Here color(country) comes before both marks, so the lines and the points both use it, and each country gets its own line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) + line + point


data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) + line + point


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:country) + line +
  point


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), color(col.country),
  line, point)






                                                                                                 1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, lines and also points.”
Written last, just after point, the same color(country) belongs to the points alone. Nothing splits the line, so one line joins the points of all five countries. A line joins its rows in x order, and here five rows share each year, so the line zigzags up and down at every year:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + point + color(country)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + line + point + color(col.country)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + point +
  color(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line, point,
  color(col.country))




gog: up to 5 rows of `line` share one value of `x(year)`, and nothing splits them, so they are joined in x order and the stroke zigzags inside that value. If you have several series, add `color(<field>)` or `group(<field>)`; for one value per `x`, summarize them with `line * mean`.




                                                                                             1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, a line and also points colored by country.”
gog prints a warning about the zigzag and suggests color(<field>) or group(<field>), although the sentence already has color(country). That color belongs to the points, so nothing splits the line.
The English sentence under each plot also says which marks a channel reaches. “Color by country” names no mark, so it reaches every mark. “Points colored by country” reaches the points only.
With one mark, it makes no difference where you write a channel: data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) and data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) + point draw the same plot. This book writes the mark first, because the mark is the subject of the sentence (The order of +). With several marks, write first what every mark shares. Then write each mark, followed by what belongs to that mark alone.
Order appears more than once in this grammar, and it does not mean the same thing every time. Which orders matter gathers all of it in one place: what you may rearrange freely, what the engine refuses, and the two arrangements that change the picture with no warning. Encoding scope gives the rule for every kind of word.

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.8 The * operator: combining
A histogram is not in your table: the bands and their counts have to be computed before anything is drawn. * is how a sentence asks for that.
* attaches a transform to a mark. The mark is always on the left; the transform is on the right. Where two transforms follow one mark, either order draws the same plot. Write them in the order they happen: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each one.
bar * bin      # histogram
line * smooth  # smoothed trend line
zone * bin     # heatmap: the same `bin`, cutting both axes
The last line, zone * bin, shows the pattern: one transform means one thing, and the mark decides where it applies. In a histogram the bar’s height carries the count, so the count takes one axis and bin cuts the other. A zone carries its count by color instead, so both axes are free, and the same bin cuts both. When one of a zone’s positions is categorical, bin cuts only the other one, because a category is already cut into slots.
The six summaries (sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile) differ from bin in one way: they take the measurement from a column you name, instead of counting rows. One channel carries the measurement: y on a bar, color on a zone, z in space(). A summary groups the rows by every position that does not carry the measurement, then reduces that channel’s column to one value inside each group. So zone * mean + x(a) + y(b) + color(v) averages v inside every cell two categories cross.
See Operators for the full rules, and Transforms for each transform in detail.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.9 The | and / operators: faceting, or composing
text:
2.9 The | and / operators: faceting, or composing
Across the world, life expectancy rises with income. One cloud of 142 countries cannot show whether that holds inside each continent. A second question, how many countries each continent has, needs a plot of its own beside the first. Two operators put both questions on one page. | puts things side by side and / puts one above the other. Whether those are panels or whole plots is decided by what you write on the right.
With facet() on the right they split one plot into panels, one per category of the column it names:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# One panel per continent, side by side
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
By default every panel shares one scale, which is what makes the panels comparable. Use both operators together and the panels form a grid. See Faceting for the full rules.
With another plot on the right they arrange the two on one page, each keeping its own coordinate space:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Two plots, side by side
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The parentheses keep each plot whole until | joins the two. Each language groups its operators in a fixed order. Arithmetic does the same: it groups * before + and reads 2 + 3 * 4 as 2 + (3 * 4). In R and Python, | groups after +, so gog would draw this sentence without the parentheses. / groups before +, so the same two plots joined by / would be refused. In Julia, gog refuses both. So whenever this book composes plots, each plot goes inside its own parentheses. Parentheses on a page shows how each language groups a page.
Composed plots share nothing by default. The arrangement decides which axis is aligned: x when one plot is above the other, y when they sit side by side. If both plots name the same column on that axis, they share it: one scale, one range of values, drawn once. That single rule is what makes a marginal plot (a scatter with a small distribution drawn along each edge) two operators rather than a chart type. See Composition.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.10 Scales: how a number becomes a position
text:
2.10 Scales: how a number becomes a position
Incomes in gapminder_2007 run from under 300 dollars to nearly 50,000. Most countries therefore crowd the left end of a linear axis, and a log scale spreads them out. A scale is written on the binding, the channel with its column in it. It is not a word of its own, because it belongs to one channel and nothing else can combine with it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”
x_label() writes your own words under the axis in place of the column name. It is a label, not a scale, and Labels, below, covers the four of them.



Scale
What it does




linear
Equal steps for equal differences. The default


log
Equal steps for equal ratios, on x, y, color, size and opacity, with any base


time
Positions dates and times, chosen from the column type: dates and date-times


category
One slot per distinct value, chosen from the column type: columns of text, and columns with a declared order


order
The order of the categories along an axis. You can also declare the order on the column: a factor in R, ordered() in the other three



A scale is not a transform: it produces no new values, only different positions for the ones you have. Scales explains what happens when you use both, such as a log scale on bar * bin or bar * sum.
The same binding takes two more arguments for the same reason. limits gives the range of values a channel covers, when you want a range other than the one in the data. tick_count says how many ticks an axis should have. Both describe the scale, so both are written where the scale is written. Scales has all three.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.11 Spaces: the surface a plot is drawn on
text:
2.11 Spaces: the surface a plot is drawn on
A space decides what a position means. Every plot so far has been drawn on the plane. That space is flat, and you never have to write it.







Space
Where the marks stand




flat
The plane: x across, y up. The default


space
The cube: x, y and z, projected onto the page


polar
The plane bent into a circle: one position becomes an angle, the other a radius


nest
Rectangles inside rectangles, each sized by its share of the one holding it


map
The earth flattened: longitude across, latitude up


globe
The earth itself, viewed: marks stand on the half of the sphere that faces you


network
The space of a graph: positions come from layout and their numbers mean nothing, so it draws no axes. State a viewing angle in network() and the layout is computed in the cube instead



One space holds the whole plot. See Space, Polar, Nest, Map, Globe and Network.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.12 Settings: values you set rather than map
text:
2.12 Settings: values you set rather than map
Every channel above asks a question about the data. color(continent) asks “which continent?”, and gets a legend so the reader can answer it.
Making every point one color asks no question about the data. It maps no column, needs no scale, and has nothing to decode, so it is not a channel. That is style:







Setting
What it fixes




style(color = )
One color for the whole layer


style(opacity = )
One opacity, 0–1


style(size = )
Point radius, or line stroke width


style(shape = )
One glyph for every point


style(pattern = )
The texture of a mark’s paint: a stroke’s dash (solid/dashed/dotted/dotdash/longdash), a fill’s hatch (hatch/crosshatch/stripes/grid/dots). Every mark but point, text and surface


palette( )
Which colors the color channel uses


theme( )
The page around the plot: grid, background, fonts, size





RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# map: color carries the continent, and a legend decodes it
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





Now the same points with one color and one opacity set for all of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# set: one color, no question asked, no legend drawn
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.5)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.5))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.5)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "tomato", opacity: 0.5 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored tomato, with opacity 0.5.”
See Setting vs mapping for the full rules.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.13 Labels: the words on the plot
text:
2.13 Labels: the words on the plot
An axis carries the name of the column bound to it. A label replaces that name when the column name is not what a reader should see.



Label
What it names




title
The plot


x_label y_label z_label
One axis each



title() is the one that adds words rather than replacing them, because a plot has no other way to say what it is about.

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.14 Facets: one panel per category
When one plot shows too many groups to compare, a facet gives each group a panel of its own.







Facet
What it cuts




facet
Splits one plot into panels, one per category of the column it names



A facet is written on the right of | or /, which is why you have already seen it drawn in the operator section: … | facet(continent). See Faceting.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.15 Selections: choosing rows in a drawn plot
text:
2.15 Selections: choosing rows in a drawn plot
A plot that is already on the screen can still answer a question, if you can select part of it.



Selection
What it does




brush
Dims the rows you did not pick, and removes none of them



A selection is the only kind that acts on a plot after it is drawn. Dragging changes what you see. It never changes the sentence, so running the sentence again gives you the selection it names, not the one you dragged. See Selection.

title: 2  The grammar
section: 2.16 Names the host language already uses
text:
2.16 Names the host language already uses
Every word in the kernel is an ordinary English word, and many ordinary words already name something else. mean names a statistic in every language that has one. data, order, range, text and box all name something in R before gog arrives. That is a consequence of choosing plain names rather than a sign that something has gone wrong, and in ordinary code almost nothing changes.
When a word is both gog’s and the language’s own, the language decides which one your call reaches. gog does not change that, and each language decides differently, so the answer is different in each one:








Language
What the language does
To reach the other one




R
Twenty kernel words collide with R names. Nine are objects, and a call skips them; eleven are functions, and those mask R’s own
base::order(x), stats::density(x)


Python
A star-import rebinds six builtins, because Python has no rule that protects them
from builtins import sum


Julia
Two modules exporting one name is an error, never a silent choice
Base.sum([1, 2, 3])


JavaScript
Nothing happens, because no name reaches your scope unless you import it
nothing to do



R’s case is the one to understand, because it has twenty collisions and only five of them can give a wrong result with no message. Most marks take no argument, and neither does a statistic like mean or max, so those words are plain objects rather than functions. When R evaluates a call it looks for a function of that name, and skips any name whose value is not a function. Base R therefore still answers mean(c(1, 2, 3)), and sapply(df, mean) works for the same reason. The message R prints when gog loads names only the eleven functions, because an ordinary call can reach only a function.
The other eleven words take arguments, so they are functions, and a function does mask R’s own. Once gog loads, range(0.25, 0.75) is gog’s band; to reach base R’s, write base::range(). Suppose you forget the masking and write range(heights) to get the smallest and largest values of a vector. The call reaches gog’s range(), which takes two numbers between 0 and 1, not a vector. For six of the eleven functions, a wrong argument like that reveals the mistake: the call is refused, and the refusal names the base R function you meant, here base::range(). Now write data(mtcars), meaning to load R’s example dataset. That call is also correct gog, naming a plot’s table, so gog answers it and cannot warn you. box(), title("..."), order(key) and palette("Set1") are the same case. A refusal needs a mistake the engine can detect, and none of these calls contains one.
There is no way to remove the collision without losing something. Prefixing the vocabulary, gog_mean and gog_range, would remove the reason for the vocabulary: a reader who has to learn a prefix learns every word twice, and none of the words is English any more. Renaming order to sort_by would take away a word every reader already knows. So the words stay, and the few places that need a qualified name write one.
Each binding chapter carries three things for its language: the full list of collisions, that language’s rule from the table above as code you can run, and the few calls the rule does not cover. R has five such calls, and they fail for two reasons. Three hand a word to one function that passes it to a second, the way aggregate(v ~ g, df, mean) passes mean on. Two use the word as a value rather than calling it, as do.call(sum, list(x)) does. See R, Python, Julia and JavaScript.

title: 2  The grammar
text:
2.17 In short
The kernel has eleven kinds of word: five build a plot, and six refine or arrange one. The minimum sentence is a table, a mark, and that mark’s required positions. A sentence gog cannot draw is refused, and the refusal says what to write instead. Most of +’s order is free, with two exceptions: the first mark is drawn at the bottom, and a channel applies to every layer only when it comes before every mark (Encoding scope).

title: 2  The grammar

title: 3  Reading practice
text:
3.11 What you just did
Those ten plots used twelve distinct words, and every plot reads left to right: data, mark, positions, refinements. A transform joined the mark and a facet came last, exactly where the first chapter put them. The same color split the bars and lines, and colored the points. The same * derived counts, means and densities. Each word meant the same thing in every plot that used it.

title: 3  Reading practice
text:
3.12 What comes next
Every sentence here was already written, so nothing asked you to choose a mark. Writing practice reverses that: it starts from a question and asks you to write the sentence.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.1 Which continents live longest?
How does a question about your data turn into a specification? Reading was recognition; writing is recall. Psychologists use those two words for two kinds of remembering. Recognition starts from something in front of you, and asks only whether you have seen it before. That is what Reading practice did: it gave you finished sentences and asked what they say. Recall starts from nothing in front of you: you produce the answer yourself. It is the harder of the two, and it is what writing a specification asks of you.
From here on, this chapter asks you to recall. Three worked examples come first. The first two show the method you will use: start with the minimum sentence, look, refine. The third asks you to write the whole sentence at once. Five questions follow with nothing in front of you, each answered by a sentence you met in Reading practice: write yours before you read on, then check it against the printed one. Last comes the other half of writing: what happens when a sentence is wrong, and what a refusal tells you to do next.

The order you want here depends on the means the plot has just computed, so the table cannot carry it.   order(col.life, desc = True))

  order(:life, desc = true)

                                                                                                                                                                               8 7 6 5 4 3 2 6 4 2 Sepal Length Sepal Width Petal Length   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal length, color by species.” The cube again, and you wrote it yourself this time.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.5 When gog says no
Every sentence so far was correct. The other half of writing is what happens when one is not.
You will write wrong sentences. Everyone does. gog promises that a wrong sentence is refused with a direction, never drawn with the wrong part quietly removed. Here are the refusals you are most likely to see first.
Forgetting to bind the table. The sentence must start with the data:

gapminder_2007 + point + x(gdp) + y(life)

Error:
! gog: a plot starts with `data()`, which names the table — columns are bare names and the nearest named table wins, so the name matters. Write `data(gapminder_2007) + point + ...`.


The message above is R’s. Each binding writes this advice with its own way of naming a column.
Quoting a column name, a habit from other packages. The refusal names the fix:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x("gdp"), y("life"))




Error:
! gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*: `x(gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.


That message is R’s too. Python and JavaScript name the fix x(col.gdp), and Julia names it x(:gdp).
Mapping a channel to a column that cannot answer its question. size encodes magnitude, and a category has none:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + size(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  size(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `size(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `size` on `point` needs a continuous (numeric) column. Use `color` or `shape` to distinguish categories.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Forgetting the column a summary reads. The refusal names the missing y, because mean must be told which column to average:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bar` needs `y()` but none is set. Add `y(<column>)` — a bar cannot be drawn without it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Binning a category. bin cuts a continuous axis, and the refusal names count, the transform that tallies rows per category:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bin` cuts a continuous axis into intervals, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows per category, `count` is the transform that does it: `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Each message names the rule and the fix. No wrong plot was drawn, and no binding was dropped to complete one. Read any refusal outside this list the same way.
The last three refusals end with a second option: set GOG_STRICT=0 and draw the plot anyway. The first two never reach the engine, so there is nothing to draw. GOG_STRICT is an environment variable, and Drawing it anyway shows which refusals GOG_STRICT affects, with the one line that sets it in each language. For now, make the fix the message asks for: at this stage the refusals are the lesson.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.6 The morning checkpoint
That is the whole method: start with the minimum sentence, look, refine, and read the refusal when one comes. If you have read this part from the start, check yourself against what it promised:

Read any sentence in this book aloud before looking at its plot.
Given a question (distribution? comparison? relationship? change over time?), name the mark and transform that answer it.
Predict whether a sentence will render or refuse, and roughly what the refusal will say.

If you can do most of that, the morning has reached its goal. You can read the next part in order, or go directly to the cookbook and answer your own questions, following a link back whenever a recipe uses a word you want explained.

title: 4  Writing practice
text:
4.7 What comes next
A morning teaches the shape of a sentence. It does not show everything one word can do. Data opens the letters with the table every sentence starts from: the shape gog needs, and what gog does with the columns it finds.

title: The letters
text:
After stating its system in brief, the 1446 book explained the letters one class at a time: the initial consonants, the vowels, the final consonants. Each class was explained by the same method.
This part does the same for gog’s letters. The marks are the initial consonants: the visible forms, such as a dot, a bar or a line. A mark draws nothing until a position says where it goes. The positions are the vowels: x, y and z. Only edge takes none of them: a layout transform computes its positions instead. Each position has a scale, which decides how a number, a category or a date becomes a place on its axis. The refining channels are the final consonants: color, size, shape, pattern, opacity. Each is optional, and each gets the legend that decodes it.
Three channels belong to none of these classes: group, label and play. On a line, group makes the same split as color: one line per category. But every line is drawn alike, so group gets no legend. It works like the space between words: it separates, but it shows nothing. label supplies a text mark’s content rather than refining the mark. Like faceting, play acts on the whole plot rather than on one mark: it cuts the plot into frames and plays them in order. Its chapter is in the next part.
The Data chapter opens this part with the table every sentence starts from, because nothing can be drawn until a table is named. The book’s data follows, saying where this book’s own tables come from and how to read one in any of the four languages. Then come the letters themselves. Choosing a mark opens them, and then each mark has a chapter of its own, fourteen in a row from point to edge. After the marks, the Scales chapter covers the scales that come with the vowels, and the Channels and legends chapter covers the final consonants and their legends. The Setting vs mapping chapter shows the difference between a column you map and a constant you set. The Transforms chapter closes the part: a transform derives new values from your columns.
Every mark chapter follows the same template, just as the 1446 book explained each letter class by the same method. It says what the mark draws, what it requires, what refines it and which transforms it takes. It then closes with three sections that have the same names in every chapter: What you can set, What it refuses and What comes next. A short summary, In short, may come between the last two. That sameness is deliberate: it is the No Exceptions law applied to this book’s structure. Learning the second mark is faster than learning the first. By the fifth you know which section answers which question, and you can read only the one you need.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.1 Binding a table
Where does a plot get its data? Every sentence starts by naming a table, and everything after that depends on the name. This chapter covers the two ways to name one, the shape the table must have, and the declarations that travel with its columns.
Most of the time the table is already loaded and you know what you want to ask. The only work left is the sentence. data() takes a table you already hold in your session. Column names after that are bare words: no quotes, no table prefix, no indexing.

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
gog looks up gdp and life inside the gapminder_2007 table automatically. This is the Bind-Once Law: name the table once, then use columns freely.
gapminder_2007 here is an ordinary table in your session, whatever your language calls one: a data frame in R, a dict of columns or a pandas DataFrame in Python. In Julia it is a named tuple of columns or a DataFrame, and in JavaScript an object of columns or an array of rows. You do not register the table or convert it to a special type first. The bindings part shows how each language builds one. The R chapter also lists the twenty names that gog and base R both use. For the eleven that are functions, it shows how to call base R’s version, such as base::order().
Writing data() does more than supply the numbers. When you write data(gapminder_2007), gog keeps the name gapminder_2007, not only the numbers inside it. The name matters as soon as a plot has more than one table. Each layer looks up its bare column names in one of those tables, and gog finds that table by its name. Leave data() out and the table arrives with no name, so gog refuses and tells you what to write:
gapminder_2007 + point + x(gdp) + y(life)

Error:
! gog: a plot starts with `data()`, which names the table — columns are bare names and the nearest named table wins, so the name matters. Write `data(gapminder_2007) + point + ...`.
gog gives the same advice for a sentence with no data at all, point + x(gdp) with nothing before it. The message above is R’s. Each binding writes this advice with its own way of naming a column.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.2 The table has to be tidy
text:
5.2 The table has to be tidy
Every table in this book has the same shape. Each row is one observation, and each column is one variable. That shape has a name, tidy data (Wickham, 2014), and gog assumes it in every sentence you write.
The reason is the rule that defines a channel in Grammar: a channel maps a column to a visual property, so anything you want to map has to be a column. Suppose you record sales for two regions, and you give each region a column of its own:

wide <- data.frame(year  = 2019:2023,
                   north = c(120, 135, 128, 152, 168),
                   south = c( 90, 101, 140, 133, 155))




wide: all 5 rows


year
north
south




2019
120
90


2020
135

2021
128
140


2022
152

2023
168

Now ask for one line per region:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(wide) + line + x(year) + y(sales) + color(region)


data(wide) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + color(col.region)


data(wide) + line + x(:year) + y(:sales) + color(:region)


plot(data(wide), line, x(col.year), y(col.sales), color(col.region))




Error:
! gog: `y(sales)` refers to a column that is not in the data. Check the spelling of `sales`.
gog: `color(region)` refers to a column that is not in the data. Check the spelling of `region`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two problems: there is no column called sales, and no column called region. It asks you to check the spelling, but the spelling is not the problem. Your two regions are column names, and a name is not a column. Your sales numbers sit in two columns instead of one. The sentence asks for columns the table does not have, so gog draws nothing.
The same numbers, one row per observation, look like this:

long <- data.frame(year   = rep(2019:2023, times = 2),
                   region = rep(c("north", "south"), each = 5),
                   sales  = c(120, 135, 128, 152, 168,
                               90, 101, 140, 133, 155))

Now sales and region are both columns, so gog draws the plot and its legend:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(long) + line + x(year) + y(sales) + color(region)


data(long) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + color(col.region)


data(long) + line + x(:year) + y(:sales) + color(:region)


plot(data(long), line, x(col.year), y(col.sales), color(col.region))






                                  2019 2020 2021 2022 2023   100 120 140 160  Sales Year  Region    north  south 





“Given the long table: lines, x is year, y is sales, color by region.”
gog never reshapes a table, and no transform turns columns into rows. You do that work before you write the sentence, in the language you are already using. R has tidyr::pivot_longer(). Python has pandas.melt(). Julia has DataFrames.stack(). JavaScript has no standard table library, so you write a short loop instead.
gog is stricter than ggplot2, but not about the shape of the table. ggplot2 does not reshape tables either, and it refuses the wide table above just as gog does. What differs is one thing: ggplot2 lets you calculate a value while you map it, so aes(x = log(gdp)) works there. gog does not allow that, because a channel takes a column name and nothing else. Some of those calculations are already part of the grammar. A log axis is one of them, written x(gdp, scale = "log"). For anything else, add the column to your table first. So a tidy table is not enough on its own. Every column your sentence names has to be in the table already.
This book does not teach you how to tidy data, and it should not, because there is a better book for it. Read R for Data Science by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Garrett Grolemund (Wickham et al., 2023), which is free online at https://r4ds.hadley.nz/. Its chapter on data tidying is the one that matters here. If the shape of your data is not settled yet, read that chapter before you read this one.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.3 The plot’s table and a layer’s table
text:
5.3 The plot’s table and a layer’s table
A line and the points it passes through come from one table. You should not have to name it twice. data() at the start of the sentence names the plot’s table: it applies to every layer that does not name its own table. The actuals table holds the sales of five years that have passed:



actuals: all 5 rows


year
sales




2019
120


2020
135


2021
128


2022
152


2023
168







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Both layers read from "actuals"
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  point


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  point)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + point


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, point)






                                            2019 2020 2021 2022 2023   120 130 140 150 160 170  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line and also points.”
A forecast continues a history of past values, and the two usually arrive as separate tables. You want both on one pair of axes. forecast holds the three years still to come:



forecast: all 3 rows


year
sales




2024
180


2025
195


2026
210





A data() that appears between two marks overrides the table for the layer that follows it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# line uses "actuals"; point uses "forecast"
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + data(forecast) + point


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, data(forecast),
  point)






                                      2020 2022 2024 2026   120 140 160 180 200  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line; then given the forecast: points.”
The rule: the first data() is the plot’s table, and each later data() applies to the mark written directly after it. A mark with no data() of its own reads the plot’s table. The refusal at the start of this chapter holds for the second table too: write + data(forecast), not + forecast.
Two things follow from the rule for a later data(). gog tells you about the first, but not about the second.
A data() at the end of a sentence has no mark after it, so its table would never be drawn. gog refuses the sentence rather than leave that table out of the plot without telling you:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  point +
  data(forecast)


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  point +
  data(forecast))


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + point + data(forecast)


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, point,
  data(forecast))




Error:
! gog: `data(forecast)` ends the sentence, so no mark comes after it to read its table. A later `data()` gives its table to the mark written directly after it: write that mark next, as in `+ data(forecast) + point`, or remove `data(forecast)`.


The message names the table and gives two ways to fix the sentence: write a mark after the data(), or remove the data().
Second, a later data() applies only to the one mark written directly after it. The mark after that one reads the plot’s table again:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# line reads actuals. point reads forecast. area reads actuals again.
data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point +
  area


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  data(forecast) + point +
  area)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + data(forecast) + point +
  area


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, data(forecast),
  point, area)






                                     2020 2022 2024 2026   0 100 200  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line; then given the forecast: points; then given the actuals again: an area.”
The two tables cover different years, which makes the change easy to see. actuals runs from 2019 to 2023, and forecast from 2024 to 2026. The area and the line both sit on the left. The points sit alone on the right. To draw two marks from the second table, write data() before each of them.
The one-mark rule fits what a second table is usually for. The axes come from the first table, and a later table adds an annotation: a threshold, a band, a note, a forecast. An annotation is one mark, so a data() that reaches one mark is enough. In this book, every table added after the first one is an annotation of this kind.
The specification above is correct, and it still reads badly. area is written on the line of code just below data(forecast), so it looks like part of the forecast. Only the rule tells you that area draws from actuals. The same specification is easier to read when each mark is written next to the table it draws from. Drawn again, it is the same picture:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line + area +
  data(forecast) + point


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line + area +
  data(forecast) + point)


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + area + data(forecast) +
  point


plot(data(actuals), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, area, data(forecast),
  point)






                                     2020 2022 2024 2026   0 100 200  Sales Year





“Given the actuals: x is year, y is sales, a line and also an area; then given the forecast: points.”
This is style, not grammar. Both spellings are legal, and both draw the same plot. The order of area and point has changed, and here that changes nothing. The two tables share no year, so neither mark is drawn over the other. gog will never refuse either spelling, because legal is not the same as clear (Law 8). Two sentences can mean the same thing and still be very different to read. That difference is yours to control.
So group the marks by the table they read. Keep each extra data() on the same line as the mark it applies to, and keep the marks that read the plot’s table together. Every line is then one table and the marks that read it, and no mark sits under a table it does not read. The rest of this book follows that layout.
The first data() is the one exception. It applies to every mark below it, so it takes a line of its own. A later data() applies to one mark only, so it shares that mark’s line of code. Alone on a line, it would seem to apply to every mark below it. That is why data(actuals) stands alone above and data(forecast) shares its line with point.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.4 When the second table names its columns differently
text:
5.4 When the second table names its columns differently
The plot above was the easy case: actuals and forecast both call their columns year and sales, so one pair of positions written at the front served both layers.
Plots often carry a note at a chosen point, and the note comes from a small table of its own. That table’s column names rarely match the first table’s. The milestones table marks two points on the income axis:



milestones: all 2 rows


at
value
note




10000
72
less steep from here


40000
80
almost flat here





Its columns are at, value and note. None of those names appear in gapminder_2007, whose columns are gdp and life. A layer may name its own columns, and the axis does not change:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(milestones) + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note) +
  style(size = 20, color = "red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(milestones) + text + x(col.at) + y(col.value) + label(col.note) +
  style(size = 20, color = "red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(milestones) +
  text + x(:at) + y(:value) + label(:note) +
  style(size = 20, color = "red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(milestones), text, x(col.at), y(col.value), label(col.note),
  style({ size: 20, color: "red" }))






                                                                                                                                                                 less steep from here almost flat here                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life; then given the milestones: text, x is at, y is value, label by note.”
There is still one x axis and one y axis, one scale each, one set of ticks. Only the names differ, because the two tables were written by different people for different reasons.
What is shared is the measurement, and that is what an axis is. at holds income and value holds years of life, the same two quantities gdp and life hold. A table whose numbers mean something else does not belong on these axes, whatever its columns are called. If you put sales figures on an income axis, gog draws the plot without an error, but nothing it shows is true. Matching names are not the test. Matching meanings are.
The same test says when a second table does not belong in the plot at all. A layer is drawn on the axes that come from the first table, so its values must measure what those axes measure. Values that measure something else need their own axes, and a second pair of axes means a second plot. Put that plot beside the first one instead. Composition shows how, with | and /.
A layer that names no position of its own reads the axis that is already there. That is why the earlier plot worked with the positions written once at the front.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.5 A table in a database
data() is the first of the two ways to name a table. This section shows the second, for a table kept in a database.
Not every table fits on one computer. Most of the data used at work is kept in a database. A warehouse, a database built to keep all of a company’s records, can hold billions of rows. gog reads those tables with one word, query(), written where data() would be.
Nothing else in the sentence changes:
data(orders)                          + bar + x(status)
query(connection, "SELECT ...")       + bar + x(status)
The SQL stays inside that one word; nothing after it is SQL. After it, the columns are still bare names. The marks, channels, transforms and operators are the ones you have already learned. You are not writing a second language for databases. You are naming the rows a different way.
Here is a real database. The code below builds a small one in memory, so it needs no server and no password:

con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "countries", gapminder_2007)

Now the sentence. The connection is the only new part:

query(con, "SELECT gdp, life, continent FROM countries WHERE gdp > 5000") +
  point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)



                                                                                                            10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Asia 





“Given the query: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
The plot is an ordinary scatterplot. gog never saw the database. It received a table of rows, as it does for every other sentence in this book. The database chose which rows to send. gog drew what arrived.
A query and a loaded table produce the same picture, byte for byte, when they hold the same rows. Every binding tests exactly that. So query() is never a different way of drawing; it is a different way of finding the rows to draw.

5.5.1 Three things to know
You open the connection yourself. gog never opens one, and it never stores a password. You connect with whatever your language already uses, and hand the open connection to query(). That also means gog adds no database driver to your install. A reader who never writes SQL never installs one.
The query runs when the plot is drawn, not when the sentence is written. Writing query(con, "...") asks the database nothing. The sentence is a specification, exactly like every other sentence in this book, and the engine draws it later. gog sends your SQL exactly as you wrote it.
Every language reaches a different set of databases. The word is the same in all four. What differs is the connection you hand it, because each language has its own database convention. Your language’s chapter says which: R, Python, Julia, JavaScript.


5.5.2 How much data comes back
query() brings every row the query returns to the computer running gog. The database does the selecting. Your machine does the drawing. Know that before you run this against a large table.
For most tables it does not matter. A few thousand rows arrive quickly, so write the simple query and stop there. Selecting the columns you need and letting gog do the rest is the normal case, and the example above is exactly that.
The number of rows starts to matter at about a hundred thousand. Above that, moving the rows costs more time than drawing them. A warehouse table can hold billions, and SELECT * FROM that_table would try to bring all of them to you.
The way to avoid it is already familiar to anyone who works with a warehouse: summarize in SQL, then draw the summary. This works because a plot is nearly always a summary anyway. A bar chart of a billion orders shows only a few bars, and a database can produce those bars far more cheaply than your laptop can.

query(con, "SELECT continent, COUNT(*) AS countries
            FROM countries GROUP BY continent") +
  bar + x(continent) + y(countries)



                              Africa Americas Asia Europe Oceania   0 20 40  Countries Continent





“Given the query: bars, x is continent, y is countries.”
The database did the counting and sent back five rows. Without the count, SELECT continent FROM countries would have sent all 142. The plot is the same one you would get by counting locally.


5.5.3 Two directions, and which one suits you
If you write the summary in SQL, you may ask whether the whole plot could be written in SQL too. There is another way to give SQL users a grammar of graphics. Posit’s ggsql (Posit Software, PBC, 2026) adds visual clauses to SQL itself: you write VISUALIZE, DRAW and SCALE inside the query, and the database returns a picture.
It has two strengths. Its clauses read like SQL, so someone who writes SQL all day stays in the language they already think in, and no host language is installed at all. And it runs the whole pipeline in the database, one query per layer, so a bar chart of ten billion rows fetches only the bar heights. On that second point ggsql does something gog does not. gog brings the rows to you, so on a large table you write the summary in SQL yourself, as the count above did.
If you write only SQL, ggsql is probably the better choice. gog would first ask you to learn R, Python, Julia or JavaScript, which is a real cost for someone who uses none of them.
gog is built in the opposite direction. The grammar stays in one place and the data comes to it, so one sentence draws a loaded table, a table in Postgres, and a table in a warehouse, in any of four languages. The sentence stays the same in every language and for every kind of table.







You work
The smaller cost




Only in SQL
ggsql: nothing to install, and the syntax is the one you use


Across several languages
gog: one grammar covers all of them, and the database too

title: 5  Data
text:
5.6 Declaring the order of categories
Wherever the table comes from, some of its categories have an order that a column of plain text does not record. Low, Medium and High have an order every reader knows. A plot that draws them in any other order makes the reader sort them. A column of plain text has no order of its own, so gog draws its categories in the order the rows happen to arrive:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


severity <- data.frame(
  level = c("High", "Low", "Medium"),
  count = c(30.0, 10.0, 20.0)
)

data(severity) + bar + x(level) + y(count) +
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in")


severity = {
  "level": ["High", "Low", "Medium"],
  "count": [30.0, 10.0, 20.0],
}
(data(severity) + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count) +
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in"))


severity = (
  level = ["High", "Low", "Medium"],
  count = [30, 10, 20],
)
data(severity) + bar + x(:level) + y(:count) +
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in")


const severity = {
  level: ["High", "Low", "Medium"],
  count: [30, 10, 20],
};
plot(data(severity), bar, x(col.level), y(col.count),
  title("Text column: the order the rows came in"))






                            High Low Medium   0 10 20 30  Text column: the order the rows came in Count Level





That order is almost never the one you mean. Declare the order you mean, where you build the table. In R the declaration is a factor. Python, Julia and JavaScript have no factor type, so gog supplies the declaration itself, under one name: ordered(). It takes the column’s values and the order its categories go in, and everything after it reads the same in all four languages:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


severity <- data.frame(
  level = factor(c("High", "Low", "Medium"), levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
  count = c(30.0, 10.0, 20.0)
)

data(severity) + bar + x(level) + y(count) +
  title("Declared: the order you asked for")


severity = {
  "level": ordered(["High", "Low", "Medium"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),
  "count": [30.0, 10.0, 20.0],
}
(data(severity) + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count) +
  title("Declared: the order you asked for"))


severity = (
  level = ordered(["High", "Low", "Medium"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),
  count = [30, 10, 20],
)
data(severity) + bar + x(:level) + y(:count) +
  title("Declared: the order you asked for")


const severity = {
  level: ordered(["High", "Low", "Medium"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),
  count: [30, 10, 20],
};
plot(data(severity), bar, x(col.level), y(col.count),
  title("Declared: the order you asked for"))






                            Low Medium High   0 10 20 30  Declared: the order you asked for Count Level





The order goes with the column, so every part of the plot agrees: the axis, the color assignment, and the legend all read in the same order. The next plot is there only to show the legend. Its x and y are both count, so the points form a diagonal line.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(severity) + point + x(count) + y(count) + color(level) +
  title("The legend follows the same order")


(data(severity) + point + x(col.count) + y(col.count) + color(col.level) +
  title("The legend follows the same order"))


data(severity) + point + x(:count) + y(:count) + color(:level) +
  title("The legend follows the same order")


plot(data(severity), point, x(col.count), y(col.count), color(col.level),
  title("The legend follows the same order"))






                                     10 15 20 25 30   10 15 20 25 30  The legend follows the same order Count Count  Level    Low  Medium  High 





The declared order stays even when gog does the counting for you. The first of the eight tickets below is High, but the axis of bar * count still shows Low, Medium, High. count makes one row per level, and the levels belong to the column, so the axis keeps their order, not the order of the rows:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


tickets <- data.frame(
  level = factor(
    c("High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"),
    levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
  )
)

data(tickets) + bar * count + x(level) +
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis")


tickets = {"level": ordered(["High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"])}
(data(tickets) + bar * count + x(col.level) +
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis"))


tickets = (level = ordered(["High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]),)
data(tickets) + bar * count + x(:level) +
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis")


const tickets = { level: ordered(["High", "Low", "High", "Medium", "High", "Low", "Medium", "High"], ["Low", "Medium", "High"]) };
plot(data(tickets), layer(bar, count), x(col.level),
  title("bar * count: the levels still order the axis"))






                              Low Medium High   0 1 2 3 4  bar * count: the levels still order the axis Count Level





“Given the tickets: bars derived by count, x is level.”
In R, the list of levels can mean two things. factor(x, levels = ...) says only which order the categories appear in. Adding ordered = TRUE says more: that Low really is less than High. gog draws the categories in the listed order either way. Most people list levels only to set the order on the page, and a plot needs nothing more than that.
In Python, a pandas table can carry the same declaration as a Categorical column, and gog reads its categories, in their order, as the levels. ordered() is for a plain dictionary of lists, so that you can declare an order without pandas installed.
Two rules apply:

Levels set the order. The data sets which categories appear. A level with no rows in the data gets no bar and no slot on the axis, because an empty labeled gap is harder to read than a shorter axis. A value in the data that the levels do not mention is not dropped. It is drawn after the listed ones. R is the exception, because of a rule in R itself. There, factor() turns a value you did not list into a missing value before gog sees it, so the row is dropped. In R, list every value you want drawn.
order() in the plot wins. The levels came with the table, so they apply to every plot drawn from it. order() is written in this one plot, so it applies here, and the more specific instruction wins. Name another column in order(), one that holds numbers, and the categories are ordered by its values instead. That is how you sort by value:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(severity) + bar + x(level) + y(count) + order(count, desc = TRUE) +
  title("order() overrides the levels")


(data(severity) + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count) + order(col.count, desc = True) +
  title("order() overrides the levels"))


data(severity) + bar + x(:level) + y(:count) +
  order(:count, desc = true) + title("order() overrides the levels")


plot(data(severity), bar, x(col.level), y(col.count),
  order(col.count, { desc: true }), title("order() overrides the levels"))






                            High Medium Low   0 10 20 30  order() overrides the levels Count Level





“Given the severity table: bars, x is level, y is count, ordered by count, largest first.”
order() can also name the categorical column itself, as in order(level). That asks for the column’s own order. For a column of plain text, that order is alphabetical. For a column with declared levels, it is the declared order. desc = TRUE reverses whichever applies. So a declared order cannot be turned alphabetical from inside the plot. To change it, change the levels where the table was built, in the language you are already using. The declaration belongs to the table, and so does the change.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.7 Missing values
A declared order is something you choose. Missing values are something you do not choose. Real data has gaps, and survey tables are usually missing many values. A row with no value where the plot needs one cannot be placed, so gog drops it and says how many, rather than changing the count without telling you:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


patchy <- data.frame(
  weight = c(3.1, 4.2, NA, 5.8, 6.0, NA, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5),
  batch  = c("A", "A", "B", "B", NA, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B")
)
data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(weight) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("Two rows have no weight")


patchy = {
  "weight": [3.1, 4.2, None, 5.8, 6.0, None, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5],
  "batch": ["A", "A", "B", "B", None, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
}
(data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(col.weight) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("Two rows have no weight"))


patchy = (
  weight = [3.1, 4.2, missing, 5.8, 6, missing, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5],
  batch = ["A", "A", "B", "B", missing, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
)
data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(:weight) + x_label("Weight") +
  title("Two rows have no weight")


const patchy = {
  weight: [3.1, 4.2, null, 5.8, 6, null, 4.9, 5.1, 3.7, 5.5],
  batch: ["A", "A", "B", "B", null, "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"],
};
plot(data(patchy), layer(bar, bin), x(col.weight), x_label("Weight"),
  title("Two rows have no weight"))




gog: dropped 2 rows of `patchy` with a missing value in `weight` — a row with no value in a column the plot maps cannot be placed, and it is left out of every layer drawn from `patchy`. To keep those rows in a layer that does not map `weight`, give that layer a table of its own.




                                    3.5 4.0 4.5 5.0 5.5   0 1 2 3  Two rows have no weight Count Weight





“Given the patchy table: bars derived by bin, x is weight.”
Only the columns the plot maps decide which rows are dropped. This plot maps weight, so the message names weight, and the two rows with no weight are left out. The table also has one row with no batch. The plot never reads batch, so that row stays in the histogram. Bind batch to color, and the same row is dropped as well, because it now has no color to take. The message then names both columns:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(weight) + color(batch) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped")


(data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(col.weight) + color(col.batch) +
  x_label("Weight") + title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped"))


data(patchy) + bar * bin + x(:weight) + color(:batch) +
  x_label("Weight") +
  title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped")


plot(data(patchy), layer(bar, bin), x(col.weight), color(col.batch),
  x_label("Weight"),
  title("One more column mapped, one more row dropped"))




gog: dropped 3 rows of `patchy` with a missing value in `batch` or `weight` — a row with no value in a column the plot maps cannot be placed, and it is left out of every layer drawn from `patchy`. To keep those rows in a layer that does not map any of them, give that layer a table of its own.




                                       3.5 4.0 4.5 5.0 5.5   0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0  One more column mapped, one more row dropped Count Weight  Batch    A  B 





“Given the patchy table: bars derived by bin, x is weight, color by batch.”
So a missing value in a column the plot never reads changes nothing. A missing value in a column the plot maps always drops the row, and the message says which column.

title: 5  Data
section: 5.8 Special characters and other writing systems
text:
5.8 Special characters and other writing systems
The people who built a table chose its names, and a plot has to print them unchanged. Category names, titles, and axis labels are drawn exactly as you wrote them. A plot is drawn as an SVG file, which is a picture written as text. Three characters have a special meaning inside one: &, < and >. gog writes them in the form the file needs, so they print as themselves, and a name like R&D needs no special handling. The plot below puts all three into its names and its title:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


special <- data.frame(
  firm  = c("R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"),
  spend = c(10, 25, 15)
)
data(special) + bar + x(firm) + y(spend) + title("Q3 <spend> & forecast")


special = {
  "firm": ["R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"],
  "spend": [10, 25, 15],
}
data(special) + bar + x(col.firm) + y(col.spend) + title("Q3 <spend> & forecast")


special = (
  firm = ["R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"],
  spend = [10, 25, 15],
)
data(special) + bar + x(:firm) + y(:spend) +
  title("Q3 <spend> & forecast")


const special = {
  firm: ["R&D", "Sales & Ops", "<10% unit"],
  spend: [10, 25, 15],
};
plot(data(special), bar, x(col.firm), y(col.spend),
  title("Q3 <spend> & forecast"))






                          R&D Sales & Ops <10% unit   0 10 20  Q3 <spend> & forecast Spend Firm





Many tables are not written in Latin letters at all. gog draws their column names as written, with no renaming first. A name in another writing system can be a bare column name as well as a label. The table below is in Korean. Its name, 지역별, means by region. Its two columns are 지역 (region) and 값 (value). The three rows are the cities 서울 (Seoul), 부산 (Busan) and 대구 (Daegu). The plot title, 한국 지역별 값, means value by region, Korea.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


지역별 <- data.frame(
  지역 = c("서울", "부산", "대구"),
  값   = c(10, 25, 15)
)
data(지역별) + bar + x(지역) + y(값) + title("한국 지역별 값")


지역별 = {
  "지역": ["서울", "부산", "대구"],
  "값": [10, 25, 15],
}
data(지역별) + bar + x(col.지역) + y(col.값) + title("한국 지역별 값")


지역별 = (
  지역 = ["서울", "부산", "대구"],
  값 = [10, 25, 15],
)
data(지역별) + bar + x(:지역) + y(:값) + title("한국 지역별 값")


const 지역별 = {
  지역: ["서울", "부산", "대구"],
  값: [10, 25, 15],
};
plot(data(지역별), bar, x(col.지역), y(col.값), title("한국 지역별 값"))






                          서울 부산 대구   0 10 20  한국 지역별 값 값 지역





A label’s width is measured from its characters, and a Korean or Chinese character is about twice as wide as a Latin one, so these labels get the margin they need and no more.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.9 In short
A table is named once, and the nearest one wins. gog refuses a sentence that names columns the table does not have; it never reshapes the table. query() is written where data() would be. A missing value drops its row only when the plot maps that column. A declared order goes with the column onto the axis and the legend; order() changes it for one plot, and the levels change it for every plot.

title: 5  Data
text:
5.10 What comes next
This chapter says what gog needs from your own table, and nothing about the tables in this book. The book’s data names them, says where they come from, and shows how to read one in your own language.




Posit Software, PBC. (2026). Ggsql: A SQL extension for declarative data visualisation based on the grammar of graphics (Versions 0.3.0 (alpha)). https://ggsql.org/


Wickham, H. (2014). Tidy data. Journal of Statistical Software, 59(10), 1–23. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10


Wickham, H., Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Grolemund, G. (2023). R for data science: Import, tidy, transform, visualize, and model data (2nd ed.). O’Reilly Media. https://r4ds.hadley.nz/

title: 6  The book’s data
text:
6.1 Reading a table
Where do gapminder_2007, medals and winds come from, and how do you get them?
Data was about a table of your own. This chapter is about the shared tables that the book’s examples draw from, listed in full under The tables. They are published beside the book as CSV files, one per table, so you can run any example in this book yourself. Each file has a fixed address:
gapminder_2007.csv holds the 142 countries drawn in the chapter A first plot. medals.csv holds the medal counts drawn in Reading practice, and winds.csv holds the wind observations drawn in Polar.
Reading one takes a single call, gog_table(), which comes with the package in all four languages. Nothing else needs to be installed.
To run the first chapter’s plot yourself, you need its table in your session. One line fetches it. gog_table() reads any of these tables by name:
gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows


country
continent
year
life
population
gdp

Asia

Argentina
Americas

12779.3796
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


gapminder_2007 <- gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)


gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


const gapminder_2007 = await gog_table("gapminder_2007");
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life));
Those four calls draw the same picture, because the table is the same file and the engine is the same program.
gog_table() also decides each column’s type. It is right for most columns, but not for a label written as a number, or for a date. A CSV is text, so numbers arrive as text and have to be converted. A column becomes numbers when every value in it is a number, and stays text otherwise. The text argument forces a column to stay text. Three columns in these tables need that, and Labels that look like numbers, below, explains which and why.
Why does a graphics package carry a table reader at all? R reads a CSV in one call, and Python and Julia in a few. JavaScript has no CSV reader in its standard library, so the same work there takes dozens of lines. A CSV reader cannot simply split each line on commas. Six countries in gapminder_2007.csv have a comma in the name, "Congo, Dem. Rep." among them, so that split gives those rows seven fields, while the header has six. Nobody should have to paste dozens of lines of parsing before drawing, so each package carries gog_table() instead.
Each package fetches the file with what its language already has: R’s read.csv(), urllib in Python, Downloads in Julia and fetch in JavaScript.
Read a file with a CSV reader of your own, and the rest of this page still applies, because data() takes any table your session holds. You then do two things yourself. First, check each column’s type: your CSV reader decides it, so the three columns named below need whatever that reader offers for keeping a column as text. Second, declare the category order, because a CSV never records one. You do this after gog_table() too. Three things a CSV cannot record covers both, and dates as well.
Reading a different table is the same call with a different name: gog_table("winds"), gog_table("medals"). A misspelled name is refused, and the refusal suggests the nearest published name, or points to the list under The tables.

title: 6  The book’s data
section: 6.2 Three things a CSV cannot record
text:
6.2 Three things a CSV cannot record
A CSV records the values in a column, and never says what kind of column it is. Three kinds of information are therefore lost when the file is written. You restore them when you read the file back. Each one changes the plot, and this page explains each one.

6.2.1 A declared order
The eight compass points have a fixed order, and a plot of them is correct only when it keeps that order. The winds table records one wind observation per row:



winds: first 5 of 264 rows


direction
bearing
speed
season




N
19.612260
10.1
Winter


N
357.049499
11.0
Winter


N
349.709737
13.8
Winter


N
2.602499
7.4
Winter


N
338.210715
3.7
Summer





The direction column of winds holds the eight compass points. Their order is N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW, clockwise from north. The Data chapter shows how a declared order sets the axis, the color assignment and the legend. A CSV cannot record that declaration. gog_table("winds") therefore returns direction as plain text, and the declaration is yours to make after reading.
Until you declare it, only the file’s own row order keeps the plot correct. The winds file lists its rows in compass order, so a plot of direction made without the declaration reads correctly. Sort the rows by speed, and the same plot changes. The compass points now follow the sorted rows, and that order is not the compass order. The plot still draws, and nothing on it shows that the compass is in the wrong order.
The example below reads the table, sorts it by speed so that the rows are no longer in compass order, and then declares the compass order:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


winds <- gog_table("winds")
# `base::order`, because gog's `order()` masks it
winds <- winds[base::order(winds$speed), ]
compass <- c("N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW")
winds$direction <- factor(winds$direction, levels = compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction)


winds = gog_table("winds")
by_speed = sorted(enumerate(winds["speed"]), key=lambda pair: pair[1])
winds = {name: [column[i] for i, _ in by_speed]
         for name, column in winds.items()}
compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
winds["direction"] = ordered(winds["direction"], compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction)


winds = gog_table("winds")
by_speed = sortperm(winds["speed"])
winds = Dict{String,Any}(name => column[by_speed] for (name, column) in winds)
compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
winds["direction"] = ordered(winds["direction"], compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction)


const winds = await gog_table("winds");
const by_speed = winds.speed.map((_, i) => i)
  .sort((a, b) => winds.speed[a] - winds.speed[b]);
for (const name in winds) winds[name] = by_speed.map((i) => winds[name][i]);
const compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"];
winds.direction = ordered(winds.direction, compass);

plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction));









                                      N NE E SE S SW W NW   0 20 40 60  Count Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction.”
The rows are in speed order, and the axis still reads N to NW. The declared order decides the axis, not the order of the rows. A declared order is kept when the space changes. The polar chapter draws this same count as a wind rose, and the change is one word. Add polar(), and the axis bends into a circle, with N at the top and the rest clockwise from it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction) + polar()


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction), polar())






                            N NE E SE S SW W NW   20 40 60  Count Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction, in polar.”
The polar chapter explains that plot. The circle starts at the first category and runs clockwise through the rest, so the compass reads correctly in the flat plot and in the circle.
The sort exists only to undo the file’s compass order. Keep the declaration in your own code, and drop the sort. winds needs a second declaration, for season: the book’s plots show Summer before Winter, and the file lists Winter first. Three other tables need a declared order too: survived in titanic (Yes, then No), slab in quakes_fiji (shallowest band first) and weekday in six_weeks (Monday first). So do age in quakes_2011 (“this week” first), and month and category in cyclones (January first, and the weakest category first). age in census needs a declared order as well, youngest band first, and so do month and cause in nightingale, April first and in the order of her legend. Their files already list them in that order. The next section explains why.


6.2.2 Labels that look like numbers
The second thing a CSV cannot record is which columns are text. Three columns in these tables hold text that gog_table() would read as numbers unless you name them. census.csv has an age column of 0, 5, 10, which are the names of age bands rather than quantities. sessions.csv has a session column of 01, 02, 03, and a number cannot keep a leading zero, so 01 comes back as 1. gm_eras.csv has an era column of 1957 and 2007. Those two values name the eras the rows compare; they do not measure anything. That is the whole reason gog_table() takes a text argument:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


census <- gog_table("census", text = "age")
sessions <- gog_table("sessions", text = "session")
gm_eras <- gog_table("gm_eras", text = "era")


census = gog_table("census", text=("age",))
sessions = gog_table("sessions", text=("session",))
gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text=("era",))


census = gog_table("census", text = ["age"])
sessions = gog_table("sessions", text = ["session"])
gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text = ["era"])


const census = await gog_table("census", ["age"]);
const sessions = await gog_table("sessions", ["session"]);
const gm_eras = await gog_table("gm_eras", ["era"]);





Without the text argument, age becomes numbers. A point or a line then places the bands along a continuous axis from 0 to 85. The plot looks reasonable, so nothing tells you the axis is wrong. The population pyramid in Many groups is refused, because it sorts the bands with order(), and order() needs a categorical axis. When age is read as text, it still needs its declared order. Without the declaration, order() sorts the bands alphabetically, one character at a time. The band 5 is then drawn between 50 and 45.
Each call above names one column, and a text argument can name more than one. gm_eras holds the same values in two columns: year as a number, era as a label. The book reads only era as text, so year stays a number. To read the year as a label too, name both columns in one text argument:



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


gm_eras <- gog_table("gm_eras", text = c("year", "era"))


gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text=("year", "era"))


gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text = ["year", "era"])


const gm_eras = await gog_table("gm_eras", ["year", "era"]);





Each language writes more than one name in its own way. R puts them inside c(), Python inside parentheses, and Julia and JavaScript inside square brackets. Python no longer needs the comma that follows a single name. Julia and JavaScript only add the second name inside the brackets.
Only census, sessions and gm_eras need a text argument; no other shared table does.


6.2.3 A date
The third thing a CSV cannot record is which columns are dates. six_weeks, revenue, monitoring and quakes_2011 each have a column of dates, and gog_table() returns it as text, so the axis gets one slot per date instead of a calendar axis. After reading, convert the column to your language’s date or timestamp type: in R, as.Date() for six_weeks, revenue and quakes_2011, and as.POSIXct() for monitoring, which also records the hour. In JavaScript, write a time after each date, so that it is midnight in local time: six_weeks.day.map((d) => new Date(d + "T00:00")). For monitoring, which has a time already, replace the space with a T: new Date(t.replace(" ", "T")). The JavaScript chapter explains why. Scales shows the calendar axis you get.
