title: 6  The book’s data
text:
6.4 What comes next
A table holds the rows, and says nothing about how they look on the page. Choosing a mark shows how to pick the mark that draws them. There are fourteen, and your question and your columns decide which one fits.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.1 One variable
Which visible form should your data take? A mark is that visible form: a dot, a bar, a line. Choosing the mark is the first decision in every plot. The answer depends on the types of your variables and the question you are asking.
There are fourteen marks, and they are not a list to learn before you draw. This chapter helps you with the choice: it shows which mark answers which question, draws the common cases, and stops. Each mark then has a chapter of its own, with examples. The tables in Quick reference are for later, when you have data in front of you and want the row that fits.
If you have used ggplot2, a mark is similar to a geom, but the two differ in one way. Many geoms compute a statistic before they draw. geom_histogram() bins your data and then draws bars. geom_smooth() fits a curve and then draws a line. A mark never does that. A mark is only the shape, and the statistic is a separate word: a histogram is bar * bin, a trend line is line * smooth. A geom tends to name a chart. A mark names a shape.
Each column of your data is one variable, and gog reads its type from the data. There are two types:
With one variable there is one question: how are its values spread out? The answer depends on whether the column is continuous or categorical.

title: 7  Choosing a mark

Are the life expectancies of 142 countries close to one value, or spread across a wide range? You can cut a continuous column into bands, or estimate a smooth curve over it. bin cuts the column into bands and counts the rows in each. bar * bin draws one bar per band, which is the histogram:

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Distribution: bar * bin")

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Distribution: bar * bin"))

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Distribution: bar * bin")

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("Distribution: bar * bin"))

When sharp changes in height from one bar to the next hide the shape, a curve shows the same spread without them. density estimates a smooth curve over the same column, and line * density draws that curve:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Smooth shape of the distribution → density curve
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Density: line * density")

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Density: line * density"))

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Density: line * density")

7.1.2 Categorical variable
A categorical column cannot be cut into bands, so the same question becomes: how often does each category occur? count tallies the rows in each category, and bar * count draws one bar per category:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# How many countries per continent? → frequency bar
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  title("Frequency: bar * count")

  title("Frequency: bar * count"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +

A count does not say what part of the whole each continent is. Africa holds 52 of the 142 countries, which is more than a third of them. proportion is the same tally as a share of the whole, so the bars sum to 1:

  title("Shares: bar * proportion")

  title("Shares: bar * proportion"))

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.2 Two variables
With two variables, the pair of column types decides the mark.

7.2.1 Continuous × Continuous
Both variables are continuous, so the questions are about relationships, trends and patterns. Do people in richer countries live longer? point places one glyph per row, and the shape those glyphs make is the first answer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Is there a relationship? → scatter
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Relationship: point")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Relationship: point"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Relationship: point")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Relationship: point"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Relationship: point Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
The direction of the cloud can matter more than any one country in it. smooth fits a trend line through the points, and line * smooth draws it over the scatter. color(continent) is written right after point, so it colors only the points, and one line is fitted to all of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Smooth the relationship → fitted trend line
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Trend: point + line * smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Trend: point + line * smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth + x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Trend: point + line * smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Trend: point + line * smooth"))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Trend: point + line * smooth Life expectancy GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
A question about two continuous columns is not always about a relationship. When one column is time and the other an amount, the question can be how much there was. The actuals table records yearly sales:

# How much, not just where → filled area
data(actuals) + area + x(year) + y(sales) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Quantity: area")


(data(actuals) + area + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Quantity: area"))


data(actuals) + area + x(:year) + y(:sales) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Quantity: area")


plot(data(actuals), area, x(col.year), y(col.sales), y_label("Sales"),
  title("Quantity: area"))

“Given the actuals: an area, x is year, y is sales.”
line and area draw the same boundary and give it different meanings. A line says where the value was; an area says how much there was, so it fills to zero and the filled region is the quantity. Choose area when zero is a true baseline for your variable, and line when it is not.
Sometimes each x has a spread to show, not one value. ribbon fills between a low boundary and a high one, and a range transform supplies that pair: the minimum and maximum at each x. Name two quantiles and range uses those instead. Add a line * mean over the ribbon, and the line of means is drawn inside the band.
When the order of the rows is what you want to show, path connects them in that order. line sorts its points by x before it joins them. path does not, so the stroke can move left as well as right, cross itself, or return to where it started. That is the connected scatterplot: the two axes carry measurements, and the joining line shows the order in time, here for five Asian countries.

“Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow end.”
Layered over any of the marks above, rule draws a straight stroke at one value on one axis, across the whole of the other: a threshold line, or a rug. A rug is a short tick at the edge of the panel for each observation, so it shows where the observations are. style(reach = "edge") shortens a rule into a rug.
How many countries have a life expectancy below 60, 70 or 80 years, and where are they on the income axis? life_bands holds three threshold values of life expectancy, each with a name:



life_bands: all 3 rows

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# One position, the panel supplies the other → rule
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Threshold and rug: rule")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(col.gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(col.band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Threshold and rug: rule"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + rule + x(:gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(:band) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Threshold and rug: rule")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), rule, x(col.gdp), style({ reach: "edge" }),
  data(life_bands), rule, color(col.band), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Threshold and rug: rule"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Threshold and rug: rule Life expectancy GDP per person  Band    Low  Middle  High 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp, with reach edge, and also rules from the life bands, colored by band.”
The rule names x(gdp) even though the points already named it. That second x(gdp) does not add an axis. Every layer shares the plot’s one x and one y. A rule sits on one axis and spans the other, so it has to say which. This rule reads the scatter’s table, which holds both gdp and life, so either column could place it. Without x(gdp), gog refuses rather than guessing; the Rule chapter shows the refusal. The three rules from life_bands need no position, because that table holds life and no gdp, so only one axis can answer.
text is also layered over other marks: it writes a label from a column at each position where point would draw a dot. Layered under the other marks, zone shades a rectangle. On an axis where you give it a pair of columns, the rectangle starts at the value in one column and ends at the value in the other. On an axis where you give it no pair, the rectangle spans the whole panel. Write zone * bin instead, and the same mark covers the panel with a grid of cells and counts the rows in each: the heatmap.


7.2.2 Categorical × Continuous
One axis groups, the other measures. The natural question is how the measurement differs across groups. mean reduces each group to one value, its average. bar * mean draws one bar per group, and the bar’s height is that value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Mean value per group → bar
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Group summary: bar * mean")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Group summary: bar * mean"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Group summary: bar * mean")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Group summary: bar * mean"))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Group summary: bar * mean Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
A mean hides how far apart the countries inside one continent are. Sometimes that spread is what you want to see. Drop the transform, and point draws every country in its continent’s slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# All individual points per group → strip plot
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Strip plot: point (one dot per country)"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Strip plot: point (one dot per country) Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life.”
Nothing is summarized: each dot is one country, placed by its continent and its life expectancy. Dots for countries with the same life expectancy overlap, so a crowded slot hides two things: how many dots it holds, and how they are spread.
There are three ways to draw a crowded group more clearly, and each shows something different. For the shape of each group rather than every point, write box + x(continent) + y(life). box draws a box between the quartiles, a line at the median, whiskers, and outliers as separate dots. ribbon * density draws the whole estimated distribution that the box summarizes: the violin plot. When every point matters but the points overlap, point * jitter spreads them sideways: the jittered strip plot.
The question is not always which group is highest. It can be how the value changes from one group to the next. line, area, step and ribbon accept a category on x too. They join one summary per group instead of drawing a bar on each, and the result is a profile:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# One value per group, joined → profile
data(gapminder_2007) + x(continent) + y(life) +
  line * mean + point * mean +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Profile: line * mean")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  line * mean + point * mean +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Profile: line * mean"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:continent) + y(:life) + line * mean +
  point * mean + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Profile: line * mean")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  layer(line, mean), layer(point, mean), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Profile: line * mean"))






                                      Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  Profile: line * mean Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: x is continent, y is life, a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean.”
A bar compares one group with another; a profile traces a change across the groups. A profile needs more care than a bar, because its segments cross parts of the panel where nothing was measured. Use it when the categories have an order, such as a rating scale or size groups from smallest to largest. Continents have no order, so that advice says not to draw this plot. gog draws it anyway. The grammar refuses a sentence that is ill-formed, never one that is only unwise; whether a profile suits your categories is your judgment (Law 8).
line is not the only mark that draws a profile. area fills under the same boundary, step holds each value flat until the next category, and ribbon * range fills the spread as a band. Drawn around a circle, the same line * mean profile is the radar chart, in Polar.

7.3.1 Swapping x and y
Long category names, such as country names, are easier to read on the vertical axis than along the bottom. In the first table, each Categorical / Continuous row whose mark sits in a slot can be drawn that way, with the two axes swapped. bar, box, interval and point sit in a slot on one axis and measure along the other, and so does the violin, ribbon * density. The column types decide which axis holds the slots: the one with the categorical column. Swapping the two positions therefore draws the same plot horizontally.
box + x(life) + y(continent) is the horizontal box plot, and bar + x(gold) + y(country), on the medals table, is the horizontal bar. Nothing else is needed. If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip() or matplotlib’s barh(), this is the same result with no extra word. gog reads the orientation from which axis carries the categories, as ggplot2 does.
Only the marks with a slot can be drawn horizontally this way. For line, step and area, x is always the domain, the axis the mark is read along, and y is the measure. The same is true of a ribbon drawn as a band rather than as a violin. Put the category on y for any of them, and gog refuses the sentence. Their two columns are often both numbers, so no column type could say which one is the domain, and the mark decides it instead. The line chapter shows what a swap of two continuous columns draws, and what to write when the domain must be the vertical axis.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.4 Mark families
The mark list looks like a set to memorize, one entry at a time. It is not. The fourteen consonants of Hangeul (한글) are not fourteen unrelated shapes either. The letters are featural: most of them are another letter with a single feature changed. ㅋ (k) is ㄱ (g) with one stroke added, so learning ㄱ teaches you most of ㅋ.
The marks are built the same way. Some pairs have the same rules for every channel: x, y, color, size and the rest. If one mark requires, accepts or refuses a channel, the other mark does the same. They differ in the geometry they draw:








Family
Same rules for every channel
They differ in




area and ribbon
✓
area closes its region on the baseline; ribbon closes it on a second data boundary


box and interval
✓
box computes its own summary of each group; interval spans two ends a transform supplies


line and step
✓
line slopes from one value to the next; step holds each value until it changes



The second member of a pair is quick to learn. It follows the same rules for every channel as its sibling, so you already know those. The grid of marks and channels in Combinations shows this: the two marks of a family have identical rows there. What is left is what the second mark draws. ribbon and interval also need a transform, such as range, to supply their two ends.
When does gog add a mark? Only for a shape that no existing mark can draw. step was added because “hold the value until it changes” is such a shape: no channel, transform or setting can say it. A thick line was not added as a mark, because style(size = ) already says it. A new chart is never the reason. A histogram, a radar and a pyramid are arrangements of marks that already exist. A new word is spelled with the letters you have, and a new chart is written with the marks you have. The families make the marks quick to learn, but gog never adds a mark only to complete a pair.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.5 Unpronounceable combinations
Just as some letter combinations cannot be pronounced, some pairs of a transform and a column type have no meaning. gog refuses each one and draws nothing.
bin, density and smooth all work along a continuous axis, so the column on that axis must be continuous. A category on that axis is refused, and each refusal names the atom that does the same job for categories:








Combination
Problem
Use instead




bar * bin + x(category)
bin cuts a continuous axis into bands
bar * count + x(category)


bar * density + x(category)
density estimates a continuous distribution
bar * proportion + x(category)


point * smooth + x(category)
smooth fits a curve along a continuous axis
bar * mean + x(category) + y(value)



All three appear as live refusals in What bin, density and smooth refuse; the table above is this page’s summary of them.

title: 7  Choosing a mark
text:
7.6 What comes next
Choosing the mark is the first decision in a plot, not the last one. Point opens the fourteen chapters that follow, each describing one mark: its channels, its transforms, its settings and its refusals.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.1 Basic usage
How does one measurement change as another changes? point draws one glyph, a small symbol, at the (x, y) position of each row. The glyph is a dot unless you choose another.
The plot it makes is the scatterplot, and it was invented later than the other basic charts. William Playfair published the line chart and the bar chart in 1786 (Playfair, 1786), and the pie chart in 1801 (Playfair, 1801). The first scatterplot was drawn about thirty years after the pie chart. Historians usually name John Herschel as the first person to plot one measured column against another. In 1833 he plotted the position of a double star against the year, then drew a smooth curve through the dots so the trend could be seen (Friendly & Denis, 2005). Other names for the same picture are scatter diagram and scattergram. When size maps a third column, the same plot is called the bubble chart.
None of those chart names is a word in gog, and that is deliberate. point is a mark, not a chart. point + x(gdp) + y(life) is a scatterplot, and point + x(continent) + y(life) is a strip plot. The mark is the same in both. The chart name belongs to the whole sentence, not to any word in the vocabulary. That is why the names are listed in an appendix, Chart names, instead of in the kernel.
Do people in richer countries live longer? Most examples in this chapter start from the smallest sentence that draws a point: a source, the mark, and its two positions.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.2 The dot as a default
Write point and you get a dot. Calling it the dot mark is accurate almost every time. But the dot is only a default, and you can change it. A point is a glyph at a position, and shape replaces the dot with one of the seven glyphs gog draws, a different one for each category of a column. Shape below names the seven, says which category gets which, and what to do with more than seven.

  title("The glyph is not always a dot")

  title("The glyph is not always a dot"))

  title("The glyph is not always a dot")

  shape(col.continent), title("The glyph is not always a dot"))

A text mark takes its glyph from a column, with label, so what you see is the value in that column. Put both on one plot and each row is located by a dot and named by its label:

title: 8  Point
section: 8.3 A categorical x: the strip plot
text:
8.3 A categorical x: the strip plot
Every plot so far has put a measurement on x, but x also accepts a categorical column. Each category gets its own slot on the axis, and every row is drawn in its category’s slot. You see the whole distribution rather than a summary of it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("One dot per country"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  One dot per country Life expectancy Continent





Every mark places a categorical column this way, bar included. Compare the strip plot with bar * mean, which reduces each group to one number:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("The same data, summarized"))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  The same data, summarized Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
mean is not the bar’s own transform. Other marks take it too, and each draws the same means in its own way:



Mark derived by mean
What it draws




point * mean
one dot at each mean


line * mean
the means joined into a profile


area * mean
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * mean
each mean held flat until the next category


bar * mean
one bar per category, the plot above



median, sum, min and max can replace mean in every row of that table. So can quantile, which needs a probability: quantile(0.9) is the value nine tenths of each group falls below. The statistic decides the number, and the mark decides how it is drawn.
The strip plot shows Africa’s spread and its overlap with Asia; the bar chart shows neither. The strip plot has one weakness: every point in a category sits on the same vertical line. Where many countries have close values, their dots cover each other, and you cannot see how many there are. opacity makes each point partly transparent, so overlap reads as a darker patch. point * jitter moves overlapping points sideways along the categorical axis, and never changes their measured value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same dots, spread sideways"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  The same dots, spread sideways Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life.”
Every dot keeps its life expectancy, so its height has not changed. Only its place inside its continent’s slot has changed, and that place means nothing: the dot still reads as its continent. jitter moves a dot’s category, never its value. In a scatterplot both axes are measurements, so a moved dot would show a value the data does not hold. gog therefore refuses point * jitter when x and y are both continuous, as What it refuses shows.
A third answer, point * dodge, also moves points sideways within their slot. Unlike jitter, it moves each point only as far as it must to touch no other point:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, set apart until none touch")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, set apart until none touch"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same dots, set apart until none touch")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same dots, set apart until none touch"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  The same dots, set apart until none touch Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life.”
No dot covers another, and every dot keeps its life expectancy. Where many countries have close values, the dots spread wide, so the outline of each group shows the shape of its distribution, one dot per country. This plot is the beeswarm. When a slot is too crowded to hold its dots, gog draws the extra ones at the slot’s edge, on top of one another, and a warning says how many overlap. It never moves them into the next continent’s slot.
A fourth answer is to count the overlapping points instead of separating them. point * bin * stack cuts the measured column into bins and piles one dot per row above each bin, which is the dot plot. It shows one distribution, with the measure on x; | facet(continent) draws one for each continent. The cookbook draws it with thirty rows, where every row is still visible. Choose among jitter, dodge and bin * stack by what you want the reader to see. jitter and dodge keep the spread: every value sits where it was measured, and with dodge no dot covers another unless its slot is full. bin * stack gives the count: how many rows fall in each bin. The result looks like a bar chart, but each row is still its own dot.

8.3.1 Either axis: a horizontal strip
gog reads the direction of a plot from its bindings. Whichever axis carries the category decides the direction, for a point exactly as for a bar. So the category can sit on y instead of x, and the strips run horizontally. The countries and the distributions are the same, and each continent’s dots now run from left to right:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  style(opacity = 0.6) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) + x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  style({ opacity: 0.6 }), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same distributions, lying down"))






                                                                                                                                                                                40 50 60 70 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  The same distributions, lying down Continent Life expectancy





If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip(), there is no such word here. Swapping the two bindings was the whole change, the same way you swap the two arguments of matplotlib’s scatter(). Use the horizontal form when the category names are too long for the bottom axis. It also helps when there are many categories, since names listed down the left side are easier to read than names crowded along the bottom.

Most African countries sit at the lower left, and most European countries at the upper right. gog adds a color legend whenever you map a column to color.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.5 Shape
Which glyph does each category get, and what happens when there are more categories than glyphs? shape maps a categorical column to one of seven glyphs. In order, they are the circle, the square, the triangle, the diamond, the cross, the star and the wye, which looks like the letter Y. The categories are ordered by where each first appears in the table, or by the order you declare. The first category gets the circle, the second the square, and so on. Here is the whole set, in the order gog assigns them:

glyph_order <- c("circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross", "star", "wye")
glyphs <- data.frame(glyph = ordered(glyph_order, levels = glyph_order),
                     row = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1))
data(glyphs) + point + x(glyph) + y(row) + shape(glyph) +
  style(size = 8) + x_label("") + y_label("") +
  title("The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned")

It is also about as many glyphs as a reader can separate on one plot. Map shape to a column with more than seven categories and the eighth category gets the circle again, so two categories share a glyph and look the same. gog says so when that happens, naming the count and the limit, and the plot still draws. Oats is the eighth food in the table, so its points are circles, the glyph salmon already has. Nothing in the picture shows which circles are salmon and which are oats, so the message counts the foods and the glyphs for you. The book has four ways to draw more than seven groups:

The name on the point instead of a glyph: a text layer with label, the labeled scatter, and repel when the names overlap. Of the four, only this one can name each of a hundred categories. In the web edition, a brush leaves only the selected names readable, as long as the text layer does not use repel.
Every category in one pale color, and the few that matter drawn again on top, in a second layer: What settings are for.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.6 Size
Once x and y are both bound, no position is free for a third measurement. The size channel can show it instead. size maps a continuous column to the point’s radius, from 3 pixels at the smallest value to 12 at the largest.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + size(col.population))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  size(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), size(col.population))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
The two largest dots are China and India, and both sit at the left, among the poorer countries. gog adds a size legend showing the column’s minimum, midpoint, and maximum.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.7 Opacity
The horizontal strip plot above made every point partly transparent with one setting, style(opacity = 0.6). opacity is also a channel: it maps a continuous column to transparency, and a larger value draws a more solid point. Population is skewed, so a linear scale would leave China and India dark and the rest faint. The log scale spreads the values across the range:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  opacity(population, scale = "log") +
  title("Opacity: population, on a log scale")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  opacity(col.population, scale = "log") +
  title("Opacity: population, on a log scale"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  opacity(:population, scale = "log") +
  title("Opacity: population, on a log scale")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  title("Opacity: population, on a log scale"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Opacity: population, on a log scale Life Gdp  Population    199.6K  16.2M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, opacity by population on a log scale.”
See Channels and legends for the opacity range and why line does not accept this channel.
That example maps opacity to a column. Often there is no column to show: the only problem is that many points overlap. Then you want one opacity on every point instead. That is a setting rather than a mapping, so you write style(opacity = ) and no legend appears; see Setting vs mapping. title: 8  Point
text:
8.8 All channels at once
A table often has more to show than two positions can hold. The refining channels carry the rest, and they can all be on one plot at once. Here continent is mapped to both color and shape, so the groups stay separate in black-and-white printing, and population is mapped to size:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  shape(continent) +
  size(population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) +
  shape(col.continent) +
  size(col.population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  shape(:continent) + size(:population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), shape(col.continent), size(col.population),
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  GDP, life expectancy, and population Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 





Four columns now show in one picture: gdp and life by position, continent by color and glyph, and population by size.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.9 What you can set
A setting changes how every point looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. These are a point’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(shape = )
circle, square, triangle, diamond, cross, star, wye


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels



A point takes more settings than most marks. It is the only mark that can set shape. Six of its seven glyphs are filled with color, so a point is also one of the marks that draw a border. size is the radius in pixels, and border_color and border_size give that border its own color and width.
A point layer can carry several settings at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue",
        border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue",
        border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue", border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ shape: "diamond", size: 7, color: "steelblue",
  border_color: "navy", border_size: 1.5 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("A shape, a size, and a border"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  A shape, a size, and a border Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored steelblue, with shape diamond, size 7, border color navy and border size 1.5.”
Where two diamonds overlap, the navy border shows where one ends and the next begins. That is what a border is for in a dense cloud of points. A cross has no fill to outline, so border_color and border_size change nothing on that glyph.
A border can also be the whole point. Set the fill color to "none" and give the border a color, and each point is drawn hollow: an outline with no fill. A hollow point can be partly transparent as well. opacity fades what color paints, and color = "none" paints nothing, so gog refuses opacity on a hollow point. Put the transparency in the border’s color instead. In "#4682b44d", the first six hex digits are steelblue, and the last two, 4d, make the outline 30% opaque. Here are all 1,704 rows of gm_all again, the table the Opacity section drew at one opacity:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 3) +
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent")


(data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 3) +
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent"))


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 3) +
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent")


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "none", border_color: "#4682b44d", size: 3 }),
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  0 50K 100K   40 60 80  Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent Life Gdp





Where hollow points overlap, every outline stays visible, and where many pile up, the outlines add up to a darker area. The plot shows each point and the crowding at once. Neither this nor opacity moves a point off its measured value, which is why they, and not jitter, are the answers for a crowded scatterplot. On a categorical axis, jitter and dodge move points apart instead, as the strip plot showed. point * jitter(0.4) spreads them 0.4 times as wide as a plain jitter.
pattern is not on the list. A hatch needs a large area and a dash needs a long stroke, and a glyph is too small for either. To separate groups by glyph, a point uses shape instead, and What it refuses shows the refusal.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the companion grid.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.10 What it refuses
Four refusals follow, each with its reason: a category on size, any pattern, jitter or dodge on a scatterplot, and opacity on a hollow point.
size shows an amount, so it needs a column of amounts:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + size(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  size(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `size(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `size` on `point` needs a continuous (numeric) column. Use `color` or `shape` to distinguish categories.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Continents are names, not amounts, and a larger dot would claim an order the data does not have. The message suggests color or shape instead: each continent gets its own color or glyph.
The second refusal is about texture. A pattern is a dash along a stroke or a hatch across an area, and a glyph is too small for either:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(pattern = "dashed")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(pattern = "dashed")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(pattern = "dashed")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ pattern: "dashed" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = )` is a stroke's dash or a fill's texture, and a `point` is a glyph, not either — a point's form is set by `shape`, a text's by its content. The strokes (`line`/`step`/`interval`/`path`/`rule`/`edge`) take a dash; the fills (`area`/`bar`/`box`/`ribbon`/`zone`) a texture.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Both messages name shape, which chooses a point’s glyph.
The third refusal is jitter on a scatterplot. In a strip plot, jitter moves a dot sideways inside its continent’s slot. A place inside a slot has no scale, so the move changes nothing a reader could measure. In a scatterplot both axes are measurements, and every place on them is a value. A jittered dot would sit at a gdp and a life expectancy that are not in the table. Two countries with the same values would no longer look the same, and a reader who reads a dot against the axes would read a number that was never measured. So gog refuses:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `point * jitter` spreads points sideways within a categorical band, but here both `x` and `y` are continuous — there is no band to spread within, and nudging a measured value would misplace it. For overplotting on two continuous axes, `style(opacity = )` reveals density without moving any point off its value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


This is a design rule, not a missing feature: jitter moves a dot’s category, never its value. ggplot2’s geom_jitter() moves points along both axes by a small random amount, and gog does not. To show overlapping points in a scatterplot, keep every point at its value and change how it is drawn. style(opacity = ), which the message suggests, makes overlap read as a darker area, as in the plot of every gapminder year under Opacity. A hollow point, an outline with no fill, keeps every point visible where points overlap, as the same table shows under What you can set.
point * dodge is refused on a scatterplot for the same reason. It moves a dot only across a category’s slot, and a scatterplot has no slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, dodge), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `point * dodge` sets points apart inside a category's slot and moves them along the category axis only, but here neither `x` nor `y` is a category — there is no slot to swarm in, and moving a measured value would misplace it. For overplotting on two continuous axes, `style(opacity = )` reveals density without moving any point off its value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The fourth refusal is opacity on a hollow point. opacity fades what color paints, and color = "none" paints nothing, so there is nothing for it to fade:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "none", border_color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.3 }))




Error:
! gog: `style(opacity = 0.3)` fades what `color` paints, and `color = "none"` paints nothing, so there is nothing here for it to fade. A border is drawn in its own color, so its transparency goes there: `style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d")` draws a steelblue outline at 30%.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests border_color = "#4682b44d" instead. In "#4682b44d" the transparency is part of the border’s own color, as in the hollow points under What you can set.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.11 In short
A point is a glyph at a position. The point mark draws one per row, unless a transform groups the rows first. It is the only mark that maps shape, because it is the only mark that picks its glyph from a fixed set. There are seven glyphs, and an eighth category gets the circle again.

title: 8  Point
text:
8.12 What comes next
The point mark draws each row as a separate glyph, and nothing joins one row to the next. When one column puts the rows in order, such as years, the change from one value to the next often matters most. Line joins the rows into one stroke that shows whether the value rose or fell.




Friendly, M., & Denis, D. (2005). The early origins and development of the scatterplot. Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences, 41(2), 103–130.


Playfair, W. (1786). The commercial and political atlas.


Playfair, W. (1801). The statistical breviary.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.1 Basic usage
How did one value change over time? line sorts the rows by x, from smallest to largest, and draws one stroke through their (x, y) points in that order, the x order. The stroke is straight pieces laid end to end, each joining one row’s point to the next, with nothing smoothed between them.
How did life expectancy change in five Asian countries? Most examples in this chapter start from the smallest sentence that draws a line: a source, the mark, and its two positions.

“Given gapminder Asia: a line, x is year, y is life.”
The stroke looks wrong, but gog drew exactly what the sentence asks for. All five countries have a row for each year, so the one stroke passes through five values at every year. The vertical segments are where it joins the five countries inside one year, before it continues to the next year. That is exactly what a line does when nothing splits the rows: it draws one series, a single stroke in x order. The message printed above the plot is gog’s warning, and it names what to add: a color or a group. Multiple series, two sections below, draws the same table as five lines, one per country.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.2 Automatic sorting by x
Rows rarely arrive in the order a line needs: a file is sorted by name, or by nothing at all. line sorts its own vertices, the points it joins, by x, so the rows may arrive in any order. The table below is deliberately shuffled, and the line still runs from left to right:



scrambled: all 5 rows


year

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(scrambled) + line + x(year) + y(life)


data(scrambled) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life)


data(scrambled) + line + x(:year) + y(:life)


plot(data(scrambled), line, x(col.year), y(col.life))






                                 1960 1970 1980 1990 2000   55 60 65 70  Life Year





That sorting is part of what the mark means. It is not an extra step that the engine performs for you. A line says this value changed along this axis, and an axis has one direction, so there is only one order the vertices could be joined in.
path is the mark that does the opposite. It joins the rows in the order your table holds them, which is what draws a route or a loop. So choosing between the two is choosing whether the order of your rows carries meaning. With line the row order cannot carry meaning; with path the row order sets the whole shape.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.3 Multiple series
The chapter’s first plot drew one stroke through all five countries, and gog asked for a color or a group. Here is the same table with color(country) added, and the single stroke splits into a line per country. color also tells the reader which line belongs to which country.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) +
  color(country)


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.country))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  color(col.country))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country.”
Each unique value in country becomes a separate line with its own color, and a color legend is generated automatically. group makes the same split without a color or a legend. Use it when the lines matter as a whole and their names do not, as in the Many groups recipe.

title: 9  Line
section: 9.4 Layering a line over other marks
text:
9.4 Layering a line over other marks
A line shows the trend and hides where the measurements were. A dot at each row shows them again, which is why line and point are so often combined. Write color before the marks and it belongs to the plot, so both layers use it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  line + point


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  line + point)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + color(:country) + line +
  point


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), color(col.country),
  line, point)






                                                                                                 1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, lines and also points.”
Both the lines and the points share the same color per country.

9.4.1 Giving each layer its own appearance
You do not have to map a column to color at all. Sometimes you want one color for the lines and another for the points, chosen by you rather than read from the data. That is a setting, written style(color = ), and no legend appears. group(country) still keeps one line per country: it splits without coloring. style() attaches to the nearest preceding mark and stops there, so each layer can be styled independently:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  point + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line + group(col.country) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  point + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  style(color = "steelblue") + point +
  style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "steelblue" }), point,
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 3 }),
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer"))






                                                                                                 1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Blue line, red points: styled per layer Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, colored steelblue, and also points, colored firebrick, with size 3.”
A channel can belong to the whole plot or to one layer. Written before any mark, it belongs to the plot and reaches every layer, as color(country) did above. Written after a mark, it belongs to that mark alone, like style(), so each layer can map a different column. The whole rule, for every atom, is one table in Encoding scope:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line  + color(country) +
  point + size(population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line  + color(col.country) +
  point + size(col.population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + color(:country) +
  point + size(:population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  color(col.country), point, size(col.population),
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points"))






                                                                                                 1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Color on the lines, size on the points Life Year  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep.   Population    20.9M  669.8M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also points sized by population.”
That works because a channel written after a mark belongs only to that mark. If it also applied to the earlier line, the line would get a size for each row, which it cannot take, and gog would refuse the plot. See Encoding scope.

title: 9  Line
section: 9.5 A category on the domain: the profile
text:
9.5 A category on the domain: the profile
In Point, swapping the two bindings turned a strip plot on its side. A line answers the same swap differently. A line’s two axes are not interchangeable. x is the domain, the axis the line is read along. y is the measure, the quantity it traces.
A bar draws horizontally when you swap its bindings, because its categorical column says which axis holds the slots. A line usually has no such column, because its two columns are both numbers, such as year and life. So gog does not read the direction from the columns: the domain is always x. The quarterly table, despite its name, holds one sales figure for each year. With the years on x, the line is the plot you expect:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + line + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years")


(data(quarterly) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years"))


data(quarterly) + line + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years")


plot(data(quarterly), line, x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years"))






                                 2005 2010 2015 2020   100 120 140 160 180  Years on x: sales read along the years Sales Year





“Given quarterly: a line, x is year, y is sales.”
Sales climbed for most of the years. They fell in 2008 and 2009, and again in 2020, and rose again after each fall. Swap the two bindings and the line still sorts along x, which is now sales. The stroke starts at 2009, the year with the lowest sales, and puts 2020 between 2012 and 2013, so the years are scrambled:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + line + x(sales) + y(year) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x")


(data(quarterly) + line + x(col.sales) + y(col.year) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x"))


data(quarterly) + line + x(:sales) + y(:year) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x")


plot(data(quarterly), line, x(col.sales), y(col.year),
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x"))






                                 100 120 140 160 180   2005 2010 2015 2020  The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x Year Sales





“Given quarterly: a line, x is sales, y is year.”
The zigzag seems to show a value that rose and fell many times. It does not. Each segment joins a year to the year with the next higher sales, not to the next year, so the rises and falls come from the sorting. Only the overall slope is real, and only because sales were mostly higher in later years.
Put a category on y instead and gog refuses it, as What it refuses shows. So the swap has two outcomes. When both columns are numbers, gog accepts it, and the line sorts along the new x and draws a different picture. When one column is a category, gog refuses the swap, because that column must stay on x.
Sometimes the domain has to run up the page, as depth does in a plot of ocean temperature, or as the years do here. Then write path instead. A path joins the rows in the order the table holds them, so a table sorted along the domain draws the vertical series the line could not:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + path + x(sales) + y(year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order")


(data(quarterly) + path + x(col.sales) + y(col.year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order"))


data(quarterly) + path + x(:sales) + y(:year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order")


plot(data(quarterly), path, x(col.sales), y(col.year),
  title("The same rows, joined in table order"))






                                 100 120 140 160 180   2005 2010 2015 2020  The same rows, joined in table order Year Sales





“Given quarterly: a path, x is sales, y is year.”

                                      Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  line * mean + x(continent): one value per category, joined Mean life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
The mean transform is what makes the profile readable. Without it, a line connects all 142 rows across five category slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(continent) + y(life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), line, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a line, x is continent, y is life.”
No reader can follow that. Inside each slot the stroke runs up and down through every country, and between slots it joins the last country of one slot to the first country of the next. gog prints a warning in your session when a line has more than five rows and nothing splits or summarizes them. A single series, such as the quarterly line, gets the same message; there one stroke is what you want. mean leaves exactly one point per category, so the stroke joins five summaries instead of 142 rows.
Does the connection mean anything? That depends on your data. Nothing was measured between Africa and the Americas, and the segment is still drawn there. If you read only the vertices, the segments help you compare the five heights. If you read the segments themselves, they claim a change that never happened. The grammar draws what you asked for. You decide whether your data supports the connection. When it does not, keep the mean and change the mark to bar. A bar stands in its own slot and claims nothing between one slot and the next. An ordered category, such as a grade, a clothing size or a survey scale, is the case that suits a line, because it has a direction for the line to follow.
Continents have no order, but a straight axis must still put one of them first and another last. A circle has no first or last place. Drop the point layer and add polar(), and the same profile bends into a circle. That is the radar chart, and it needs no new atom:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), polar(), title("line * mean + polar(): the radar"))






                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   60 70 80  line * mean + polar(): the radar Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, in polar.”
Look at the segment from Oceania back to Asia. On the flat profile the line has two ends, because a straight axis has two ends. In the circle the five categories are spread around the whole ring, so the last one sits beside the first and the line closes. No atom was added to close the ring. A categorical angular axis wraps, and the mark follows the space it is drawn in. The Polar chapter covers this in full.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.6 Smoothed trend line
People in richer countries tend to live longer. The relationship between gdp and life is positive: as one rises, the other tends to rise as well. Sometimes the direction of a relationship is all a reader needs to know. Combine line with the smooth transform to draw a trend line fitted through all the rows instead of the rows themselves:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
The point layer keeps every country visible, and smooth reduces the same rows to one fitted curve. Only the line layer carries the transform, so the points are untouched.
smooth is not the line’s own transform. Four other marks take it too, and each draws the same fitted curve in its own way:



Mark derived by smooth
What it draws




point * smooth
one dot at each fitted value


area * smooth
the curve filled to the baseline


bar * smooth
one thin bar at each fitted value


step * smooth
the curve as a staircase


line * smooth
the fitted curve above

title: 9  Line
text:
9.7 Two boundaries from a pair
Sometimes the answer at each x is two values rather than one: a lowest and a highest, or the spread around a mean. Most transforms give a line one value per x. A pair transform gives it two, a low and a high. A line then draws both boundaries as two separate lines, not one zigzag joining them. A ribbon takes the same pair and fills the band between the two boundaries; a line draws only the boundaries. There are five pair transforms: range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band and bounds. Here are the lowest and the highest life expectancy among the five countries in each year, drawn as two lines:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(line, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines"))






                                1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines Life expectancy Year





“Given gapminder Asia: a line derived by range, x is year, y is life.”
Add style(pattern = "dashed") for the dashed band often used in published figures. Ribbon shows the same pair filled and then unfilled.

title: 9  Line
text:
9.8 Stroke width and opacity
You may want thicker lines for a slide, or fainter ones where many lines cross. Each line is drawn as a single stroke from its first point to its last. So size and opacity are not channels here: one stroke has one width and one opacity, and no row can change them. That one stroke still has a width and an opacity, and style() sets them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ size: 4, opacity: 0.45 }),
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer"))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  One width, one opacity, for the whole layer Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, with size 4 and opacity 0.45.”
Two questions look alike and are not the same: “Does this mark have this property?” and “Can a column be mapped here?” For a line’s width, the first answer is yes and the second is no. Setting vs mapping uses a line as its clearest case.
Setting one pale color on a layer is the usual way to make another layer easier to see:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line + group(col.country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + line * smooth +
  style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, smooth),
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 3 }),
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red"))






                                      1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Every country in gray, the trend in red Life Year





Each layer here carries its own style(). Unlike a channel, style() cannot belong to the whole plot: written before any mark, it is an error, because a plot has no appearance of its own to style.

9.9 Each country and its continent’s mean or median
The plot above draws five countries and one trend. The gm_all table holds 142 countries, measured every five years from 1952 to 2007. In one panel, 142 gray lines are too many to read. One trend through all of them would also hide how the continents differ. So draw one panel for each continent, with its countries in gray and their mean as one blue line.
The sentence below has two line layers. The first draws one gray line for each country, as above. The second is line * mean. In each year, mean averages the values of the countries, so it leaves one value per year, and the line joins those values. | facet(continent) splits the whole plot into one panel per continent. Every layer is split the same way, so the blue line in each panel is the mean of that continent’s countries. Faceting explains the operator in full.

  style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, mean),

                                                              1960 1980 2000   40 60 80                                                         1960 1980 2000                                                                                 1960 1980 2000                                                      1960 1980 2000                               1960 1980 2000      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Every country, and the continent's mean Life expectancy Year





“Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, and also a line derived by mean, split into panel columns by continent.”
The blue line is the continent’s mean, and the gray lines show how far each country was from it. Every continent’s mean rose, but Africa’s stopped rising for fifteen years. It rose from 39 years in 1952 to 53 in 1987, and in 2002 it was still 53. In 22 of Africa’s 52 countries, life expectancy was lower in 2002 than in 1987. In Zimbabwe it fell from 62 years to 40. The table has only two countries in Oceania, Australia and New Zealand, so the blue line almost covers their two gray lines.
Income is a second way to compare the continents. The same two layers can draw GDP per person, with two changes to the sentence. The first change is the scale. GDP per person runs from a few hundred dollars to more than a hundred thousand, so the next plot draws it on a log scale. On this scale each labeled tick is ten times the one below it, so the poorer countries are not crowded together at the bottom.
The second change is the summary. gog computes mean in dollars, and only then places the result on the log axis (The measured value keeps its own units). In dollars, one very rich country can raise the mean far above most of the others. In 1952, Kuwait’s GDP per person was 108,382 dollars, and Asia’s mean was 5,195. Sorted from poorest to richest, the middle one of Asia’s 33 countries had 1,207, less than a quarter of the mean. In the Asia panel, a mean line would therefore run above most of the gray lines. The median is that middle value, and sorting the countries gives the same order in dollars as in logarithms. So line * median has half of the gray lines above it and half below, on a log axis too:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(gdp, scale = "log") +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * median + style(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  y_label("GDP per person") +
  title("GDP per person on five continents") | facet(continent)


(data(gm_all) + x(col.year) + y(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
  line + group(col.country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * median + style(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  y_label("GDP per person") +
  title("GDP per person on five continents") | facet(col.continent))


data(gm_all) + x(:year) + y(:gdp, scale = "log") + line +
  group(:country) + style(color = "lightgray") + line * median +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 3) + y_label("GDP per person") +
  title("GDP per person on five continents") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gm_all), x(col.year), y(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, median),
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 3 }), y_label("GDP per person"),
  title("GDP per person on five continents"), across(col.continent))
