                                     setosa versicolor virginica    Uncertainty of the mean Species






“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length, beside intervals derived by confidence, x is species, y is petal length.”
The whiskers on the right are less than a third as long, and the data is identical. The ratio is the same in all three species. The two statistics do not contradict each other. deviation describes how far the flowers are from their average, and measuring more of them does not make that whisker shorter. confidence describes how precisely the average itself is known. More flowers make its whisker shorter: four times as many flowers make it half as long. So the ratio between the two whiskers comes from the group size. With only a few flowers per species, the confidence whisker can be the longer one, because a t-interval widens when the group is small.
So choose the statistic by asking which caption you would write under the plot. “A versicolor petal is usually within half a centimeter of its species average” describes the left panel. “The average versicolor petal is 4.26 cm, and the interval reaches 0.13 cm on either side” describes the right one. Reporting one and meaning the other is the mistake the name error bar allows, and the reason gog requires the statistic in the sentence.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.6 Why interval needs a transform
Every plot so far has named a transform. A mark needs one when it draws a number that nothing else supplies. A bar needs no transform, because the grammar already supplies its baseline: zero. bar + x + y draws. An interval has no such default. A low and a high are two numbers, and a plain y() supplies one. So the shortest interval that will draw is a mark, its positions, and a pair transform. That is its minimum syllable. Ask for an interval without a transform and the engine refuses the sentence rather than drawing an empty panel. What it refuses shows that refusal.
This is the design choice that keeps the channel vocabulary small. The obvious alternative would add ymin and ymax as two more channels, useful to only a few marks, and a box plot would then need five. Instead a transform computes the extents, the way mean computes one value per group, so the channel set never grows. ribbon reads the same low and high values, and box computes its five numbers inside the mark. The pair transform bounds(lower, upper) takes a low and a high you already have as two columns of the table, and Horizontal whiskers draws a coefficient plot with it.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.7 Horizontal whiskers
Whiskers turn horizontal for the reasons bars do: the names are long, or there are many of them. A tall list of horizontal whiskers is then easier to read than a crowded row of vertical ones. An interval takes its orientation from the bindings, the way a bar and a box do. Put the categories on y and the measured column on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(petal_length) + y(species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.petal_length) + y(col.species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:petal_length) +
  y(:species) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") + y_label("Species") +
  title("The same 95% CI, horizontal")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.petal_length), y(col.species), x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  y_label("Species"), title("The same 95% CI, horizontal"))






                                        2 3 4 5   virginica versicolor setosa  The same 95% CI, horizontal Species Petal length (cm)





The caps turn too, since a cap always crosses the span at its end, and the center dot stays at the center. The sections after this one work the same way on horizontal whiskers. color, dodge, caps, center and pattern, all introduced below, behave the same whichever axis carries the categories.
This is the usual shape for a coefficient plot, where each row is a named estimate and the reader reads the intervals from top to bottom. Estimates like these normally arrive already computed, from a model rather than from raw observations. That is what bounds is for: it reads two columns you already have as the low and the high, and computes nothing. The term column goes on y. In coefs, lo and hi are the ends of a 95% confidence interval for each term. bounds supplies the values for the other axis, so there is no x() to write:

title: 13  Interval

13.8 Splitting by color
With color, a reader can see which whisker is which without reading the axis. color splits an interval into one whisker per group, the same categorical split line and bar make. The statistic is computed inside each group, so every group gets its own interval. Here color repeats the species already on x, so each species gets its own hue, and one legend names them all:

  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species")

  color(col.species) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("95% CI of mean petal length, by species"))

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.9 Caps, or a linerange
The caps are the short lines across each end of a whisker. They are decoration rather than data, because they only mark where a whisker stops. A crowded plot is often easier to read without them. So whether to draw them is a setting. style(caps = FALSE) removes them, and a whisker with no caps is a linerange. caps = TRUE, the default, keeps the capped error bar. Here is the confidence interval from Splitting by color with its caps off:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  color(species) + style(caps = FALSE) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) + style(caps = False) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + style(caps = false) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  style({ caps: false }), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("The same CI, drawn as a linerange"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length, color by species, with caps off.”
caps belongs to the two marks that draw whiskers, interval and box. On any other mark, style(caps = ) is refused, and the message says what to use instead. A bar’s border_size is refused on a line the same way. caps combines with all five pair transforms. So the error bar, the linerange and the pointrange are all the same mark. Only the transform and one setting change.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.10 Hiding the center dot
Whether a center exists is decided by the statistic, not by a setting. confidence and deviation compute a mean as their center, and smooth_band computes the fitted value. range and bounds compute none. So the first three draw a pointrange, and range and bounds draw a bare error bar. A second layer can add a center where the statistic has none. point * mean over interval * range draws a pointrange from two layers, as Three layers instead of one mark shows with the median.
A setting can only hide a center that exists. A pointrange’s dot is the center the statistic computed. Sometimes you want the whisker without it. style(center = FALSE) drops the dot and leaves a bare error bar. center = TRUE, the default, keeps it:

  color(species) + style(center = FALSE) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, without its center dots")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) + style(center = False) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, without its center dots"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + style(center = false) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("The same CI, without its center dots")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),
  style({ center: false }), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("The same CI, without its center dots"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length, color by species, with center off.”
center and caps each show or hide one part of an interval: center its middle dot, caps its ends. Each takes two values, so a confidence interval can be drawn in four ways. A capped pointrange is the default. A capped bare error bar is center = FALSE. A linerange with a dot is caps = FALSE. Setting both to FALSE gives a bare linerange. style(center = ) belongs to interval alone, because a box has no center dot: its middle is the median line. On any other mark it is refused, and the message says what to use instead.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.11 A dashed whisker
A dash separates one layer from another without a second color, and it still separates them when the plot is printed in black and white. A whisker is a stroke, so it takes style(pattern = ) the same way a line does. This is the settable rule: a dash is the pattern on every path-stroke mark (line, step, interval, path, rule, edge). The dash is drawn on the whisker span only. The caps and the center dot stay solid, since a dashed cap would not look like a cap and a dot has no line to dash:

  title("A dashed 95% CI")

  color(col.species) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A dashed 95% CI"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:species) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A dashed 95% CI")

  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), color(col.species),

section: 13.12 A bar with its error bar
text:
13.12 A bar with its error bar
Two marks can answer two questions about the same groups. A bar shows where each group’s mean sits. An interval shows how well that mean is known. Layer them and you have a plot that appears throughout the social sciences, usually with a bare error bar rather than a pointrange:

  x_label("Species") + y_label("Mean petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval")

  interval * confidence(0.95) + style(center = False, color = "black") +
  x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Mean petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval"))


data(iris_flowers) + bar * mean + style(color = "lightgray") +
  interval * confidence(0.95) + style(center = false, color = "black") +
  x(:species) + y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") +
  y_label("Mean petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, mean), style({ color: "lightgray" }),
  layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  style({ center: false, color: "black" }), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Mean petal length (cm)"),
  title("Mean petal length, with a 95% confidence interval"))

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by mean, colored lightgray, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95%, with center off, colored black, x is species, y is petal length.”
Each layer names its own statistic. bar * mean reduces each group to one number, and interval * confidence(0.95) computes the interval around that number. Both read the same column and report different things, and the sentence says which is which. The dot is turned off because it would sit exactly on the top of the bar, which already marks the mean.
A bar with an error bar is where the three quantities named at the start of this chapter are most often confused, and nothing in the picture separates them. In gog the sentence names the statistic: this one says confidence(0.95), and deviation in its place would give a different sentence and a much longer whisker.
The groups of a second category go side by side, with the same dodge that separates grouped bars. Bind color to the bars and group to the whiskers. group splits the whiskers into the same slots as the bars but draws no legend of its own, so the plot keeps one:

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, colored by era, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95% and dodge, grouped by era, with center off, colored black, x is continent, y is life.”
Oceania has both the shortest whisker and the longest, from the same two countries. A confidence interval from two values is wide compared with the distance between them, because two values say little about the spread. In 2007 Australia and New Zealand were a year apart, and the interval is thirteen years wide. In 1957 the two countries were 0.07 years apart, and the confidence interval is still nine tenths of a year wide. That is more than twelve times the 1957 range, which showed as a single cap in Splitting by color.
What this plot does not show is the data. Two groups can have the same mean and the same interval and still hold very different values, and a bar reports only the one number. Three layers instead of one mark draws the spread itself, and box draws five numbers at once.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.15 In short
An interval computes nothing. Its transform decides which two numbers it spans, and whether there is a center to draw. caps and center are settings, so neither reads a column. A dash can be set for the whole layer, or mapped to a column, which splits the whiskers the way color does.

title: 13  Interval
text:
13.16 What comes next
Which two numbers an interval spans is the transform’s answer, never the mark’s. Box answers it inside the mark: it computes the quartiles and the median itself, and draws them as a box and two whiskers.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.1 A summary per group
How is each group spread out? box draws the box-and-whisker of a distribution, one per group. In each category it summarizes the measured column. A box spans the lower quartile to the upper, with a line at the median. Whiskers reach to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) of the box. Any values beyond that limit are outliers, drawn individually as dots. bar * mean gives only one number per group, while box shows how the whole group is spread. An interval needs a transform to supply its low and high values, while a box computes its whole summary itself. Boxes are vertical when the categories are on x and horizontal when they are on y; see Horizontal boxes.
The construction is John Tukey’s, from Exploratory Data Analysis (Tukey, 1977), where he called it a schematic plot. The name readers kept was his informal one, box-and-whisker, now usually shortened to box plot. Mary Eleanor Spear’s range bar of 1952 (Spear, 1952) had drawn the box and the extremes a quarter century earlier. The range bar had no rule for the fence, the cutoff that decides which values are outliers. That rule, 1.5 times the IQR, is Tukey’s: it decides where ordinary values stop and unusual ones begin.
There is one difference from his book. Tukey’s box spans hinges. Sort the values and cut the sorted list in half; when the count is odd, the middle value belongs to both halves. Take the median of each half: those two medians are the hinges. gog spans the lower and upper quartiles instead, as most software does. The two agree when a group has an odd number of values, and can differ slightly when the number is even. A box drawn by gog is therefore not always the box Tukey’s own rule gives.
How do the three species differ in petal length, not only on average but in how widely each varies? Put the categorical column, species, on x, and put the measured column, petal_length, on y. The mark computes the summary itself:

"range" draws the whole five-number summary. whiskers changes only how the summary is computed; the settings that change how a box looks are in What you can set.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.5 Why box needs no transform
An interval cannot draw without a transform to give it a low and a high. A box never needs one. An interval is only a shape, a span from a low value to a high one. Which low and high it spans is a real choice: a min–max range, a confidence interval, or a pre-computed pair. A box is a shape with one fixed statistical meaning: the summary is what a box plot means. A statistic that is always drawn by the same mark belongs inside that mark, not in a separate transform. So the whole box is box + x + y. Adding any transform other than dodge is refused, and the message says what to write instead, as What it refuses shows.
The same principle keeps the channel vocabulary small: something that only one mark can use belongs inside that mark, not in the shared vocabulary. Taking ggplot2’s ymin, lower, middle, upper and ymax as channels would add five channels meaningful to a single mark. Instead the summary is computed inside the mark, and the channel vocabulary does not grow.
The table below sets the four marks side by side. Three of them read a low and a high value from a transform, and box computes its own summary:



Mark
The spread it draws




interval * range
a whisker from the low value to the high


ribbon * range
the band between the two values, filled


line * range
the two values as two separate strokes


box
quartiles, median and whiskers, with no transform to write



box is also one of several marks that draw a distribution, and each answers a different question. bar * bin draws one variable’s histogram, and interval draws a range or an error bar. box gives the summary per group. The violin (ribbon * density) draws an estimate of the whole distribution that summary is computed from. See Transforms for how mean, median and range differ from the box’s own summary.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.9 In short
The summary is inside the mark: a box refuses every statistic, and takes only dodge, which moves boxes and computes nothing. whiskers is its one parameter. A box’s width is fixed by its slot, so no column can vary it. gog’s box spans the quartiles, and Tukey’s spans hinges, so on a group with an even number of values the two can differ slightly.

title: 14  Box
text:
14.10 What comes next
A box occupies one position on its axis, and its width carries no value from the table. Ribbon fills the band between a low value and a high one at every position along the axis.




Spear, M. E. (1952). Charting statistics. McGraw-Hill.


Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory data analysis. Addison-Wesley.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.1 A band from a range
How far apart were the lowest and highest values at each date? ribbon draws a filled band from a low boundary to a high one across x: a confidence band, a spread band, the shaded region around a trend. It fills one region, the way an area does. It reads a low value and a high value at each position, the way an interval does. An area fills from the data down to a baseline at zero. A ribbon has no baseline, and both of its edges come from the data, usually through a transform. With a category on one axis and density, the same mark draws a violin plot.
The gapminder_asia table holds five Asian countries, measured every five years. Did those five move closer together over the years, or further apart? The gap between the lowest and the highest in each year answers that. A band drawn between those two values shows every year at once, as one shape. The two boundaries come from a transform, exactly as an interval’s two extents do. range reduces y to its minimum and maximum within each x, and the ribbon fills between them. Here, the spread of life expectancy across five Asian countries, year by year:

15.2 A band with a mean line
On its own, a band shows the spread but not the center. A band is usually drawn with a line through the middle. You compose the two by layering, not by adding an option to either mark. A ribbon * range for the spread, a line * mean for the trend, sharing one x and y:

  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band")

  ribbon * range + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) +

  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band"))

  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.25) + line * mean +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 2) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band")

  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.25 }), layer(line, mean),

  title("Mean life expectancy, with its min–max band"))

This is the most common ribbon plot: a trend with its uncertainty or spread drawn around it. It is two marks the grammar already has, added with +.

title: 15  Ribbon
section: 15.4 Why a ribbon needs a transform
text:
15.4 Why a ribbon needs a transform
A low and a high are two numbers, and a plain y() supplies one. An area closes on zero: its region’s other edge is zero, which the grammar supplies. A ribbon has no such second number. Like interval, a ribbon needs a transform that supplies both boundaries, and that transform is part of its minimum syllable. Write a ribbon without one and the engine refuses it, rather than drawing an empty panel. What it refuses shows the message.
Computing the boundaries in a transform also keeps the channel vocabulary small. The alternative would add ymin and ymax as two more channels, useful to only a few marks. A box plot would then need five such channels, one for each number it summarizes. With a transform instead, the same low and high values can be drawn as a whisker, as two lines, or as a filled band. See Transforms for the range, confidence, deviation and smooth_band statistics.
Usually that transform is one of the five pair transforms: range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band and bounds. density over a category also works. It gives one curve per category, and the ribbon draws that curve and its mirror image as the two boundaries. That is the violin, later in this chapter.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.5 A confidence band
How well is the mean life expectancy known in each year? That is a different question from how far the five countries spread. range shows the full spread. For the uncertainty of the mean, use confidence. It computes a t-interval for the mean at each x, and the ribbon fills between its two boundaries. Here is the 95% band for the same five countries:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy")


(data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy"))


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, confidence(0.95)), x(col.year),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("95% confidence band for mean life expectancy"))






                               1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  95% confidence band for mean life expectancy Life expectancy Year





“Given gapminder Asia: a ribbon derived by confidence at 95%, x is year, y is life.”
The band is wide because each mean comes from only five countries. Those five differ by more than fifteen years, so the interval around their mean is wide. A confidence level above 0.95 draws a wider band still.
Compare it with the first plot in this chapter: the two bands are almost the same width. That comes from having only five values, not from the two statistics agreeing. Over the 142 countries of gm_all, the 95% band in 2007 is about 4 years wide, and their range is 43 years. What the band means is decided by the statistic you name: range draws the observed spread, and confidence draws the uncertainty of the mean. The mark stays the same in both plots, exactly as it does for interval.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.6 A pre-computed band
range, confidence, deviation and smooth_band compute the band from the raw values in the table, at the moment gog draws the plot. Many bands are computed earlier, by the analysis itself. A model’s standard error, a standard error of measurement, a bootstrap interval: each of these is computed before the plot. Each gives a low value and a high one, and those two become two columns in the table. gog draws what you computed, and it does not re-fit the model. The score_band table holds one row per raw score on a test scored from 0 to 20. Each row also holds the expected true score for that raw score, the score a model predicts, and the two ends of a 95% band around it. In this table the expected true score equals the raw score, so a line through it is a diagonal:

This is the one case range, confidence, deviation and smooth_band cannot produce: a band that was computed outside the plot, before gog ever read the table.
A band like this is usually drawn together with the values it surrounds. Here those values are the expected true scores. A dashed line draws them, with a point at every raw score. The band, the line and the points are three layers composed with +:

The dash on that line comes from style(pattern = ). That style() is written after line, so it belongs to that layer, and the band is not dashed. On a stroke the texture is a dash. The band takes the same setting, with different values. On a fill the texture is a hatch: "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid" or "dots", never "dashed".

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.7 Filled, or two dashed edges
Some plots need the band without a fill. A band starts as a low and high pair, and the mark decides how that pair is drawn. This follows the No Exceptions law. One bin draws as a bar chart, as a line and as a step histogram, and one pair draws in just as many ways: filled, as two strokes, or as two staircases. ribbon fills the pair. A line traces its two boundaries instead, which is the unfilled band many journals prefer. With style(pattern = ) it becomes the dashed pair of curves those journals often print:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + x(score) + y(expected) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges")


(data(score_band) + x(col.score) + y(col.expected) +
  line * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) +
  line + style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  point + style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges"))


data(score_band) + x(:score) + y(:expected) +
  line * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "gray", pattern = "dashed", size = 1.2) + line +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) + point +
  style(color = "steelblue", size = 2.4) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges")


plot(data(score_band), x(col.score), y(col.expected),
  layer(line, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "gray", pattern: "dashed", size: 1.2 }), line,
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 1.5 }), point,
  style({ color: "steelblue", size: 2.4 }),
  y_label("Expected true score"), x_label("Raw score"),
  title("The same band, unfilled: two dashed edges"))

“Given the score band: x is score, y is expected, lines from lower to upper, and also a line and points.”
line * bounds is one layer that draws both edges, splitting the pair into a low curve and a high one. So you do not write one y() for the low edge and another for the high edge. Two plain line layers can draw two columns you already have. They cannot split a pair that range computes, because that pair never becomes a column you can name. A line draws every pair transform the same way. line * range traces the lowest and the highest values, and line * confidence traces the two ends of a confidence interval. step * bounds draws the same two edges as staircases. Filled or unfilled, solid or dashed, it is one pair and a choice of mark, never a new option added to the band.
Four marks draw a low and high pair: interval draws it as a whisker at each x, line and step trace its two boundaries, and ribbon fills between them. All four marks draw range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band and bounds.

Europe’s band narrows from about 29 years wide in 1952 to about 10 in 2007, and the Americas’ from 31 to 20. Asia’s stays about 37 to 40 years wide, except for a dip in its lower edge in 1977.
The bands overlap where two continents cover the same range of life expectancy. A split area draws each region nearly opaque, as it draws a single one, so little of the region behind shows through. For an area, stack solves this: it starts each region at the top of the ones below, so no two regions overlap. A ribbon split into groups draws each band translucent by default instead, so a band behind another stays readable. The difference follows from what each mark measures. An area measures a height from the baseline, so its groups can be piled into a total. A ribbon already spans a low to a high and measures no such height, so there is nothing to stack. Overlapping bands are read through transparency and never stacked, which is why ribbon * stack is refused and the refusal names style(opacity = ).

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.9 One region, one fill
A ribbon is a single filled region, so opacity is a setting here, not a channel, exactly as on area. Its two boundaries pass through the low and high values at each x, and its inside belongs to no single row. So a column cannot make one part of the band lighter or darker than another. What it refuses shows the refusal.
size is refused both ways: a ribbon neither maps it nor sets it. A band’s shape comes entirely from its x values and its two boundaries, so there is no width to choose. To outline the band, layer a line along its boundaries rather than setting an outline on the mark. The plot in What you can set does this with line * bounds.

data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + line * mean + x(:continent) +
  y(:life) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * range + line * mean: spread and center, per continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, range), layer(line, mean),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * range + line * mean: spread and center, per continent"))






                                      Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  ribbon * range + line * mean: spread and center, per continent Life expectancy Continent





The band runs from each continent’s lowest life expectancy to its highest, and the line marks each continent’s mean.
For most such data an interval is the better sentence. It draws a separate whisker at each category and claims nothing about the space between them. A ribbon instead slopes from one category to the next, across positions where no rows exist. The grammar does not decide that for you: both sentences are well formed, and which one fits your data is a question about the data.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + interval * range + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("interval * range: the same numbers, claiming less")


(data(gapminder_2007) + interval * range + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("interval * range: the same numbers, claiming less"))


data(gapminder_2007) + interval * range + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("interval * range: the same numbers, claiming less")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(interval, range), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("interval * range: the same numbers, claiming less"))






                                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  interval * range: the same numbers, claiming less Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: intervals derived by range, x is continent, y is life.”
Each whisker spans the same lowest and highest values as the band, and nothing is drawn between the continents.

title: 15  Ribbon
section: 15.11 The violin: a distribution per category
text:
15.11 The violin: a distribution per category
A range on a category gives two numbers per group, the lowest and the highest. density gives a whole shape per group, and a ribbon can draw that shape. The curve runs along y, the measure. Its height at each life expectancy is drawn as a width across the continent’s slot, on both sides, so the two halves are the same curve facing opposite ways. That is the violin plot (Hintze & Nelson, 1998), and it is the band across the continents drawn above, with density in place of range and without the line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent"))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * density: one distribution per continent"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  ribbon * density: one distribution per continent Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
density is not the ribbon’s own transform. Five other marks draw the same estimated curve, and only the shape changes. That is the No Exceptions law: a mark draws whatever rows a transform produces, in the mark’s own way.



Mark derived by density
Shape




line * density
the curve as a stroke


step * density
the curve as a staircase


area * density
the curve filled to the baseline


point * density
one dot at each point the curve was estimated


bar * density
one thin bar at each of those points


ribbon * density
the curve mirrored, the violin above



line, step and area also read a category on one axis, exactly as the violin does. point and bar need a continuous axis instead: one dot or one thin bar per estimated point cannot be read inside a category’s slot, so gog refuses both there.
Nothing new was added to the grammar to draw the violin. A ribbon closes on a second boundary the data supplies, and a violin closes on the mirror image of its own curve. density estimates a distribution, and this plot computes one estimate for each group. There is no violin word to learn. Such a word would have to say four things at once: the mark, the statistic, the mirror and the slot. The sentence already says all four: ribbon is the mark and supplies the mirror, density is the statistic, and the category on x gives the slot.
Compare it with the box drawn from the same two columns:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized"))


data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized"))






                                                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  box + x + y: the same distributions, summarized Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life.”
A box gives you five numbers you can name. The violin gives you the shape those five numbers summarize. Africa’s violin is widest near 52 years, and it has a second, smaller bulge near 73. Africa’s median is 53, and none of the box’s five numbers shows that second cluster.

15.11.1 What the width means
Every group’s density integrates to 1 on its own. If that were the whole estimate, the widths would say nothing about how many rows each group has. A continent of two countries would be drawn as large as a continent of fifty-two. So by default the estimate is weighted by the group’s row count, and width means the same thing across the whole panel. Oceania holds two countries, so it is the narrowest of the five violins.
The weighting is on the shape’s area, the space it covers, not on its width, which is why Europe’s violin is wider than Africa’s. Europe’s thirty countries differ in life expectancy by no more than ten years, so Europe’s area is packed into a short stretch of the axis and the shape has to be wide. Africa’s fifty-two countries cover thirty-seven years of life expectancy, so its larger area is spread across a much longer stretch of the axis. What the width reports at any height is countries per year of life expectancy, and that reading is the same in every slot.
compare = "shape" removes that weighting and draws every violin to the same area. It is the right choice when your question is about the shapes alone. It is the wrong one when a group whose values are packed together is drawn so wide that every other violin is drawn thin:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area')


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title('density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area'))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density(compare = "shape") +
  x(:continent) + y(:life) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("density(compare = \"shape\"): every violin the same area")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density({ compare: "shape" })),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("density(compare = \"shape\"): every violin the same area"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  density(compare = "shape"): every violin the same area Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density compared by shape, x is continent, y is life.”
Oceania is now the widest violin and Africa the thinnest, so two countries are drawn wider than fifty-two. Oceania’s two values are one year apart, so its shape covers the shortest stretch of the axis. To hold the same area as the others in that short stretch, it has to be the widest. The widest shape in a panel sets the scale, so every other violin is drawn in proportion to it. Each plot answers a different question, so gog weights each area by row count unless you write compare = "shape".


15.11.2 Compared with ggplot2’s violin
If you have used ggplot2, you will notice that gog’s violins differ from those geom_violin() draws on the same data. Three choices cause the difference, and gog makes each one on purpose.
First, the ends narrow to a point. A violin is the density curve mirrored, and gog draws the whole curve. The curve runs three bandwidths past each group’s smallest and largest value. The bandwidth is the width of the bell-shaped kernel that density places on each value. No row in the table lies in these tails. Oceania’s two countries lie at 80.2 and 81.2 years, but with the bandwidth of 2.04 years that all five violins share, its violin runs from 74.1 to 87.4. Split by color(continent), line * density draws these same tails, so the violin and the curve show one estimate. geom_violin() stops each violin at its group’s smallest and largest value, so its ends are flat. With trim = FALSE, it draws tails the same way, three bandwidths long.
Second, each violin’s area is weighted by its row count, as What the width means explains. geom_violin() draws every violin to the same area, which is what compare = "shape" draws in gog.
Third, every violin in a plot is smoothed by one bandwidth, so a difference in shape comes from the data and not from the smoothing (One transform, four readings). geom_violin() gives each violin its own bandwidth.
In gog, only the second choice can be changed to match geom_violin(). The ends always narrow to a point, and every violin shares one bandwidth, whether gog chooses it or you set it.


15.11.3 Sideways, and halved
A band cannot turn, because its x is always the domain. A violin can: density makes the category a slot, and gog reads the orientation from the bindings, as it does for a bar or a box. A category on y is the form with room for long category names:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways")


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways"))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same violins, turned sideways")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same violins, turned sideways"))






                                   40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  The same violins, turned sideways Continent Life expectancy





An area draws the same estimate closed on the slot’s center line instead of on its mirror image. So area draws one half of the shape, and ribbon draws both halves:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin")


(data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin"))


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density: the half violin")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(area, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("area * density: the half violin"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  area * density: the half violin Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
There are two choices here, and they are made independently: which mark closes the region, and which axis carries the category. That gives four plots. The one this chapter has not drawn yet, an area with the category on y, has a name of its own. Halve the violin and turn it sideways. Each category then gets a filled curve rising from its slot’s center line, above one shared measure axis. That is the ridgeline plot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline")


(data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline"))


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(area, density), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("area * density + x(life): the ridgeline"))






                                   40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  area * density + x(life): the ridgeline Continent Life expectancy





Nothing was added for it either. It is the half violin’s sentence with x and y exchanged.
Read the four plots together and you can see what orthogonality gives you here. One idea draws all four plots: density estimated per category, filled on one side of the slot’s center line or on both, with the category on either axis. A word for the violin and a word for the ridgeline would name two of the four. The other two would have no word, and neither would the idea behind all four.


15.11.4 Letting the ridges overlap
The ridgeline above keeps every ridge inside its own slot. That comes from how far a shape reaches by default. The widest shape in a panel reaches 0.4 of a slot from the slot’s center line, and every other shape is drawn in proportion to it. A slot ends 0.5 from that line, so each shape stays inside its own slot, with empty space before the next category. Bars follow the same rule, for the same reason: the gap shows that the categories are separate groups, not pieces of one continuous scale.
A ridgeline, as it is usually drawn, breaks that rule on purpose: its ridges are tall enough to reach into the slot above, and that overlap is part of the design. density(reach = ) says how far, in slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall")


(data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall"))


data(gapminder_2007) + area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(:life) +
  y(:continent) + x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(area, density({ reach: 2.5 })),
  x(col.life), y(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall"))






                                   40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  reach = 2.5: each ridge two and a half slots tall Continent Life expectancy





“Given gapminder 2007: areas derived by density reaching 2.5 slots, x is life, y is continent.”
The number is measured from the slot’s center line to the shape’s furthest point. That is why the number means the same thing to both marks. A ribbon reaches that far on each side, an area on one side only. The half violin therefore stays exactly half of the violin, at any reach. Past 0.5 the shapes leave their own slots. gog does not refuse this, because a reach above 0.5 is what your sentence asks for. Where two ridges overlap, the lower one is drawn later and covers the one above it.
The category axis grows to hold the ridges. Normally the axis leaves half a slot of space beyond the first and last categories, which is enough for a bar or a box, since each stays inside its slot. A ridge 2.5 slots tall does not stay in its slot, so the axis adds the room it needs. Without that room, the panel edge would hide the top of the highest ridge.
The edge is a layer here, as it is for every filled band in this chapter. Neither area nor ribbon takes a border setting. A line given the same transform traces the outline of the fill. That is the Filled, or two dashed edges rule again, this time inside a category’s slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.5) +
  style(color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.9) +
  line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black", size = 1) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  layer(area, density({ reach: 2.5 })),
  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.9 }),
  layer(line, density({ reach: 2.5 })),
  style({ color: "black", size: 1 }), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same ridges, with their edges drawn"))






                                          40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  The same ridges, with their edges drawn Continent Life expectancy





Both layers read the same density(reach = 2.5), so the stroke lies exactly on the outline of the fill. That is why no border setting is needed: a layer draws the outline, with its own color, width and dash. Color each ridge by its own category and the plot is complete:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(col.continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  area * density(reach = 2.2) + color(:continent) +
  line * density(reach = 2.2) + style(color = "black", size = 0.9) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("One hue per ridge")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  layer(area, density({ reach: 2.2 })), color(col.continent),
  layer(line, density({ reach: 2.2 })),
  style({ color: "black", size: 0.9 }), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One hue per ridge"))






                                          40 60 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  One hue per ridge Continent Life expectancy  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





The color(continent) is written after the area, so it belongs to that layer alone. Written before both marks it would color the line too. A layer cannot both map color and set it, so the sentence would be refused. Where a channel sits in the sentence is what decides its scope, and Encoding scope explains that in full.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.12 What you can set
A setting changes how the band looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. These are a ribbon’s, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(pattern = )
solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots



A ribbon takes area’s list, and for area’s reasons. There is no size, because the band’s shape comes from the two boundaries its transform supplies. There is no border, because the edge is a line traced along the same pair.
One setting this chapter has not shown on a band is a fill pattern. Here is a band hatched with a grid, with a dashed line along both of its boundaries:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(score_band) + x(score) +
  ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges")


(data(score_band) + x(col.score) +
  ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) +
    style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + title("A textured band, and its two edges"))


data(score_band) + x(:score) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "grid", opacity = 0.45) +
  line * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "slateblue", pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Expected true score") +
  title("A textured band, and its two edges")


plot(data(score_band), x(col.score),
  layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "slateblue", pattern: "grid", opacity: 0.45 }),
  layer(line, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "slateblue", pattern: "dashed" }),
  y_label("Expected true score"),
  title("A textured band, and its two edges"))






                                    0 5 10 15 20   0 10 20  A textured band, and its two edges Expected true score Score





“Given the score band: x is score, a ribbon from lower to upper, with pattern grid, and also lines from lower to upper, with pattern dashed.”
Both marks read the same bounds(lower, upper) there, exactly as the two ridge layers did, so the edges stay on the band. The two pattern values follow the rule from A pre-computed band: a hatch on the fill, a dash on the stroke.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the companion grid.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.13 What it refuses
The first refusal concerns the measure, which must be continuous. A band from range spans a low value to a high one, and both are quantities, so a category on y is refused. The violins above put a category on y, but there density makes it a slot rather than the measure:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(life) + y(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(col.life) + y(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * range + x(:life) + y(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.life),
  y(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `y(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `y` on `ribbon` needs a continuous (numeric) column. On these marks `x` is the domain and `y` the measure, and a category is not a quantity to measure: a mean of category names is not a number, and a region has no categorical baseline to close on. Put the category on `x` instead — `line * mean + x(<category>) + y(<number>)` is the profile plot, and `area * mean` fills it. Unlike `bar`/`box`/`interval`, these marks do not read their orientation off the bindings, because their two axes do not have the same role.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A bare ribbon is the second refusal. A plain y() supplies one number, and a band needs two boundaries, as Why a ribbon needs a transform explained. The engine says so rather than drawing an empty panel:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(year) + y(life)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(col.year) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon + x(:year) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), ribbon, x(col.year), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `ribbon` draws a span from a low value to a high one, but nothing here produces those extents. Add a range transform — `ribbon * range + x(t) + y(value)` draws a band between the min and max at each x, or `ribbon * bounds(lo, hi)` a pre-computed one.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message calls them range transforms. It names two of the four, range and bounds, and writes out a sentence the engine would accept.
A mapped opacity is the third. The inside of the band belongs to no single row, as One region, one fill explained. Opacity is set with style(opacity = ) and never mapped:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + opacity(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + ribbon * range + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  opacity(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(ribbon, range), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `ribbon` — a ribbon takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `gdp` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`, or use a mark that maps `opacity`: `point`, `bar` or `surface`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.14 In short
A ribbon fills the space between two boundaries, and refuses to draw until a transform supplies them. The transform decides what the band means: the extremes from range, the middle from two quantiles, the mean’s uncertainty from confidence, and a band computed elsewhere from bounds. Over a category, density makes the ribbon a violin. Both edges come from the data, so the band’s shape is never a setting.

title: 15  Ribbon
text:
15.15 What comes next
A ribbon shows a region and names nothing inside it. Text draws a string at each position, read from a column.




Hintze, J. L., & Nelson, R. D. (1998). Violin plots: A box plot–density trace synergism. The American Statistician, 52(2), 181–184. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1998.10480559

title: 16  Text
text:
16.1 The mark and its content
Which point is which? text draws a string, a piece of text such as a name or a number, at each (x, y) position. It is point’s sibling: both place one glyph per row. A point’s glyph is a dot by default. A text mark’s glyph is a string, and that string comes from a column, through the label channel. This chapter uses it three ways: to name the points of a scatter, to print a value on a bar, and to write a note on a plot.
A point tells you where a row sits; it cannot tell you which row. Five countries drawn as dots are five points with nothing to say which country is which:

data(medals) + point + x(gold) + y(silver) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Five countries, and no names")


(data(medals) + point + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Five countries, and no names"))


data(medals) + point + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Five countries, and no names")

RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named"))

  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("The same five, named")

That is the whole difference between the two marks. point draws the same dot at every row’s position. text draws one of the row’s own values there instead.

title: 16  Text
section: 16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter
text:
16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter
A dot marks one position on the panel. A word is much wider than a dot, so a name on its own only shows roughly where its row sits. The two marks can be drawn together: layer a point mark and a text mark on the same x and y, with the + operator. The dot gives the exact position and the string gives the name. That is a labeled scatter, built from two marks rather than a third mark of its own.
Each style() applies to the mark written before it, so style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") colors the dots and not the words. Without a nudge, each label is drawn centered on its dot, so style(nudge = "up") moves every label above its dot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Located by the dot, named just above")


(data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Located by the dot, named just above"))


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Located by the dot, named just above")


plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Located by the dot, named just above"))






                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Located by the dot, named just above Silver Gold





“Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge up.”

16.2.1 Nudging the label off its point
Up is only one of four directions, and it is not always the side with room. A dot near the top of the panel, or one with a neighbor just above it, has no space for its name there. Those labels need a different direction. style(nudge = ) shifts a text label off its (x, y). It takes one direction: "up", "down", "left", or "right":


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same, nudged right")


(data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same, nudged right"))


data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("The same, nudged right")


plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "right" }), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("The same, nudged right"))






                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  The same, nudged right Silver Gold





You do not give a distance. The engine sets it from the font size, far enough that the word does not touch a dot of the default size. That is why nudge asks only for a direction. A nudge is one fixed shift, the same for every label, and nothing in the data changes it. jitter and dodge work differently: they compute each mark’s offset from the data, so marks can move by different amounts. Only text accepts a nudge. A point or a bar has no label to move, so the engine refuses the setting there and names the mark that does.


16.2.2 repel: moving labels off each other
A nudge shifts every label the same way, so it moves each label off its own dot and does nothing else. When the labels collide with each other, one fixed shift moves them all together and the words still overlap. Thirty European countries are enough to show it:

Every name is drawn on its own dot, and where the countries crowd together the words overlap. A nudge would move all thirty words the same distance in the same direction, so the same words would still overlap.
repel solves that. It is one of the four collision modifiers, with jitter, dodge and stack, so it is written after the mark with *, not inside style(). It measures where the labels and the dots actually are, then moves each label off the words around it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same thirty, moved apart")


(data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same thirty, moved apart"))


data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text * repel +
  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same thirty, moved apart")


plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same thirty, moved apart"))






                                                 Albania Austria Belgium Bosnia and Herzegovina Bulgaria Croatia Czech Republic Denmark Finland France Germany Greece Hungary Iceland Ireland Italy Montenegro Netherlands Norway Poland Portugal Romania Serbia Slovak Republic Slovenia Spain Sweden Switzerland Turkey United Kingdom                    10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   72 74 76 78 80 82  The same thirty, moved apart Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”
Notice three things in this plot. Every label is drawn just outside its dot, so no word covers the dot it names. A label with other words near it moves to whichever side has room. A label with space around it stays where it started, directly above its dot. The first two follow from one rule: repel pulls each label toward its own dot, and pushes it away from every other word and every dot, its own included.
In a more crowded plot, repel can move a label much further from its dot. Once the gap is larger than the height of one line of text, gog draws a thin line from the dot to the word, so you can still see which dot the name belongs to. No label in this plot moved that far, so none has a line.
The placement is deterministic. It uses no random-number generator and does not read the computer’s clock, so the same specification draws the same picture every time. It does depend on the order of the rows, though. repel settles the overlaps pair by pair, in the order of the rows, so the same rows in a different order can end with some labels in different places.
Sometimes no arrangement keeps every label apart. repel then still draws every label, and gog prints a message saying how many still overlap. Which names to leave out is your decision, so repel never removes one. In this plot all thirty fit, so gog prints no message.
Three things give crowded labels more room: fewer rows, a smaller style(size = ), and a larger plot. theme(width =, height =) sets the plot’s size in pixels, and the Composition chapter explains it.
Fewer rows is often the right choice. On a large table you usually name only the few rows that matter: give the text layer its own table that holds just those rows, as A note is a layer does with one row. In the web edition, clicking a dot on a plot with brush() shows its values beside it, which Selection calls a stamp. Stamps help you choose those rows. A stamp is gone when the page reloads, while a text label is part of the specification and is drawn every time.

title: 16  Text
section: 16.3 Number labels: the value on each mark
text:
16.3 Number labels: the value on each mark
A label does not have to be a name, and it does not have to sit on a scatter. A bar shows which country won more. To read how much more, a reader has to measure each bar against the axis, and that measurement is only an estimate. Sometimes the number itself is the answer. Bind a column that holds numbers and each row’s value is drawn. A whole number is printed without a decimal point. Layer text over bar to print each bar’s height at its top:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(country) + y(gold) + label(gold) +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height")


(data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + label(col.gold) +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height"))


data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") + text + x(:country) +
  y(:gold) + label(:gold) + y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height")


plot(data(medals), bar, style({ color: "steelblue" }), text,
  x(col.country), y(col.gold), label(col.gold), y_label("Gold medals"),
  title("Each bar labeled with its height"))






                  46 38 29 19 17                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany   0 10 20 30 40  Each bar labeled with its height Gold medals Country





“Given the medals: bars and also text, x is country, y is gold, label by gold.”
Each bar now carries its count, so the gap between the USA’s 46 and China’s 38 can be read without the axis.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.4 Color
You see a hue faster than you can read a word, so a color split shows you the groups before you read a single name. Every label so far has been printed in one color, which is the default. Map a categorical column to color and the labels split by that column; a column of numbers is refused on a text mark. The mapping gets a legend to name the groups, and the colors come from the same palette that points and bars use. In the plot below each country is its own group, so the hue repeats the name:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + color(country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + color(col.country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  color(:country) + x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  color(col.country), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("One hue per country"))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, color by country.”
The legend names the five hues. With a column that several rows share, such as a continent, one hue would mark every name in a group before you read any of them.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.5 Styling: one color, one size
The color channel takes its hues from a column. When the words are the whole plot, with no dots or bars beside them, you may want one color of your own and a larger font, because the default is often too small to read comfortably. Neither comes from a column, so both are settings rather than mappings. style(color = ) sets the color of the words, and style(size = ) sets the font size in pixels. Each applies to every label in the layer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels")


(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels"))


data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Bigger, greener labels")


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ color: "seagreen", size: 17 }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("Bigger, greener labels"))






            USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Bigger, greener labels Silver Gold





“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, colored seagreen, with size 17.”
gog refuses a size mapped to a column on a text mark, so every label in a layer has one font size. A word cloud sizes each word by how often it occurs, so it needs a size per row, and that is one reason gog draws no word cloud.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.6 A halo around each label
A label drawn over a dot or a line can be hard to read, because the mark shows around its letters. style(border_size = ) draws a halo: a band of the panel’s background color around each letter, drawn under the text. It hides the mark next to each letter and does not change the letters:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 9) +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(size = 12, border_size = 3) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Names with a halo")


(data(medals) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 9) +
  text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  style(size = 12, border_size = 3) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Names with a halo"))


data(medals) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 9) + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  style(size = 12, border_size = 3) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Names with a halo")


plot(data(medals), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e", size: 9 }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ size: 12, border_size: 3 }), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Names with a halo"))






                   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany   USA China Great Britain Russia Germany               20 30 40   10 20 30  Names with a halo Silver Gold





“Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with size 12 and border size 3.”
A thin band of the panel’s color now separates each name from the gray dot behind it. border_size sets the width of the stroke in pixels. Half of it lies under the letters, so a width of 3 shows as a band 1.5 pixels wide. border_color sets its color, if you want one other than the background. Either setting alone draws a halo: an unset width is 3 pixels, and an unset color is the panel’s background color. With neither, a label has no halo.
A halo hides the marks it covers, so use it where the words matter more than those marks. It never hides another label’s letters, because every halo in a layer is drawn before any letter. It does not move overlapping labels apart. That is the job of repel.

title: 16  Text

16.7 Turning a label
A note beside a vertical line is easiest to read when it is written along the line, not across it. style(angle = ) turns every label in its layer by the number of degrees you give, counterclockwise from horizontal, so 90 reads upward and -90 downward. Each label turns around its own position, the point its x and y give. The milestones table holds two notes. Each is drawn at the income in at and the height in value:

Each note is now parallel to its line, and the halo from the section above hides the line behind its letters. gog measures a turned label by the space it takes after turning. repel uses that space to keep labels apart, and in nest a name is drawn only if it fits its rectangle when turned. A flow draws every name, so turning is how a long name stays inside its tall, narrow slot.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.8 Why label is a channel
A setting is a value you type into the sentence. You might expect to type a label into the sentence in the same way, like a title. A label is not a title: it is one value per row, and that makes it data. One rule of the grammar decides whether a label is a setting or a channel: data reaches a mark only through a channel. That makes label a channel, so no mark takes the words themselves as an argument. A fixed note is therefore a table with one row, given to data(), and never a value given to style().
Only text accepts label; every other mark refuses it, which is why a labeled scatter is point + text and never a label on point. text requires a label: the label is part of the mark’s minimum syllable, as x and y are. Ask for a text mark with no label and the engine refuses, and says what to write instead, as What it refuses shows. text is the mark, and label is the channel that carries the column it draws.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.9 A note is a layer
A plot often needs one note written on it, at a place you choose. It may say what a region of the scatter means, or why a point sits where it does. If you have used ggplot2, a note there is a separate function, annotate(). In gog it is a table with one row, and the plot below draws it. A second data() gives the next layer its own table (the Data chapter’s rule), and a table with one row in it puts one string on the plot:



income_note: its one row

  data(income_note) + text + label(what) +
  title("A note is a layer, not a function")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(income_note) + text + label(col.what) +
  title("A note is a layer, not a function"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(income_note) +
  text + label(:what) + title("A note is a layer, not a function")

  data(income_note), text, label(col.what),
  title("A note is a layer, not a function"))
