“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also text from the income note, label by what.”
The note sits in an empty corner of the scatter: no country in 2007 has an income that high with lives that short.
That plot needed nothing new in the grammar. A mark written directly after a data() already reads that table, and text already draws one string per row. The note is data like any other, so it is scaled like any other. Give the note an x far from the points, and the axes stretch to cover it, so check the axes each time you place a note.
One rule applies while writing a note. The text layer names no position of its own, so it reads the columns the axes use, gdp and life, from its own table. That is why income_note has a column with each of those names. A note with its own names writes its positions after text: + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(what). Any other mark at a place you choose is written the same way: a small table, and a layer over it. A dot on the plot is a point over the same one-row table, and several notes are several rows.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.10 Text that a transform places
You choose where a note goes. A transform can choose the place instead, and then the text names whatever that transform built. In the first three rows, a second layer with the same transform draws the shape the text labels:



Text derived by
What it labels




text * layout
the nodes of a network, beside point * layout and edge * layout


text * flow
each stage’s slots in a flow, beside ribbon * flow and zone * flow


text * partition
the regions of a hierarchy, beside zone * partition


text * repel
the scatter labels of repel, moved off each other



The chapters that draw them are Network, Flow and Transforms. In each one the text is a layer over the mark that drew the shape, and both layers read the same transform.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.11 What you can set
The Styling section set a color and a size. Those are two entries in a longer list, and the whole of it is here: which color, how transparent, which size, which way to shift the label, by how many degrees to turn it, and the color and width of its halo. None of that is in a column, so it is set rather than mapped, and each mark takes its own settings. These are a text mark’s, with the values each accepts:



Setting
Value

style(border_color = )

style(border_size = )

style(nudge = )
up, down, left, right


style(angle = )
degrees, counterclockwise from horizontal

  y_label("Gold medals") + title("Labels nudged off their points")

title: 16  Text
text:
16.12 What it refuses
A text mark refuses three things: a missing label, the shape channel, and any pattern. The label is part of the mark’s minimum syllable, as x and y are: with no string, a text mark has nothing to draw. The engine refuses and names the channel to add:

data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver)


data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver)

plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver))

A reader who knows point will try its channels on text. color draws with a categorical column, and size and opacity are legal but not drawn. shape is refused outright, because it cannot change a string. A point’s glyph can change shape because the dot itself says nothing. A text mark’s glyph is the string itself, so there is nothing for shape to change:

  shape(:country)

  shape(col.country))

A string takes no texture either. pattern dashes a stroke or hatches a filled region, and a word is neither:

  style(pattern = "hatch")

  style(pattern = "hatch"))

  style(pattern = "hatch")

  style({ pattern: "hatch" }))

! gog: `style(pattern = )` is a stroke's dash or a fill's texture, and a `text` is a glyph, not either — a point's form is set by `shape`, a text's by its content. The strokes (`line`/`step`/`interval`/`path`/`rule`/`edge`) take a dash; the fills (`area`/`bar`/`box`/`ribbon`/`zone`) a texture.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.13 In short
A text mark will not draw without a label, and no other mark accepts one. Its words come from a column, so a fixed note is a table with one row. repel draws every label and reports how many still overlap, because which names to leave out is your decision.

title: 16  Text
text:
16.14 What comes next
Without repel, row order never moves a word: each one is drawn at the position its own row gives it. For a path, row order decides which rows are joined: the mark joins each row to the next, in the order the table holds them.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.1 The connected scatterplot
How did income and life expectancy change together in each country, year by year? path draws one stroke through the rows’ points, in the order the table gives them. That is the whole definition of the mark, and it is the one thing line does not do. A line sorts its vertices by x first, because a line draws a function: one y for each x, read left to right along a domain. A path draws a route. It visits row 1, then row 2, and it may turn back, cross itself, or return to where it started.
The two marks draw the same kind of stroke, and they take the same color and group splits and the same style(size = ) and style(pattern = ) settings. One question separates them: does the order of the rows mean something? A path keeps that order, and three things follow from it. It can carry an arrowhead, because its last vertex is the table’s last row. In polar it can go around the circle more than once, because two rows with the same angle stay apart, each on its own turn. And it can run through the cube, because the row order does not depend on any axis. None of the three is a special case.
Two measures that change over time can be drawn as two separate time series, one above the other. The reader then has to find the same year in both plots before comparing them. One plot can show both measures and time together, if the rows are already in time order. Here are five Asian countries, each measured twelve times from 1952 to 2007. Put income on one axis and life expectancy on the other, and connect each country’s measurements in the order they were taken:

Each route is one country’s history. The plot has no time axis, but it still shows time: time is the order in which the points are joined. China’s route goes almost straight up at very low income. That shape belongs to a country whose life expectancy rose long before its income did, and India’s and Indonesia’s routes rise the same way. Korea’s route starts upward and then turns a sharp corner to the right. Past that corner its income climbs fast and its life expectancy rises more slowly. Japan’s route is the flattest of the five. It begins where Korea’s route turns: Japan had that income and life expectancy in 1952, twenty years before Korea. This is a connected scatterplot, and path is the only mark that draws it.

17.2 What line draws instead
line is the mark you would probably write first, because it is the familiar way to join rows with a stroke. So compare what line draws from the same table. One word changes in the specification, and three of the five routes change shape:

  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("the same data, sorted by x"))

  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("the same data, sorted by x")

  color(col.country), x_label("GDP per person"),

“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is gdp, y is life, color by country.”
Look at China’s route. Its income did not rise steadily: it fell once and then rose again, so the year order and the income order differ, and line joins the points in income order. Every point is still in the right place, but the stroke between them no longer follows the years. Indonesia’s and Japan’s routes change the same way, Japan’s only slightly. India’s and Korea’s income rose at every measurement, so for them both marks draw the same picture. This is not a defect in line. A line draws a function, and a function has one value for each x. Sorting the rows by x cannot change which value belongs to which x. For a time series read along a date axis, the sort simply puts the rows in date order.
The two marks answer different questions. If a specification names the wrong one, the engine still draws a plot, and the plot still looks reasonable. Nothing reports the mistake. The rule is this. If the reader should follow the points in any order other than left to right, that order has to come from the table, and only path takes its order from the table.

title: 17  Path
section: 17.3 Which end is the last row?

  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("style(arrow = \"end\"): the head sits at 2007")

Now each route points at its last row. arrow takes "end", "start", or "both": an arrowhead (a head, for short) at the last row, at the first row, or at both ends.
Two marks take it: path, and edge, whose direction comes from the two columns of its layout. Every other mark refuses it. A line’s last vertex is the row with the largest x, so a head there would point at the end of the sort, not at the last row. A path’s end comes from the data. What it refuses shows a line refusing an arrowhead.

title: 17  Path
section: 17.5 Two transforms, and the rest refused
text:
17.5 Two transforms, and the rest refused
Every path so far has been drawn directly from the rows. The next question is what happens when a transform changes the rows before the path draws them. line, step, area and ribbon compose with many transforms. path composes with two, density and cluster, and refuses every other transform. The summaries show the reason most clearly. What it refuses shows path * mean being refused.
A summary replaces the rows. mean reduces each country to one number, and what is left to connect is one point per country, in whatever order the summary produced them. One point per country, joined left to right, is what line already draws. A path’s meaning is the row order, and a summary discards that order. That is why this mark refuses almost every transform, and why its row on the Combinations grid is nearly empty.
density is the transform this chapter shows, and Cluster shows the other. Like a summary, density replaces the rows. Unlike a summary, its new rows have an order that means something: they are the points around each ring, in the order the ring is traced.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.6 The contour: path * density
Where are the flowers most crowded, and how tightly? A scatterplot of these 150 flowers would show two groups. Where several flowers share a position their dots are drawn on top of each other, and you cannot tell how many are there. A contour plot draws the shape of the cloud as closed rings, without drawing the points. Bind both positions and compose density. gog estimates the density of points at every place on the plane, then traces the rings on which that density is the same:

“Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length.”
Over two positions a density is a field: one estimated value at every place on the plane. Three marks read that field, and each one draws it differently:







Mark derived by density, over two positions
Shape




zone * density
the field as filled cells


surface * density
the field as a sheet in the cube


path * density
the field as contour rings, the shape this section draws



Surface draws all three from one table, one after another.
That contour needed nothing new in the grammar. One rule produced it, and the same rule makes zone * bin draw a heatmap. The rule is that the mark decides how many axes a transform cuts. You never state the number yourself. In bar * density you bind only one position, so one axis is still free. The density is estimated along the bound axis and drawn on the free one, as one thin bar at each point where it was estimated. A path is a route through two columns and treats them equally, so it has no axis left over. density therefore cuts both. There is no contour atom for the same reason there is no pie() (Polar makes that argument): the atoms you already have spell it.
Read the outermost ring, then the ones inside it. The outermost is a single ring around both groups, and the next level inward splits into two separate rings. One level can therefore be several separate rings. So a level is not one stroke, the way one color value is one line. Each ring is drawn as its own stroke, and the level decides only its color. The two inner rings are never joined across the gap between them.

17.6.1 The parameters
The rings are colored by their level, and you did not bind color to get that. The rows density produces carry a new column, level, and gog bound color to it for you, the same way bar * bin binds y for you. Bind it yourself if you prefer, and change how many rings are traced:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 10) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + color(level) +
  title("ten levels, named out loud")


(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 10) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + color(col.level) +
  title("ten levels, named out loud"))


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 10) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + color(:level) + title("ten levels, named out loud")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(path, density({ levels: 10 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), color(col.level),
  title("ten levels, named out loud"))

“Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density at 10 levels, x is sepal length, y is petal length, color by level.”
The rings now come in ten levels instead of the default six, so they sit closer together.
density is one transform, and the mark decides what it computes. With line it computes a curve over one column. With zone or path it computes a field over two columns: a zone fills the field, and a path draws its rings. The parameters follow from this. A width suits the curve, and a number of levels suits the field.
levels cuts the field into that many steps. Of the three marks that read the field, zone and path accept it, and surface refuses it, for a reason Surface gives. A one-dimensional density is a single curve, and a curve has no field to cut, so a line refuses it.
bandwidth is how far each row is spread when the density is estimated, in the column’s own units, so it belongs to the curve over one column. A contour spreads over two columns, and two columns are usually in different units, such as dollars and years. One number cannot be a width in both. Sepal length and petal length are both in centimeters, but gog refuses bandwidth here too, because the rule is about two columns, whatever their units. What it refuses shows both refusals.
adjust multiplies the bandwidth gog chooses by itself. It is a plain number rather than a length, so it means the same thing on either axis. It is the one parameter line, zone, surface and path all accept:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(adjust = 1.6) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
  title("the same cloud, smoothed harder")


(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(adjust = 1.6) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) +
  title("the same cloud, smoothed harder"))


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(adjust = 1.6) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + title("the same cloud, smoothed harder")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(path, density({ adjust: 1.6 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length),
  title("the same cloud, smoothed harder"))






                                       4 5 6 7 8   0 2 4 6  the same cloud, smoothed harder Petal Length Sepal Length  Level         0.0872 0.0509 0.0145 





“Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density adjusted by 1.6, x is sepal length, y is petal length.”
Each flower now spreads further when the density is estimated, so the rings are smoother.
To estimate one field per category, split the rows with group. The level is already on color, which is why the split has to be group. Versicolor and virginica overlap on this plot, so the chunk below first keeps only their rows, in a table named petals:

petals <- iris_flowers[iris_flowers$species != "setosa", ]

data(petals) + path * density(levels = 4) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + group(species) +
  title("two species, estimated separately")



                                        5 6 7 8   3 4 5 6 7  two species, estimated separately Petal Length Sepal Length  Level         0.547 0.339 0.131 





“Given the petals: paths derived by density at 4 levels, x is sepal length, y is petal length, grouped by species.”
Each species has its own set of rings. Both sets take their colors from the levels, so the lower set, with the shorter petals, is versicolor. The two fields are smoothed alike. On each axis, the two species share the same bandwidth: the average of the bandwidths each species would get alone. A difference between the two sets of rings therefore comes from the flowers and not from the smoothing.


17.6.2 One field, two marks
A path has no axis left over, and a zone has none either, so a zone also reads density over both positions. The difference is in the geometry. A path draws the rings as strokes. A zone given levels fills the bands between them, and without levels it fills small cells. Give both marks the same levels and you get the same curves twice: once as strokes, once as the edges of filled bands. The filled version is the filled contour, and zone * density draws it; the zone chapter covers the color ramp it uses. One field, two marks. It is the same division of work as in bar * bin and line * bin: the mark chooses the geometry, and the transform stays the same.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.7 A path in polar
The arrowhead was the first of the three things the row order gives a path. The second appears in polar, when the same angle appears in more than one row. Some routes turn: a bearing that moves through all 360 degrees, or a value that cycles through the hours while another grows. The spiral table holds two days of readings, one every 15 minutes. a is the hour of the day, and r grows the whole time:



spiral: first 5 of 192 rows


a
r

On flat axes the route has to jump back at midnight:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(spiral) + path + x(a) + y(r) +
  title("a path on flat axes")


(data(spiral) + path + x(col.a) + y(col.r) +
  title("a path on flat axes"))


data(spiral) + path + x(:a) + y(:r) + title("a path on flat axes")


plot(data(spiral), path, x(col.a), y(col.r), title("a path on flat axes"))






                               0 10 20   0 1 2 3 4  a path on flat axes R A





“Given the spiral: a path, x is a, y is r.”
The long stroke across the middle joins 23:45 on the first day to midnight on the second, and no reading lies along it. On a straight axis the end of one day is drawn far from the start of the next. On a circle the two are at the same angle, so the route continues instead of jumping. path works in polar like every other mark:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(spiral) + path + x(a) + y(r) + polar() +
  title("a path in polar")


(data(spiral) + path + x(col.a) + y(col.r) + polar() +
  title("a path in polar"))


data(spiral) + path + x(:a) + y(:r) + polar() + title("a path in polar")


plot(data(spiral), path, x(col.a), y(col.r), polar(),
  title("a path in polar"))






                  0 10 20   0 1 2 3 4  a path in polar R A





“Given the spiral: a path, x is a, y is r, in polar.”
The route goes around twice, one day after the other, and turns outward in a spiral. A line cannot draw this. It sorts the rows by a, so each moment of the first day is joined to the same moment of the second, and the stroke zigzags between them inside one turn:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(spiral) + line + x(a) + y(r) + polar() +
  title("a line in polar")


(data(spiral) + line + x(col.a) + y(col.r) + polar() +
  title("a line in polar"))


data(spiral) + line + x(:a) + y(:r) + polar() + title("a line in polar")


plot(data(spiral), line, x(col.a), y(col.r), polar(),
  title("a line in polar"))






                  0 10 20   0 1 2 3 4  a line in polar R A





“Given the spiral: a line, x is a, y is r, in polar.”
There is one thing path does not copy from line: the segment that closes a radar chart, like the one in Line. A categorical line in polar joins its last vertex back to its first, because the categories fill the whole turn, and a gap there would leave one sector blank. A path puts each category on the same spoke as a line does, but it does not join its last vertex back to its first. Its last vertex is where the data stopped, so closing the route would add a segment that is not in the table. If a route does return to its start, say so by repeating the first row.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.8 A path in the cube
In polar the path still joined the same rows in the same order. A third axis does not change that either, because the row order does not depend on any axis. A glider’s route has three positions: east, north and altitude. A flat page holds only two of them. Drawn flat, two circling gliders are two rings, one inside the other, and nothing on the page shows that they are rising. The thermals table holds one row for each recorded position of two gliders. Both circle the same thermal, a rising column of warm air, as they climb:

Bind z and the route runs through the cube instead of across the page. Of the marks that join their rows into one stroke, path is the only one that takes the third position. The reason is the row order this whole chapter is about:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + color(col.glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + title("Two gliders, one thermal")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), title("Two gliders, one thermal"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude  Two gliders, one thermal  Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider.”
An order is not a property of any axis, so adding a third axis does not change it. The route joins the same rows in the same sequence, whatever angle the scene is turned to. A line sorts by x, and the cube has no left to right. In the cube x is one of three equal positions. At some viewing angles x points straight into the page, so a line would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see. So a line’s sort by x has no meaning in the cube, and line, step, area and ribbon refuse z rather than draw a stroke the reader cannot read, as What it refuses shows.
Look again at the two routes in the cube. They cross several times. At each crossing the route nearer to the eye is drawn over the one behind it, and which route is nearer changes as the two gliders climb. To draw the cube on a flat page, gog draws the pieces farthest from the eye first and the nearest last, so that near pieces cover far ones. This drawing order is the depth sort. A glyph sits at one distance from the eye, so it takes one place in that order. A stroke through the cube has a far end and a near end, so each segment takes its own place. The segments of both routes share one depth sort. If each stroke took one place in the depth sort, one glider’s route would be drawn entirely in front of the other’s, and the two coils could not pass through each other as they do here. An arrowhead takes its place the same way, at the depth of its own tip. A head far from the eye is covered by whatever is drawn in front of it.
As on a flat line, color can vary along the route, because a color belongs to one place on the stroke rather than to the whole stroke. Bind altitude to color as well as to z. The climb is then said twice: once by where the route is, once by what color it is:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(altitude) + group(glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Altitude, said twice")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) +
  color(col.altitude) + group(col.glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) +
  title("Altitude, said twice"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:altitude) + group(:glider) + palette("viridis") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) + title("Altitude, said twice")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.altitude), group(col.glider), palette("viridis"),
  space({ turn: -25, tilt: 20 }), title("Altitude, said twice"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude  Altitude, said twice  Altitude            2513.2 1706.6 900 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by altitude, grouped by glider, with the viridis palette.”
palette("viridis") chooses the color ramp that shows the altitudes. space(turn = -25, tilt = 20) sets the viewing angle, which Space explains; a z binding alone would draw the cube from its default angle. group(glider) tells gog that the rows belong to two routes rather than one. Remove group(glider) and the plot is wrong. A category on color splits the mark into one stroke per group, but a measure has no categories to split on. Without group the two gliders would be joined into a single route, with one straight segment from the last row of one glider to the first row of the other. color shows a value along the route; group says which route each row belongs to. They are two different questions, so they need two atoms.
The depth sort draws the route as separate segments. Left alone, the dash pattern would start again at every segment, so gog continues it from one segment to the next:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) +
  style(pattern = "dashed") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20)


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + color(col.glider) +
  style(pattern = "dashed") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + style(pattern = "dashed") +
  space(turn = -25, tilt = 20)


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), style({ pattern: "dashed" }),
  space({ turn: -25, tilt: 20 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude   Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider, with pattern dashed.”
The dashes run along the route rather than resetting at every row. The dash belongs to the route, not to the segments the depth sort needs.
Space owns the third dimension and the viewing angle.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.9 What a path is for
In the three spaces this chapter used (the flat plane, polar and the cube), the path did one thing: it joined the rows in the table’s order. The connected scatterplot is the best known use, but the mark is more general than that. A path is the right mark whenever the reader should follow the rows in the order the table gives them. A route through space is one, and so is a cycle that returns to where it began. So is a hysteresis loop, which is a cycle whose outward and return routes differ, and so is an arrow. The test is always the same question. Does the order of the rows mean something? If it does, the mark is path; if the reader should read left to right, it is line.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.10 What you can set
A plain stroke does not show which way the route runs, and it looks like every other stroke on the panel. The table has no column for the direction or for the look of the stroke, so both are set rather than mapped, and each mark takes its own settings. These are a path’s, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash, longdash


style(arrow = )
end, start, both



arrow belongs to path and edge only, for the reason Which end is the last row? gave.
A route can carry the heads, a width and a dash together:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route")


(data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route"))


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:country) +
  style(arrow = "both", size = 2.5, pattern = "dotted") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), path, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.country),
  style({ arrow: "both", size: 2.5, pattern: "dotted" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Both ends marked, on a dotted route"))






                                               0 10K 20K 30K   40 50 60 70 80  Both ends marked, on a dotted route Life expectancy GDP per person  Country    China  India  Indonesia  Japan  Korea, Rep. 





“Given gapminder Asia: paths, x is gdp, y is life, color by country, with arrow both, size 2.5 and pattern dotted.”
arrow takes a value rather than a true-or-false flag. "both" is an ordinary thing to ask for, and a flag would have needed a second setting to say it. The heads are drawn solid on a dotted path. The dash is the route’s texture, and a head cut into dashes no longer reads as an arrow.
This chapter covers the parameters of one transform, density: levels, bandwidth and adjust, in The parameters. Cluster covers those of cluster. Every other property of a path is either mapped to a column or set with style().
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the companion grid.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.11 What it refuses
You might want the route to thicken as income rises, so that the stroke itself carries a third measure. size reads one value from every row. A path joins all of its rows into a single stroke, and a stroke is drawn at one width from end to end. There is nowhere to put a second width:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + size(col.gdp)


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + size(:gdp)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), path, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), size(col.gdp))




Error:
! gog: `size` cannot be bound to `path` — a path takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `gdp` mapping and set it with `style(size = )`, or use a mark that maps `size`: `point`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Set it instead and every segment takes the same width, which is the Setting vs mapping distinction again.
A summary is the second refusal. A path draws the rows in their order, and a summary replaces those rows, as Two transforms, and the rest refused explained:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + path * mean + x(country) + y(life)


data(gapminder_asia) + path * mean + x(col.country) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_asia) + path * mean + x(:country) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), layer(path, mean), x(col.country), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `path` strokes the rows in the order the table gives them, and `mean` replaces those rows with one summary per key — after which the order is the keys' and the path is a `line`. Use `line * mean`, which sorts by `x` and is the mark a statistic is drawn on.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


density(bandwidth = ) is the third. It is a width in one column’s own units, and the two columns of a contour are usually in different units, so one number cannot be a width in both:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length)


(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length))


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(bandwidth = 0.5) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(path, density({ bandwidth: 0.5 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length))




Error:
! gog: `density(bandwidth = )` is a width in one column's own units, and `path * density` spreads over *two* columns measuring different quantities — one number cannot be a width in both. Use `density(adjust = )`, which scales the automatic bandwidth on each axis by the same dimensionless factor.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Three more refusals follow. In each one, line refuses something that path accepts, and two of them come from the sort. An arrowhead is the first of them. A line sorts its rows by x, so its last vertex is simply the largest x in the table. A head there would point at the result of the sort, not at the last measurement taken:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + style(arrow = "end")


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + style(arrow = "end")


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + style(arrow = "end")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  style({ arrow: "end" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(arrow = )` is a `path` setting, and a `line` cannot carry it — a line sorts its vertices by `x`, so its last point is wherever the domain ends rather than where the data stopped — a head there would point at the sort. Use `path`, which strokes the rows in the data's own order and so has an end the data chose.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Here x is the year, so the sort and the table order agree, and the head would land on 2007. gog refuses it anyway, because on a line the end of the stroke always comes from the sort.
density(levels = ) is the second. It cuts the estimated field into steps, and a one-dimensional density is a single curve with no field to cut:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + line * density(levels = 8) + x(sepal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + line * density(levels = 8) + x(col.sepal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + line * density(levels = 8) + x(:sepal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(line, density({ levels: 8 })),
  x(col.sepal_length))




Error:
! gog: `density(levels = )` cuts a field into levels, and a `line` estimates *one curve* — a curve has no levels to cut. Drop it for a density curve, or read the density over both axes: `path * density(levels = )` traces the contours, `zone * density(levels = )` fills the bands between them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


z is the third. A line sorts by x, and the cube has no left to right, so the sort has no meaning in the cube, as A path in the cube explained:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + line + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude)


data(thermals) + line + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude)


data(thermals) + line + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude)


plot(data(thermals), line, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude))




Error:
! gog: `line` reads a *domain* left to right — it sorts by `x` and draws one value for each — and a cube has no left to right: `x` is one of three equal positions, and at some viewing angles it runs into the page and becomes depth. A `line` in space would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see, so this is refused rather than drawn. For a route through three dimensions use `path`, which is `line` with that sort removed: `path + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(altitude)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Two of the three have one cause: a line’s shape comes from the sort, and a path’s comes from the rows. The third has another. A curve over one column has no field to cut into levels.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.12 In short
A path joins the rows in the order the table holds them, so sorting the table changes the picture. That order is the mark’s meaning. The arrowhead belongs to path and edge only, and the two transforms a path takes are density and cluster.

title: 17  Path
text:
17.13 What comes next
Every part of a path comes from the data. Rule draws a different kind of stroke, one that crosses the whole panel at a value you give it.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.1 A line at a threshold
Where is the line you want to compare every value against? Most marks read two positions. rule reads one, and draws a line there. Along the other axis, the line crosses the whole panel. That gives two familiar plots: a reference line at a threshold, and a rug of ticks showing where the observations sit.
Most plotting libraries draw these two plots with three marks: a vertical reference line, a horizontal one, and a rug. gog has one. A vertical and a horizontal reference line differ only in which axis holds the position. gog works that out from the columns, as it does for a bar.
How many countries have a life expectancy above 70? On a scatter the reader has to find 70 on the axis and judge each point against it. With a line at 70, each point is compared with the line instead of with the axis. “Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands.”
The sentence names rule once, and the plot draws three lines. That is the mark’s most useful property: its position is a column, not a number. life_bands holds three values, one per line. Add a fourth row and a fourth line appears with no change to the plot’s sentence at all.
Every channel works this way: color(band) names a column, not a color. That is why there is no rule(70). A number typed into the plot would be one value for the whole plot. A column is data, so it can hold a different threshold for each panel of a faceted plot, and it follows the scale and the space like every other column.
A rule takes no transform, so it cannot compute a reference for you. What it refuses shows that refusal. Which reference you need decides which mark you write:
For a line at the overall mean, compute the mean yourself and give it to rule as a column.

title: 18  Rule
text:
Mark
The reference it draws




rule
a line at each value in a column you supply


line * mean
the means joined into a profile


ribbon * bounds
a band between a low column and a high one


zone * bounds
a block across the panel, between the same two

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.2 Horizontal or vertical
Nothing in the read-aloud sentence under that plot said “horizontal”. The mark took the direction from the columns instead. life_bands has a life column and no gdp column, and the plot’s y is life. One axis answers and the other does not. The rule sits on the axis that answers, and spans the axis that does not.
A threshold on income needs a vertical line, and there is no second mark for it. Give the rule a table that holds gdp instead, and the same word draws the line vertically:



gdp_threshold: its one row


gdp




10000







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(gdp_threshold) + rule + style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(gdp_threshold) + rule + style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(gdp_threshold) +
  rule + style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same mark, the other axis")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(gdp_threshold), rule,
  style({ color: "firebrick", pattern: "dashed" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same mark, the other axis"))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  The same mark, the other axis Life expectancy GDP per person





gdp_threshold holds gdp, the plot’s x, so the line is vertical. gog draws both directions with one rule. ggplot2 needs two marks for them, geom_vline() and geom_hline(), and matplotlib needs axvline() and axhline().

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.3 A rug of ticks
A scatter shows where each country sits on two axes at once. A second question is only about how the countries spread along the income axis. A rug tick reads one position too. It sits at one value and extends a short distance into the panel from its edge. That is a threshold line, only shorter. One setting makes the line short, so a rug needs no second mark:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries sit on the income axis")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(col.gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries sit on the income axis"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + rule + x(:gdp) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the countries sit on the income axis")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), rule, x(col.gdp), style({ reach: "edge" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Where the countries sit on the income axis"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Where the countries sit on the income axis Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules, x is gdp, with reach edge.”
The rule names x(gdp) even though the points already named it. This layer has no table of its own, so it reads the scatter’s, which holds both gdp and life. Both axes answer, so the rule has to say which one it sits on. The life_bands table holds only life, which is why those rules named no position.
Look along the bottom. Each tick is one country, drawn at its own income. Below $5,000 the ticks merge into one solid block: 66 of the 142 countries sit in the first tenth of the income axis. The scatter holds the same countries but spreads them up the other axis, so the crowding is harder to see.
In general a rug puts the one-dimensional distribution of one column in the margin of a plot that already shows something else. You read the spread of gdp and still see the scatter, with no second plot whose axis you would have to match.
Everything else about the mark is unchanged. style(reach = ) takes one of two words: panel, the default, and edge. You do not give it a length. A tick’s length comes from the panel: a small share of it, held between 4 and 14 pixels so that it stays visible in a small facet. A number in place of edge would be a pixel count, and it would mean something different in every facet and at every plot size.

18.3.1 The other axis
The rug so far has been along the bottom, on income. Life expectancy has a distribution of its own, and the overlapping points hide it the same way. A rug is not only for the horizontal axis. The position you name on the layer decides which axis it sits on. Write y(life) instead of x(gdp) and the ticks run up the left edge. Write both, as two layers, and the scatter has a rug along the bottom and another up the left at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(gdp)  + style(reach = "edge") +
  rule + y(life) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both margins, from two layers")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.45) +
  rule + x(col.gdp)  + style(reach = "edge") +
  rule + y(col.life) + style(reach = "edge") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Both margins, from two layers"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.45) + rule + x(:gdp) + style(reach = "edge") + rule +
  y(:life) + style(reach = "edge") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Both margins, from two layers")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.45 }), rule, x(col.gdp), style({ reach: "edge" }),
  rule, y(col.life), style({ reach: "edge" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Both margins, from two layers"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Both margins, from two layers Life expectancy GDP per person





Each rug names one axis, and both read the scatter’s table. A single rule layer that names both is refused, because a rule draws one line per row, placed by one column. The message suggests the two layers above, as What it refuses shows.
The left edge shows a different distribution from the bottom edge. The ticks are dense above 70, thinnest between 60 and 70, and a little denser again from 60 down to 40. Of the 142 countries, 83 sit above 70 and 43 below 60, with only 16 between. This is a distribution with two groups and a thin stretch between them, not a single group. The bottom rug cannot show this, because its ticks are placed by income. In the scatter it is harder to see, because the same countries are spread over two axes.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.4 Coloring the lines
The three threshold lines in the first plot are all drawn alike, and nothing says what each one stands for. Give each line its own color instead, and the legend prints the band’s name beside that color. A rule draws one line per row of its table, so color gives each row its own color. life_bands has a band column naming each threshold, and that is the column to use:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(life_bands) + rule + color(col.band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + data(life_bands) + rule + color(:band) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per band, named in the legend")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "lightgray" }), data(life_bands), rule, color(col.band),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One line per band, named in the legend"))






                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  One line per band, named in the legend Life expectancy GDP per person  Band    Low  Middle  High 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands, colored by band.”
A line colored by a number changes shade along its length. A rule is one segment in one shade, and a single shade on a thin line is too hard to read a number from. So color on a rule takes categories, not a continuous ramp.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.5 Thickening a rule
A thin line marks a threshold, but it is not the first thing a reader sees. Sometimes the thresholds are the reason the plot exists. Then the reader should find those lines first, before reading the data around them. style(size = ) sets a rule’s width, and a wide, faint rule reads as a highlighted band:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.55) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.20) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.55) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.20) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.55) + data(life_bands) + rule +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 26, opacity = 0.2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.55 }), data(life_bands), rule,
  style({ color: "seagreen", size: 26, opacity: 0.2 }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels"))






                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  A thick rule: emphasis, measured in pixels Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands, colored seagreen, with size 26 and opacity 0.20.”
That is a good way to mark a value. The width is measured in pixels, not in data. Each wide rule in that plot covers a little over two years of life expectancy, only because this axis runs from 40 to 80. Facet the plot, resize it, or change the range of the data, and the same size = 26 covers a different number of years while looking identical. Nothing is wrong with that as long as the width is decoration. It is wrong as soon as the width is supposed to mean something.

18.5.1 Thickness as data
Sometimes the thickness is itself a measurement: “the healthy range is 65 to 75”, not “look here”. Then the two edges are data, and you need a mark whose edges are positions. That mark is ribbon. You give it a low column and a high column. healthy_band has two rows, one at the lowest income and one at the highest. The band therefore runs from the poorest country to the richest:



healthy_band: all 2 rows


gdp
lo
hi




277.5519
65
75


49357.1902
65
75







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(healthy_band) + ribbon * bounds(lo, hi) + style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
  data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A band whose edges are 65 and 75, and rules on top")


(data(healthy_band) + ribbon * bounds(col.lo, col.hi) + style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) +
  data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A band whose edges are 65 and 75, and rules on top"))


data(healthy_band) + ribbon * bounds(:lo, :hi) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.18) + data(gapminder_2007) +
  point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(life_bands) + rule +
  style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A band whose edges are 65 and 75, and rules on top")


plot(data(healthy_band), layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lo, col.hi)),
  style({ color: "seagreen", opacity: 0.18 }), data(gapminder_2007),
  point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), data(life_bands), rule,
  style({ color: "seagreen", pattern: "dashed" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("A band whose edges are 65 and 75, and rules on top"))






                                                                                                                                                                                          0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  A band whose edges are 65 and 75, and rules on top Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given the healthy band table: a ribbon from lo to hi; then given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also rules from the life bands.”
Now 65 and 75 are positions. They rescale with the axis and keep the same values in every facet. On a log axis they are still drawn at 65 and 75, not a fixed number of pixels apart. The band is written first, and layers are drawn in the order they are written, so the points are drawn over it.
Give that same table two different gdp values instead of the data’s range, and the band becomes a box bounded on both axes. That is how you shade a corner of a scatter, or one period of a time series.
Neither the band nor the box extends to the edge of the panel. A ribbon is bounded by its data, so it stops exactly at the numbers you gave it. Give it wider values and the scale grows to fit them, so a ribbon never touches the edge. For a rectangle whose sides come from the data on one axis and from the panel on the other, use zone. A zone takes a pair of values on one axis and spans the other, as a rule takes one value and spans the other.

title: 18  Rule
section: 18.6 In polar: the ring and the spoke
text:
18.6 In polar: the ring and the spoke
Wind comes from a compass direction, so its speed can be drawn on a circle, as a radar chart. A target speed on that chart is a threshold like any other. In polar one of the two axes is bent into a circle. The question is what shape the line takes then. The mark does one thing: it draws a line at one position and spans the whole of the other axis. In polar that is unchanged. A polar plot has two axes, the angle and the radius. A rule that spans the angle is a ring, and one that spans the radius is a spoke: a straight line from the center to the rim, the outer edge of the circle. The Polar chapter explains how the circle itself is built.
winds is the table that The book’s data introduced. speed_target holds one target speed:

The angular axis runs all the way around the circle, and one full circle of it is called the turn. A rule that spans the whole turn closes into a ring. Here it marks a target speed on the radar chart of mean wind speed by direction, and speed is on the radial axis, the one that runs from the center outward:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed) + polar() +
  data(speed_target) + rule + style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring")


(data(winds) + line * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.speed) + polar() +
  data(speed_target) + rule + style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring"))


data(winds) + line * mean + x(:direction) + y(:speed) + polar() +
  data(speed_target) + rule +
  style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring")


plot(data(winds), layer(line, mean), x(col.direction), y(col.speed),
  polar(), data(speed_target), rule,
  style({ color: "firebrick", pattern: "dashed" }),
  title("A target speed, drawn as a ring"))






                        N NE E SE S SW W NW   10 15 20  A target speed, drawn as a ring Speed Direction





“Given the winds: a line derived by mean, x is direction, y is speed, in polar, and also rules from the speed target.”
A rule that spans the whole radius draws a spoke. Give the rule a table holding direction instead of speed, and the line sits at that compass point:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + line * mean + x(direction) + y(speed) + polar() +
  data(data.frame(direction = "E")) + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("One compass point, center to rim")


(data(winds) + line * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.speed) + polar() +
  data({"direction": ["E"]}, name='data.frame(direction = "E")') + rule +
    style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("One compass point, center to rim"))


data(winds) + line * mean + x(:direction) + y(:speed) + polar() +
  data((direction = ["E"],)) + rule +
  style(color = "firebrick", pattern = "dashed") +
  title("One compass point, center to rim")


plot(data(winds), layer(line, mean), x(col.direction), y(col.speed),
  polar(), data({ direction: ["E"] }), rule,
  style({ color: "firebrick", pattern: "dashed" }),
  title("One compass point, center to rim"))






                        N NE E SE S SW W NW   10 15 20  One compass point, center to rim Speed Direction





“Given the winds: a line derived by mean, x is direction, y is speed, in polar; then given one row with direction E: a rule.”
Neither shape is a special case in the sentence you write. rule is still one mark in polar because nothing about it changed. It is written the same way, it takes its axis from its column, and it means the same thing in every space. A rule that needed a special case in polar would not be one mark. It would be three: a flat line, a ring, and a spoke.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.7 What you can set
A threshold line has to look different from the data it crosses, and no column in the data says how it should look. You say it with a setting, and each mark accepts its own list. These are a rule’s settings, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash, longdash


style(reach = )
panel, edge



Four of those are a stroke’s ordinary controls, and one is the mark’s own. style(reach = ) sets how far the rule reaches across the panel. The value edge shortens it to a tick. The other four behave here as on line or path:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data(data.frame(life = 50.0)) + rule + style(color = "firebrick", size = 4) +
  data(data.frame(life = 60.0)) + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  data(data.frame(life = 70.0)) + rule +
    style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "dotted", size = 2.5) +
  data(data.frame(life = 80.0)) + rule +
    style(color = "black", size = 6, opacity = 0.25) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Bottom to top: thick, dashed, dotted, faded")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  data({"life": [50.0]}, name='data.frame(life = 50.0)') + rule + style(color = "firebrick", size = 4) +
  data({"life": [60.0]}, name='data.frame(life = 60.0)') + rule + style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  data({"life": [70.0]}, name='data.frame(life = 70.0)') + rule +
    style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "dotted", size = 2.5) +
  data({"life": [80.0]}, name='data.frame(life = 80.0)') + rule +
    style(color = "black", size = 6, opacity = 0.25) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Bottom to top: thick, dashed, dotted, faded"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + data((life = [50],)) + rule +
  style(color = "firebrick", size = 4) + data((life = [60],)) + rule +
  style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") + data((life = [70],)) +
  rule + style(color = "steelblue", pattern = "dotted", size = 2.5) +
  data((life = [80],)) + rule +
  style(color = "black", size = 6, opacity = 0.25) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Bottom to top: thick, dashed, dotted, faded")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "lightgray" }), data({ life: [50] }), rule,
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 4 }), data({ life: [60] }), rule,
  style({ color: "seagreen", pattern: "dashed" }), data({ life: [70] }),
  rule, style({ color: "steelblue", pattern: "dotted", size: 2.5 }),
  data({ life: [80] }), rule,
  style({ color: "black", size: 6, opacity: 0.25 }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Bottom to top: thick, dashed, dotted, faded"))






                                                                                                                                                                                              0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Bottom to top: thick, dashed, dotted, faded Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored lightgray; then given one row with life 50: a rule colored firebrick, with size 4; then given one row with life 60: a rule colored seagreen, with pattern dashed; then given one row with life 70: a rule colored steelblue, with pattern dotted and size 2.5; then given one row with life 80: a rule colored black, with size 6 and opacity 0.25.”
The pattern values are the five dashes, solid among them, because a rule is a stroke. style(pattern = "hatch") is refused, and the message lists the dashes instead. A hatch is a fill’s texture. bar, area, box and ribbon take it, and so does zone, the next chapter. The setting has one name, and each mark draws it the way its shape allows. A stroke takes a dash, and a fill takes a hatch.
What a rule refuses follows from the same geometry. There is no shape, because a stroke has no glyph to choose, and there is no border. What it refuses shows the border refused.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. The companion grid has a row per mark, listing what it maps rather than sets.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.8 What it refuses
The first sentence you are likely to try is a bare rule on the plot’s own table. That table holds both position columns, so both axes answer. Nothing in the sentence says which axis is meant, so gog refuses rather than choosing one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + rule


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + rule


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + rule


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), rule)




Error:
! gog: `rule` marks a value on one axis and spans the other, but this table has a column for both — `x(gdp)` and `y(life)` — so there is nothing to say which axis is meant. Say it on the layer: `rule + x(gdp)` places every line by `gdp`, `rule + y(life)` by `life`. Giving the rule its own table holding just the one column works too.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


That refusal is why every rug in this chapter names its axis, rule + x(gdp) or rule + y(life). A threshold with a table of its own needs no position. That table holds only one of the two columns, so the axis is taken from it. A bar also takes its direction from its columns, and gog refuses a bar with categories on both axes. The rule had a column for both axes. The bar has the reverse problem: neither axis holds a number, so the bar has nothing to measure, and gog will not guess.
The opposite, one layer that names both positions, is refused too. A rule draws one line per row, placed by one column, so only one of the two columns could be drawn:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  rule + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(reach = "edge")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  rule + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(reach = "edge"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + rule + x(:gdp) +
  y(:life) + style(reach = "edge")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), rule,
  x(col.gdp), y(col.life), style({ reach: "edge" }))




Error:
! gog: `rule` draws one line per row, placed by one column, and this layer names two — `x(gdp)` and `y(life)` — so only one of them could be drawn. For lines on both axes, write two layers, one per axis: `rule + x(gdp) + rule + y(life)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message suggests two layers, one per axis, as in the plot under The other axis.
A rule takes no transform either. It is placed by one column and spans the whole panel on the other axis. A statistic such as mean summarizes one axis for each value of the other, and a rule reads only one position:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule * mean


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule * mean)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(life_bands) +
  rule * mean


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(life_bands), layer(rule, mean))




Error:
! gog: `rule` is placed by one column and spans the other axis, so it has no measure for `mean` to compute and nowhere to put the answer. Compute the value where your data lives and give the rule a table of the results — one row per line — which is what a rule's position always is: a column.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message restates what a rule is. To draw a line at the mean, compute the mean yourself and supply it as a column. A rule’s position always comes from a column.
A rule has no border either. A border is the outline of a filled shape, and a rule is a line with no inside to outline:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(border_color = "black")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(life_bands) + rule + style(border_color = "black"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(life_bands) +
  rule + style(border_color = "black")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(life_bands), rule, style({ border_color: "black" }))




Error:
! gog: a `rule` is drawn with a stroke, not a filled shape — it has no separate border. `style(color = )` sets its color and `style(size = )` its width.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


So style(color = ) is a rule’s color and style(size = ) its width. That is the same answer line, step and path give, because it is the same geometry.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.9 In short
A rule’s position is a column and never a number, so three thresholds are three rows. With its column on x the line is vertical, and on y horizontal. style(reach = "edge") makes it a rug tick, and in polar it is a ring or a spoke. A rule on the plot’s own table must name exactly one axis, or gog refuses it. It takes no transform: compute the value yourself and give the rule that column.

title: 18  Rule
text:
18.10 What comes next
A rule marks one value. Its width is measured in pixels rather than in data. Zone is the region between two values, a rectangle across the panel rather than a line.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.1 A band across the panel
Which region of the plot should the values stay inside? zone shades a rectangle. It is rule’s sibling: a rule is a line and a zone is an area, and both work the same way. A rule takes one position and spans the axis it was not given. A zone takes a pair and spans the axis it was given no pair for. Give it pairs on both axes and it is a rectangle you placed.
Spanning the axis you gave no pair for is what first sets this mark apart. No other mark draws a rectangle that reaches the edge of the panel.
Were sales inside the target each year? You could print the two target numbers in the caption. A reader would then have to check one year at a time. A band shaded behind the line shows every year together. The quarterly table holds one sales figure for each year, and target_band holds the two edges of a target band:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A target band, 150 to 175")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A target band, 150 to 175"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point + y_label("Sales") +
  title("A target band, 150 to 175")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)), style({ color: "seagreen" }),
  data(quarterly), line, point, y_label("Sales"),
  title("A target band, 150 to 175"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper, and also a line and points.”
bounds(lower, upper) names the two columns holding the bottom and top. Nothing names a left or a right, so the zone takes those from the panel and runs edge to edge. The zone is written before the line so the data draws on top of it; a highlight belongs behind what it highlights.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.2 A band up the panel
Some highlights are periods of time rather than ranges of value. The years of a recession are one such period, when the question is how sales changed during them. Name the other pair, start and end, and the rectangle runs up the panel instead of across it. The recessions table holds the two slumps, each with a start year and an end year:



recessions: all 2 rows


start
end

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "indianred") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Two slumps, from one table")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(color = "indianred") +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Two slumps, from one table"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(recessions) +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "indianred") + data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Two slumps, from one table")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(recessions),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "indianred" }), data(quarterly), line, point,
  y_label("Sales"), title("Two slumps, from one table"))






                                                          2005 2010 2015 2020   100 120 140 160 180  Two slumps, from one table Sales Year





“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end, and also a line and points.”
Two shaded periods, and only one zone in the sentence. One row is one rectangle, so a two-row table draws two bands, the same property that lets one rule table draw three thresholds. Add a row and a third band appears with no change to the sentence.
Look at where the red reaches: the top and bottom of the panel exactly. That is the thing a ribbon cannot do. A ribbon is bounded by its data, so it stops at whatever numbers you give it. Any number big enough to reach the top would widen the axis to include it, so the highlight would change the plot it was meant to mark.
The pair is called start/end rather than left/right on purpose. Left and right are facts about a screen. This grammar takes orientation from the bindings, so the same words still apply when the domain is drawn as an angle, in polar coordinates.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.3 Both pairs: a rectangle
Sometimes the region to highlight is bounded on both axes: these five years, this range of sales, and nothing outside either. That is a box rather than a band. Name all four and neither axis comes from the panel:
