data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(lower, upper, start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A box over five years of sales")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper, start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A box over five years of sales"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(sales_box) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper, start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) + data(quarterly) + line +
  point + y_label("Sales") + title("A box over five years of sales")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(sales_box),
  layer(zone,
  bounds(col.lower, col.upper, { start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "goldenrod", opacity: 0.3 }), data(quarterly), line,
  point, y_label("Sales"), title("A box over five years of sales"))






                                                         2005 2010 2015 2020   100 120 140 160 180  A box over five years of sales Sales Year





“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a sales box zone from lower to upper and from start to end, and also a line and points.”
So one atom covers the three shapes a highlight needs: a band across the panel, a band up it, and a box. The pairs you name decide which one you get, so there is no separate atom for each.

title: 19  Zone
section: 19.4 Which axis the pair bounds: the funnel
text:
19.4 Which axis the pair bounds: the funnel
A funnel counts how many people are left at each stage, from website visits down to invoices sent. Its usual picture is a stack of centered blocks, one per stage, measured across the page rather than up it. Drawing it means moving the measurement to x, and a category on y is what moves it.
lower and upper bound the measure axis, the axis that carries the measured numbers. Every plot to this point has measured along y, so every lower/upper band has run across the panel. Now put a category on y instead. The measure moves to x, and the same two columns bound it there:

stage <- c("Website visit", "Downloads", "Potential customers",
           "Requested price", "Invoice sent")
n     <- c(39, 27.4, 20.6, 11, 2)
funnel <- data.frame(stage = factor(stage, levels = stage),
                     n = n, lo = -n / 2, hi = n / 2, mid = 0)



RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(funnel) + zone * bounds(lo, hi) + y(stage) + style(opacity = 1) +
  text + label(n) + x(mid) +
  x_label("") + y_label("Stage") + title("A funnel, and no funnel atom")


(data(funnel) + zone * bounds(col.lo, col.hi) + y(col.stage) + style(opacity = 1) +
  text + label(col.n) + x(col.mid) +
  x_label("") + y_label("Stage") + title("A funnel, and no funnel atom"))


data(funnel) + zone * bounds(:lo, :hi) + y(:stage) + style(opacity = 1) +
  text + label(:n) + x(:mid) + x_label("") + y_label("Stage") +
  title("A funnel, and no funnel atom")


plot(data(funnel), layer(zone, bounds(col.lo, col.hi)), y(col.stage),
  style({ opacity: 1 }), text, label(col.n), x(col.mid), x_label(""),
  y_label("Stage"), title("A funnel, and no funnel atom"))






                       39 27.4 20.6 11 2                   -20 -10 0 10 20   Invoice sent Requested price Potential customers Downloads Website visit  A funnel, and no funnel atom Stage





“Given the funnel: zones from lo to hi, y is stage, and also text, x is mid, label by n.”
That is a funnel chart. No atom in the sentence is a funnel.
Each block is a zone. The table gives one row per block. The columns lo and hi hold -n/2 and n/2, computed in R before the plot. The numbers inside the blocks are a second layer, drawn by text. The waterfall later in this chapter computes its running total the same way.
A funnel is a bar chart whose blocks are centered on zero. A bar grows from a baseline and refuses bounds, so the centered blocks are zones with both ends named.
The plot works because lower and upper name the measure axis and not the bottom and the top of a screen. gog never asks which way the screen runs; it asks what each axis carries. Here y carries a category, so y holds slots, and the measurement can only go on x. This is the rule bar already follows: one categorical position, one measured position, and their types decide the orientation. It is why there is nothing like ggplot2’s coord_flip() to write.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.5 Coloring the zones
The two recession bands in the sales plot are both the same red, which leaves them unnamed. Color each by its name and the legend says which is which, with no note on the plot. Each row is its own rectangle, so color maps per row. recessions carries a name for each slump:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) + color(slump) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Named, and keyed by the legend")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) + color(col.slump) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Named, and keyed by the legend"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(recessions) +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) + color(:slump) +
  data(quarterly) + line + point + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Named, and keyed by the legend")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(recessions),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  color(col.slump), data(quarterly), line, point, y_label("Sales"),
  title("Named, and keyed by the legend"))






                                                          2005 2010 2015 2020   100 120 140 160 180  Named, and keyed by the legend Sales Year  Slump    Financial crisis  Pandemic 





“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end colored by slump, and also a line and points.”
A zone’s color also takes a number, drawn from a continuous ramp of colors, while bar, area and ribbon accept only categories. A rectangle is large enough for the eye to compare its shade with the legend. That is what a heatmap needs, so a heatmap cell is this mark rather than a new one. Cells cut from the data draws that plot, after the sections on rectangles you place yourself.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.6 Rectangles that are the data
The funnel’s blocks were the data, but every other zone so far has been a highlight: a rectangle behind a line, saying where to look. Nothing requires it to sit behind anything. Give a zone a pair on the measure axis and a categorical position. Each category’s rectangle then runs from one number to another, with no plot underneath. Two common finance charts are made of exactly that.

19.6.1 The waterfall
A waterfall is a running total, broken into the steps that made it. gog has no transform for that and the omission is deliberate: stack accumulates within a position, one pile per slot, and a waterfall accumulates across positions. So the running total is arithmetic, and arithmetic belongs with the data, in the host language. The cashflow table holds one row per step of a cash statement: a delta for the step, and a total flag marking the subtotals:



cashflow: first 5 of 6 rows


step
delta
total




Opening
120
TRUE


Sales

FALSE


Refunds

FALSE


Costs
-32

-14

w <- cashflow
w$top  <- cumsum(w$delta)          # where each step ends
w$base <- c(0, head(w$top, -1))    # and where it started: the step before
w$base[w$total] <- 0               # except the subtotals, which start at zero
w$dir  <- ifelse(w$total, "total", ifelse(w$delta >= 0, "gain", "loss"))

slot <- seq_len(nrow(w)) - 1       # category k sits at k, counting from 0
w$left  <- slot - 0.35             # so a side named at k ± 0.35 is inside its slot
w$right <- slot + 0.35

That chunk is R; the other three bindings compute the same columns in their own language. The sentence has four spellings like every other:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(w) + zone * bounds(base, top, start = left, end = right) +
  x(step) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
  palette(c("steelblue", "seagreen", "indianred")) +
  y_label("Cash (thousands)") + title("Where the money went")


(data(w) + zone * bounds(col.base, col.top, start=col.left, end=col.right) +
  x(col.step) + color(col.dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
  palette(["steelblue", "seagreen", "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Cash (thousands)") + title("Where the money went"))


data(w) + zone * bounds(:base, :top, start = :left, var"end" = :right) +
  x(:step) + color(:dir) + style(opacity = 1) +
  palette(["steelblue", "seagreen", "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Cash (thousands)") + title("Where the money went")


plot(data(w),
  layer(zone,
  bounds(col.base, col.top, { start: col.left, end: col.right })),
  x(col.step), color(col.dir), style({ opacity: 1 }),
  palette(["steelblue", "seagreen", "indianred"]),
  y_label("Cash (thousands)"), title("Where the money went"))






                                        Opening Sales Refunds Costs Tax Closing   0 50 100 150  Where the money went Cash (thousands) Step  Dir    total  gain  loss 





“Given the w table: zones from base to top and from left to right, x is step, color by dir, with opacity 1.”
A few lines of host arithmetic and one sentence. The blocks that start at zero are not a special case. They are rows whose base is 0, a number the table supplies like every other.
Two parts of that sentence need explaining, because both override one of this mark’s defaults on purpose.
style(opacity = 1) is there because a zone whose sides you named is drawn translucent, at 20%. A rectangle someone chose is nearly always a highlight, with something drawn over it. Here nothing is drawn over it: the rectangle is the measurement. A cut zone (a heatmap cell) is already opaque for the same reason, and this is how you say the named one is data too.
The left/right pair makes the gap between the blocks. Without start and end, a zone fills its slot whole, while a bar takes four fifths of it and leaves one fifth empty, which is what separates the categories. A zone’s width normally means something: it is the region the category owns. A waterfall block’s width means nothing, so it should leave a gap the way bar does, and naming the sides is how to ask for one. The arithmetic works because a categorical axis puts its categories at 0, 1, 2 and so on. Category k owns the slot from k−½ to k+½, and k ± 0.35 sits inside it. Drop those two columns and the rectangles touch, which reads as one connected shape rather than six steps.


19.6.2 The candlestick
A candlestick shows how a price moved in each trading session. Each session has four numbers: the price at the start (open) and the end (close), and the highest (high) and lowest (low) prices in between. gog needs no new channels for them, because a rectangle’s sides read the pair a ribbon and an interval already read. Low to high is a whisker; open to close is a rectangle; that is two layers over one table:

s$body_hi <- pmax(s$open, s$close)

  interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) +

  zone * bounds(:body_lo, :body_hi, start = :left, var"end" = :right) +
  color(:dir) + style(opacity = 1) + palette(["seagreen", "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions")


plot(data(s), x(col.session), layer(interval, bounds(col.low, col.high)),
  color(col.dir),
  layer(zone,
  bounds(col.body_lo, col.body_hi, { start: col.left, end: col.right })),
  color(col.dir), style({ opacity: 1 }),
  palette(["seagreen", "indianred"]), y_label("Price"),

“Given the s table: x is session, intervals from low to high colored by dir, and also zones from body lo to body hi and from left to right colored by dir.”
color(dir) is said twice, once per layer, and both are needed because of scope. A channel written after a mark belongs to that mark, so the whisker takes its session’s color along with the body. Both uses of the column share one legend, because it is one column.
There is no candlestick atom, and the grammar does not need one. The chart is made of things that already exist, which is the claim the whole grammar makes. Chart names lists it beside the pie and the rose, which are also sentences rather than words. Each candlestick row carries four numbers: two for the whisker and two for the body. ribbon and interval already read a low and a high, and a rectangle’s bottom and top are the same pair. That is why neither finance chart needs a new channel.

  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Where the country-years actually are")

  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Where the country-years actually are"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  Where the country-years actually are Life expectancy GDP per person  Count         40 20.5 1 





“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”
bin is not the zone’s own transform. What the mark changes is how many axes the cut runs along:







Mark derived by bin
Shape




bar * bin
one axis cut, drawn as the bars of a histogram


zone * bin
two axes cut, drawn as the cells above


surface * bin
the same two axes, with the count raised into the cube



Read the dark cells that rise from lower left to upper right: wealth and life expectancy rise together. The darkest cell says how many country-years sit at that combination, which overlapping dots cannot show.
Three things in that sentence need explaining.
bin cut both axes, and nothing asked it to. It is the same transform that makes a histogram, and how many axes it cuts is taken from the mark rather than requested. A bar leaves one axis free to measure a height along, so bar * bin cuts the other one. A zone’s cell needs an extent on both axes before it can be a rectangle at all, so zone * bin cuts every axis that has a width to cut, which here is both of them. One transform, one word, readings decided by what the mark needs. There is no bin2d. Note the words has a width to cut: the mixed mesh is where they matter, because a categorical axis arrives already cut, and bin does not cut it.
The count became the color, although no color() was written. Both positions were taken, so the measurement went to the one channel left that can carry a number, and the legend is titled Count. This is what bar * bin already does for the y axis: a transform that invents a column also says where it goes.
The column it invents is called count, and you may name it out loud. That is not a different plot. It is the same sentence with nothing left implied:

short <- data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life)
long  <- data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
           color(count)

identical(render_svg(short), render_svg(long))

[1] FALSE


render_svg() returns the drawn picture as text, so comparing the two texts shows that the pictures are the same.
Writing it has one use: a binding is where a scale goes, and the short form has nowhere to put one. Counts are strongly skewed here: the fullest cell holds forty country-years while half of them hold four or fewer. On a linear ramp nearly every cell is the same pale blue. Name the channel and you can say scale = "log" on it, the same way you already did on x:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(count, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.count, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp"))


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:count, scale = "log") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.count, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  The same cells, counted on a log ramp Life expectancy GDP per person  Count         40 6.32 1 





“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by count on a log scale.”
Now the cells with few rows get distinct shades, and the dark diagonal shows a gradient rather than one flat patch of color. The legend’s middle label is 6.32, not 20.5: on a log ramp the middle color stands for the geometric mean of the two ends.
The white gaps are cells where no country-year fell. They are left as panel, not painted the pale end of the ramp, because that end stands for a count of one. The uneven edge you get instead is the region the data actually covers, which is information rather than a gap the renderer failed to fill.
bin(24) sets the mesh, the grid of cells the cut makes, exactly as it does on a histogram, and one number cuts both axes into that many bins. A coarser mesh shows less detail, and claims less precision:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side"))


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(8)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same data, eight bins a side"))






                                                                      1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  The same data, eight bins a side Life expectancy GDP per person  Count         212 106.5 1 





Notice that the log scale still applies. The cells are cut in log space, so they are even on the page rather than even in dollars. That is what you want when the variable ranges from a few hundred dollars to a hundred thousand.
These cells are also drawn solid rather than translucent, for the reason the waterfall gave: here the zone is the data, with nothing behind it to show through.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.8 Hexagons: the other mesh
Does the grid pattern in a heatmap come from the data or from the mesh? The cells above are rectangles, and that is a choice rather than a fact about binning. Say tiling = "hex" and the plane is cut a different way:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same country-years, hexagonal cells")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  palette("viridis") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same country-years, hexagonal cells"))


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + palette("viridis") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same country-years, hexagonal cells")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20, { tiling: "hex" })),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), palette("viridis"),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same country-years, hexagonal cells"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  The same country-years, hexagonal cells Life expectancy GDP per person  Count            43 22 1 





“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 on hexagons, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette.”
Two things changed there, and only one of them is the mesh. palette("viridis") replaces the default sequential ramp, and it is the right choice for a count. Viridis is built so equal steps in the number are equal steps in perceived brightness. On a plot whose entire message is how many, that is the difference between reading the diagonal and guessing. The palette is a free choice on either mesh, though, so do not read it as something hexagons require.
The hexagonal mesh is chosen for a reason, not for its looks: the rectangular mesh has a defect. A square grid lines up its cell centers in rows and columns, and the eye is very good at seeing rows and columns: it reads that alignment as if it were structure in the data. Wilkinson states it directly: rectangular bins “lead the eye to align bin centers and to see regularity where there is none” (Wilkinson, 2005). That is why Carr and colleagues devised hexagon binning in 1987 (Carr et al., 1987). A hexagonal mesh staggers alternate rows, so there is no aligned lattice left to mistake for a finding.
To see that on its own, keep the palette the same and change only the mesh:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Rectangular cells, same palette")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  palette("viridis") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Rectangular cells, same palette"))


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  palette("viridis") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Rectangular cells, same palette")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), palette("viridis"), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Rectangular cells, same palette"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                         1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  Rectangular cells, same palette Life expectancy GDP per person  Count            45 23 1 





Look along the sparse edges of the two plots. The rectangular cells line up in straight rows and columns, so the edge of the data is made of horizontal and vertical pieces. The hexagons do not line up, so the edge follows the data rather than the mesh.

19.8.1 Why the mesh belongs to bin
In the rest of this book, a transform computes and the mark decides how the result is drawn. bar * bin, line * bin and step * bin are one histogram drawn three ways. So it would be reasonable to expect the hexagon to be a mark, or a setting on one. It is neither, and the reason is in the numbers themselves.
Those three marks all receive the same numbers. A hexagonal mesh staggers alternate rows of cells, which changes which cell each observation falls in, so the counts themselves differ. You cannot draw a hexagonal plot from data binned into rectangles, whatever the mark does with it. The mesh is decided before anything is drawn, so it belongs to the transform that does the cutting.
That is also how Wilkinson organizes it. His bin is not one method but a family of ways to partition a plane, with rect and hex among the members. The mesh both shapes the cells and tags each row with the cell it fell in. One operation, both effects.
One consequence follows for the other marks: a tiling means nothing to a bin that cuts one axis, because there the cells are intervals and an interval has no shape. So bar * bin(tiling = "hex") is refused, as What it refuses shows.


19.8.2 Hexagons and the shape of the panel
The hexagonal cells are not quite regular, meaning their six sides are not all the same length. They are regular in the space the mesh is cut in, because that cut gives both axes the same number of steps. The panel then stretches that space by whatever its own proportions are, so on a wide panel the cells are drawn slightly wide. Look closely at the hexagonal cells and you can see it.
This is what the original hexbin package exposes as its shape argument. A panel kept at equal proportions removes it. theme(ratio = 1) asks for that panel, and the hexagons are then regular.

Both meshes so far have counted the rows that fell in each cell. A count is exact, and when the table is small it is also ragged: the 150 flowers spread over a mesh would leave most cells holding one or two, or none.
bin counts what landed in each cell. There is a second thing worth measuring at a cell, and it needs no new mark either: how dense the cloud of points is there. That is density, the transform that gives a line its smooth curve. A zone reads it across both axes, for the reason it reads bin across both, and so paints the field that path traces as contours.

Most of what the heatmap showed is true here too. Both axes were cut without being asked, the measurement went to color, and color(density) names it out loud and draws the identical plot. zone * bin and zone * density are one plot measured two ways, counted and estimated.
The white gaps are the one difference between the two plots. This plot has none. A count of zero says no row fell in that cell, so bin leaves it unpainted. An estimate exists at every point of the plane, so the estimator returns a value for every cell and the mesh is painted edge to edge. What it paints is a real density rather than an arbitrary color value. The cell values times the cell areas sum to one, the same property that makes the curve’s y a density.
palette() chooses the ramp, exactly as it does for a binned heatmap, and the argument for viridis on a count is the argument for it here:

  title("Filled density, viridis")

  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density, viridis"))


data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") + title("Filled density, viridis")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density), x(col.sepal_length),
  y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),

Look at the dark area away from the two clusters: it is even, and the cells meet with no gaps. gog draws each cell’s edges on whole screen pixels. Smoothed edges would leave thin lines of panel between the cells, and on a dark ramp they would look like a grid laid over the data.
One parameter a painted field takes is adjust, the multiplier on the bandwidth the estimator computed from the data. It is a multiplier rather than a width in either column’s units, which is why it is the one parameter that means the same thing on both axes:

  title("The same cloud, smoothed harder"))

The same field traced rather than painted is path * density, the contour. The difference between them is the one between bar * bin and line * bin: the mark chooses the shape, and the transform stays the same.

section: 19.10 Bands the data cut: zone * density(levels = )

19.10 Bands the data cut: zone * density(levels = )
A smooth ramp is hard to read a value from: two nearby cells differ by a shade the eye cannot name. Cut the field into a few steps and each band has a level a reader can point to. Ask for levels and the field stops being continuous. It is cut into that many steps, and a zone fills between them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density bands")


(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density bands"))


data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") + title("Filled density bands")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density({ levels: 8 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("Filled density bands"))






                                        4 5 6 7 8   0 2 4 6  Filled density bands Petal Length Sepal Length  Level            0.146 0.082 0.0182 





“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density at 8 levels, x is sepal length, y is petal length.”
That is the filled contour, and levels is the same parameter path takes. levels means one thing, cut the field into this many steps, and each mark then draws that cut its own way: a path traces the boundaries, a zone fills between them. So the two are not two features but one transform read by two marks, and a band’s edge falls exactly on the contour line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced")


(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced"))


data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(path, density({ levels: 8 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("The same eight levels, traced"))






                                              4 5 6 7 8   0 2 4 6  The same eight levels, traced Petal Length Sepal Length  Level            0.146 0.082 0.0182 





“Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density at 8 levels, x is sepal length, y is petal length.”
That makes three readings of one transform: line * density is a curve, zone * density a painted field, and path * density a contour.
The bands lie one inside another. A denser region usually lies inside a less dense one, so gog paints the outermost band first and each inner band over it. A band can also have a hole. When points lie around a circle, the density in the middle is low, so each band has a hole there. gog cuts the hole out of the band, and the middle stays unpainted.

title: 19  Zone
section: 19.11 Cells the axes already made: the tile plot
text:
19.11 Cells the axes already made: the tile plot
So far the sides have been made in three ways: bounds named them, bin cut them, and density estimated them. The funnel already used a fourth way without naming it: a category’s slot, which needs no column at all.
Six weeks of daily orders is already a grid: weeks across, weekdays down, one count in each cell. The grid itself is the picture you want, and two categorical axes already divide the panel into its cells.
A categorical axis is already divided. Six weeks on the x axis is six slots. “Week 3” owns one of those slots, a place on the panel with a left edge and a right edge, and the axis fixes both when it lays out the categories. So a category bounds its own axis, and two categorical positions bound a zone completely, with no transform in the sentence:

data(six_weeks) + zone + x(week) + y(weekday) + color(orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time")


(data(six_weeks) + zone + x(col.week) + y(col.weekday) + color(col.orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time"))


data(six_weeks) + zone + x(:week) + y(:weekday) + color(:orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time")


plot(data(six_weeks), zone, x(col.week), y(col.weekday),
  color(col.orders), title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time"))






                                                                                  Week 1 Week 2 Week 3 Week 4 Week 5 Week 6   Sun Sat Fri Thu Wed Tue Mon  Six weeks of orders, a day at a time Weekday Week  Orders         34 23.5 13 





“Given the six weeks table: zones, x is week, y is weekday, color by orders.”
That is a tile plot, here in the form called a calendar heatmap, and the whole of it is zone + x + y + color. What makes it worth drawing is that 42 daily counts carry two patterns at once. A list of numbers shows neither, while a grid separates them by direction. Read down a column for the week (week four is the pale one, the lowest week) and across a row for the weekday, where the Thursday row is the darkest overall and the Friday row the palest. The extremes are the cells where the two patterns agree: the darkest cell is Thursday of week six, and the palest are the Friday and Saturday of week four.
The rule underneath is short: a category owns a slot, a number is a point. A point has no width, so two continuous positions leave a zone with nothing to bound it until bin is written into the sentence. Nothing else changed, and nothing was added to the kernel: no mark, no transform, no channel.

19.11.1 bin cuts, count tallies
The calendar table has one row per cell already. Often a table does not: you hold the raw observations and want to know how many fell in each cell. The transform that tallies them is count, exactly as it is for a bar chart:

data(winds) + zone * count + x(direction) + y(season) +
  title("Wind observations by direction and season")


(data(winds) + zone * count + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) +
  title("Wind observations by direction and season"))

“Given the winds: zones derived by count, x is direction, y is season.”
That is the shape of a confusion matrix, the table that counts predicted classes against actual ones. A confusion matrix is the same sentence with different columns: zone * count + x(actual) + y(predicted).
Notice what was not needed there. bin cuts a continuous axis into cells before anything can be counted in them; a categorical axis arrives already cut, so there is nothing left to do but tally. bar * bin and bar * count follow the same rule on one axis; here both axes follow it. So each refusal names the other transform: give zone * count a continuous axis and it names bin, and give zone * bin two categorical axes and it names count.
A tile plot has two categorical positions where a bar chart has one. That second position changes only where the tally is written. A bar has a length to put it on, so bar * count writes its tally to the y axis. A tile plot’s two positions are both taken by categories, so zone * count writes its tally to color, and the legend is titled Count.
proportion is the same tally as a share of the whole, which is the plot to draw when the absolute numbers are not what you want to read:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone * proportion + x(direction) + y(season) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares")

  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares"))

  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares")

  y(col.season), palette("viridis"),
  title("The same observations, as shares"))

“Given the winds: zones derived by proportion, x is direction, y is season.”
That share is of every row counted, not of a row or a column of the grid. A confusion matrix divided by the total of each true class needs a different denominator. proportion always divides by the whole table, so compute row shares in the host language and draw them as a tile plot.
proportion reads a cut mesh the same way. Compose it with bin and the heatmap’s counts come back as fractions of the whole, the relative-frequency histogram with a second axis:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows"))


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20), proportion),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), palette("viridis"),
  title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                         1K 10K 100K   40 60 80  The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows Life Gdp  Proportion            0.0264 0.0135 0.000587 





proportion leaves the cells exactly where bin cut them, and the legend now reads in shares: the fullest one holds about three percent of the 1704 rows.


19.11.2 count tallies rows, mean reduces a column
The wind table records more than which cell each observation fell in. Each row also carries a speed, and the question “how fast, on average, in each cell?” is not a tally at all; it is a summary of one column.
The first sentence to try is a plain tile plot, and it is refused. A zone draws one opaque rectangle for each row, and here many rows share each cell. Their rectangles would be drawn one on top of another, so each cell would show only the color of its last row. gog counts the rows that would be hidden, and names the summary to write instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)

Compare that with zone * count in the section above. The sentence has the same shape, with mean for count and one more binding. count was handed no column, so it counts rows and labels the result count. mean was handed one, and color(speed) says which column it reduced. All six summaries read a mesh this way (sum, mean, median, max, min and quantile), and each writes its answer back into the column it reduced.
The first heatmap said that the measurement goes to color when both positions are taken. The rule has a second half: color is also the channel that names the column, because a summary writes its result back into the column it read. On an ordinary two-axis bar chart, bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) names life with y and puts the mean back on y; the source and the destination are one binding. A zone measures by color, so color is both the source and the destination.
The whole rule is short. A summary reduces the column on the channel that carries the measurement: y on a bar, color on a zone. It groups by every position that does not carry it. A bar measures with y, so it groups by x. A zone measures with nothing positional, so it groups by both. In the cube a bar measures with z, so it groups by the pair as well.
A summary composes with proportion too: each cell’s summary becomes a share of the total over all cells. The titanic table already holds counts: each row is a group of people aboard, and n is the size of the group. So sum adds up the people in each cell, and proportion turns each sum into a share of everyone aboard. Counting rows would be wrong here: zone * proportion gives every cell 0.125, because each cell holds 4 of the table’s 32 rows.

19.12 Sides the data drew: the choropleth

19.13 What you can set
A highlight has to stay in the background, and a heatmap cell has to be solid. gog gives each kind its own default, and a value in style() overrides it for the whole layer. Each mark takes its own settings. These are a zone’s, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(pattern = )
solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels



A zone is a filled region, so those five are exactly what a fill takes, and no more. One of them has a default that matters. opacity is 0.2 for a placed zone: one whose sides you named with bounds, or one that spans the panel on an axis. It is 1 when the data gives every side: cells bin cut, cells density estimated, the slots two categories own, and the regions a boundary drew. A placed zone is a highlight. It stays pale so the gridlines, and any layer written before it, show through. A zone of the second kind is the data, with nothing behind it to reveal.

Use the hatch when a plot will be printed in gray, or when two overlapping zones need more than color to separate them. 19.14 What it refuses
A point or a line draws from the plot’s own x and y, so a bare zone over the same table is the natural first attempt. Two continuous positions give a rectangle no width and no height, so it is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

Error:
! gog: `zone` shades a rectangle, but nothing here says where its sides are. Five things can: a categorical position, whose category owns a slot — `zone + x(method) + y(dataset) + color(score)` fills every cell where two categories cross; `bounds`, which names the sides from columns you hold — `zone * bounds(lo, hi)` on the measure axis, `zone * bounds(start = a, end = b)` on the domain axis, all four for a box, and the axis you leave out spans the panel; `bin`, which cuts them out of two continuous axes and counts the rows in each cell; `density`, which cuts the same cells and estimates a value at each; and a boundary, many rows around one region, named by `group` in `map()` or `globe()` — `zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(<region>) + map()`. A continuous position on its own is none of them — a number is a point, and a point has no width.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A category on one axis and a number on the other do not make a cell either. The category bounds its own axis, but the number gives the zone no width on the other axis. Each zone would span the whole panel, and the number would be dropped. gog refuses the sentence, and the message names three ways to fix it. Cut the number into ranges with zone * bin * mean, as in the summary heatmap. Or declare the column’s categories before plotting. A cell that then holds more than one row needs zone * mean, or the rows in one cell are drawn on top of each other, and you see only the last. Or leave the position out of the zone, so each slot spans the panel, as in the column highlight:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone + x(year) + y(continent) + color(life)


data(gm_all) + zone + x(col.year) + y(col.continent) + color(col.life)


data(gm_all) + zone + x(:year) + y(:continent) + color(:life)

A zone needs two answers: where its cells are, and what is in each. bounds answers only where. count answers only what, inside cells your categories already made. density answers both. bin answers both, and it can also answer only where, which is how bin * mean works. proportion gives the tally as shares of the whole. Two transforms that give the same answer contradict each other. A summary such as mean answers what, inside the cells the positions make, but a rectangle whose sides you named is one row on its own, so there are no cells for it to group rows into:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * mean +
  line

  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) * mean +
  line)

  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) * mean + line

  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper), mean), line)

Keep whichever you meant: `zone * bounds(...)` to shade a region you chose, or `zone * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + color(<column>)` to summarize one within every cell two categories cross. To shade a band the data computed, `ribbon * range` is the mark that spans a statistic.

To shade a region the data computed rather than one you chose, use ribbon, the mark that fills between two computed values: ribbon * range fills between the minimum and maximum at each x. A zone shades where you say; a ribbon shades what the data says.
Asking for two measurements is also a contradiction. count makes one measurement and mean makes another, but a cell holds a single number. count cuts nothing, so with mean measuring the cells there is nothing left for it to do:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone * count * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)

  color(:speed)

  y(col.season), color(col.speed))

Keep whichever you meant: `zone * count` to measure what `count` computes, or `zone * mean + color(<column>)` to reduce the column you name. To cut a continuous axis into cells and reduce a column inside each, `bin` is the transform that cuts without keeping the measurement: `zone * bin * mean + x(<number>)`.

bin * mean in the summary heatmap has the same shape and is not a contradiction: bin supplies the cells, and mean supplies the measurement inside them.
Say mean with no column to reduce and gog asks for one rather than guessing. A zone measures by color, so color is the binding the refusal names:

Name it: `zone * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + color(<column>)`. To count the rows in each cell instead of reducing a column, `count` needs no such binding: `zone * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>)`.

A bin needs something to cut, and two categorical axes leave it nothing: each category is one slot, and a slot cannot be cut smaller. The refusal goes further: a cell per pair of categories is the tile plot, which does no binning at all, so it names the transform that tallies into cells you already have:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

! gog: `zone * bin` cuts an axis into cells, and there is no axis here it can cut — `x(weekday)` and `y(week)` are both categorical. A category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows into the cells two categorical axes already make, `count` is the transform that does it: `zone * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>)` draws a cell per pair, colored by how many rows fell there. (With *one* categorical axis `zone * bin` draws the mixed mesh — the continuous axis cut into cells, one row of them per category.)

One categorical axis is allowed, and it draws. That is the mixed mesh. density differs from bin here, and the reason is the estimate itself. A field is estimated between the data points, so it needs somewhere to spread on both axes. A density per category would be normalized inside each slot on its own, which makes its cells incomparable across slots while the color ramp claims otherwise. A density per category is a different plot, so a field asks for two continuous axes and names what to use instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

! gog: `zone * density` estimates a density over the *plane*, and `y(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no interval for the estimate to spread along. Both axes must be continuous. To compare one continuous distribution across categories, `line * density + color(continent)` draws a curve per group.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A tiling is refused for a reason of its own, and that reason is distance. A hexagon is regular only when a step up and a step across can be compared, so hex needs a distance on both axes. A category’s slots have an order but no distance, so a mixed mesh always has rectangular cells:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  y(col.continent))

! gog: `bin(tiling = "hex")` partitions a *plane*, and `y` here is categorical — its slots are an order, not a distance, so there is nothing for a hexagon to be regular against. This plot is the mixed mesh: one axis cut into cells, one row of them per category, and its cells are rectangles by construction. Drop the tiling, or bind both axes to numbers for `bin(tiling = "hex")` to have a plane to cut.

When bin cuts only one axis, a tiling has nothing to shape. bar * bin cuts intervals, and an interval has no shape, so the refusal names zone as the mark a tiling belongs to:

To cut a continuous axis into cells first, `bin` is the transform that does it: `zone * bin` counts the rows in each, which is the heatmap.

The six summaries follow the same rule. mean reduces a column inside a cell, and a continuous position gives it no cell. The refusal names both fixes: a category on each position, or bin on the continuous axis first:

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.15 In short
A zone’s sides come from five places: bounds, bin, density, a category’s slot, or a boundary named by group. Where nothing gives sides, the zone reaches the panel edge, which a ribbon cannot do. The pair you name decides which axis it bounds; the column types decide which one measures.

title: 19  Zone
text:
19.16 What comes next
Color is how a zone carries a measure, read back from a legend. Surface gives that measure a height instead, and the same field is raised into the cube as a sheet.

Wilkinson, L. (2005). The grammar of graphics (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.1 A sheet through the samples
What shape does a landscape have, sampled on a grid? surface draws a sheet through your samples. It is a sheet through three positions, x, y and z. Without the third position there is no sheet at all. That makes it the only mark that must be drawn in the cube. Every other mark draws in the plane, and several of them also draw in the cube once you bind a z.
It is not area with a z. An area fills the space between a curve and a baseline. A surface has no baseline. Both are fills, and that is all they share.
A grid of elevations is a table of numbers, 1364 of them here. Nobody can see a hill in a column of numbers. Draw the same numbers as a sheet and the hill appears. Here is Maunga Whau, a volcano in Auckland. The book’s copy keeps every second row and every second column of the original grid, so these samples are 20 m apart. Ross Ihaka digitized the elevations from a topographic map, and R’s datasets package is where the book reads them (R Core Team, 2026):

There is no space() in that sentence and none is needed: binding z is what puts a plot in the cube, exactly as it is for a 3-D scatter. space(turn =, tilt =) still sets the angle when you want a different one. z_label() names the third axis, the way x_label() names the first, and Space explains it.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.2 One row per crossing
What shape must a table have before a surface can draw it? A scatter’s table does not have that shape, and knowing why tells you which of your tables can become a sheet. Given two position columns and no transform, a surface reads each row as a crossing: the point where one x value meets one y value. The sheet is the faces between the crossings. The grid those faces make is the sheet’s mesh. You never declare which crossings are neighbors. gog recovers that from your two position columns: the distinct east values and the distinct north values become the mesh lines, one set in each direction. A face is drawn wherever all four corners of a cell are present.
So this reading needs a table with one row per (x, y) crossing: every x value paired with every y value.
Maunga Whau has that shape. It holds 1364 rows, 31 distinct east values and 44 distinct north values: 31 × 44 = 1364, so the grid is full, and 30 × 43 = 1290 faces get drawn.
The same count shows why a scatter cannot be a surface. The gapminder 2007 table below holds 142 countries, and no two of them share a gdp value or a life value. That makes a grid 142 wide and 142 deep holding only 142 crossings, so no cell has all four corners. The sheet would be empty:

That refusal names the two sentences that do draw: a point with a z for the cloud itself, and surface * density for a field estimated from it. A field is one value at every place on the plane. The third geometry of one field draws surface * density for the iris flowers.
Because a face needs all four of its corners, a gap in the grid is an opening in the sheet rather than a face drawn across it. Drop the crossings around the summit and the sheet opens there rather than covering the gap:

peak <- maunga_whau[!(maunga_whau$east > 300 & maunga_whau$east < 440 &
                        maunga_whau$north > 400 & maunga_whau$north < 560), ]

data(peak) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("A gap in the grid, left open")

The note above the plot counts the crossings gog did find: 1322 of 1364, so 42 crossings are missing. Each missing crossing removes every face that needed it, so more than 42 faces are missing: 1234 are drawn here, where the full grid draws 1290. The note is advice rather than a refusal, because a grid with gaps is a legitimate thing to have and a sheet with openings is a true picture of one. What would not be legitimate is quietly spanning a gap, which claims a height nobody measured. The note also says what to check if you expected a whole sheet: each position value must repeat exactly. If one row holds 1.2 and another 1.2000001, gog makes two mesh lines where you meant one, and the sheet gets openings you did not intend.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.3 A continuous floor
A table with a continent in one column and a year in another looks like the grids above, and a sheet over it is a reasonable thing to ask for. The two position columns make the sheet’s floor, the plane under it, and both have to be continuous. A face stretches from one sample to the next and so claims every height between them, and between one category and the next there is nothing to claim. So a category on either position is refused.
Numbers cut into cells are different, and a surface takes those, as When each cell holds one value shows. Cut cells meet edge to edge, and the edge between two cells is itself a number on the axis. A category instead owns a slot, a share of the axis that is its own, and the line between two slots stands for no value at all. So a surface refuses the slot, not the cut. The flat marks show the same difference: bars over categories stand apart, and the bars of a histogram touch.
The refusal, shown in What it refuses, names the mark that does take a category on both positions: the 3-D bar. A 3-D bar sits in its slot and claims nothing about the space between slots. So bar * count + x(a) + y(b) + space() draws one bar over each pair of categories. A surface cannot draw that grid, because tiles with empty space between them are not a sheet.

“Given the iris flowers: a surface derived by density, x is petal length, y is sepal length, in the cube, turned 120.”
The sheet is turned to 120 degrees because of where the two peaks are. They sit on a diagonal of the floor. At the default angle the near peak stands directly in front of the far one and hides it, so the sheet would show one peak where the data has two. One sheet, four angles returns to that, because every 3-D view has this problem, not only this one.
All three plots say the same thing about these two clusters: they are nearly equally dense at their centers. The cluster with long petals is the denser one, by about four percent. What each plot asks of the reader is different. In the cells you compare two shades against a legend. In the contours you count rings. On the sheet you compare two heights, and that needs no legend at all. Which of the three you want depends on what you are asking, not on which mark is better.
One transform, three marks, and the estimate itself is the same in all three. What differs is where each mark puts the measurement. A zone puts it in color. A path puts it in the level each contour was cut at. A surface puts it in height. That is why the third sentence never binds z() and still gets a third axis, labeled Density. The transform supplies the measurement, and the mark puts it on the height. A flat bar * bin does the same for y.







Mark derived by density, over two positions
Where the measurement goes




zone * density
into the color of each cell


path * density
into the level each contour was cut at


surface * density
into the height of the sheet, the third plot above



Here the transform stays the same, and each mark supplies its own geometry. That is the rule that already made the contour and the estimated heatmap one feature instead of two.
The third sentence above writes space(), and the chapter’s first sentence, for the volcano, did not. The reason matters. A bound z says there are three columns here, which nothing else can mean. An invented height says only this layer has a measure of its own. density invents one in the plane too, so space() is what tells gog to put the answer on a third axis.

title: 20  Surface
section: 20.5 When each cell holds one value
text:
20.5 When each cell holds one value
The volcano’s sheet joins its samples with sloping faces. Does the ground rise smoothly between your samples, or does each cell hold one value that says nothing about its neighbors? bin is the other transform that tiles a floor. It cuts the floor into cells, and mean gives each cell the average elevation of the rows inside it. The surface is then flat across each cell, with a step at each boundary. The density sheet above is drawn the same way, from much smaller cells. Here is the same volcano, read as a coarse grid rather than a fine one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface * bin(12) * mean + x(:east) + y(:north) +
  z(:elevation) + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell")


plot(data(maunga_whau), layer(surface, bin(12), mean), x(col.east),
  y(col.north), z(col.elevation), z_label("Elevation (m)"),
  title("Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                600 400 200 800 600 400 200 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Maunga Whau, one elevation per cell





“Given Maunga Whau: a surface derived by bin into 12 and mean, x is east, y is north, z is elevation.”
Nothing about the volcano changed. What changed is the claim. The sheet at the top of this chapter says the ground rises smoothly between its samples. This one gives each cell one elevation, the mean of its samples, and says nothing about how the ground varies inside the cell. Each claim is right for a different kind of data, and which one you want is a question about how yours was measured.
That question has a clear answer in an experiment or a simulation, where the conditions form a grid with exactly one number in each cell. Read as crossings, such a table gives fewer faces than it has values. Nine values make a 3 × 3 grid of crossings. A face needs four crossings at its corners, so the sheet has 2 × 2 = 4 faces, and no face stands for any one value:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


cells <- data.frame(
  a = c(-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2),
  b = c(-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2),
  v = c(0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039)
)

data(cells) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) + title("Nine values, four faces")


cells = {
  "a": [-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2],
  "b": [-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2],
  "v": [0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039],
}
data(cells) + surface + x(col.a) + y(col.b) + z(col.v) + title("Nine values, four faces")


cells = (
  a = [-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2],
  b = [-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2],
  v = [0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039],
)
data(cells) + surface + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  title("Nine values, four faces")


const cells = {
  a: [-2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2, -2, 0, 2],
  b: [-2, -2, -2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2],
  v: [0.039, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.019, 0.029, 0.039, 0.029, 0.039],

  title("Nine values, four faces"))






                             2 1 0 -1 -2 2 1 0 -1 -2 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Nine values, four faces





Nine numbers became four faces, and each face slopes between the four values at its corners. Cut the floor into cells instead, and each cell gets a flat top of its own, a plateau:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
  color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus")


(data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(col.a) + y(col.b) + z(col.v) +
  color(col.v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus"))


data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  color(:v) + palette("plasma") + title("Nine values, nine plateaus")


plot(data(cells), layer(surface, bin(3), mean), x(col.a), y(col.b),
  z(col.v), color(col.v), palette("plasma"),
  title("Nine values, nine plateaus"))






                                              1 0 -1 1 0 -1 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Nine values, nine plateaus  V            0.039 0.029 0.019 





“Given the cells: a surface derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v, color by v, with the plasma palette.”
Nine plateaus, and three colors. The nine values make a symmetric bowl: the four corner cells share the highest value, the four edge cells share the middle one, and the center cell holds the lowest. The ramp makes that symmetry visible. In the plain sheet above, you had to read the symmetry from the axis.
A 3-D bar uses the same sentence: bin cuts the x and y axes into cells, and mean averages the column named on z inside each one. The transforms mean the same thing on both marks, and only the geometry laid on the cell differs. Here mean does no averaging, because this table holds one row per cell. It is still needed: without it, bin counts the rows in each cell and draws that count as the height.
The step between two plateaus is drawn, as a vertical face standing on the line the two cells share. That line has no width, so the vertical face claims nothing about any area: it is simply what a jump looks like. Without it the mark would draw disconnected tiles floating at their own heights, and a reader could not tell a step from a missing cell.
A vertical face spans the difference between two neighbors, and a 3-D bar on every cell does not. A bar always reaches down to the baseline, so a grid of bars hides its own back rows as soon as you turn it. A vertical face is only as tall as its own step. The next plot turns both to 60 degrees, so you can see which one is still legible. Both are set to one color, so the only thing that differs between them is the shape:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(cells) + bar * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
    space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
   (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
      space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Plateaus, turned"))) +
  theme(height = 430)


(((data(cells) + bar * bin(3) * mean + x(col.a) + y(col.b) + z(col.v) +
    space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
   (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(col.a) + y(col.b) + z(col.v) +
      space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Plateaus, turned"))) +
  theme(height = 430))


((data(cells) + bar * bin(3) * mean + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") + title("Bars, turned")) |
  (data(cells) + surface * bin(3) * mean + x(:a) + y(:b) + z(:v) +
  space(turn = 60) + style(color = "#76b7b2") +
  title("Plateaus, turned"))) + theme(height = 430)


beside(plot(data(cells), layer(bar, bin(3), mean), x(col.a), y(col.b),
  z(col.v), space({ turn: 60 }), style({ color: "#76b7b2" }),
  title("Bars, turned")),
  plot(data(cells), layer(surface, bin(3), mean), x(col.a), y(col.b),
  z(col.v), space({ turn: 60 }), style({ color: "#76b7b2" }),
  title("Plateaus, turned")), theme({ height: 430 }))






                                                      1 0 -1 1 0 -1 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Bars, turned


                                              1 0 -1 1 0 -1 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Plateaus, turned






“Given the cells: bars derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v, beside a surface derived by bin into 3 and mean, x is a, y is b, z is v.”
| composes them (Composition), so the two are one figure and turn together. That is what makes this a fair comparison, rather than two pictures the reader has to match angle by angle.
theme(height = ) sets the whole figure’s height in pixels. It is set here because two cubes side by side each get half the page’s width but the full height, so each panel is tall and narrow. A cube keeps its proportions on the page, so it never stretches to fill a tall panel. Without the setting, blank space would be left above and below each cube.
Empty cells need no special rule and get none. bin leaves them out, because a cell with no rows is not a measurement of zero. A plateau claims only its own cell, so a cell with nothing in it is simply a cell with no top. It is the same opening a missing crossing makes in the mesh, for a different reason.
What a surface refuses is a grid of slots, the cells two categories make. What it refuses shows that refusal.

title: 20  Surface
section: 20.6 The mesh, and what the shading means
text:
20.6 The mesh, and what the shading means
A smooth sheet hides where its samples were, the way a line hides its rows. Drawing the mesh lines shows the grid again, so a reader can see how fine the sampling was. border_color and border_size draw them. A face is a closed fill like a bar’s or a box’s, so the settable rule gives it a border. On a surface, those borders are the mesh lines:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 0.4) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The mesh, drawn")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 0.4 }),
  z_label("Elevation (m)"), title("The mesh, drawn"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  The mesh, drawn





“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, with border color white and border size 0.4.”
The mesh lines add no shapes to the picture, because every face is already stroked in its own shade. That thin stroke covers the pale seam that would otherwise show between neighboring faces. border_color replaces the stroke’s color, and border_size its width. Leave both out for a seamless sheet. A border_size of 0 removes the stroke, and the pale seams appear.
Look at the shading on the sheet above, and on the turned one below it. The faces are shaded by their slope: a steep one is darker, a flat one keeps its full color. That is a fact about the terrain, not about where a light is, so turning the scene rearranges the faces on the page and repaints none of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  space(turn = 130, tilt = 35) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Turned, with the same shades")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  space(turn = 130, tilt = 35) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Turned, with the same shades"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  space(turn = 130, tilt = 35) + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Turned, with the same shades")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), space({ turn: 130, tilt: 35 }),
  z_label("Elevation (m)"), title("Turned, with the same shades"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Turned, with the same shades





“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, turned 130, tilted 35.”
Compare the crater walls here with the first plot. Same faces, same shades, seen from the other side. A light that stayed in one place on the screen would have changed the shade of every face. A color that changed while the data did not would mislead a reader, with no way to notice.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.7 Color by height, per face
Slope shading says how steep a face is, not how high it stands. How high is the summit, and how deep is the crater? color maps on a surface, and a continuous column colors it face by face along a ramp. palette() chooses which ramp. "viridis" suits a topographic sheet, because it gets steadily lighter from its lowest color to its highest:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + color(elevation) +
  palette("viridis") +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) + color(col.elevation) +
  palette("viridis") +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  color(:elevation) + palette("viridis") + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), color(col.elevation), palette("viridis"),
  z_label("Elevation (m)"),
  title("Height twice: as a position and as a ramp"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Height twice: as a position and as a ramp  Elevation            193 143.5 94 





Compare that with the first plot in this chapter. The summit and the crater rim are in that plot too. With slope shading alone you have to infer them from which faces are dark. The ramp states the heights, and the legend decodes them.
Mapping the height to color when z already shows it is redundant on purpose. It is what a reader of a topographic map expects. It also shows why a surface can take a continuous color when an area cannot. An area has one interior, and coloring it by a measure would make a gradient fill, which is a different and much larger job. A surface has faces, and a face is small enough to hold one value.
A face has four corners and one color. Its color is the mean of its four corner values, which stands for the field at its center. So the ramp describes the mesh you have, not only the field you sampled from. Here is one bowl-shaped field, sampled coarsely and then finely:

bowl <- function(n) {
  g <- expand.grid(a = seq(-2, 2, length.out = n), b = seq(-2, 2, length.out = n))
  g$v <- 0.019 + 0.0025 * (g$a^2 + g$b^2)
  g
}
coarse <- bowl(3)
fine   <- bowl(7)

((data(coarse) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
    color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Sampled 3 by 3: four faces")) |
   (data(fine) + surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) +
      color(v) + palette("plasma") + title("Sampled 7 by 7: thirty-six faces"))) +
  theme(height = 320)



                               2 1 0 -1 2 1 0 -1 -2 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Sampled 3 by 3: four faces  V            0.039 0.029 0.019 


                                                             2 1 0 -1 2 1 0 -1 -2 0.040 0.035 0.030 0.025 0.020 A B V  Sampled 7 by 7: thirty-six faces  V            0.039 0.029 0.019 






“Given coarse: a surface, x is a, y is b, z is v, color by v, with the plasma palette, beside the same given fine.”
Two tables share this page, and data() keeps each table’s name, coarse or fine. gog finds each layer’s table by that name, so it refuses two different tables under one name (Data).
The left sheet is one uniform color, and that is correct rather than broken. Every face has one high corner, one low corner and two middle ones, so all four faces get the same average. The mesh is too coarse to hold the shape, and the ramp says so instead of inventing a gradient across it. The right sheet has the same field under it and enough faces to resolve it, so the bowl appears.
This is the reading that makes the legend trustworthy. A color is the height at one stated place, the center of a face, so two faces of one color really are at one height there, and a sheet of one color has all its face centers at one height.
The slope shading is still underneath the ramp, and the two combine rather than cancel: a face takes its color from the ramp and is then darkened by how steep it is. Viridis stays readable because only the low ground takes its dark colors, and low ground is usually flat. A flat face is barely darkened by its slope, so few faces are darkened by both the ramp and the slope.
An estimated height takes a ramp the same way, and you name it the same way. density writes its estimate into a column called density, so density is the name you give color, exactly as on a zone or a path:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space() + color(density) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The estimate, as a height and as a ramp")


(data(iris_flowers) + surface * density +
  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + space() + color(col.density) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The estimate, as a height and as a ramp"))


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density + x(:petal_length) +
  y(:sepal_length) + space() + color(:density) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The estimate, as a height and as a ramp")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(surface, density), x(col.petal_length),
  y(col.sepal_length), space(), color(col.density), palette("viridis"),
  title("The estimate, as a height and as a ramp"))
