





Nothing there is a special case. The transform makes a column, the column has a name, and a name can be bound. Whether the height came from your table or from an estimate is only a difference in source. It does not change what you may say about it.
Whether you want the color as well as the height is a separate question. The plain sheet in A sheet through the samples already shows the height by position alone. Use the ramp when the low ground matters. Slope shading darkens a steep face but not a flat one, so a broad, low mound and the flat ground around it are drawn almost the same color. The ramp is what separates them.
A categorical color splits the mark instead, one sheet per group. gog puts every face of both sheets into one depth order, the back-to-front order in which faces are drawn, rather than drawing one sheet and then the other:

band <- maunga_whau
band$side <- ifelse(band$north > 440, "north slope", "south slope")

data(band) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + color(side) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Two sheets, sorted together")



                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Two sheets, sorted together  Side    south slope  north slope 





The two sheets meet along the line where side changes. Depth order runs across that line rather than stopping at it. Each face is placed by its own distance from you, whichever sheet it belongs to, so the two sheets are correct wherever they overlap. Drawing one whole sheet and then the other would put every face of the second in front, and the line where they meet would be drawn wrong.

title: 20  Surface
section: 20.8 Opacity by a measure, per face
text:
20.8 Opacity by a measure, per face
A color decides what a face says. An opacity decides whether you can see through it. Part of a sheet is often not the subject. The flat ground around a hill only hides what is behind it, and fading those faces makes the hill the solid part of the picture. opacity maps on a surface, and it maps for the reason color does. A face is small enough to hold one value, so it can hold an opacity too. Every face takes its own opacity, and a face fades where its measure is small:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + opacity(elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Faint where the ground is low")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface +
  x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) + opacity(col.elevation) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Faint where the ground is low"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  opacity(:elevation) + z_label("Elevation (m)") +
  title("Faint where the ground is low")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), opacity(col.elevation), z_label("Elevation (m)"),
  title("Faint where the ground is low"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Faint where the ground is low  Elevation    94  143.5  193 





“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, opacity by elevation.”
Over the low ground the fill fades to almost nothing and each face keeps its outline, so that part of the sheet shows as mesh lines alone. A ramp cannot do that; an opacity can. The legend beside the plot reads the same way color’s does, with the smallest, middle and largest values of the column.
No face disappears completely. A mapped opacity runs from 0.15 to 0.95, so the faintest face here is still drawn, which is the rule every mapped opacity follows (Channels).
A face reads its opacity the way it reads its color, from the mean of its four corners. A plateau reads its own cell’s row. A vertical face stands between two cells and reads the taller one’s row, the way a bar’s side takes the bar’s color. Either way one face has one reading, whichever channel asks for it.
The sentence behind the first plot in this section binds elevation twice: once to z and once to opacity. A second column is the more useful case: the shape stays in z, and another measure decides which faces fade.

relief <- maunga_whau
h <- matrix(relief$elevation, nrow = length(unique(relief$north)))
up   <- rbind(h[-1, ], h[nrow(h), ])
side <- cbind(h[, -1], h[, ncol(h)])
relief$steepness <- as.vector(sqrt((up - h)^2 + (side - h)^2))

data(relief) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) + opacity(steepness) +
  z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Solid where the ground is steep")



                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   600 400 200 0 800 600 400 200 0 180 160 140 120 100 East North Elevation (m)  Solid where the ground is steep  Steepness    0  9.86  19.72 





steepness combines the two elevation changes at each crossing, one toward the next east value and one toward the next north value. The steep sides of the hill stay solid, and the flat ground around them fades away. The sheet is the same shape as the one above it, and a different part of it is solid.
An area refuses a mapped opacity for the same reason it refuses a continuous color. A region has one interior and one fill, so a row there is a corner of the outline rather than a part that can carry a value. A surface has faces, and each face can carry both.
One value for the whole sheet is still style(opacity = ). Set it when you want to see one sheet through another, and map it when you want each face to fade by its own value.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.9 One sheet, four angles
A still 3-D plot hides something at every angle, and which thing it hides depends on the angle you pick. So turn the same sheet rather than trust one view of it. Each of these changes exactly one of turn/tilt from the first:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 30, tilt = 25) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("The default view")) |
 (data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 140, tilt = 25) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Turned: the same sheet from the west"))) /

    color(elevation) + palette("viridis") + space(turn = 30, tilt = 70) +
    z_label("Elevation (m)") + title("Tilted up: the crater appears")) |

“Given Maunga Whau: a surface, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by elevation, with the viridis palette, turned 30, tilted 25, beside the same turned 140; above the same tilted 70, beside the same tilted 5.”
Read them as a set and you can see what each angle hides. The crater is the most interesting thing about this hill, and the first two plots do not show it. The rim nearest you stands in front of the crater, so turning alone does not show it while the tilt is low. Tilt up and you can see into the crater, because you are now looking down from above. The same tilt flattens the heights, until the sheet looks like a flat colored map. Tilt down instead and you get the opposite: the heights read clearly, the view from above is gone, and the sheet shows as an outline. One or the other, never both.
These four plots show why you would want to turn a plot. Here you need both the view from above and the view from the side, and no single still view shows this hill whole. So turn the four with the pointer. Raise the tilt until the crater opens, and watch the heights flatten as it does. The four still views show the problem; dragging them lets you check it yourself.
All four turn together, because | and / composed them into one figure. Each panel keeps the angle its own sentence asked for, and the drag adds the same change to every one. Reset returns each to where it began. To turn one alone, write it alone.
That is composition rather than faceting, and the two share the same pair of operators. A facet names a column (Faceting), and a viewing angle is not a column: it is a property of the coordinate space, the way a polar() start angle is. gog does build small multiples of cubes, one cube for each value of a column, but these four panels are not small multiples. Space has that example.
One limit shows in these four plots, and it belongs to the cube rather than to the mark. Notice the Elevation axis in the tilted-up panel. You are looking down along it, so it is drawn at about a third of its full length. gog labels three heights there where the reference view labels five, because it drops numbers rather than let them overlap. Space says which numbers a crowded axis drops, and why the scale itself never changes.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.10 What a surface is for
A surface is for anything that is a height over a plane. Terrain, and the sea floor. A response surface from a designed experiment. A model’s fit measured over two of its parameters. A model’s predictions over a grid of two predictors. And, through density, the shape of a two-dimensional distribution.
What it is not for is data that merely has three numbers per row. That is a 3-D scatter, and the refusal in One row per crossing names it for you. The question to ask is whether the space between two of your samples means anything. On a grid it does; in a cloud it does not.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.11 What you can set
No column says whether the mesh lines show, or how far you can see through a sheet. A setting decides both without reading any column, and each mark takes its own settings. These are a surface’s, with the values each accepts:



Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(border_color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(border_size = )
pixels



A surface is a closed fill, so it takes what a bar and a box take: a color, an opacity, and a border. pattern is the one fill setting it refuses, and like a bar it has no size. The next section says why for both.
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the companion grid.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.12 What it refuses
Every flat mark is written with only x and y as positions, so it is easy to write a surface that way by mistake. Leaving out the height and leaving the plot in the plane are one mistake, not two, so there is one refusal. It names both ways into the cube, and it names the two marks that draw a field in the plane instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north)


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(col.east) + y(col.north)


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north)


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north))




Error:
! gog: a `surface` is a sheet through three positions, so it needs the cube. Bind the height — `surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(h)` — or let a transform invent it: `surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space()`. For the same field drawn in the plane, `zone` paints it as cells and `path` traces its contours.

plot(data(gm_eras), surface, x(col.continent), y(col.year), z(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent)` maps a categorical (text) column, but `x` on `surface` needs a continuous (numeric) column. A face spans the gap between two samples, and between two categories there is nothing to span. Over two categories, stand a column in each cell instead: `bar * count + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + space()` — a column stands in its own cell and claims nothing in between.

The message names the mark that draws one bar in each category’s slot instead, the 3-D bar. The transforms that tally into slots are refused by the same rule. count and proportion count rows into the cells two categories make:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  space())




Error:
! gog: a `surface` is a sheet over a floor whose cells tile without gaps. `count` tallies into the cells two categories make, and slots leave air between them, so the tiles would not join into a sheet. `bin` and `density` tile a floor, and `sum`, `mean`, `median`, `max`, `min` and `quantile` reduce a column inside the cells `bin` cuts: `surface * bin * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(<column>)`, while `surface * density + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + space()` estimates the field. Over categories, `bar` is the mark, where the column under each tile says which cell it belongs to.

A face spans the gap between two samples, and between two categories there is nothing to span. A face spans the gap between two samples, and between two categories there is nothing to span. That refusal lists the two transforms that do tile a floor, bin and density.
density(levels = ) cuts a field into level sets, and a level set is a region in the plane. A surface has already given the third axis to the measurement, so a band drawn on it could only be a color. zone already draws those bands in the plane, as colored regions, so the sentence is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + space()


(data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) +
  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + space())


data(iris_flowers) + surface * density(levels = 5) + x(:petal_length) +
  y(:sepal_length) + space()


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(surface, density({ levels: 5 })),
  x(col.petal_length), y(col.sepal_length), space())




Error:
! gog: `density(levels = )` cuts a field into level sets, which are regions in the plane — a `surface` draws the field itself, with the estimate as its height, so it has no axis left to put a band on. Drop `levels` for the sheet, or `zone * density(levels = )` to fill the bands and `path * density(levels = )` to trace their boundaries. For a sheet in steps, cut the floor rather than the height: `surface * bin * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(<column>)` lays a flat plateau on every cell.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A stepped sheet can be cut on either of two axes, and only one of the two draws. Cutting the floor into cells is surface * bin, which When each cell holds one value draws. Cutting the height into bands is what levels asks for, and that one is refused. It would cut the measurement rather than the grid, so the plateaus would be contours of equal height rather than one per cell.
bandwidth is refused for the reason it is refused on every two-dimensional field. It is a length in one column’s own units, and a field spreads over two columns that measure different quantities. One number cannot be a width in both. Use density(adjust = ), which is dimensionless and scales both.
There is no size on a surface. Its extent is the grid it is drawn on, so a size would be a second and contradictory answer to how big it is. area refuses a size for the same reason. And a surface is the one fill mark that refuses pattern:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")


(data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch"))


data(maunga_whau) + surface + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")


plot(data(maunga_whau), surface, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), style({ pattern: "hatch" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = )` textures a fill, and a `surface` is a mesh of fills — but a hatch tile is a texture in *screen* space, and a projected mesh foreshortens every face differently, so one tile would read as a different density on every face. That is a texture that changes with the viewing angle instead of with the data. A surface says its shape with slope shading; `style(border_color = )` draws its mesh lines, and `color` ramps it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A hatch tile is a texture in screen space, and every face of a projected mesh is foreshortened differently, so one tile size would read as a different line spacing on every face. The texture would then follow the viewing angle rather than the data, which is the one thing this mark’s shading is built to avoid.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.13 In short
A surface stretches between neighboring samples, so it needs a floor whose cells tile. A scatter’s table does not give it one. A face needs all four of its corners, so a missing crossing leaves an opening rather than a guessed height.

title: 20  Surface
text:
20.14 What comes next
A surface needs two continuous positions under it. Edge is the mark for tables with no positions at all: rows naming two things and saying they are connected.




R Core Team. (2026). R: A language and environment for statistical computing. R Foundation for Statistical Computing. https://www.R-project.org/

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.1 The network diagram
Which things in your table are connected to which? edge draws one stroke per row of the table, between the two things named in that row. Every other mark that draws a stroke is placed by the axes. A line and a path join points at their x and y values, and an interval spans two values on one axis. An edge is different: each row gives it only two names, and no column says where a name sits on the page. The picture an edge layer makes is the network diagram.
So an edge takes no x and no y, and no other mark refuses both. An edge’s endpoints come from a layout, a transform that reads the two columns of names and places each distinct name once. Write the from column first and the to column second, so the sentence states the direction of each relation. If you swap the two columns, the picture does not change. It changes only when you add arrowheads: style(arrow = "end") points each edge from the first column to the second (What you can set).
A network diagram needs a table with one row per relation. In trade_partners, each row names an exporter and an importer, and gives the value of the goods in billions of dollars, rounded:

Name the table, then write three things: the mark, the layout that derives it, and the space network():
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network())
“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The 15 countries become 15 positions on the panel, and the 22 rows become 22 strokes. Five pairs of countries trade in both directions, and each pair’s two strokes lie on one line. So you can count only 17 lines, and those five look slightly darker than the rest. No country is labeled: the layout placed the countries, but no layer draws their names.
An edge draws only inside network(). A layout computes its positions from the graph. Here a graph is not a chart: it is a set of things and the relations between them. Each thing is a node, and each row is one relation between two nodes. A node is one name, however many rows it appears in: Germany is one node in seven rows. A layout chooses positions that keep the picture readable, so the distance between two nodes is not a quantity. An axis would put numbers on that distance, so gog refuses every other space.
A layout is not for edges alone. It gives every node one position, and it adds a column, name, that holds each node’s name. Two other marks read a layout and draw at those same positions:
The next section gives each stroke a value from its row, and adds the first of those three: a dot at each node. The Network chapter draws all three in one plot.

text:

Shape




point * layout
one dot per node


text * layout + label(name)
each node’s name


edge * layout
one stroke per relation, the plot above

title: 21  Edge
section: 21.2 Color, opacity and dash, one per row
text:
21.2 Color, opacity and dash, one per row
In the first plot every stroke is drawn the same way, so a relation worth 500 billion dollars looks like one worth 50 billion. The table holds that value, and a stroke can carry it as opacity. Each edge is drawn from one row, so it can take its color, its opacity and its dash from that row’s values. opacity takes a continuous column such as billions. A faint stroke’s ends are hard to find. So a second layer, point * layout(exporter, importer), reads the same layout and draws a dot at each node:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("More trade, darker stroke"))






                                            More trade, darker stroke  Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The three darkest lines meet at one node. The table shows which: China, Mexico and Canada each export more than 400 billion dollars of goods to the United States. On line, opacity is only a setting, because a line joins many rows into one stroke. An edge draws one stroke per row, so each row gives its stroke an opacity of its own.
Which strokes share an exporter? color needs a categorical column such as exporter, and each stroke takes its exporter’s color. So the five strokes with Germany as exporter share one color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(exporter) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + color(col.exporter) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  color(:exporter) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), color(col.exporter),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter"))






                                            Each stroke, colored by its exporter  Exporter    China  Mexico  Canada  United States  Korea  Germany  Netherlands  Japan  Australia  Brazil  India  France 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, colored by exporter, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
Mexico, Canada and the Netherlands are in the legend, but no stroke shows their color. Each trades both ways with one partner, and the partner’s stroke is drawn on top of theirs.
The dash can come from a column too. pattern(exporter) gives each exporter a dash, the way color(exporter) gave each a color above. There are only five dashes: solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash and longdash. When a column has more than five categories, some of them share a dash, and gog prints a message that says how many:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + pattern(exporter) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, dashed by its exporter")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + pattern(col.exporter) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, dashed by its exporter"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  pattern(:exporter) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network() +
  title("Each stroke, dashed by its exporter")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), pattern(col.exporter),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("Each stroke, dashed by its exporter"))




gog: `pattern(exporter)` has 12 categories and `edge` draws 5 dashes, so the set starts over: 7 categories share a dash with an earlier one. Use `color(exporter)`, whose default palette has twenty, or give each category its own panel with `facet(exporter)`.




                                            Each stroke, dashed by its exporter  Exporter    China  Mexico  Canada  United States  Korea  Germany  Netherlands  Japan  Australia  Brazil  India  France 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, patterned by exporter, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The legend lists the exporters in the order the table first names them, and the dashes start again after the fifth. So Germany, sixth, has China’s solid stroke, and so does India, eleventh. Where two countries trade both ways, their two strokes lie on one line, and the lower dash shows through the gaps in the upper one. color(exporter) gave each of the twelve its own color.

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.3 What you can set
Some choices come from no column: how thick every stroke is, or one dash for all of them. You set those in the sentence, with style(), and each mark takes its own settings. These are an edge’s, with the values each accepts:







Setting
Value




style(color = )
any CSS color name or hex


style(opacity = )
0 to 1


style(size = )
pixels


style(pattern = )
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash, longdash


style(arrow = )
end, start, both



style(size = ) sets the stroke width for the whole layer. style(color = ), style(opacity = ) and style(pattern = ) give every stroke one value, when no column is mapped to that channel. The settings table above lists every dash that style(pattern = ) accepts.
style(arrow = ) draws an arrowhead on each stroke. With "end", it is at the node in the second column of layout(), the to column. With "start", it is at the node in the first column, and with "both", at both nodes. Each arrowhead ends outside the dot that a point * layout layer draws at the node, so the dot does not cover it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + style(arrow = "end") +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke points at its importer")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + style(arrow = "end") +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke points at its importer"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  style(arrow = "end") + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  network() + title("Each stroke points at its importer")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  style({ arrow: "end" }),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network(),
  title("Each stroke points at its importer"))






                                                                  Each stroke points at its importer





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, with arrow end, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the companion grid.

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.4 What it refuses
The other marks take their positions from x and y, so binding them to an edge is the first thing most readers try. An edge with no layout has no endpoints to draw, and x and y cannot supply them. gog refuses the sentence, because no layer gives network() a layout to draw:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge + x(billions) + y(exporter) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge + x(col.billions) + y(col.exporter) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge + x(:billions) + y(:exporter) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners), edge, x(col.billions), y(col.exporter),
  network())




Error:
! gog: `network()` draws what a `layout` places, and nothing here carries one. Compose the syllable: `edge * layout(from, to) + network()`, with `point * layout(...)` for the nodes and `text * layout(...) + label(name)` for their names.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A layout is read only inside network(), so the sentence has to name that space:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer)


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)))




Error:
! gog: a `layout`'s positions are the graph's, not the data's — an axis under them would number something no reader can mean. Draw it in the network: `+ network()` flat, or `+ network(turn = 30, tilt = 25)` for the cube.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The Network chapter adds a label beside each dot and sizes each dot by its number of relations. It also draws the same graph in a cube, and lists the other refusals.

title: 21  Edge
text:
21.5 What comes next
An edge never has an axis, because a layout places both of its endpoints. Most marks are placed by an axis instead, and Scales is where a value becomes a position on an axis.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.1 A scale is not a transform
What do you do when most of your data is crowded into one corner? You change the scale, which decides how a number becomes a position. It is written on the binding, not as an atom of its own:
A scale belongs to one channel, so it is written where that channel is bound. There is no scale() atom to write separately. A separate atom would make you name the channel twice, once to bind it and once to scale it, and the two could then disagree.
Writing the scale on the binding also makes a sentence easier to read. To see how gdp is placed, you look at x(gdp, scale = "log") and nowhere else. Nothing else in the sentence can change it, and there is no second function to look up.
A log scale is not the only way to see a spread of incomes. You could take the logarithm of the column yourself and plot the result. That is a different operation, and the difference decides what the axis says.
bin and mean are transforms: they read your table and compute new values from it. A scale produces no new values at all. It changes how far along the axis a number lands and what the ticks say, and nothing else.
The difference is visible in the finished plot. Here is gdp plotted with a log scale:

  color(continent) +

  color(col.continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Income and life expectancy: log scale"))

  color(:continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Income and life expectancy: log scale")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Income and life expectancy: log scale"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Income and life expectancy: log scale Life GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
The axis reads 1K and 10K. Those are dollars, the units you supplied.
The word log appears nowhere on the axis, and that is deliberate. The units did not change, so the axis label does not claim they did. The ticks are the only sign: each is a whole power of ten, so equal steps along the axis mean equal ratios. Write x_label("GDP per person (log scale)") when a reader needs the scale named in words. The axis label is yours, and gog never writes the scale into it.
Now the same picture, drawn after taking the logarithm of the column yourself:
gm_logged <- gapminder_2007
gm_logged$log_gdp <- log10(gm_logged$gdp)

data(gm_logged) + point + x(log_gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  title("The same shape, with the axis in log units")



                                                                                                                                                                                2.5 3.0 3.5 4.0 4.5   40 50 60 70 80  The same shape, with the axis in log units Life Log Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
Every point is in the same place as in the first plot, but the axis now reads 2.5 to 4.5. Those numbers are logarithms, not dollars. The tick at 3.0 sits where the first plot has 1K, because ten to the power of 3 is 1,000. The tick at 3.5 means ten to the power of 3.5. That is about 3,162 dollars, a number most readers need a calculator to find. A log scale does that calculation for the reader: its ticks are already in dollars.
So the choice between the two is about what the quantity is. Take the logarithm of the column when that logarithm is itself the quantity of interest: a log-odds, a decibel, a pH. Use a log scale when the quantity is still dollars or people, and you only want to see it across orders of magnitude.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.2 The order of a scale and a transform
text:
22.2 The order of a scale and a transform
Once a transform is in the plot, a scale is no longer only about display, because a transform has to choose which numbers to work on. gog follows one rule, and it has no per-transform exceptions:

A transform groups by one axis and measures on the other. The scale is applied before the transform on the grouping axis, and after it on the measured axis.


22.2.1 Scaling the grouping axis
A histogram of income is the first plot where that rule changes the result. Its bins have to be cut somewhere, either in dollars or in the logarithms of those dollars.
bin groups by x, so a log x is applied first. The bins are cut on the logarithms, not on the dollars. Each bin then spans one constant ratio. Every bar is therefore the same width, and the bars fill the axis from end to end:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Bins cut in log space are evenly spaced")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Bins cut in log space are evenly spaced"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Bins cut in log space are evenly spaced")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Bins cut in log space are evenly spaced"))






                                 1K 10K   0 10 20  Bins cut in log space are evenly spaced Count GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp on a log scale.”
Suppose the bins had been cut in dollars and only the drawing had been logarithmic. The first bin alone would cover most of the axis, and the rest would crowd into the right edge. That reads as a mistake rather than as a modeling choice, which is why the grouping axis is scaled first.


22.2.2 The measured value keeps its own units
Put the log on the measured axis instead and a different question follows. Does a bar on a log scale stand for a sum of dollars, or for a sum of logarithms?
sum writes to y, so a log y is applied after the sum. The two bars in this plot stand for 100 and 10:

data(receipts) + bar * sum + x(store) + y(sales, scale = "log") +
  title("A sum is still a sum")


(data(receipts) + bar * sum + x(col.store) + y(col.sales, scale = "log") +
  title("A sum is still a sum"))


data(receipts) + bar * sum + x(:store) + y(:sales, scale = "log") +
  title("A sum is still a sum")


plot(data(receipts), layer(bar, sum), x(col.store),
  y(col.sales, { scale: "log" }), title("A sum is still a sum"))






                          North South   10 20 50 100  A sum is still a sum Sales Store





“Given the receipts: bars derived by sum, x is store, y is sales on a log scale.”
If the scale had been applied first, gog would have added the logarithms, giving the log of a product, which is not a quantity anyone asked for. gog adds the dollars first and scales the total afterwards, so sum reports a sum of dollars.
If you have used ggplot2, note the order, because ggplot2 does the opposite. Under scale_y_log10(), a stat_summary(fun = mean) averages the logarithms of the values. The result is a geometric mean, the average computed on the logarithms. gog computes the summary in your data’s units and scales the result, so the number the bar stands for is the number you would get by taking the sum or the mean yourself.


22.2.3 smooth: a curve on a log axis
The grouping axis raises the same question for smooth: is the curve fitted to dollars, or to their logarithms? On incomes that run from a few hundred dollars to nearly fifty thousand, the answer changes the shape of the curve.
smooth groups by x, so with a log x the curve is fitted against log income. Life expectancy rises by about the same amount for each tenfold rise in income, so the curve is close to a straight line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A trend fitted against log income")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A trend fitted against log income"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + line * smooth + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A trend fitted against log income")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, smooth),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("A trend fitted against log income"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, and also a line derived by smooth, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

22.3 What a log scale refuses
Some columns cannot take a log scale, and they are not rare: a depth that goes below zero, a balance that went negative, a count of zero.
A logarithm is undefined at zero and below, so rows with such values have no position on the axis. gog says so rather than dropping them quietly:

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.4 Choosing the base
Not every quantity is best read in powers of ten. Ten is the usual base for money and for population, but a pitch doubles with every octave, and a decay is counted in factors of e.
scale = "log" means base 10 unless you say otherwise:
x(freq, scale = "log", base = 2)
The base is a number, not a name. There is no "log2" or "ln" scale. One base argument already covers every base, so a separate name for each would add words without adding meaning. The same objection rules out ggplot2’s scale_x_log10 family.

22.4.1 The base changes the labels, not the picture
You might expect a new base to move the points. It does not move a single one. Any two logarithms of the same column differ by a constant factor, and gog normalizes every axis by its own range. The factor cancels, so the points land in the same places in every base. The transforms are unaffected too: bins of equal width in base 2 are equal width in base 10, so bar * bin cuts at the same values whichever base you name.
What the base actually chooses is where the gridlines fall and how they read. Here are six frequencies, each one an octave above the one before it, on base 10 and then base 2:

The points have not moved. The second plot puts a gridline on each doubling, which is what “an octave” means. So for pitch, bits, or doubling times, base 2 is the one whose labels name what you are counting.


22.4.2 Natural log
The natural base is for a quantity that decays at a constant rate. The amounts in the decay table shrink by a factor of e every hour, so there is one gridline between each reading and the next. A change by a factor of e is called an e-folding.
R has no constant named e, so you write base = exp(1). The other three bindings have one: Python’s math.e, Julia’s ℯ, and JavaScript’s Math.E.

  title("Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e"))






                                          1 e e² e³ e⁴   0 1 2 3 4 5  Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e Hours Amount remaining





Notice the labels: e, e², e³, e⁴, not 2.718, 7.389, 20.086, 54.598. That follows from one rule gog applies to every base:

Label the quantity when it is a short number; otherwise label the power.

Base 10 gives 1, 10, 100, 1K, 10K and so on, up to 100B. K means a thousand, M a million, and B a billion (10⁹). The letters stop at B, so 10¹² would read 1000B, with four digits before the letter. From 10¹² upward, a tick is labeled as a power instead, such as 10¹². Base 2 gives 1, 2, 4 and so on, up to 8388608. A number with more than seven digits is labeled as a power instead, such as 2²⁴. Base e has no short quantity above 1, so every tick past the first reads as a power, which is what a reader counting e-foldings wants. If instead you want the axis to read 0, 1, 2, 3 in ln units, you do not want a log scale at all. You want log() applied to the column, and an axis labeled in log units, like the log_gdp plot earlier in this chapter. A scale keeps the reader’s units; a column of logarithms changes them.
A base only means something as the base of a logarithm, so gog refuses one that has no log scale to belong to:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(octaves) + point + x(freq, base = 2) + y(level)


data(octaves) + point + x(col.freq, base = 2) + y(col.level)


data(octaves) + point + x(:freq, base = 2) + y(:level)


plot(data(octaves), point, x(col.freq, { base: 2 }), y(col.level))




Error:
! gog: `x(freq, base = …)` has no scale to be the base of. A base belongs to a logarithm — add `scale = "log"`, or remove the base.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.5 Time: a date column gets a calendar axis
text:
22.5 Time: a date column gets a calendar axis
A column of dates raises a question the other columns do not. Where do the ticks go, and what do they say, when the units are years and months rather than tens and hundreds?
The time scale is one you never have to write. A column of dates or date-times (Date or POSIXct in R) is temporal, because its type already says so. gog reads the calendar from the type, the same way a column of text already gets a categorical axis:



revenue: first 5 of 26 rows


day
sales




1994-06-30
52


1995-06-30
57


1996-06-30
55


1997-06-30
61


1998-06-30
64







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + line + x(day) + y(sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years")


(data(revenue) + line + x(col.day) + y(col.sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years"))


data(revenue) + line + x(:day) + y(:sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years")


plot(data(revenue), line, x(col.day), y(col.sales),
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years"))






                                 1995 2000 2005 2010 2015 2020   60 80 100  Twenty-six years, ticked in years Sales Day





The sentence names no scale at all. Writing scale = "time" is allowed and adds nothing, exactly like writing scale = "linear" on a number.
The ticks land on calendar boundaries, because the calendar is not decimal. An axis of years steps 1, 2 or 5 like any number line. For units smaller than a year those steps mean nothing: nobody reads an axis cut into fifths of a year. Months step by 1, 2, 3 or 6, and each of those divides twelve. A gridline therefore always falls on January, and a 3-month step marks each quarter. Days step by 1 or 2, and weeks by 1 or 2, always on Mondays. Hours and minutes step in the units a clock uses.



six_weeks: first 5 of 42 rows


day
orders
weekday
week




2024-03-01
20
Fri
Week 1


2024-03-02

2024-03-03

Mon

2024-03-05

Week 1







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# six_weeks is the cast's daily orders table, see the Preface
data(six_weeks) + line + x(day) + y(orders) +
  title("Six weeks, ticked on Mondays")


(data(six_weeks) + line + x(col.day) + y(col.orders) +
  title("Six weeks, ticked on Mondays"))


data(six_weeks) + line + x(:day) + y(:orders) +
  title("Six weeks, ticked on Mondays")


plot(data(six_weeks), line, x(col.day), y(col.orders),
  title("Six weeks, ticked on Mondays"))






                                     Mar 4 Mar 11 Mar 18 Mar 25 Apr 1 Apr 8   15 20 25 30 35  Six weeks, ticked on Mondays Orders Day





A tick is labeled at its own resolution: 2010 for a year step, Jan 2024 for a month step, Mar 4 for a day step. A column of dates never gets clock ticks, however narrow its range. A column of date-times (POSIXct in R) can, because it stores a time of day:



monitoring: first 5 of 37 rows


at
load




2024-03-04 06:00:00
40


2024-03-04 07:00:00
47


2024-03-04 08:00:00
54


2024-03-04 09:00:00
60


2024-03-04 10:00:00
65







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(monitoring) + line + x(at) + y(load) +
  title("A day and a half, ticked by the clock")


(data(monitoring) + line + x(col.at) + y(col.load) +
  title("A day and a half, ticked by the clock"))


data(monitoring) + line + x(:at) + y(:load) +
  title("A day and a half, ticked by the clock")


plot(data(monitoring), line, x(col.at), y(col.load),
  title("A day and a half, ticked by the clock"))






                                   06:00 12:00 18:00 Mar 5 06:00 12:00 18:00   20 40 60  A day and a half, ticked by the clock Load At





00:00 happens every day, so that label names no particular day. The midnight tick shows the date instead. Every other label on a time axis follows one rule: a tick is labeled at its own resolution, and it leaves out what it shares with its neighbors.

22.5.1 Bars on a date axis
Daily orders make a natural bar chart, one bar per day, and forty-two bars raise the question of where the ticks go.
Bars positioned at dates are an ordinary time series. The ticks still come from the calendar, and there is not a tick for every bar. Wilkinson’s stock-price example puts its ticks on Sundays rather than on every trading day (Wilkinson, 2005), and gog ticks these six weeks at the start of each week:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(day) + y(orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks")


(data(six_weeks) + bar + x(col.day) + y(col.orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks"))


data(six_weeks) + bar + x(:day) + y(:orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks")


plot(data(six_weeks), bar, x(col.day), y(col.orders),
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks"))






                                                                      Mar 4 Mar 11 Mar 18 Mar 25 Apr 1 Apr 8   0 10 20 30  Daily bars, weekly ticks Orders Day





A bar that measures a date is refused. A bar’s length is an amount, and a moment in time is not an amount. A bar “reaching” 2007 would be measured from 1970, the year a stored date counts from, which nobody chose as a baseline:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + bar + x(sales) + y(day)


data(revenue) + bar + x(col.sales) + y(col.day)


data(revenue) + bar + x(:sales) + y(:day)


plot(data(revenue), bar, x(col.sales), y(col.day))




Error:
! gog: `bar` measures its length along `day`, but that is a date column — a bar's length is an amount, and a moment in time is not an amount. Put the date on `x()` and measure a number, or use `point`/`line` for values that are dates.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.




22.5.2 What a time axis refuses
A date is stored as a number underneath. You might therefore expect a date to take a log scale, and a number to take a time scale. Neither is allowed.
A moment has no logarithm. The calendar’s zero is an arbitrary convention, and a logarithm measured from an arbitrary zero measures nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + line + x(day, scale = "log") + y(sales)


data(revenue) + line + x(col.day, scale = "log") + y(col.sales)


data(revenue) + line + x(:day, scale = "log") + y(:sales)


plot(data(revenue), line, x(col.day, { scale: "log" }), y(col.sales))




Error:
! gog: `x(day, scale = "log")` — `day` is a date column, and a moment in time has no logarithm: the calendar's zero is an arbitrary origin. Log the measured axis instead, or remove the scale.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


gog can read the calendar off a date column, but you cannot declare a plain number temporal at the binding. The engine cannot know whether a number like 20656 counts days, seconds, or years:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(revenue) + point + x(sales, scale = "time") + y(sales)


data(revenue) + point + x(col.sales, scale = "time") + y(col.sales)


data(revenue) + point + x(:sales, scale = "time") + y(:sales)


plot(data(revenue), point, x(col.sales, { scale: "time" }), y(col.sales))




Error:
! gog: `x(sales, scale = "time")` — `sales` is not a date column, and a number alone does not say what moment it is. Store it as dates, or as date-times, before plotting; gog reads the calendar from the column's type.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The fix belongs in the data, where the answer is known: convert the column to your language’s date or timestamp type, which in R is as.Date() or as.POSIXct().
For the same reason, a plain number cannot set the width of a bin on a time axis. bin(width = 7) does not say whether 7 counts days or seconds. The engine measures time in seconds, so these bins would be seven seconds wide, far too thin to see:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(day)


data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(col.day)


data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(:day)


plot(data(six_weeks), layer(bar, bin({ width: 7 })), x(col.day))




Error:
! gog: `bin(width = 7)` does not say what unit 7 is in, and `x(day)` holds dates. gog measures time in seconds, so these bins would be 7 seconds wide. Give the number of bins instead, such as `bin(30)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


To cut a time axis into bins, give the number of bins instead: bin(6) cuts these six weeks into six bins.
Time zones are never converted. The engine draws the clock time you gave it. In R, a POSIXct is formatted in its own time zone when it is drawn, so the axis shows the times your session showed you. In JavaScript, a Date is drawn as your computer’s clock shows it, in local time. If two series must share an axis, put them in one time zone before plotting; that decision belongs to the analysis, not the engine.


22.5.3 Time on the other channels
A scale answers how far along? on every channel that measures, and a date column is no exception. Coloring rows by how recent they are is common. An axis tick can read Mar 4, because the ticks beside it place it in a sequence. A legend row stands alone, so each row carries the full date:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + point + x(day) + y(orders) + color(day) +
  title("Recent days, darker")


(data(six_weeks) + point + x(col.day) + y(col.orders) + color(col.day) +
  title("Recent days, darker"))


data(six_weeks) + point + x(:day) + y(:orders) + color(:day) +
  title("Recent days, darker")


plot(data(six_weeks), point, x(col.day), y(col.orders), color(col.day),
  title("Recent days, darker"))






                                                                              Mar 4 Mar 11 Mar 18 Mar 25 Apr 1 Apr 8   15 20 25 30 35  Recent days, darker Orders Day  Day         2024-04-11 2024-03-21 2024-03-01

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.6 The scales
The chapter has used linear, log and time so far, and category comes later, in The column’s type picks the axis. The table names all four and what each one does.







Scale
What it does




linear
Equal steps for equal differences. The default


log
Equal steps for equal ratios, on x, y, color, size and opacity, with any base above 1


time
Positions dates and times, chosen from the column type: columns of dates and date-times, on every channel that measures


category
One slot per distinct value, chosen from the column type: columns of text, and columns with a declared order

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.7 The axis fits your data
Where should an axis end, on the data or on the next round number past it? Padding to a round number leaves part of the panel blank, and implies that the data reaches further than it does.
An axis shows round numbers on its ticks, but the range follows your data, not the round numbers. Each tick is a round number that falls inside the data, or at most a little past it into the margin. The axis does not extend to the next multiple of ten only to end on a round number. A span of 1952–2007 is drawn as 1952–2007, with ticks at 1960, 1980 and 2000, not padded to 1940–2020 with a third of the panel left blank:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(year) + y(life) +
  group(country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it")


(data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  group(col.country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it"))


data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), area, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ opacity: 0.4 }),
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it"))






                                   1960 1980 2000   0 20 40 60 80  The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: areas, x is year, y is life, grouped by country.”
Two more rules refine that fit. When the data sets an end, that end is a free end, and a free end leaves a small margin, so a glyph never touches the panel edge. A point at the exact maximum would otherwise be cut in half by that edge:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("No point touches the panel edge"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  No point touches the panel edge Life GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





A baseline gets no margin. The area of Asian life expectancies above shows it: the shape starts on the panel’s bottom edge, not a little way above it. When a bar or an area measures from zero, the zero is part of what it measures. A gap beneath it would show a stretch of axis below zero that no bar can reach, so the baseline sits on the panel edge. An area has no glyph for the edge to cut, so it runs from the left edge of the panel to the right. That is why the area plot above spans the full width while the scatterplot of incomes keeps its margins. An area ends exactly at its first and last values. A point’s circle reaches past its value by its radius, so it needs the margin.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.8 A scale is not only for axes
text:
22.8 A scale is not only for axes
Most of this chapter has put a scale on an axis. A color ramp can crowd its data into one end, just as a linear axis can crowd it into one corner of the panel. x and y turn a number into a position, but so do color, size and opacity: a ramp position, a radius, a transparency. All five answer how far along?, so all five take a scale. In three dimensions z takes a scale too, but it refuses log: see Space.
This matters most for a column spread across orders of magnitude. population runs from about 200 thousand to 1.3 billion. On a linear ramp the median country sits in the bottom one percent of that range, so nearly every point gets the same color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear color: nearly one flat color")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear color: nearly one flat color"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Linear color: nearly one flat color")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Linear color: nearly one flat color"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Linear color: nearly one flat color Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 659.4M 199.6K 







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log color: the whole ramp is used")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log color: the whole ramp is used"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Log color: the whole ramp is used")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("Log color: the whole ramp is used"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Log color: the whole ramp is used Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 16.2M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population on a log scale.”
The same is true of size, where a linear scale leaves almost every point at the minimum radius:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  size(population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  size(col.population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  size(:population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), size(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  style({ color: "steelblue" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Log size"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Log size Life GDP per person  Population    199.6K  16.2M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, size by population on a log scale.”
Look again at the middle row of each of the two color legends. On a linear ramp it is the arithmetic midpoint; on a log ramp it is the geometric one: √(min · max), about 16M rather than 660M. The label has to be the geometric midpoint, because it names the color painted at the middle of the ramp.
shape, pattern and group answer which one?, not how far along?: there is no distance between a circle and a square. So gog refuses scale on all three, as shown here for shape:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  shape(continent, scale = "log")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  shape(col.continent, scale = "log"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  shape(:continent, scale = "log")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  shape(col.continent, { scale: "log" }))




Error:
! gog: `scale` on `shape(continent)`: `shape` distinguishes categories rather than measuring them, so there is no scale for it to run along. Drop `scale`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.9 limits: stating the range yourself
Every rule so far takes the range from the data. That is the right default, but it is wrong when the data does not cover every value the axis should show. The range an axis should cover is its domain, and it is not always the range the data reaches. The tide table holds a gauge’s readings, one height every three hours from hour 1 to hour 22, so none falls at midnight. polar() draws an axis as a circle, and Polar teaches that space in full. Nothing in a column of hours tells that circle that hour 24 is the same place as hour 0. limits states the domain:



tide: first 5 of 8 rows


hour
height




1
2.1


4
4.4


7
3.6


10
1.2


13
0.9







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(tide) + line + x(hour, limits = c(0, 24)) + y(height) + polar() +
  title("The whole day, whatever hours the gauge recorded")


(data(tide) + line + x(col.hour, limits = [0, 24]) + y(col.height) + polar() +
  title("The whole day, whatever hours the gauge recorded"))


data(tide) + line + x(:hour, limits = [0, 24]) + y(:height) + polar() +
  title("The whole day, whatever hours the gauge recorded")


plot(data(tide), line, x(col.hour, { limits: [0, 24] }), y(col.height),
  polar(), title("The whole day, whatever hours the gauge recorded"))






                 0 10 20   1 2 3 4  The whole day, whatever hours the gauge recorded Height Hour





“Given the tide: a line, x is hour from 0 to 24, y is height, in polar.”
Without limits, one turn would cover only 1 to 22, and the first and last readings would be drawn on the same spoke. With limits, each hour sits at its share of the day: hour 6 a quarter of the way around, hour 12 halfway. The curve still does not close, and should not. The gauge took no reading at midnight, and a domain says what range the axis covers rather than inventing an observation. The gap is in the readings, and the plot shows it at its true size, the three hours from 22 to 1. Polar describes three cases: two in which the curve closes, and this one, in which it does not.
limits is written on the binding, beside scale and base, for the same reason they are: a domain belongs to one channel, and an atom of its own would name that channel twice. A stated end is drawn exactly where you state it. The margin exists to keep a glyph off the panel edge, and an end you chose is not a data extreme that needs the room.
A domain can widen the axis as easily as it narrows it. Nothing was dropped in that plot: the readings run 1 through 22 and all of them lie inside 0 through 24. Narrowing is the direction that removes rows, and gog reports how many rows it removes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, limits = c(0, 30000)) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A domain of 0 to $30,000")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, limits = [0, 30000]) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A domain of 0 to $30,000"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, limits = [0, 30000]) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A domain of 0 to \$30,000")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { limits: [0, 30000] }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("A domain of 0 to $30,000"))




gog: `x(gdp, limits = …)` excludes 20 of 142 rows, which fall outside [0, 30000]. Stating a domain is what removes them — widen the limits if they should be drawn.




                                                                                                                                                          0 10K 20K 30K   40 50 60 70 80  A domain of 0 to $30,000 Life GDP per person  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





The note above the plot is that report: it names how many rows fell outside and what the domain was. The plot still draws, because removing those rows is what you asked for, but gog does not remove data without saying so. Ask for a domain no row can satisfy and gog refuses instead, because the alternative is an empty panel with axes drawn over nothing.
Keeping every country on the page and marking one group of them is a different operation, and it has a different word. limits removes rows before the plot is drawn. brush removes nothing: it dims the rows outside its range. Selection shows the two side by side.
When a transform computes the values on an axis, as count does, a domain leaves out each bar or point whose value falls outside it. Here the count axis stops at 40, below Africa’s count of 52:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y(count, limits = c(0, 40))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + y(col.count, limits = [0, 40])


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  y(:count, limits = [0, 40])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  y(col.count, { limits: [0, 40] }))




gog: `y(count, limits = …)` leaves out 1 of 5 computed values, which fall outside [0, 40]. Stating a domain is what removes them — widen the limits if they should be drawn.




                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 10 20 30 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, y is count from 0 to 40.”
Africa keeps its label and has no bar. A bar stopped at the top edge would show 40, not 52. The note above the plot says how many values were left out, so the empty space above Africa does not mean zero.
You can state one end alone. The end you leave out stays a free end, which is how you start an axis at zero and let the top follow the data:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  title("y from zero, top still fitted to the data")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life, limits = [0, None]) +
  title("y from zero, top still fitted to the data"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(:continent) +
  y(:life, limits = [0, missing]) +
  title("y from zero, top still fitted to the data")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life, { limits: [0, null] }),
  title("y from zero, top still fitted to the data"))






                                       Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  y from zero, top still fitted to the data Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by mean, x is continent, y is life from 0.”
limits reaches more than the axes. A domain is a property of the scale, so it reaches every channel that measures. That is how you keep one color ramp the same across plots built from different data:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log", limits = c(1e5, 2e9)) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log", limits = [1e5, 2e9]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log", limits = [1e+05, 2e+09]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life),
  color(col.population, { scale: "log", limits: [1e+05, 2e+09] }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B Life GDP per person  Population         2B 14.1M 100K 





On a categorical axis limits is refused, and the refusal names the two ways to get what you meant. A category has no range to lie inside. Choosing which categories appear is filtering your table, and choosing what order they appear in is order().


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, limits = c(0, 3)) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent, limits = [0, 3]) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent, limits = [0, 3]) +
  y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean),
  x(col.continent, { limits: [0, 3] }), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent, limits = …)` — `continent` is text, and a category has no range to lie inside. To choose which categories appear, filter the table before plotting; to change the order they appear in, use `order(continent)`.
