title: 22  Scales
section: 22.10 The column’s type picks the axis
text:
22.10 The column’s type picks the axis
The time section showed a column of dates choosing its own axis without being asked. A column of text does the same, and this section states the rule behind both. Other tools make you name a scale whenever you want to change one, so you may expect to write scale = "category".
The four scales are not all chosen the same way. You ask for log. You do not ask for time or category. gog reads those off the column: a column of dates gets a calendar axis, and a column of text gets one slot per distinct value.
You may still write them. As with scale = "time" on a date column, writing scale = "category" on a categorical column is allowed and changes nothing. The plot below is identical to the same sentence with the scale left off:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, scale = "category") + y(life) +
  title("Writing it changes nothing")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent, scale = "category") + y(col.life) +
  title("Writing it changes nothing"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent, scale = "category") +
  y(:life) + title("Writing it changes nothing")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean),
  x(col.continent, { scale: "category" }), y(col.life),
  title("Writing it changes nothing"))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Writing it changes nothing Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent as a category, y is life.”
What you cannot do is use a scale to contradict the column. Ask for a categorical axis on a number and gog refuses:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "category") + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "category") + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "category") + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "category" }),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(gdp, scale = "category")` — a scale says how a measured column is placed; whether an axis measures at all is the column's type. Removing the scale alone would leave the continuous axis you were trying to escape. Store `gdp` as text or categories before plotting, and drop the scale. To cut the numbers into ranges instead, use `bin`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The reason behind that refusal also explains the others in this chapter. A scale says how a measured column is placed. The column’s type decides whether the axis measures at all. So log on a categorical column is refused, and time on a plain number is refused. A date column cannot be turned back into raw numbers by asking for linear either. None of those refusals offers another scale. Each tells you to change the column or remove the scale, because the column’s type is what the axis reads.
There are two things you might mean by “draw this number as categories”, and there is a different answer for each. For one slot per distinct value, declare the column’s categories: factor() in R and ordered() in the other three bindings, both shown in Data. For ranges, use bin, which cuts the numbers into intervals and is covered in Transforms.

title: 22  Scales
section: 22.11 tick_count: how many ticks the axis aims for
text:
22.11 tick_count: how many ticks the axis aims for
An axis picks about five ticks by default. After limits, the count is the second thing about an axis you can choose. A crowded axis is easier to read with fewer; an axis someone will take numbers from is easier with more. tick_count is written on the binding, beside scale, base and limits, and for the same reason. How many ticks an axis gets is a property of the scale, so it belongs to the sentence that describes the scale rather than to theme(), which controls the page.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A high count: for reading values off"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(col.life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A high count: for reading values off")))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("A high count: for reading values off"))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 12 }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("A high count: for reading values off")))






                                                                                                                                                                              0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80  A low count: the shape, not the numbers Life GDP per person


                                                                                                                                                                                       0 5K 10K 15K 20K 25K 30K 35K 40K 45K 50K    A high count: for reading values off GDP per person






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, beside the same with 12 ticks.”
The count is a target, not an exact number. The count sets the step between ticks, and the step is then rounded to 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten. So asking for eight ticks on an axis from 0 to 100 gives a step of 10, and eleven ticks. What you can rely on is the direction: a higher count never gives fewer ticks than a lower one. Every tick is a round number. The count also has an upper limit: an axis draws at most 26 ticks. If the rounded step would give more than 26 ticks, the engine uses a larger round step. The axis is still labeled from one end to the other, and a message names both steps.
Both panels in the plot above cover the same range. That is the rule the count obeys: it changes how densely an axis is labeled, never where the axis stops. Ask for two ticks and the axis does not shrink to the two values it draws.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year, tick_count = 2) + y(life) +
  group(country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year, tick_count = 2) + y(col.life) +
  group(col.country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year, tick_count = 2) + y(:life) +
  group(:country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year, { tick_count: 2 }),
  y(col.life), group(col.country), style({ opacity: 0.4 }),
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007"))






                                 1950 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007 Life Year





A log axis and a date axis take a count too, but their steps are rounded to different values. On a log axis the ticks can be at every power of the base, or skip one or more powers between them. In base 10 they can also be at 1, 2 and 5 times each power. A date axis uses calendar steps, such as a day, a week, a month or a year. The time section describes these steps. On these two axes, the engine picks the step whose number of ticks is closest to your count.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log", tick_count = 12) + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Seven ticks: 1, 2 and 5 times each power")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log", tick_count = 12) + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Seven ticks: 1, 2 and 5 times each power"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log", tick_count = 12) +
  y(:life) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Seven ticks: 1, 2 and 5 times each power")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point,
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log", tick_count: 12 }), y(col.life),
  x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Seven ticks: 1, 2 and 5 times each power"))






                                                                                                                                                                                    500 1K 2K 5K 10K 20K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Seven ticks: 1, 2 and 5 times each power Life GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale with 12 ticks, y is life.”
The sentence asks for twelve ticks, and the axis draws seven. In base 10 no log step is finer than 1, 2 and 5 times each power, so seven is the closest count to twelve. Without a count, this axis reads only 1K and 10K, as at the start of the chapter.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(six_weeks) + line + x(day, tick_count = 3) + y(orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks")


(data(six_weeks) + line + x(col.day, tick_count = 3) + y(col.orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks"))


data(six_weeks) + line + x(:day, tick_count = 3) + y(:orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks")


plot(data(six_weeks), line, x(col.day, { tick_count: 3 }), y(col.orders),
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks"))






                               Mar 4 Mar 18 Apr 1   15 20 25 30 35  Three ticks: one every two weeks Orders Day





“Given the six weeks table: a line, x is day with 3 ticks, y is orders.”
By default these six weeks get a tick every Monday, six in all. Asked for three, the axis steps two weeks at a time, still on Mondays.
A categorical axis has one place per category, so the data sets the count and you do not. The refusal names the same two fixes the limits refusal named:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, tick_count = 3) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent, tick_count = 3) +
  y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean),
  x(col.continent, { tick_count: 3 }), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent, tick_count = 3)` — `continent` is text, and a categorical axis has one tick per category, so the count is the data's rather than yours. To change which categories appear, filter the table before plotting; to change their order, use `order(continent)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A legend is not an axis, and it takes no tick count. limits reaches every channel that measures, because every one of them has a domain; tick_count reaches only the three position channels that draw an axis: x, y and z. A color legend names three rows, both ends and the middle, and the scale, linear or log, sets their values, not a count you choose. The middle row is the midpoint explained above: the label for the color painted halfway along the ramp. So gog refuses a tick count on color(), size() or opacity(), the same way it refuses scale and limits on shape(): there is nothing for the count to describe.

22.11.1 Crowding in the plane and in the cube
A flat panel and a cube follow one rule for crowded numbers: no number may be printed over another. A flat continuous axis draws every tick it chose, as long as no two numbers overlap. Where panels are side by side, an end number that would reach past its panel is moved inward. In narrow panels, such as the five panels of a plot faceted by continent (Faceting), the numbers can still overlap. The axis then draws fewer numbers, and the ticks and gridlines of the others are left out too. The numbers it keeps are the ones a larger round step would choose, so 0, 10K, 20K, 30K and 40K become 0, 20K and 40K. A number left out can be read from the numbers on either side, so no message is printed. If you stated a tick_count, a message says how many ticks were drawn. A polar plot, a map, and an axis freed with free = TRUE still draw every number they chose.
The sentence below asks for twelve ticks, but each panel has room for three, and a message says so:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(life) |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(:life) |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 12 }),
  y(col.life), across(col.continent))




gog: `x(gdp, tick_count = 12)` asks for about 12 ticks, and the 11 ticks it chose do not fit side by side at this size, so 3 of them are drawn. A smaller `tick_count`, or a wider plot (`theme(width = )`), draws them all.




                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 12 ticks, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
A cube can also have too little room for its numbers. In a 3-D plot (Space), each axis is longer or shorter depending on the viewing angle. Turning the cube lengthens one axis and shortens another. The cube then draws as many numbers as fit and leaves the rest out. When a count you stated cannot fit, the engine says so rather than quietly drawing fewer.
Names on a categorical axis follow the same rule: no name may be printed over another. The axis tries to name every category, and a name is usually much wider than a number. When names do not fit side by side, a flat axis first turns them 90 degrees, to read upward. A turned name needs room along the axis only for its height, not its width. When even turned names are too close, the flat axis leaves some out, as the cube does. It draws one name in every two or three, each with its tick, and prints a message. The 142 countries of 2007 do not fit, even turned:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(country) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(:country) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), bar, x(col.country), y(col.life))




gog: the 142 names of `country` on the x axis do not fit side by side, even turned to read upward: they are 5.1px apart, and a name needs 8.9px. One in every 2 is drawn (71 of 142), with its tick; the rest keep their places, unnamed. To name every one, swap the two axes so `country` runs down the y axis, in a taller plot (`theme(height = 1330)`), or draw fewer rows.

Cote d'Ivoire Cuba Denmark Dominican Republic Egypt Equatorial Guinea Ethiopia France Gambia Ghana Guatemala Guinea-Bissau Honduras Hungary India Iran Ireland Italy Japan Kenya Korea, Rep. Lebanon Liberia Madagascar Malaysia Mauritania Mexico Montenegro Mozambique Namibia Netherlands Nicaragua Nigeria Oman Panama Peru Poland Puerto Rico Romania Sao Tome and Principe Senegal Sierra Leone Slovak Republic Somalia Spain Sudan Sweden Syria Tanzania Togo Tunisia Uganda United States Venezuela West Bank and Gaza Zambia   0 20 40 60 80  Life Country





Every bar is still drawn, and a bar without a name keeps its place between two named ones. The message gives two ways to name every country: put country on the y axis in a taller plot, or draw fewer rows.

22.12 axis: leaving an axis out
An axis lets a reader decode a position, as a legend lets a reader decode a color. Sometimes the reader does not need it. On a map, a reader finds a place by its shape and its neighbors, not by its longitude and latitude. Write axis = FALSE on the binding, beside scale and limits, and the axis is left out: its tick marks, its numbers and its name.   group(piece) + map() + title("The coastlines, without axes")

“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon without an axis, y is lat without an axis, grouped by piece, in the map space.”
The scale is unchanged, so every point is drawn where it would be with the axes. The panel takes the room the axes would have used. The gridlines stay, and so does the frame: the two lines along the bottom and the left of the panel. Both belong to the whole plot rather than to one axis. theme() removes them with grid = "none" and frame = "none". In Map, three small maps of Ohio leave out both axes, the gridlines and the frame.
axis is written on the three positions, x, y and z, because they are the channels that draw an axis. On any other channel gog refuses it and names the three. The name is part of the axis, so gog refuses x_label() for an axis that is left out, even x_label(""):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  x_label("GDP per person")

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.13 In short
A scale changes where a number lands on the axis. It never changes the number itself. limits states the domain: narrowing it removes rows and reports how many, while a brush removes none. tick_count is a target, not an exact number. A crowded continuous axis, flat or in a cube, draws fewer numbers. A crowded categorical axis turns its names, then leaves some out and says so. axis = FALSE leaves an axis out and keeps its scale.

title: 22  Scales
text:
22.14 What comes next
A scale decides how far along a channel a number lands. It does not decide which visual property shows the column. Channels covers that: which property carries a column, and what guide it gets.




Wilkinson, L. (2005). The grammar of graphics (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.1 color
Which visual property should carry which column? A channel binds a data column to a visual property of a mark, and the channels do not all do the same work. x, y and z are the vowels: without one a mark does not render. Five other channels get a legend: color, size, shape, pattern and opacity. Those five are the final consonants, the optional ㅁ (m) that turns 가 (ga) into 감 (gam): never required, and each one changes what the plot says. Every channel atom has the same form:
No exceptions. x and y are channels too: the same rule applies everywhere.
Different fields use different words for this, so you may know it by another name. Bertin wrote the vocabulary down first, in Sémiologie graphique (Bertin, 1967). He separated the two dimensions of the page from six retinal variables: size, value (his word for lightness), texture, color, orientation, and shape. The eye does not read the two groups the same way. Wilkinson and ggplot2 both say aesthetic, which is why ggplot2 code has aes() and gog code has nothing like it. The visualization literature chose channel instead, paired with the mark it modifies (Munzner, 2014), and that is the word gog uses. In everyday English, a channel carries a signal. Here the column is the signal, and color or size is the channel that carries it to the reader. Choosing an everyday word follows gog’s Plain Names law. Encoding is the same idea named as an act rather than a thing, and this book keeps both words. A channel is what you write; an encoding is what it does. Encoding scope is about the second.
A legend is generated automatically whenever one of the five refining channels (color, size, shape, pattern, opacity) is bound to a column, with no configuration required. x, y and z get an axis instead, and group gets neither: it splits a mark without encoding anything, so there is nothing for a legend to decode. label belongs to the text mark, and play has a chapter of its own.
Which points belong together? A plain scatter cannot say, so the grouping has to come from a column.
color(field) maps a column to color, and a legend appears automatically. On point, line, step, path, zone and surface it takes either kind of column, and the kind decides what color means. On the other marks it takes only a categorical column.
It is spelled color, and only color. gog writes American English throughout and accepts no second spelling, so colour, which ggplot2 accepts, does not exist here. Writing it is refused, and the refusal names the fix (see Law 3).
A categorical column answers “which one?” Each category gets its own color from the palette:

A continuous column answers “how much?” Its values run along a ramp. A ramp is a range of colors that a number is placed along, the way an axis is a range of positions. This one runs light to dark, and the legend is the ramp itself, labeled at its minimum, midpoint, and maximum:

Notice the legend: color gets one continuous strip. The size and opacity legends later in this chapter show three sampled examples instead. A legend should show the scale. A range of colors fits in one strip, but there is no way to draw a continuum of circles. The rule is the same for every channel; only the form of the legend changes. The difference matters most for a multi-hue ramp. Three sampled colors from viridis, one of the ramps below, say nothing about the colors between them. Three circles of growing size do, because a reader can imagine the sizes in between and cannot imagine the colors.
The default ramp is one hue, not a rainbow, and that is deliberate. A sequential ramp, one that runs from low values to high, encodes magnitude. A reader reads a darker color as more, so lightness is what such a ramp varies. One hue running light to dark is read quickly, stays readable in grayscale and under color blindness, and matches the categorical palette when both appear in one figure. A rainbow encodes magnitude as hue, which has no intrinsic order, so the reader has to consult the legend for every point. gog’s default is a single blue built on the same hue as the first categorical color, so the two scales read as one system. Ramps has the multi-hue alternatives, and the sections after it have the diverging ramps and the ramps you build from colors you choose.

23.3 shape
A journal prints your figure in black and white, and the colors you chose print as grays that look almost the same. The grouping has to come from the glyph instead.
shape(field) maps a categorical column to one of seven glyphs: circle, square, triangle, diamond, cross, star, wye (a Y shape). Seven is the whole set. It is also about as many shapes as a reader can recognize quickly. Map shape to a column with more than seven categories and the eighth category starts again at the circle. Two categories then share a glyph, and gog prints a message to say so. The Shape section of the point chapter shows what to do when a column has more than seven categories.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  shape(continent)

  shape(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + shape(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  shape(col.continent))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, shape by continent.”
color and shape can be bound to the same column. Binding one column to two channels is redundant encoding, and it makes the plot easier to read:

  color(continent) + shape(continent)

  color(col.continent) + shape(col.continent))

  shape(:continent)

Either channel alone would separate the continents. Using both separates them in two ways, so a reader who cannot see the colors still has the shapes. gog draws one legend for the two, with each glyph in its continent’s color.

23.4 pattern
shape answers the black-and-white problem for points. A bar or a line has no glyph to change, so it needs a different answer, and that answer is texture.
pattern(field) maps a categorical column to a texture, the way shape maps one to a glyph. The mark’s geometry decides which one: a hatch, a repeated pattern of lines or dots, on the filled regions (bar, box, area, ribbon, zone), and a dash on the strokes (line, step, interval, path, rule, edge). Textures do not depend on color, so they work in grayscale and for a colorblind reader. The first category is always the plain one (solid), the rest textured:

title: 23  Channels and legends

23.5 opacity
Sometimes a number should decide how faint a mark is drawn, so that small values fade and large ones stay opaque.
opacity(field) maps a continuous column to transparency: a larger value draws a more opaque mark.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + opacity(population) +
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more solidly")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + opacity(col.population) +
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more solidly"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + opacity(:population) +
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more solidly")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.population),
  title("Opacity: larger populations drawn more solidly"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Opacity: larger populations drawn more solidly Life Gdp  Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, opacity by population.”
Only China and India are drawn nearly opaque, because their populations are several times larger than any other country’s. A ramp on a skewed column shows the fix, a log scale, and it works on opacity too.
Mapped opacities run from 0.15 to 0.95 rather than 0 to 1: a fully transparent mark is invisible, which is never what a reader wants. With no opacity binding, a filled mark is drawn at 0.82 so that overlapping fills show through each other, while most strokes and a text are drawn fully opaque. A zone sets its own: a highlight is drawn pale so the plot behind it shows, and a zone of cells, such as the heatmaps below, is drawn fully opaque. style(opacity = ) overrides any of them.
Like size, opacity produces a legend showing the minimum, midpoint, and maximum of the column.
On line, opacity cannot be mapped: a stroke has one opacity, and one value cannot carry a column. This is the same rule that refuses a per-row size on a line, not a special case for opacity:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + opacity(population)

plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  opacity(col.population))

gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


That one stroke still has an opacity, so you can set it for the whole line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(opacity = 0.4)

  style(opacity = 0.4))

  style(opacity = 0.4)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ opacity: 0.4 }))

“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, with opacity 0.4.”
To split the rows into one line per country, use group, as above; to give each line its own color as well, use color.
That refusal looks like an inconsistency: color maps onto a line and opacity does not. It is not one. A width, an opacity and a dash are properties of the whole stroke: ask where along the line the width is 3px and the question has no answer. A color is not like that. You can point at one place on a line and ask what color it is, so a measure can vary along it, and color on line, step and path accepts either kind of column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  color(gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person")

  color(col.gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  color(:gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), color(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  palette("viridis"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One line per country, colored by GDP per person"))






                                                                                     1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  One line per country, colored by GDP per person Life expectancy Year  Gdp            31.7K 3560.4 400.4 





“Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, color by gdp on a log scale, with the viridis palette.”
A category on color splits the mark into one stroke per group. A measure varies the color along each stroke and gets a ramp legend, not one swatch (a small sample of the color) per series. One channel and one mark give two behaviors, and the column’s type decides which behavior you get. group still splits the mark either way, which is why the sentence above draws one line per country and runs the ramp along each line. See Setting vs mapping.

23.6 group
The section above used group twice without saying what it does. It is the one channel that splits a mark and encodes nothing.
group(field) splits the mark into one series per value in the column. On a line, that is one stroke per value, and every stroke gets the same color. Use it when the lines must be kept apart but one color is what you want.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) +
  group(country)


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  group(col.country))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Life Year





When you want color and grouping, use a categorical color(field) alone: it implies grouping automatically.

title: 23  Channels and legends

23.7 Multiple channels
Two positions and one refining channel carry three columns. A table usually has a fourth you want on the page.
You have already seen two refining channels on one mark several times. Channels compose freely, so you can bind more of them at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Two positions and three refining channels
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) + shape(continent) +
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + size(col.population) + shape(col.continent) +
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  size(:population) + shape(:continent) +
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007")

  color(col.continent), size(col.population), shape(col.continent),
  title("GDP and life expectancy, 2007"))

Five channels carry four columns here. The three refining channels draw only two legends, because shape repeats color and the two share one. Each column on a refining channel adds a legend for the reader to check. So add a channel only when the plot needs its column, or when it makes a column easier to read, as shape does here.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.8 Palettes
Most plots so far used the colors gog chose by default. To choose your own, use palette().
palette() chooses the colors the color channel assigns. There is no separate atom for ramps, which ggplot2 calls gradients. One atom serves both, because the column’s type decides which meaning the colors get. For a categorical column, gog reads a set of colors as one color per category. For a continuous column, it reads the same set as stops, the fixed colors a ramp passes through.
There are three kinds of named palette, and they say three different things: a categorical palette gives each category its own color, a sequential ramp runs from low values to high, and a diverging ramp measures distance from a center in either direction. The type of the column decides which kinds you may name: a categorical column takes a categorical palette, and a continuous column takes a sequential or a diverging ramp. The sections below follow that order.
gog’s default palette holds 20 colors, which is more than most tables need. When a column has more categories than that, gog builds the extra colors from the HSL color wheel (hue, saturation and lightness), which places every hue around a circle. No two categories share a color.

23.8.1 Categorical palettes
Most of the time the default is what you want. You change it when a reader may be colorblind, when a journal requires particular colors, or when the marks are large enough that the default is too strong.
A categorical palette gives one color to each category, so a reader matches a swatch in the legend to a name. gog provides three, and the last column says which one to pick:



Name
Colors
Best for




"gog"
20 (default)
General use


"okabe"
8 base + 8 light variants
Colorblind accessibility


"soft"
8, lighter
Filled marks: bars, areas, zones



"okabe" is Okabe and Ito’s set (Okabe & Ito, 2008), chosen so that its eight colors stay distinct for readers with the common forms of color blindness. gog adds eight lighter versions of these colors, used when a column has more than eight categories:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("okabe")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("okabe"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("okabe")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("okabe"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





The default is designed for points and lines, where a color occupies a few pixels and must stay visible at reading distance. A fill is large, so it is already easy to see, and a color strong enough to make a small point easy to find is more than a bar needs. In a row of such bars, the strong color takes attention away from the heights, which are what the bars show. soft is a different set of eight colors, lighter than the default. Compare these two. Apart from the title, the palette is the only difference:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  title("The default, over filled bars")

  title("The default, over filled bars"))

  title("The default, over filled bars")

  color(col.continent), title("The default, over filled bars"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, color by continent.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + color(continent) +
  palette("soft") + title("palette(\"soft\")")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + color(col.continent) +
  palette("soft") + title("palette(\"soft\")"))

  palette("soft") + title("palette(\"soft\")")

  color(col.continent), palette("soft"), title("palette(\"soft\")"))

The default still works on bars, and on a scatter of the same data it would be the better choice. The difference is what the color is doing: a point has to be easy to find, while a bar is already visible and only has to differ from its neighbors.


23.8.2 Sequential ramps
A continuous column has no categories to give a color to, so a palette has to mean something else. For a continuous color column, palette() names a ramp instead. The ramps below run one way, from low values to high. Lightness changes steadily along the ramp, and that is what shows the order.








Name
What it is
Use it when




"blue"
the default: one hue, light→dark
almost always


"viridis"
many hues, with equal color steps for equal value steps
dense data where small differences must stay visible


"magma"
viridis’s family: black through purple to cream
a dark plot with strong contrast


"inferno"
the same family: black through red and orange to pale yellow
as for magma, with more red and orange


"plasma"
the same family, blue through magenta to yellow
a dark plot with strong contrast, starting at dark blue rather than black


"cividis"
the family’s colorblind-optimized member
the ramp itself has to stay readable under two-color vision (dichromacy)


"gray"
no hue at all: light gray to near-black
figures that will be printed in black and white

The volcano is cut into cells, each colored by its mean elevation. A dense grid of continuous values like this is what a ramp is for. palette() is a property of the plot, so six ramps means six plots, and | and / put them on one page:

“Given Maunga Whau: zones derived by bin into 16 and mean, x is east, y is north, color by elevation, with the viridis palette, beside the same with magma; above the same pair with inferno and plasma; above the same pair with cividis and gray.”
That is the same sentence six times with one word changed. It is written out in full because a loop or a variable is written differently in each of the book’s four languages.
Those six plots show four things, one in each paragraph.
gray runs from light to dark, and the other five run from dark to light. In the gray plot the summit is dark, while in the other five it is bright. Both directions are correct. gog’s own ramps (gray and the default blue) run light to dark, because with one hue a darker color reads as a larger value, and a photocopier keeps those lightness differences. The viridis-family ramps run dark to light because their designers made them that way, and reversing them would give a ramp named magma that no longer looks like magma. In any plot, the legend shows which end is high: its top label names the value at that end of the ramp.
Of the five viridis-family ramps, magma and inferno end on a near-white. magma’s last stop is nearly the same color as the panel behind it, so the very top of the scale almost disappears. You can see this in the pale, flat summits in the magma and inferno plots. The viridis family ends on very light colors by design. blue and gray never reach white, so their pale end stays visible against the panel, and that is why blue is the default rather than one of these.
cividis uses the fewest hues of the five, and that is deliberate: it uses only the two that stay distinct under the common forms of color blindness. The other four run through many more, so they separate neighboring values by hue as well as by lightness. cividis separates them mostly by lightness, and that loss is acceptable whenever the ramp has to stay readable for a colorblind reader.
gray is for the figure that will be photocopied. It is a ramp only, and there is no categorical gray palette. Grays differ only in lightness, so readers can distinguish only a few of them. For categories in a print figure, use shape on points and pattern on bars and lines, which separate them and leave the color channel free. gog refuses palette("gray") on a categorical column, and the refusal says why:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("gray")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("gray"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("gray")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("gray"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("gray")` is a sequential ramp for numbers, but `color` is bound to a text column. Use a categorical palette — `gog`, `okabe`, or `soft` — or list one color per category. For categories in a figure that has to print in black and white, reach for `shape(<column>)` instead — it tells them apart without spending color.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.




23.8.3 Diverging ramps
A sequential ramp means more. A diverging ramp means away from a center, in two directions. A change, a residual, a correlation and an anomaly all fall on both sides of zero. gog provides two:








Name
What it is
Use it when




"blue_red"
blue → neutral → red
the usual choice


"brown_teal"
brown → neutral → teal
the sign of the value is what matters, and readers may be colorblind



The name reads low to high, so blue_red paints the smallest values blue and the largest red. Both pass through the same gray at the center of the scale.
The palette does not decide which value gets the neutral color. That value is the middle of the scale’s domain, which limits sets. Without limits, the middle falls on the data’s own midpoint. Here delta runs from -32 to 120, so the midpoint is 44. That value is painted gray, and zero is painted blue.



cashflow: first 5 of 6 rows

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(cashflow) + point + x(step) + y(delta) +
  color(delta) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0")


(data(cashflow) + point + x(col.step) + y(col.delta) +
  color(col.delta) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0"))


data(cashflow) + point + x(:step) + y(:delta) + color(:delta) +
  palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0")


plot(data(cashflow), point, x(col.step), y(col.delta), color(col.delta),
  palette("blue_red"), style({ size: 9 }),
  title("44 is painted gray, not 0"))






                                      Opening Sales Refunds Costs Tax Closing   0 50 100  44 is painted gray, not 0 Delta Step  Delta           120 44 -32 





State a symmetric domain and zero becomes the center of the scale, so zero is the value painted gray. Read the “Closing” point, which is exactly zero:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(cashflow) + point + x(step) + y(delta) +
  color(delta, limits = c(-120, 120)) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray")


(data(cashflow) + point + x(col.step) + y(col.delta) +
  color(col.delta, limits = [-120, 120]) + palette("blue_red") + style(size = 9) +
  title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray"))


data(cashflow) + point + x(:step) + y(:delta) +
  color(:delta, limits = [-120, 120]) + palette("blue_red") +
  style(size = 9) + title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray")


plot(data(cashflow), point, x(col.step), y(col.delta),
  color(col.delta, { limits: [-120, 120] }), palette("blue_red"),
  style({ size: 9 }), title("Symmetric limits paint zero gray"))






                                      Opening Sales Refunds Costs Tax Closing   0 50 100  Symmetric limits paint zero gray Delta Step  Delta           120 0 -120 





“Given the cashflow table: points, x is step, y is delta, color by delta from -120 to 120, with the blue red palette.”
Two things follow from centering the ramp with limits. The ramp stays linear: equal distance in color is equal distance in the data on both sides of the center. Some scales set a midpoint and then rescale each side to the data’s own ends, and a scale built that way is no longer linear. And limits removes rows outside it, so the domain has to be wide enough to hold the data: c(-50, 50) here would drop the opening balance, and gog would say so.
Symmetric limits have one drawback. If a column runs from -2 to 100, limits of -100 to 100 leave almost all of the blue half unused, because the data reaches only a little way below zero. Accept that when the sign is what matters, since zero has to be painted gray. When the sign does not matter, a sequential ramp such as blue uses its whole range.


23.8.4 Stops of your own
Sometimes you need a ramp between two particular colors, and no named ramp runs between them. Pass those colors to palette(): they become the stops, and gog fills in the colors between them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(life) + palette(c("white", "navy")) + style(size = 6) +
  title("Custom stops")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.life) + palette(["white", "navy"]) + style(size = 6) +
  title("Custom stops"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:life) +
  palette(["white", "navy"]) + style(size = 6) + title("Custom stops")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.life), palette(["white", "navy"]), style({ size: 6 }),
  title("Custom stops"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by life, with a palette of white and navy.”
gog refuses a palette that does not match the column, rather than guessing what you meant. A categorical palette cannot serve a continuous column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(life) + palette("okabe")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.life) + palette("okabe"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:life) +
  palette("okabe")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.life), palette("okabe"))

Use a ramp — `blue`, `viridis`, `magma`, `inferno`, `plasma`, `cividis`, or `gray` run one way, `blue_red` or `brown_teal` diverge from a center — or give `palette()` your own stops, the colors themselves, such as "white" and "navy".

23.8.5 A ramp on a skewed column
No ramp reads well on a skewed column, and changing the palette does not fix it. A linear ramp spreads its colors evenly across the domain, so when most rows sit in a narrow part of it they all receive almost the same color. When you color by population, nearly every country falls at the light end:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(population) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.population) +
  x_label("GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:population) +
  x_label("GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.population), x_label("GDP per person"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 659.4M 199.6K 





The two dark points are China and India, whose populations are several times larger than any other country’s. The cause is the data, not the palette, so the fix is a log scale on the channel, and on x as well, since GDP per person is skewed the same way:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log") + x_label("GDP per person")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life GDP per person  Population         1.3B 16.2M 199.6K 





On the log scale the colors spread along the whole ramp, so countries of different sizes get different colors.
color, size and opacity all take scale =, because all three answer “how far along?”. gog refuses it on shape, pattern and group: they answer “which one?”.


23.8.6 Custom colors
Often the colors are decided before you begin: a journal asks for them, or an earlier figure already used them.
Pass the colors yourself: hex values, CSS color names such as firebrick, or a mix of the two:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  palette(c("#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) +
  palette(["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette(["#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#4daf4a", "#984ea3", "#ff7f00"]))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





The same call takes CSS color names, which are easier to recognize when you read the code later:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  palette(c("firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple", "darkorange"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) +
  palette(["firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple", "darkorange"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple", "darkorange"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette(["firebrick", "steelblue", "seagreen", "rebeccapurple",
  "darkorange"]))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





gog refuses a color it cannot recognize, and offers the nearest match. Otherwise the misspelled name would go into the plot, and a browser draws an unknown color as black:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette(c("firebrick", "stelblue"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette(["firebrick", "stelblue"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["firebrick", "stelblue"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette(["firebrick", "stelblue"]))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` entry "stelblue" is not a color. Did you mean "steelblue"? Use a CSS color name, or a hex value like "#4e79a7".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Colors are assigned in first-appearance order: the first unique value gets the first palette color, the second gets the second, and so on. If the column declares its order, that order is used instead. Either way, the same rows in the same order always get the same colors.
One mistake to know about: a single color is not a palette. palette() reads a single word as a palette name, and "red" is not one. What palette("red") attempts is one constant color, which is style(color = "red"):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("red"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("red")` is not a known palette. Named palettes are gog, okabe, soft for categories; blue, viridis, magma, inferno, plasma, cividis, gray for numbers; blue_red, brown_teal for numbers that diverge from a center. `"red"` is a color, not a palette. To paint every mark one color use `style(color = "red")`; to give each category its own color, give `palette()` several colors, "red" among them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.




23.8.7 Colors by name
Colors passed without names are assigned in first-appearance order, so a category’s color depends on where it falls in that order. Sorting the rows can change a category’s color, and so can another table that lists the categories in a different order. Two plots placed side by side in a report then disagree about which color a continent is. To assign a color to a category, write the category’s name beside the color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c(Africa = "seagreen", Americas = "goldenrod", Asia = "tomato",
            Europe = "steelblue", Oceania = "orchid"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette({"Africa": "seagreen", "Americas": "goldenrod", "Asia": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue", "Oceania": "orchid"}))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["Africa" => "seagreen", "Americas" => "goldenrod", "Asia" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue", "Oceania" => "orchid"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette({ Africa: "seagreen", Americas: "goldenrod", Asia: "tomato",
  Europe: "steelblue", Oceania: "orchid" }))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with a palette naming Africa seagreen, Americas goldenrod, Asia tomato, Europe steelblue and Oceania orchid.”
Each continent now takes the color written beside its name, whatever order the rows arrive in. The legend still lists the continents in first-appearance order, with Asia first. Once colors are named, the names and the categories must match. A name that is not a category would color nothing. A category without a name would get a color nobody chose. gog refuses both. So a palette that names all five continents is refused on a table that holds only three, unless the column’s declared order includes all five. Usually a mismatch is a misspelled name, and the message suggests the category you probably meant:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c(Africa = "seagreen", Americas = "goldenrod", Asai = "tomato",
            Europe = "steelblue", Oceania = "orchid"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette({"Africa": "seagreen", "Americas": "goldenrod", "Asai": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue", "Oceania": "orchid"}))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["Africa" => "seagreen", "Americas" => "goldenrod", "Asai" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue", "Oceania" => "orchid"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette({ Africa: "seagreen", Americas: "goldenrod", Asai: "tomato",
  Europe: "steelblue", Oceania: "orchid" }))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` names "Asai", and `continent` has no level called that, so its color would go to nothing. Did you mean "Asia"? The levels of `continent` are "Asia", "Europe", "Africa", "Americas", and "Oceania".

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.9 Legend placement
Every plot above that maps a refining channel drew a legend automatically, to the right of the panel. The panel shrinks by itself to make room, so there is no margin to set. To move all of a plot’s legends to another side, write theme(legend = ) with "bottom", "top" or "left". Above or below the panel, a legend’s entries are placed side by side, and they continue on a new line when the plot is too narrow. The panel then gets shorter instead of narrower. The legend of a continuous color is drawn horizontally there, with the smallest value on the left. Style draws a plot with its legend below the panel. A legend too big for the plot is left out rather than drawn outside the image. gog says so, and names the theme() width or height that would give it room.

23.9.1 Leaving a legend out
A legend decodes a channel, and sometimes an axis already decodes the same channel. Here color and x map the same column, so the axis already names the continent under every bar. A legend would repeat those names. Write legend = FALSE on the channel and the legend is left out:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  color(continent, legend = FALSE)


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  color(col.continent, legend = False))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  color(:continent, legend = false)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  color(col.continent, { legend: false }))






                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, color by continent, without a legend.”
The bars keep their colors, because the channel still maps the column. Only the legend is gone, and the panel takes the legend’s space. legend belongs to the five refining channels, the ones that draw a legend. x, y and z are read from their axes, and group, label and play draw no legend. gog refuses legend on all six:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent, legend = FALSE)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent, legend = False)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent, legend = false)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count),
  x(col.continent, { legend: false }))




Error:
! gog: `x(continent)` is given `legend` — `x` is read off its axis, so there is no legend to show or leave out. `legend` belongs on the five channels that draw one: `color`, `size`, `shape`, `pattern` and `opacity`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A legend is one kind of guide, the part of a plot that decodes a channel. A position’s guide is its axis, and axis = FALSE on the position leaves it out, as Scales shows.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.10 In short
A channel takes a column, never a value: gog refuses color("red") and points to style(). The five refining channels get a legend, and x, y and z get an axis; legend = FALSE and axis = FALSE leave them out. group and label get neither, and play gets a strip that names the frame. A mark’s geometry decides which channels it accepts. palette() chooses the colors: a categorical palette for a categorical column, a ramp for a continuous one.

title: 23  Channels and legends
text:
23.11 What comes next
Every channel here reads a column, so every plot answers a question about the data. Setting vs mapping covers the opposite case: a value you choose yourself, which reads no column and gets no legend.




Bertin, J. (1967). Sémiologie graphique: Les diagrammes, les réseaux, les cartes. Gauthier-Villars.


Munzner, T. (2014). Visualization analysis and design. CRC Press.


Okabe, M., & Ito, K. (2008). Color universal design (CUD): How to make figures and presentations that are friendly to colorblind people. J*FLY Data Depository for Drosophila Researchers. https://jfly.uni-koeln.de/color/

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.1 Why a constant is not a channel
Should a mark’s color come from your data, or from you? There are two ways to make something red, and gog keeps them apart on purpose.
Mapping lets the data decide a visual property. color(continent) says let the continent decide the color, so gog builds a scale, assigns a color per continent, and draws a legend to decode it.
Setting means you give the property a value yourself. style(color = "tomato") says make them all tomato. No column is read, no scale is built, and no legend appears, because there is nothing to decode.
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent.”
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored tomato.”
Every channel in gog maps a data column to a visual property. A constant maps nothing, so it does not meet the definition. The same test settles a question from later in the book. Rotating a 3-D plot is not a channel either, because it is a property of the coordinate space.
A practical test gives the same answer: a mapping to color, size, shape, pattern or opacity draws a legend, and a setting draws none. If the plot needs a legend to be read, it was a mapping. A mapping written with legend = FALSE leaves its legend out, so a plot with no legend can still use a mapping.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:

In the grid below, every setting is a row and every mark is a column. The grid shows what each mark takes and what it refuses, including combinations you would not have guessed were legal. Legal is not the same as useful. Law 8 says the grammar guarantees a plot is legal, and you judge whether it is useful. The grid shows the limit of what can be expressed. Those rows are every setting there is. x, y, z, group, label and play are absent because they are channels and nothing else, which Two questions, not one explains.
color (CSS name or hex) and opacity (0–1) can be set on every mark. The other rows follow from each mark’s geometry rather than from a list someone chose. A setting is available on every mark whose geometry can carry it, and it behaves the same way on all of them. That is the settable rule: a setting covers its whole geometry class, the group of marks drawn with the same kind of shape.
size is a measurement in pixels: a radius, a stroke width, or a font size. It belongs to point, text, every stroke mark, and the lines of a box. The grid marks it — for bar, area, ribbon, zone and surface. Their positions already decide their size, so there is nothing to set. shape chooses one of seven glyphs. Only point takes it.
pattern is the texture of a mark’s paint. It is one property drawn differently by each geometry, the way color is a fill on a bar and a stroke on a line. On the six stroke marks (line, step, path, interval, rule, edge) it is the dash: "solid"/"dashed"/"dotted"/"dotdash"/"longdash", so an error bar can be dashed too. On the five filled regions (bar, box, area, ribbon, zone) it is a fill texture: "solid"/"hatch"/"crosshatch"/"stripes"/ "grid"/"dots". A surface takes no hatch: the hatch is drawn flat on the screen, so on a tilted sheet it would look denser on some faces than on others. Those hatchings keep a plot readable in grayscale or in black-and-white print. It changes the paint, never the shape: a dashed line and a solid one pass through the same points. A step is a different mark because it holds each value until it changes.

border_color and border_size draw an outline separate from the fill. A border_size of 0 means no border. Both belong to the five closed-shape fills (bar, box, point, zone and surface). On those marks you cannot draw the outline as a second layer. A setting is the only way to get it. color fills the shape; border_color outlines it; the two are independent, so a box can be pale inside and dark-edged:

  style({ color: "steelblue", opacity: 0.7, size: 5,
  border_color: "white", border_size: 1 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("A point with a white border"))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  A point with a white border Life expectancy GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored steelblue, with opacity 0.7, size 5, border color white and border size 1.”
opacity fades what color paints, which here is the fill. The white outline stays fully opaque. To make an outline partly transparent, put the transparency in border_color: in "#4682b44d", the last two hex digits make steelblue 30% opaque.
On text, the same two settings draw a halo, a band of color under the letters. The Text chapter shows one.
A curve fill (area, ribbon) takes no border. Its edge is a data curve, so you draw it as a line layer (area + line, line * bounds), and a line can be dashed, which a border cannot. And a cross point has no fill to outline, so a border on a cross-shaped glyph has nothing to draw on, and gog refuses it. When shape is mapped to a column, the categories drawn as crosses go without a border, and gog prints a message that names them.
The last six rows of the grid above each control one part of a mark’s drawing. caps shows or hides the caps at the ends of a whisker, on an interval and a box. center shows or hides an interval’s center dot. nudge moves a text label off its position. arrow draws an arrowhead at one end, or both ends, of a path or an edge. reach says how far a rule reaches across the panel. And angle turns the labels of a text layer by a number of degrees (Turning a label). A row has a ✓︎ under every mark that has the part its setting controls. For caps that part is a whisker; for arrow, a start and an end that come from the data.
A line shows why arrow does not belong to it. An arrowhead marks the direction the data runs in. A line sorts its vertices by x, so its last point is simply the largest x in the table, not the last row, and an arrowhead there would mark the largest x rather than the end of the data.

data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each path ends at 2007")


(data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.country) +
  style(arrow = "end") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each path ends at 2007"))


data(gapminder_asia) + path + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:country) +
  style(arrow = "end") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Each path ends at 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), path, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.country), style({ arrow: "end" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Each path ends at 2007"))

24.2.3 CSS colors
A color usually comes as a hex value copied from a design document, or as a name remembered from another tool. Not every name you remember is one gog knows.
A name from CSS, the language web pages are styled with, and a hex value both work anywhere a color is accepted, in style() and in palette():

R’s colors() includes numbered shades (gray80, gray50, steelblue3) that CSS does not have. gog uses CSS colors because that is what SVG accepts and what the other three bindings use too, so the vocabulary is the same in every language:

For an exact shade, give the hex value.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  0 50K 100K   40 60 80  1704 points: low opacity reveals the density Life Gdp





Where many points overlap, the cloud is darker, so its dense regions show.
A reference layer. When one layer is what the plot is about, the others should be drawn faintly:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Five countries in gray; the trend in red")


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line + group(col.country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Five countries in gray; the trend in red"))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + line * smooth +
  style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Five countries in gray; the trend in red")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, smooth),
  style({ color: "firebrick", size: 3 }),
  title("Five countries in gray; the trend in red"))






                                      1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Five countries in gray; the trend in red Life Year





“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines, grouped by country, colored lightgray, and also a line derived by smooth, colored firebrick, with size 3.”

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.4 Two questions, not one
A mapped opacity works on a point. Try the same binding on a line and gog refuses it.
A line is drawn with one stroke from its first point to its last. The stroke has one width and one opacity, so size and opacity are not channels on line:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + group(country) + opacity(life)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + line + group(col.country) + opacity(col.life)


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + group(:country) +
  opacity(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_asia), x(col.year), y(col.life), line,
  group(col.country), opacity(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `opacity` cannot be bound to `line` — a line takes one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. Drop the `life` mapping and set it with `style(opacity = )`, or use a mark that maps `opacity`: `point`, `bar` or `surface`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


But one stroke still has a width and an opacity. Those are settings:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.5) +
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity")


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.5) +
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity"))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.5) +
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity")


plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), style({ size: 4, opacity: 0.5 }),
  title("Set on a line: one width, one opacity"))






                                   1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  Set on a line: one width, one opacity Life Year





This is where the distinction matters most. “Can a column be mapped here?” and “Does this mark have this property?” are different questions, and line is where the answers differ.
Every mark answers both. Five properties are a channel and a setting under the same name, and this is what each mark says about them:
