A set only cell means the mark has the property, but one value for the whole layer, not one per row: a line has one width, and a rule layer one opacity. Bind a column there and the refusal explains that, and names the setting to write instead.
Two set only cells are exceptions. The grammar allows size and opacity on a text, but the engine does not draw them. gog refuses the mapping as Unsupported rather than Illegal, and the message names no setting. Set either one with style() instead. Combinations marks these two cells with a symbol of their own, ◌.
The table above has a column for five of the kernel’s eleven channels. The other six, x, y, z, group, label and play, are only ever mapped, and they have no row on the settings grid either. Positions, groups, labels and the steps of an animation come from data, or they do not exist at all. There is nothing to set. Eight settings are only ever set, and never appear on the mapping grid. border_color, border_size, caps, center, nudge, angle, arrow and reach decorate a mark and read no column.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.5 Mapping and setting the same property
text:
24.5 Mapping and setting the same property
It is easy to write both by accident: a color(continent) left from an earlier draft, and a style(color = ) added to try one shade.
Doing both would mean one of the two instructions is silently discarded, which gog never does:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + style(color = "tomato")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + style(color = "tomato"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  style(color = "tomato")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), style({ color: "tomato" }))




Error:
! gog: `color(continent)` maps color and `style(color = "tomato")` sets it — one layer cannot do both. Keep `color(continent)` to show the data, or `style(color = "tomato")` to fix every point at one value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Write the one you meant.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.6 style and the layer it follows
text:
24.6 style and the layer it follows
A trend line is easiest to see when the points under it are faint and the line is not, so the two layers need different settings.
color() written before any mark applies to every layer that can take it. style() attaches to the nearest mark before it, and to no other mark, because a setting written for one layer should not change another:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  line * smooth +
  point + style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Only the points are tomato")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  line * smooth +
  point + style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Only the points are tomato"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + line * smooth + point +
  style(color = "tomato", opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Only the points are tomato")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), layer(line, smooth),
  point, style({ color: "tomato", opacity: 0.4 }),
  title("Only the points are tomato"))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Only the points are tomato Life Gdp





To style both layers, write a style() after each mark.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.7 palette: choosing the colors a mapping uses
text:
24.7 palette: choosing the colors a mapping uses
Setting a color and mapping a column are the two choices this chapter has kept apart. Sometimes you want part of each: the continents separated by color, and those five colors chosen by you rather than by gog.
style(color = ) is written instead of a mapping. palette() keeps the mapping and chooses which colors the categories receive:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette(c("tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette(["tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette(["tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent),
  palette(["tomato", "steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod", "orchid"]))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, with a palette of tomato, steelblue, seagreen, goldenrod and orchid.”
A palette needs a mapping to give its colors to. With no column bound to color it has nothing to color, so it is refused rather than accepted and then ignored:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + palette("okabe")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + palette("okabe")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + palette("okabe")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  palette("okabe"))




Error:
! gog: `palette()` chooses the colors a `color` mapping hands out, and nothing here maps `color`, so it would have no effect. Bind a column with `color(<column>)` to use it — or, to paint every mark one color, that is a setting rather than a palette: `style(color = "…")`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names two fixes, because there are two things you may have meant. To give each category its own color, bind the column with color(continent). To paint every mark one color, write style(color = "steelblue"), which is a setting rather than a palette.
A plot can have a color mapping that you did not write. A zone * density colors its cells by a measure it computes itself (Zone), so palette() works on that plot.
One color, though, is not a palette. palette() takes either a palette name ("gog", "okabe") or the colors themselves, and it reads a single word as a palette name. "red" is not a palette name, so gog refuses it rather than quietly using the default palette:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  palette("red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  palette("red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("red"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("red")` is not a known palette. Named palettes are gog, okabe, soft for categories; blue, viridis, magma, inferno, plasma, cividis, gray for numbers; blue_red, brown_teal for numbers that diverge from a center. `"red"` is a color, not a palette. To paint every mark one color use `style(color = "red")`; to give each category its own color, give `palette()` several colors, "red" among them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Making everything one color is setting, not choosing a palette, so use style(color = "red").

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.8 theme: settings that belong to no mark
text:
24.8 theme: settings that belong to no mark
The gridlines distract on a slide. You want the category names along the bottom at 45 degrees.
style() sets a mark’s own appearance. The gridlines, the shape of the panel and the angle of the tick labels belong to no mark, so they have a word of their own: theme().


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(grid = "none")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(grid = "none"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme(grid = "none")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), theme({ grid: "none" }))






                                                                                                                                                                   1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
The gridlines are gone, and nothing about the points changed, because theme() never changes a mark.
grid names each set of gridlines by the axis whose ticks they mark, not by the direction they run. So "x" keeps the lines belonging to the x axis and removes the rest. That naming is the same when the plane is bent into a circle. The next plot keeps the x axis gridlines in polar, a space later in the book. They radiate from the center instead of running from bottom to top:



winds: first 5 of 264 rows

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar() + theme(grid = "x")


data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction) + polar() + theme(grid = "x")


data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction) + polar() + theme(grid = "x")


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction), polar(),
  theme({ grid: "x" }))






                         N NE E SE S SW W NW   20 40 60  Count Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction, in polar.”
ratio sets the panel’s width divided by its height. The image keeps the size it was given and the panel shrinks inside it, so the plot still takes the same room on a page:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + theme(ratio = 1)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + theme(ratio = 1)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(ratio = 1)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ ratio: 1 }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





tick_angle turns the x tick labels to the angle you give, in degrees. You do not need it to keep names apart. When category names do not fit side by side, gog turns them 90 degrees by itself, to read upward. Scales shows what gog does when even turned names do not fit. tick_angle is for choosing the angle yourself. gog keeps the angle you choose, even when fewer names fit at it, and says so. The bottom margin grows to hold the turned labels, and the axis name sits below them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  theme(tick_angle = 45)


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  theme(tick_angle = 45))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  theme(tick_angle = 45)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), theme({ tick_angle: 45 }))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





axis_label says where an axis’s name sits. By default each name is centered along its own axis, so the y name is turned through 90 degrees. Ask for "end" and both names move to their axis’s far end and stay horizontal, so nothing on the plot has to be read sideways. It is one property, not one per axis, so the two names never follow different rules:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme(axis_label = "end")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme(axis_label = "end"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme(axis_label = "end")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)"), theme({ axis_label: "end" }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life expectancy (years) GDP per person





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the axis names at their ends.”
A legend on the right makes the panel narrower by the legend’s own width. On a narrow figure, such as one column of a journal page, that leaves little room for the data. legend says which side of the plot the legends sit on. The default is "right", and the other sides are "left", "top" and "bottom". Above or below the panel, a legend’s entries are placed side by side, so the panel gets shorter instead of narrower:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(legend = "bottom")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(legend = "bottom"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme(legend = "bottom")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), theme({ legend: "bottom" }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, with the legend at the bottom.”
The panel now takes the width the legend used beside it, and the five continents are listed side by side under the x axis’s name. To leave one legend out instead, write legend = FALSE on its channel (Leaving a legend out).
font_size sets how big the plot’s text is. It is one number, not three. The number itself is the size of a tick label, in pixels. The axis names and the title are a fixed proportion larger. The default of 11 draws tick labels at 11, axis names at 13 and the title at 16. Ask for 16 and those three become 16, 19 and 23:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Bigger text, one number") + theme(font_size = 16)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Bigger text, one number") + theme(font_size = 16))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  title("Bigger text, one number") + theme(font_size = 16)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), title("Bigger text, one number"), theme({ font_size: 16 }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Bigger text, one number Life Gdp





Look at the margins. They grew with the text, because the room an axis needs is measured from the labels that go in it. Larger text therefore never overlaps the panel.
A smaller number leaves more room for the data in a small figure:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Smaller text, same plot") + theme(font_size = 8)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Smaller text, same plot") + theme(font_size = 8))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  title("Smaller text, same plot") + theme(font_size = 8)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), title("Smaller text, same plot"), theme({ font_size: 8 }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Smaller text, same plot Life Gdp





One number sets all the text, so one plot never carries three unrelated text sizes. You cannot ask for a bigger title on its own: the title grows only when the tick labels grow.
The number is a measurement in pixels, not a multiplier. font_size = 1.5 is refused, because a number that small is almost always meant as a multiplier:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(font_size = 1.5)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(font_size = 1.5)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + theme(font_size = 1.5)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ font_size: 1.5 }))




Error:
! gog: `theme(font_size = )` is how many pixels a tick label is, not a multiplier, so it needs one number of at least 4. The default is 11, and the axis names and the title are derived from it.


font_size does not name a typeface. The engine measures text with its own table of character widths, so it can lay out a plot with no font installed. It asks for the reader’s system font, and the computer that opens the plot supplies the letters.
A preset is a named bundle of these properties, and you ask for one by its name. You can still change any property in it, so one small change never means writing every property yourself:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  theme("minimal", ratio = 1)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  theme("minimal", ratio = 1))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme("minimal", ratio = 1)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme("minimal", { ratio: 1 }))






                                                                                                                                                                   1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





gog has three presets: "gog", the default, "minimal" and "bw". "minimal" removes the gridlines, the same as theme(grid = "none"), and ratio = 1 then makes the panel square.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.9 Axes, legends, gridlines and the frame
text:
24.9 Axes, legends, gridlines and the frame
A map, a small figure or a slide often needs less around the data than gog draws by default. The settings that leave each part out are explained in different places, so this section collects them in one table. An axis and a legend are guides: each one decodes a channel, so you leave it out inside that channel’s call, as in color(continent, legend = FALSE). The gridlines and the side where the legends sit belong to the whole plot, so theme() sets them. theme() also sets the frame: by default, the two lines along the bottom and the left of the panel.



To
Write
Explained in




leave out an axis: its tick marks, its numbers and its name
x(gdp, axis = FALSE)
Scales


leave out only an axis’s name
x_label("")
this section, below


leave out a legend
color(continent, legend = FALSE)
Channels


leave out the gridlines
theme(grid = "none"), or "x" or "y" to keep one set
theme, above


leave out the frame, or draw all four sides
theme(frame = "none"), or "full" for all four sides
this section, below


put the legends on another side
theme(legend = "bottom"), "top" or "left"
theme, above, and Channels



The plot below uses four of them at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life, axis = FALSE) +
  color(continent) + theme(grid = "x", frame = "none", legend = "bottom")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life, axis = False) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(grid = "x", frame = "none", legend = "bottom"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life, axis = false) + color(:continent) +
  theme(grid = "x", frame = "none", legend = "bottom")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life, { axis: false }), color(col.continent),
  theme({ grid: "x", frame: "none", legend: "bottom" }))






                                                                                                                                                            1K 10K    Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life without an axis, color by continent, with the legend at the bottom.”
The y axis is gone, with its numbers and its name, and grid = "x" keeps only the gridlines of the x axis. The panel has no frame, and the legend lists the continents side by side under the x axis’s name. Each point keeps its place among the others, because none of these settings changes the data. With the y axis left out, though, a reader can see which points are higher, but not by how many years. So leave out an axis only when its numbers are not needed, as on a map.
To leave out only an axis’s name, give it an empty one: x_label(""). The tick marks and the numbers stay, so the reader can still read values from the axis.
frame says which sides of the panel get a line, and it takes three values. "axes", the default, draws one line along the bottom and one along the left, where the axes sit. "full" draws all four sides, and "none" draws none:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  theme(frame = "full", grid = "y")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  theme(frame = "full", grid = "y"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  theme(frame = "full", grid = "y")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), theme({ frame: "full", grid: "y" }))






                                 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





The panel now has a line on all four sides. It is called frame and not border because style(border_color = ) already uses that word for something else. A border belongs to a mark, such as a bar or a point. A frame surrounds the panel.
A flow whose two columns name one set of places, flow(a, b, shared = TRUE), has two other defaults. It has no numbers to read values from, so its panel has no frame and is white instead of gray. frame and background change both, as on any other plot.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.10 A figure for a journal
A journal often asks for a figure on a white background inside a framed panel.
theme("bw") is the preset most often wanted for publication: a white panel inside a full rectangle.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme("bw")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme("bw"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme("bw")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), theme("bw"))






                                                                                                                                                                         1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





"bw" stands for black and white, and the name misleads. What becomes black and white is everything around the data, never the data itself. The continents in that plot keep every color the palette gave them. In a “bw” plot only the data carries color, and everything around it is black, white or gray.
The whole preset is three settings, written out below. This sentence draws the same picture theme("bw") just drew:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + theme(background = "white", frame = "full", strip = "white")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + theme(background = "white", frame = "full", strip = "white"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) +
  theme(background = "white", frame = "full", strip = "white")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent),
  theme({ background: "white", frame: "full", strip: "white" }))






                                                                                                                                                                         1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





Here background makes the panel white and frame draws a rectangle around it. frame is explained in the section above, strip in the next section, and background in The panel’s background.
Every preset in gog follows the same rule: a preset only names settings you could have written yourself. A preset that did more than that would be a second set of words to learn.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
section: 24.11 The strip, and how it prints
text:
24.11 The strip, and how it prints
The third setting inside theme("bw") is strip. It colors the band above each panel, the band that names the category the panel holds. You only see it on a faceted plot, and its color matters more in print than on screen.
By default the band is a light gray. On a screen that is fine, and it shows which panel each name belongs to:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
On paper it is not fine. A light gray is printed as many tiny black dots, and those dots sit directly under small text. The label gets harder to read, and a photocopy makes it worse. This is the same reason pattern exists for fills: what is easy to see on a screen can be hard to see on paper.
So theme("bw") makes the band white as well. The framed panel already separates one panel from the next, so the tint is no longer needed:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) + theme("bw") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) + theme("bw") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme("bw") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), theme("bw"), across(col.continent))






                                                              0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                       0 20K 40K                                                                               0 20K 40K                                                    0 20K 40K                             0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





You can also name the color yourself, for a poster or a slide where a tint makes the name easier to read rather than harder:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
  theme(strip = "#dce8f0", frame = "full") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
  theme(strip = "#dce8f0", frame = "full") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme(strip = "#dce8f0", frame = "full") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), theme({ strip: "#dce8f0", frame: "full" }),
  across(col.continent))






                                                              0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                       0 20K 40K                                                                               0 20K 40K                                                    0 20K 40K                             0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





An animated plot has the same band (Play, later in the book). It names the moment the animation shows, such as the year, the way a panel band names its category. theme(strip = ) colors that one too. A property that colored one band and not the other would be exactly the kind of exception Law 2 forbids.

24.11.1 The label color on a dark band
Some plots use a dark band on purpose, and that creates one problem: the default label is dark too.
A dark band with light text is often wanted, and you need only one property for it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
  theme(strip = "#22223b", frame = "full") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
  theme(strip = "#22223b", frame = "full") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme(strip = "#22223b", frame = "full") | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life), theme({ strip: "#22223b", frame: "full" }),
  across(col.continent))






                                                              0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                       0 20K 40K                                                                               0 20K 40K                                                    0 20K 40K                             0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





You did not name a text color, and the text is drawn white. gog reads the band color you asked for. It has two default label colors, and it picks the one that contrasts more with that band. On a pale band the label stays dark, which is why the faceted plots earlier in this chapter have dark labels.
gog chooses the label color because an unreadable name is a defect, not to save you a line of code. Without that rule, theme(strip = "black") would paint the near-black default label onto a black band. Every panel name would be unreadable while the rest of the plot looked correct. So when you do not name a label color, gog chooses a readable one.
When you want a particular label color, and not only a readable one, name it. gog then uses the color you name as written, without checking it against the band:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
  theme(strip = "navy", strip_text = "gold", frame = "full") |
  facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(col.life) +
  theme(strip = "navy", strip_text = "gold", frame = "full") |
  facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(:life) +
  theme(strip = "navy", strip_text = "gold", frame = "full") |
  facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { tick_count: 3 }),
  y(col.life),
  theme({ strip: "navy", strip_text: "gold", frame: "full" }),
  across(col.continent))






                                                              0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                       0 20K 40K                                                                               0 20K 40K                                                    0 20K 40K                             0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





Every default in gog works this way: it decides what you did not say, and stops deciding as soon as you say it. The engine guarantees the plot is well-formed and leaves taste to you, which is Law 8.
A "transparent" band gives gog no color to read, because it shows whatever is behind it. So the label stays dark, which suits the white page a band usually sits on.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.12 The panel’s background
A slide or a journal may need a panel in a color other than gog’s light gray. background colors the panel, and it takes any color the rest of the grammar takes, a CSS name such as linen among them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  theme(background = "linen", frame = "full")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  theme(background = "linen", frame = "full"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(background = "linen", frame = "full")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ background: "linen", frame: "full" }))






                                                                                                                                                                         1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





"transparent" is the one value that changes more than the panel. If only the panel were transparent, the margin around it would still be painted. So "transparent" also leaves the margin and the legend’s box unpainted, and the page under the figure shows through. A journal often asks for this, because it prints the figure on a page whose color gog does not know.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.13 What theme() refuses
theme() checks every name you give it, and refuses one it does not know rather than ignoring it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme("dark")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme("dark")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + theme("dark")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), theme("dark"))




Error:
! gog: `theme("dark")` is not a theme. gog has `gog`, `minimal`, or `bw`. A theme is a named preset you can then adjust — `theme("minimal", ratio = 1)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The gridlines are named by their axis, "x" or "y", and not by the direction they run, so grid = "vertical" is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(grid = "vertical")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(grid = "vertical")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(grid = "vertical")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ grid: "vertical" }))




Error:
! gog: `theme(grid = )` is one of "both", "x", "y" or "none".

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.14 style and theme
style() and theme() differ in what they belong to. style() belongs to a mark, and a plot with three layers can carry three different ones. theme() belongs to the whole plot, and there is only one of it: no single layer has gridlines or a background of its own. The two never set the same property, and that is why they are two words rather than one.
Text size shows the split best: both atoms have a size setting, but each sets the size of different text. style(size = 17) on a text layer sets how big those labels are, and they are labels that come from a column. theme(font_size = 16) sets how big the tick labels, the axis names and the title are, and those belong to the whole plot. One is a property of a mark and the other is a property of the plot, so neither can replace the other.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.15 In short
A mapping to color, size, shape, pattern or opacity gets a legend, and a setting gets none. That is the quickest test for which one you wrote; a mapping with legend = FALSE also has none. Five names are a channel and a setting at once: color, size, shape, pattern and opacity. Which call you write decides which you get.

title: 24  Setting vs mapping
text:
24.16 What comes next
A setting changes how a mark looks and computes nothing from the rows. Transforms shows how gog derives values the table does not hold: counts, means, bins, densities, and the low and high values an interval needs.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.1 One variable, or two?
How do you plot a number your table does not hold? A transform computes it for you and hands the result to a mark. It runs after the table is read and before anything is drawn, and the mark stays what it is: bar * bin still draws bars.
The family has other names. ggplot2 says stat, and the chapter Wilkinson devotes to it says statistics (Wilkinson, 2005); SQL says aggregate, dplyr says summarize, a spreadsheet says pivot. Each of those covers about half of what gog groups here. mean, count and density really are statistics, and they replace rows with a summary. But bin cuts an axis into cells. bounds reshapes two columns you already have and computes nothing at all. stack, dodge, jitter and repel are about collisions between marks rather than about the values behind them. Calling all of that a statistic would misname most of it, so the word here is the most general one that is still accurate: a transform is anything that changes what reaches the mark.
Transforms are applied with the * operator:
The result is the same mark drawing derived values, not a new atom to memorize.
The middle six (sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile) form the aggregation family. All share the same pattern: group by x, reduce y to one value. range, confidence and deviation group the same way but write a low and a high, the extents an interval spans. smooth_band writes the same pair along smooth’s curve. These four and bounds, which comes later in this chapter, are the pair transforms.
Grouping the transforms by what they compute is not the only useful way to sort them. Fifteen of them also fall into two families by how many columns they read, and reading one column or two is what decides whether you write y(). The other nine of the kernel’s twenty-four transforms come later in this chapter. bounds reshapes rather than computes. partition, flow, layout and cluster each compute a whole picture, such as a mosaic or a network. dodge, stack, jitter and repel move marks that would otherwise overlap.
Inventing transforms (bin, count, density) read a single variable and make the measure axis from it. proportion joins them whenever it stands alone, because the only measurement it then has to rescale is the tally it makes itself. You name only the variable whose shape you are asking about, and the transform invents the y column and labels it (“Count”, “Proportion”, “Density”). bar * bin + x(life) and line * density + x(life) are the same grammatical shape: one name in, a new axis out. Leaving out y() here is not a mistake. There is exactly one sensible y, the count or the density, and the engine supplies it. If you name a column of the table on that axis, as in bar * count + x(continent) + y(life), gog refuses it, because the transform would never read that column.
Reading transforms (smooth, sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band) read two columns and summarize the second as it varies with the first. They fit or aggregate an existing y, so you must bind one: without y(gold), bar * mean + x(country) has no way to guess which column to average. Leave y() off and the engine invents nothing: only you know which column was meant, so it stops and names what is missing (add y(<column>)). range, confidence, deviation and smooth_band are the four that read a y like the others but write more than one: range a low and a high, the other three a low, high and center.
So whether you write y() is not an arbitrary rule to memorize for each transform. The family a transform belongs to decides it. This is one instance of Explicit Over Implicit: the short form is allowed exactly when it cannot be misread, and refused when it could.
Both families replace your rows with a summary of them, and this chapter calls any transform that does so a statistic. A statistic runs within each group when a channel that splits the rows into groups is bound: color, group, pattern or shape. bar * bin + color(species) draws one histogram per species, not one combined bar that has discarded the split (see overlaid histograms). The same rule gives a density curve, a count, or a mean per group. Each output row keeps the group it came from. The mark colors it by that group, and the legend lists the same groups.

  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")

                                       50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Histogram of life expectancy, 2007 Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life.”
bin is not the bar’s own transform. Four other marks cut the same bins, and only the shape changes:







Mark derived by bin
Shape




point * bin
one dot at the top of each bin


line * bin
the frequency polygon: straight lines through the bin centers


area * bin
the same polygon, filled to the baseline


step * bin
the staircase outline


bar * bin
filled bars, the histogram above



zone * bin cuts two axes instead of one, which is the heatmap, and surface * bin raises the same cells into the cube.
Bin count defaults to Sturges’ rule (Sturges, 1926): k = ⌈log₂(n)⌉ + 1, where n is the number of rows and k the number of bins. In words, each time the number of rows doubles, the histogram gets one more bin. Notice there is no y() in the expression: bin invents the count column internally, and the y axis is labeled “Count” automatically.

25.2.1 Choosing the bin count
A histogram’s shape depends on how it is cut, and the default cut may hide a gap or split a peak. You will often want a finer cut, or bins whose width means something in the data’s units.
Sturges’ rule is a sensible default, not a mandate. Pass a number to set the bin count, or name a width to fix the bin width in the data’s own units:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(30)), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram"))






                                                             40 50 60 70 80   0 5 10 15  Thirty bins: a finer histogram Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin into 30, x is life.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin({ width: 5 })), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("Bins five years wide"))






                                            40 50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30 40  Bins five years wide Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life.”
The positional number is the count: bin(30) is thirty bins. A width is the less common request, so it is said out loud, bin(width = 5); the two are mutually exclusive. gog refuses bin(30, width = 5) rather than guess which one you meant. For the same reason a bare number always means a count: on this data, five bins and bins five years wide are very different plots.
A width also decides where the bins start: every edge is a multiple of the width. The five-year bins above therefore run from 35 to 40, from 40 to 45, and so on, not from the smallest value, 39.6. Where the bin edges fall explains why, and how ggplot2 places its edges instead.


25.2.2 Choosing a width
When you give a count of bins, you decide only how much detail to show: bin(20) draws fewer, wider bars than bin(30) on any column. When you give a width, you decide more, because a width is measured in the column’s own units. Use a width when each bin should cover a span that means something, such as five years of life expectancy or half a centimeter of petal length. Because every edge is a multiple of the width, two histograms cut at the same width share their edges, even when their data cover different ranges. You can then compare them bin by bin.
To choose a width, first decide roughly how many bars you want. Divide the column’s range, its largest value minus its smallest, by that number. Then take a nearby round number in the column’s units, such as 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 or 10. Life expectancy runs from 39.6 to 82.6 years, a range of 43. Ten bars would each be 4.3 years wide, and the nearest round number is 5.
One more rule prevents tall bars and empty bins that come from the cut rather than from the data. The width should be a whole multiple of the distance between two neighboring values the column can hold. quakes_fiji holds a thousand earthquakes near Fiji, and it records each magnitude to one decimal place, so its possible values are 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and so on, 0.1 apart:

The bar from 4.5 to 4.75 is far taller than the bars on either side. It holds 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7, while each neighbor holds two: 4.3 and 4.4 before it, 4.8 and 4.9 after it. A width of 0.2 puts two possible values in every bin, and the shape is smooth:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.2) + x(magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin")


(data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.2) + x(col.magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin"))


data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.2) + x(:magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin")


plot(data(quakes_fiji), layer(bar, bin({ width: 0.2 })), x(col.magnitude),
  x_label("Magnitude"), title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin"))






                                      4 5 6   0 100 200  Width 0.2: two values in every bin Count Magnitude





The same rule applies when you give a number of bins, because the number sets the width. Suppose a column holds whole numbers from 9 to 35, so only 27 values are possible. Thirty bins are each 0.87 wide, and at least three must stay empty. For one bar per value, use bar * count, which counts the rows at each value instead of binning them.
Two kinds of axis treat a width differently. A time axis refuses a width, as What a time axis refuses shows, so give the number of bins there. On a log axis the bins are cut on the logarithms, so a width counts powers of the base. In the default base 10, bin(width = 1) makes bins from 100 to 1,000 and from 1,000 to 10,000. In base 2, each bin ends at twice its start.


25.2.3 Why bar * bin, not a histogram() shortcut?
Because bin does the same computation regardless of the mark, and the mark decides how the bins are drawn. bar * bin fills bars. line * bin connects the bin centers into a frequency polygon, and step * bin traces the histogram as a staircase outline. Add stack and a fourth reading appears, the dot plot further down this chapter: one dot per observation rather than one mark per bin. Adding a histogram() shortcut would violate Law 2 (No Exceptions) by special-casing a particular mark+transform pair.


25.2.4 The same bin, cutting two axes
All twelve gapminder years on one scatter make 1704 points, and where they overlap you cannot see how dense the cloud is. The answer is to count rows in cells of the plane, not only along one axis.
The mark decides something else too: how many axes get cut. Each mark above leaves one axis free to measure the count along, so bin cuts the other one. A zone measures nothing by length, and it needs an extent on both axes to be a rectangle. So the same word cuts both, and the count goes to color, the only channel left holding a number:

That is a heatmap, with no atom added to the kernel.


25.2.5 One of each: the mixed mesh
Five continents make five histograms, and comparing five panels is harder than comparing five rows of one picture.
The rule that a zone cuts both axes needs one qualification. What bin cuts is every axis that has a width to cut, and a categorical axis has none, because it arrived already cut: a category is a cell. Give a zone one of each and the transform does the only coherent thing, which is to cut the continuous axis and not the categorical one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut")

  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut"))

  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut")

  palette("viridis"), title("One axis cut, one already cut"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, x is life, y is continent, with the viridis palette.”
Each continent gets a row of cells, and every row is cut on the same edges, so you can compare the continents by reading straight down. It is a distribution per category shown as shade rather than as height, which is why five of them fit where one histogram would go. The Zone chapter explains this plot, the heatmap and the tile plot below with one rule.


25.2.6 Which mesh: tiling
bin also decides the shape of the cells it cuts, because a different mesh puts different rows in different cells and so changes the counts. Rectangles are the default. Hexagons stagger alternate rows, so a reader does not mistake the straight rows of the mesh for a pattern in the data (Carr et al., 1987):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex")


(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex"))


data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20, { tiling: "hex" })),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 on hexagons, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”
A tiling means nothing to a bin that cuts one axis, since there the cells are intervals and an interval has no shape, so bar * bin(tiling = ) is refused pointing at zone. The Zone chapter works through both meshes, including why an empty cell is left unpainted.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.3 count: frequency aggregation
The first question to ask of a categorical column is how many rows fall in each category. A table with one row per country does not hold that number anywhere.
count counts the number of rows for each unique value of x, and it works on both categorical and continuous columns. It is the categorical counterpart to bin: bin groups a continuous column; count groups a categorical one.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# How many countries are in each continent?
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  title("Countries per continent, 2007"))






                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Countries per continent, 2007 Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”
count is not the bar’s own transform. Five other marks tally the same rows, and only the shape changes:







Mark derived by count
Shape




point * count
one dot at each count


line * count
the counts joined into a profile


area * count
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * count
each count held flat across its slot


zone * count
one cell per pair of categories, colored by its count


bar * count
one bar per category, the plot above



Compare these bars with the histogram at the start of the chapter. Histogram bars touch, because the bins are cut from one continuous axis and no value falls between them. Bar chart bars are drawn with a gap between them, because the categories are separate.
Like bin, count writes its own y column and labels the axis “Count”. To title that axis yourself, use y_label().

25.3.1 The same count, tallying two axes
With two categorical columns the question becomes how often each pair occurs, such as how many winds came from the west in winter.
bin cuts one axis on a bar and two on a zone, and count works the same way, for the same reason. A bar has a length to show the tally along, so it groups by one axis; a zone measures nothing by length, so it tallies rows into the cell where two categories cross and the count goes to color:

  title("One count, two axes: the tile plot")

  title("One count, two axes: the tile plot"))

That is the tile plot (a confusion matrix is the same sentence with different columns), and like the heatmap, no atom was added to the kernel.
Together, bin and count state the whole rule: bin cuts, count tallies. A continuous axis has to be cut into cells before there is anything to count in; a categorical axis arrives already cut, because a category is a cell. So on a zone each is refused where the other belongs, and each refusal names the other.
Taking the two axes one at a time gives three plots, not two. Cut both axes and it is the heatmap; cut neither and it is the tile plot; cut one of two and it is the mixed mesh above. A bin is refused only where there is nothing left for it to cut at all.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.4 proportion: relative frequency
Fifty-two of the 142 countries are in Africa, and that fact reads differently as a count than as a share of the whole.
proportion divides a measurement by its total, producing shares in [0, 1] that sum to 1. In statistics they are called relative frequencies. Used on its own it has nothing to divide yet, so it tallies the rows first exactly as count does:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# What share of countries belongs to each continent?
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("Continent share, 2007"))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  Continent share, 2007 Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent.”
The same six marks read a share as they read a count:







Mark derived by proportion
Shape




point * proportion
one dot at each share


line * proportion
the shares joined into a profile


area * proportion
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * proportion
each share held flat across its slot


zone * proportion
one cell per pair of categories, colored by its share


bar * proportion
one bar per category, the plot above



Use proportion when you care about relative composition rather than raw counts, for example “what fraction of respondents chose each option?” count and proportion differ only by a constant factor, which is the total. So order works the same on both: sorting by the y column gives the same order either way.
It follows count into two dimensions as well, so zone * proportion reads a tile plot as shares (see Zone).

25.4.1 The total is the whole plot, always
Once a second column splits the bars, each segment could be a share of its own bar or of the whole plot.
The denominator is every row the plot draws, in every context. That is the one thing the word is allowed to mean. Split the bars by a second column and they still sum to 1 between them, so each bar reads as this pair’s share of everything:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(direction) + color(season) +
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations")


(data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(col.direction) + color(col.season) +
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations"))


data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(:direction) + color(:season) +
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations")


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.direction),
  color(col.season),
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations"))






                                              N NE E SE S SW W NW   0.00 0.05 0.10 0.15  Every bar is a share of all 264 observations Proportion Direction  Season    Summer  Winter 





“Given the winds: bars derived by proportion, x is direction, color by season.”
Add up the sixteen segments there and you get 1, not 2. What you cannot get that way is the conditional reading: “of the summer winds, what share came from the west”. That reading is the facet. It cuts the data into panels before any of this runs, so each panel normalizes inside itself:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(direction) | facet(season)


data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(col.direction) | facet(col.season)


data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(:direction) | facet(:season)


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.direction),
  across(col.season))






                                      N NE E SE S SW W NW   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3                                   N NE E SE S SW W NW      Summer  Winter  Proportion Direction





“Given the winds: bars derived by proportion, x is direction, split into panel columns by season.”
Compare the two plots. In the first, summer’s bars and winter’s bars share one total. In the second, each season has its own.


25.4.2 Normalizing something other than a tally
Two histograms from tables of different sizes cannot be compared by their counts, and a continent’s population means more as a share of the world’s.
Because proportion divides whatever measurement it finds, it composes with any transform that leaves one number per cell. Put it after a bin and the histogram’s own counts come back as fractions, the relative-frequency histogram, on exactly the mesh a plain bar * bin cuts:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * proportion + x(life) +
  title("Shares, not counts")


(data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * proportion + x(col.life) +
  title("Shares, not counts"))


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * proportion + x(:life) +
  title("Shares, not counts")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin(20), proportion), x(col.life),
  title("Shares, not counts"))

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20 and proportion, x is life.”
Put it after a summary and the column you named is the thing rescaled, so each slot reads as its share of the grand total:

  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007")

  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) +
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population),
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007"))

What it refuses is what leaves it nothing to divide by. A density already integrates to 1, and its cells are sample points rather than parts of a whole. A smooth gives a value at each x, so the sum of those values has no meaning. A pair transform writes a low and a high, which leaves two numbers per cell, and a span is not part of any total.

data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(col.life)

plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, density, proportion), x(col.life))
