title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.5 density: kernel density estimate
A histogram’s outline changes with every choice of bin, and its steps belong to the bins rather than to the data. A smooth curve describes the same distribution without the steps.
density is the third inventing transform: it estimates the same distribution that bin counts, but as a smooth curve. The curve is the probability density function of x, estimated with a Gaussian kernel and evaluated at 256 evenly spaced points. By default the bandwidth (how wide each kernel is, and so how smooth the curve) is chosen automatically by Silverman’s rule (Silverman, 1986), which uses the interquartile range so that a few extreme values do not widen it.
Combine it with line to draw a smooth density curve:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))






                               40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007 Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life.”
density is not the line’s own transform. Five other marks estimate the same curve, and only the shape changes:



Mark derived by density
Shape




area * density
the curve filled to the baseline


step * density
the curve as a staircase


point * density
one dot at each point the curve was estimated


bar * density
one thin bar at each of those points


ribbon * density
the curve mirrored, which is the violin


line * density
the curve as a stroke, the plot above



Bind two positions instead of one and density cuts both axes. zone then draws the field as cells, path as contour rings, and surface as a sheet.
As with the other inventing transforms, there is no y() to write: the density column and its axis label are both made for you.

25.5.1 Choosing the bandwidth
The automatic curve can be smoother than the data supports, hiding a second peak, or rougher, showing bumps that are only noise.
The automatic bandwidth is a sensible default, not a mandate, and it is the parameter you will change most often, as the bin count is for bin. It is set the same two ways. A positional number is an adjust multiplier on the automatic bandwidth: density(2) is twice as smooth, density(0.5) half as smooth and so more jagged.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(2): twice as smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(2): twice as smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("density(2): twice as smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density(2)), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("density(2): twice as smooth"))






                                 20 40 60 80 100   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03  density(2): twice as smooth Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density adjusted by 2, x is life.”
To fix the bandwidth in the data’s own units instead, name it. Here bandwidth = 1 sets each kernel one year wide, narrower than the default, so the curve keeps more of the distribution’s fine structure:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ bandwidth: 1 })),
  x(col.life), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width"))






                                 40 50 60 70 80   0.00 0.02 0.04 0.06  bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density at bandwidth 1, x is life.”
This works exactly as bin does. The positional number is the adjust multiplier: the common request, since you rarely know the bandwidth you want in advance and only need the automatic one a little smoother or rougher. An absolute width is the less common request, so it is said out loud, density(bandwidth = 1); the two are mutually exclusive, and density(2, bandwidth = 1) refuses with direction rather than guessing which you meant.


25.5.2 One transform, four readings
Once you have a curve for one column, you will want the same estimate over two columns, or one curve per category, side by side. Each of those is still density.
density estimates a distribution, and how it is drawn depends on what you bind and on the mark. There are four readings, and they are one transform rather than four transforms sharing a name.
Bind one continuous column and it is a curve over that column, with its height on the other axis, which is everything above. Bind two continuous columns to a mark with no measure axis and it is a field over the plane: zone * density paints it cell by cell, and surface * density raises it into the cube. Cut that field into steps of equal density and it becomes a set of levels: path * density traces their edges as contour lines, and zone * density(levels = 8) fills the bands between them. Bind a category and a continuous column and both axes are taken, so the estimate is drawn across the category’s slot, one distribution per group, which is the violin:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading")


(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading"))


data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * density: the slot reading"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 60 80  ribbon * density: the slot reading Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”
This plot draws five estimates, one per continent, and all five are smoothed by the same bandwidth. By default it is the average of the bandwidths Silverman’s rule gives each continent on its own. If each continent kept its own bandwidth, Oceania’s two countries would get one about a ninth of Africa’s, and the two shapes would differ partly because of that. With one bandwidth, a difference in shape comes from the data and not from the smoothing. The same sharing applies whenever one layer draws several estimates: curves split by color, the panels of a facet whose axes are shared, and the frames of an animation made with play. adjust multiplies the shared bandwidth, and a stated bandwidth replaces it.
Split the curve by color, and each continent gets its own curve, smoothed by the same shared bandwidth:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("line * density + color: one curve per continent")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("line * density + color: one curve per continent"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) + color(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("line * density + color: one curve per continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("line * density + color: one curve per continent"))






                                 40 60 80   0.00 0.05 0.10 0.15  line * density + color: one curve per continent Density Life expectancy  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: lines derived by density, x is life, color by continent.”
Each curve encloses the same area, so a continent whose countries sit close together draws a tall, narrow curve. Oceania’s two countries are one year apart, so its curve is the tallest. With its own, much smaller bandwidth, it would be nearly three times as tall, and the other four curves would be pressed down against the axis.
Each of density’s parameters belongs to one of the four readings, and gog refuses a parameter in a reading where it has no meaning, rather than ignoring it. bandwidth is a length in one column’s units, so it means nothing to a field, whose two axes measure different quantities. levels counts lines of equal density, and a curve has none to count. The slot reading has two parameters of its own. compare says what a violin’s width means from one slot to the next. reach says how far the shape extends, measured in slots, and past half a slot the shapes reach into their neighbors: the ridgeline. Neither means anything to a plot with no slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ compare: "count" })),
  x(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `density(compare = )` says what a violin's width means from one slot to the next, and `line * density` here has no slots — it estimates one curve along one axis. Bind a category to give it slots to compare: `ribbon * density(compare = "count") + x(<category>) + y(<number>)`. Otherwise drop `compare`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.6 What bin, density and smooth refuse
text:
25.6 What bin, density and smooth refuse
A histogram of continent is an easy thing to ask for, and gog refuses it. smooth, which fits a trend line, has its own section later in this chapter; it is included here because it is refused for the same reason as bin and density. The refusal is easier to act on once you know what these three transforms share.
One variable, or two? sorted the transforms by how many columns they read. A second property divides them a different way: these three all describe how values are spread along an axis, so the axis they read has to carry a number. A category is one slot rather than a stretch of line, so there is nothing to cut into intervals, nothing for a curve to spread over, and nothing to fit through.
The violin above looks like an exception, but it is not one. There the category is not the axis being estimated along: y(life) is, and the category only says which rows each estimate is made from. Take the number away and there is nothing left to spread over, so the refusal returns. That is why the first two examples below bind a category and nothing else.
Each refusal names the atom that asks the same question of categories. Binning one is really counting it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bin` cuts a continuous axis into intervals, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows per category, `count` is the transform that does it: `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A density over categories is really a share of the total:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, density), x(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `density` estimates a continuous distribution, and `x(continent)` is categorical — there is no number line for the curve to spread along. For the share of rows in each category, that is `bar * proportion`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And a curve fitted across categories is really a summary within each one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, smooth), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `smooth` fits a curve of `y` against `x`, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a fit needs a number line to run along. For a typical value per category, `bar * mean` (or `point * mean`) says it directly.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Which axis must be continuous is taken from the bindings rather than fixed to x. The horizontal histogram is bar * bin + y(life): it cuts y, because y is the axis it was handed and x is the one it invents. smooth is the strict one of the three, since it fits y against x and so needs a number on both.

25.6.1 A fit needs rows to fit through
It is easy to ask for a trend through very few rows: a table filtered to its latest years, or a group with two members.
Having numbers is not the same as having enough of them. smooth fits a curve, and two points are a straight line while one is a point, so it asks for at least three:

two_readings <- subset(gm_all, country == "France" & year >= 2002)
data(two_readings) + line * smooth + x(year) + y(life)

Error:
! gog: `smooth` fits a curve through the rows and needs at least 3 of them. This data has 2. Plot what you have with `point` and no transform, which draws the rows as rows rather than as a curve through them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The count that matters is the count inside each group, not in the table. A statistic runs within every group you split by, and faceting splits the rows before any of that. So a table with plenty of rows can still be asked for a fit through two:

recent <- subset(gm_all, year >= 2002)
data(recent) + line * smooth + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) |
  facet(continent)

Error:
! gog: `smooth` fits a curve through the rows and needs at least 3 of them. Split by `continent` or `country`, the smallest group has 2. Drop the split so the fit reads the rows together, or plot what you have with `point` and no transform, which draws the rows as rows rather than as a curve through them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


There are 284 rows there and gog still refuses, because each country in each panel is its own fit and each has only two rows. The message names both splits, so you know which one to remove. Drop group(country) and each panel fits one curve through a continent’s rows, and every continent has more than the three rows a fit needs.
The refusal matters because of what the plot would show without it. Below three rows the curve cannot be computed, so what would be drawn is the rows themselves, connected in order. A two-point group would draw a straight segment beside a hundred-point curve, with nothing to say that one is a fit and the other is the data. An unfinished plot that looks finished is worse than a refusal.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.7 Chaining transforms
Some questions need two transforms. To show life expectancy across income bands, cut income into bands and take a mean of life inside each one.
Two transforms on one mark have to divide the work, and there are only four jobs to divide. A transform can say where the cells are, it can say what is in them, it can say what scale the answer is read on, and it can say where the marks sit. bounds names where each band starts and ends. count tallies into the cells your categories already own, and says nothing about where those cells are. mean and its five siblings reduce a column you name, and say nothing about where the cells are either. proportion does the third job and only the third: it divides by a total, which is why it can stand after almost anything. dodge, stack, jitter and repel do the fourth, moving marks that would otherwise land on top of one another. Several of these transforms, mean, bounds and the four that move marks among them, have their own sections later in this chapter. Here they appear only as examples of how two transforms combine.
Two transforms compose when they do different jobs, and contradict when they do the same one. A cell holds one extent, one measurement, one scale and one arrangement. A second transform doing a job the first already did therefore leaves no reading that keeps both. The engine refuses, rather than drawing one and quietly discarding the other. Combinations has the whole grid, generated from the same rule.
Because each job is filled once, the order you write them in does not change the picture. Still, write them in the order they are computed, so the sentence reads in the same order as the work.
bin does two of the four jobs, and it is the only transform that can drop one of them. Cutting an axis is what makes it a bin; the tally it hands back is a by-product of the cut. So when you compose it with another statistic, bin keeps the cut and the other statistic keeps the measurement:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * mean + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band")


(data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * mean + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band"))


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * mean + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin(20), mean),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band"))






                                                  1K 10K 100K   0 20 40 60 80  Mean life expectancy by income band Life Gdp





“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20 and mean, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”
Read the sentence as three separate claims. bin(20) cuts income into twenty bands. mean reduces life within each one. bar draws the result as a length from zero. The bars touch because the bands tile the axis, exactly as a histogram’s do, and the y axis is now labeled for the column that was actually reduced.
Any mark that accepts both transforms accepts the pair. Here the same cut is drawn as points, with median in place of mean:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point * bin(20) * median + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Median life expectancy by income band")


(data(gm_all) + point * bin(20) * median + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Median life expectancy by income band"))


data(gm_all) + point * bin(20) * median + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + title("Median life expectancy by income band")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(point, bin(20), median),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  title("Median life expectancy by income band"))






                                                1K 10K 100K   50 60 70 80  Median life expectancy by income band Life Gdp





“Given all the gapminder years: points derived by bin into 20 and median, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

25.7.1 What cannot be chained, and why
Having seen bin * mean work, you will want to know which other pairs do.
The other two inventing transforms cannot drop their measurement, because measuring is all they do. Take it away from count and nothing is left of it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * count * mean + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gm_all) + bar * count * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gm_all) + bar * count * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * count * mean` measures each cell twice — `count` supplies only a measurement: its cells are the slots the positions already own, so with `mean` measuring them too the cell is measured twice and `count` has nothing left to contribute. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * count` to measure what `count` computes, or `bar * mean` to reduce the column you name. To cut a continuous axis into cells and reduce a column inside each, `bin` is the transform that cuts without keeping the measurement: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


density fails a different test. Its cells are the points where the estimate was sampled, and the estimate exists between your observations rather than inside cells that hold rows, so there is nothing inside one for a statistic to reduce:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * density * mean + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gm_all) + bar * density * mean + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gm_all) + bar * density * mean + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, density, mean), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * density * mean` measures each cell twice — a `density` cell is a point where the estimate was sampled, not a bucket holding rows — the estimate exists *between* your observations — so there is nothing inside one for `mean` to reduce. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * density` to measure what `density` computes, or `bar * mean` to reduce the column you name. To cut a continuous axis into cells and reduce a column inside each, `bin` is the transform that cuts without keeping the measurement: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


smooth is refused against all three, including bin, for a reason none of them share. It fits a curve through the rows and already averages locally while it fits, so cutting them into cells first asks the same question a second time:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin * smooth + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gm_all) + bar * bin * smooth + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gm_all) + bar * bin * smooth + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin, smooth), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * bin * smooth` asks one question twice — `smooth` fits a curve through the rows and already averages locally as it goes, so cutting them into cells first changes nothing it was not doing. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * smooth + x(<a>) + y(<b>)` for the fitted curve, or `bar * bin` for the shape `bin` measures. For a summary per cell rather than a fitted curve, name the statistic: `bar * bin * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And two transforms that each invent their own measurement are the same contradiction. bin gives up its tally only to a transform that reads a column you named, and count reads none, so a cell would be measured twice:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin * count + x(life)


data(gm_all) + bar * bin * count + x(col.life)


data(gm_all) + bar * bin * count + x(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin, count), x(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * bin * count` measures each cell twice — `bin` and `count` each invent their own measurement from the rows, and neither was handed a column to give way to, so there is no reading that keeps both. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * bin` or `bar * count`. To cut an axis into cells and measure something else inside them, the second transform has to be one you hand a column: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>) + y(<column>)`. To read either as shares of the whole rather than as counts, `proportion` rescales whichever you keep: `bar * bin * proportion`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Each refusal names both transforms you could drop. Each also names a third option, bar * bin * mean, because bin is the one transform that cuts without keeping its measurement.
The same rule applies to transforms that write a low and a high, and to the transforms that arrange marks. Two transforms that both produce a low and a high measure the cell twice. So range and confidence cannot stand together. A minimum and a maximum are not a 95% confidence interval, and one of the two would have to be discarded:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + interval * range * confidence + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gm_all) + interval * range * confidence + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gm_all) + interval * range * confidence + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(interval, range, confidence), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `interval * range * confidence` measures each cell twice — `range` and `confidence` both reduce the column you named, and a cell holds one answer, so drawing both would mean drawing one of them and discarding the other. Keep whichever you meant: `interval * range` or `interval * confidence`. To show both, draw them as two layers: `interval * range + interval * confidence`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The same is true when one transform writes a single value and the other writes two:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + line * sum * range + x(year) + y(population)


data(gm_all) + line * sum * range + x(col.year) + y(col.population)


data(gm_all) + line * sum * range + x(:year) + y(:population)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, sum, range), x(col.year),
  y(col.population))




Error:
! gog: `line * sum * range` measures each cell twice — `sum` and `range` both reduce the column you named, and a cell holds one answer, so drawing both would mean drawing one of them and discarding the other. Keep whichever you meant: `line * sum` or `line * range`. To show both, draw them as two layers: `line * sum + line * range`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And two arrangements are the same contradiction on the fourth job. A bar cannot be set beside its neighbor and piled on top of it at once, because it sits in one place:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * count * dodge * stack + x(continent) + color(continent)


data(gm_all) + bar * count * dodge * stack + x(col.continent) + color(col.continent)


data(gm_all) + bar * count * dodge * stack + x(:continent) +
  color(:continent)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count, dodge, stack), x(col.continent),
  color(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bar * dodge * stack` arranges the same marks twice — `dodge` and `stack` each decide where colliding groups go, and a mark sits in one place, so one of the two would be discarded. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * dodge` or `bar * stack`. To show both readings, draw them as two plots side by side rather than as one layer.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A transform can also be unnecessary rather than contradictory, and that is a different answer. proportion divides a tally by its total, so it already counts the rows, which leaves count beside it with nothing to add. The plot is still exactly the plot you asked for, so the engine draws it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * count * proportion + x(continent) +
  title("Share of countries by continent")


(data(gm_all) + bar * count * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  title("Share of countries by continent"))


data(gm_all) + bar * count * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("Share of countries by continent")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("Share of countries by continent"))




gog: `bar * count * proportion` draws the same plot as `bar * proportion` — a share is a share *of* a tally, so `proportion` already counts the rows and `count` adds nothing. Drop it, or keep `bar * count` on its own to read the tallies themselves rather than their shares.




                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  Share of countries by continent Proportion Continent





“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by count and proportion, x is continent.”
The note printed with the plot names the shorter sentence, bar * proportion, that draws the same picture.
That is the difference between the two answers. When the two transforms cannot both be used, the engine refuses rather than discard one. When both can stay and one of them simply changes nothing, it draws and says so. Neither answer is silence, which is the rule underneath both: a word you wrote is never read and then ignored.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.8 smooth: LOESS trend line
The inventing transforms make a new measurement from one column. The reading transforms summarize a measurement you already have: each one reads a column you name, usually on y, and answers with a summary of it. smooth is the first of them.
Income and life expectancy rise together across the scatter, and one curve through the cloud states that relationship more plainly than 142 separate points.
smooth fits a locally weighted linear regression (LOESS) through the (x, y) points and evaluates it at 100 evenly spaced x positions (Cleveland, 1979). Each local regression is fitted once, with no second fit that gives outliers less weight. The curve is the engine’s own, so it is identical in all four languages.
Combine smooth with line to overlay a trend line on a scatterplot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth + title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth),
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
smooth is not the line’s own transform. Four other marks fit the same curve, and only the shape changes:



Mark derived by smooth
Shape




point * smooth
one dot at each fitted value


area * smooth
the curve filled to the baseline


bar * smooth
one thin bar at each fitted value


step * smooth
the curve as a staircase


line * smooth
the fitted curve above



Span is fixed at 0.75: each local regression uses the nearest 75% of the data. A larger span would give a smoother curve, but smooth takes no argument, so the span cannot be changed. smooth needs continuous columns on x and y, and at least three rows in each group. Both refusals are earlier in this chapter, under What bin, density and smooth refuse. It writes its fitted values under the same x and y names, so the axes keep their labels.
ggplot2’s geom_smooth() uses the same span, 0.75, but differs in two ways. First, its default fit is a local quadratic: a small parabola around each x position, not a straight line. So the two curves can differ where the relationship is curved, most often at their left and right ends. Second, when any group has 1,000 rows or more, geom_smooth() fits a generalized additive model instead of LOESS. In that case, the two curves come from different methods, and the difference can be larger.

25.8.1 smooth_band: the band around the curve
A curve through a cloud says where the trend lies. A band around it says how precisely the trend is known. confidence adds a low and a high around a mean; smooth_band adds them around smooth’s curve. At the 100 x positions smooth uses, smooth_band writes the curve’s confidence band as a low and a high, with the fitted value as the center. A ribbon fills the band, and line * smooth draws the curve inside it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point +
  ribbon * smooth_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * smooth +
  title("The trend, and how precisely it is known")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point +
  ribbon * smooth_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * smooth +
  title("The trend, and how precisely it is known"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + ribbon * smooth_band +
  style(opacity = 0.3) + line * smooth +
  title("The trend, and how precisely it is known")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  layer(ribbon, smooth_band), style({ opacity: 0.3 }),
  layer(line, smooth), title("The trend, and how precisely it is known"))






                                                                                                                                                                                          0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80 90  The trend, and how precisely it is known Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points, and also a ribbon derived by smooth_band, and also a line derived by smooth.”
The band widens at the right, where only a few rich countries lie. Where fewer rows lie near an x position, the trend there is known less precisely. The band shows the uncertainty of the curve, not the spread of the countries, so three countries in four lie outside it. Its center is smooth’s curve exactly. The confidence level is 0.95 unless you name another, and smooth_band(0.99) draws a wider band.
Like smooth, smooth_band needs two continuous columns, but it needs five rows in each group, not three. The band’s width is computed from how far the rows lie from the curve. With three or four rows, the curve passes through every row, so no width can be computed. line * smooth_band draws the band’s two edges instead of filling it.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.9 Aggregation family: sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile
text:
25.9 Aggregation family: sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile
The six summaries are the simplest members of the reading family. A table can hold several rows for the same x value, for example medals from different years all labeled “USA”. bar alone then draws one bar per row, and the bars for one country are drawn over each other in one slot.
The aggregation family groups rows by x and reduces y to a single value per group. All six follow exactly the same grammar:
bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * mean + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * median + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * max + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * min + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * quantile(0.9) + x(country) + y(gold)
sum, total y per group, the most common aggregation for counts and amounts:



medal_repeats: all 5 rows


country
gold




USA
10


USA
5


GBR
8


GBR
4


JPN
6







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medal_repeats) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Total gold medals") + title("Sum per country: bar * sum")


(data(medal_repeats) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Total gold medals") + title("Sum per country: bar * sum"))


data(medal_repeats) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Total gold medals") +
  title("Sum per country: bar * sum")


plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Total gold medals"),
  title("Sum per country: bar * sum"))






                            USA GBR JPN   0 5 10 15  Sum per country: bar * sum Total gold medals Country





“Given the medal repeats table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”
sum is not the bar’s own transform, and the whole family behaves alike:



Mark derived by sum
Shape




point * sum
one dot at each total


line * sum
the totals joined into a profile


area * sum
the same profile, filled to the baseline


step * sum
each total held flat across its slot


zone * sum
one cell per pair of categories, colored by its total


bar * sum
one bar per category, the plot above



You can put mean, median, min, max or quantile in place of sum in every row of that table. The statistic decides the number, and the mark decides the shape.
mean, average y per group, useful for comparing typical values:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medal_repeats) + bar * mean + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Mean gold medals") + title("Mean per country: bar * mean")


(data(medal_repeats) + bar * mean + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Mean gold medals") + title("Mean per country: bar * mean"))


data(medal_repeats) + bar * mean + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Mean gold medals") +
  title("Mean per country: bar * mean")


plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, mean), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Mean gold medals"),
  title("Mean per country: bar * mean"))






                            USA GBR JPN   0 2 4 6  Mean per country: bar * mean Mean gold medals Country





median, the middle value, robust to outliers:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medal_repeats) + bar * median + x(country) + y(gold) +

25.9.1 The same six, grouping by a pair
Mean wind speed by direction is one bar chart. Mean wind speed by direction and season is a grid of cells, with one mean in each.
On a zone, count tallies two axes instead of one, and these six do the same, for the same reason. A bar has a length to show the answer along, so it groups by one position and measures along the other. A zone measures nothing by length. Both its positions are free to be grouping columns, and the answer goes to color:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed) +
  title("The same mean, grouped by a pair")

  title("The same mean, grouped by a pair"))

  title("The same mean, grouped by a pair")

  color(col.speed), title("The same mean, grouped by a pair"))

The cells for west are the darkest in both rows: winds from the west average about 21 in summer and in winter alike. Each direction changes little from one season to the other, so on this table the direction a wind comes from says more about its speed than the season does.
The channel that names the column to reduce is also the channel that shows the result. That is not a special case for the zone: a summary reduces in place everywhere, and on bar * mean + x(country) + y(gold) it is y that both names gold and receives the average. A zone measures by color, so there color both names the column and shows the result.
So the whole rule fits in one sentence: a summary groups by every position the mark does not measure with, and reduces the column named on the one it does.

The middle two rows are identical, and that is the rule working rather than a coincidence: a 3-D bar and a surface have the same three positions and measure along the same one, so they group and reduce alike. Only the shape drawn on each (x, y) cell differs: a standing bar, or a flat plateau.
What separates these six from count, bin and density is not the number of axes, since all nine can group by one axis or two. It is whether a column was named for them. Those three invent their measurement. They need no column named, and they write their answer into a column of their own name. These six are given a column instead, so the sentence has to say which one, and the answer replaces it. proportion belongs to neither group: it divides whatever measurement the sentence has already made.


25.9.2 Why these names?
The six names follow one rule. sum, mean, median, max, min and quantile each name an operation on y, not a data type and not a chart name. The * operator makes this explicit: bar * sum reads as “a bar that sums”. Every aggregation is the word a statistics course already uses (Law 3: Plain Names).

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.10 quantile: one point in the distribution
text:
25.10 quantile: one point in the distribution
sum, mean, median, max and min each answer a fixed question. quantile takes the question as its argument: quantile(0.9) is the value below which nine tenths of the group falls, which is the 90th percentile.
Many reported numbers have exactly that form. A service level is the 95th percentile of response time. A growth chart is a set of percentiles by age. A pay band is usually quoted at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles. Here are three of them across every country, year by year:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line * quantile(0.9) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  line * median + style(color = "gray") +
  line * quantile(0.1) + style(color = "tomato") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th")


(data(gm_all) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line * quantile(0.9) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  line * median + style(color = "gray") +
  line * quantile(0.1) + style(color = "tomato") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th"))


data(gm_all) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line * quantile(0.9) +
  style(color = "steelblue") + line * median + style(color = "gray") +
  line * quantile(0.1) + style(color = "tomato") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th")


plot(data(gm_all), x(col.year), y(col.life), layer(line, quantile(0.9)),
  style({ color: "steelblue" }), layer(line, median),
  style({ color: "gray" }), layer(line, quantile(0.1)),
  style({ color: "tomato" }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th"))






                                     1960 1980 2000   40 50 60 70 80  The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th Life expectancy Year





“Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, a line derived by quantile at 0.9, colored steelblue, and also a line derived by median, colored gray, and also a line derived by quantile at 0.1, colored tomato.”
The three lines are three sentences over one table, and they say different things about the same 142 countries. The middle rose steadily. The top rose more slowly, because it was already high. The bottom rose and then declined for a decade, which neither of the others shows.
Each of those three lines named its own probability: 0.9, 0.5 written as median, and 0.1. Leave the probability out and nothing can run, because quantile has no default the way bin and density do. Every other transform whose parameter is a number works bare, and this one is refused:

The plot draws, and gog says that median is the plain name for it. quantile(0) and quantile(1) say the same about min and max.   y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Petal length range per species"))






                                   setosa versicolor virginica   2 4 6  Petal length range per species Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range, x is species, y is petal length.”
range is not the interval’s own transform. Three other marks read the same low and high value, and only the shape changes:



Mark derived by range
Shape




ribbon * range
the band between the two values, filled


line * range
the two values as two separate strokes


step * range
the same two boundaries, as staircases


interval * range
one whisker per group, the plot above



You can put confidence, deviation or bounds in place of range in every row of that table, and bounds adds zone, which shades the region between its two columns.
range reads a y and groups by x exactly like the aggregation family: it needs a y() and works the same whether x is continuous or categorical. What differs is the output: two rows per group instead of one. This low/high-rows shape is reused elsewhere. The box mark encodes its own summary the same way, with the two whisker ends as the pair of rows and the quartiles alongside. The ribbon mark fills between the same pair as a continuous band. See Interval for the whisker, and for why its extents are invented here rather than bound to two extra channels the kernel would never otherwise have.

25.11.1 A band between two quantiles
The minimum and the maximum each come from a single row, so one unusual row moves the whole span. To show the middle of a group instead of its extremes, give range two quantiles:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range(0.25, 0.75)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Middle half of petal length per species"))






                                       setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5 6  Middle half of petal length per species Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, x is species, y is petal length.”
The two numbers are quantile probabilities, so range(0.25, 0.75) spans the first quartile to the third. That span is the interquartile range, and it is the same one a box draws as its body, computed by the same rule. Any other pair works the same way: range(0.1, 0.9) keeps the middle 80%, and range(0.05, 0.95) the middle 90%.
Bare range is range(0, 1), because the quantile at 0 is the minimum and the quantile at 1 is the maximum. So interval * range is unchanged, and the two arguments only make its default visible. Naming one end leaves the other at its extreme, so range(high = 0.9) runs from the smallest value to the 90th percentile.
Both ends are probabilities. A number below 0 or above 1 is refused, not corrected:

  y(:petal_length)

  y(col.petal_length))

For a low and a high you computed yourself, in the data’s own units, use bounds instead.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.12 confidence: the interval of the mean
text:
25.12 confidence: the interval of the mean
range shows the full spread of a group. Often the question is the uncertainty of the mean instead, which is what an error bar shows. confidence computes the mean’s confidence interval per group (mean ± t·se, with se the standard error: the t-interval), emitting a low, a high, and a center. That center is what turns the whisker into a pointrange, a whisker with a dot at its center:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("95% CI of mean petal length"))






                                        setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5  95% CI of mean petal length Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length.”
The level is a parameter, exactly like bin(30) and density(2): confidence alone is 95%, confidence(0.99) is wider. It uses the t-distribution (not a fixed 1.96), so a small group’s interval is genuinely wider. A group of one has no spread, and its interval collapses to a point.
The center dot appears because the statistic has a center; range has none, so it draws a bare whisker. That is the rule for every pair transform: the transform decides whether there is a center, and the mark draws what it is given. So the difference between an error bar and a pointrange is which statistic you ask for, not another mark to remember.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.13 deviation: the spread of the data
text:
25.13 deviation: the spread of the data
confidence says how precisely a mean is known. deviation says how far the values behind it spread. That is a different question, drawn as the same picture: deviation emits the same low, high and center, so it also draws a pointrange:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")


(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))


data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, deviation), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))






                                          setosa versicolor virginica   2 3 4 5 6  Mean petal length, with one standard deviation Petal length (cm) Species





“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length.”
The number of standard deviations is a parameter, like confidence’s level: deviation alone reaches one standard deviation on each side of the mean, and deviation(2) reaches two, so that band is four standard deviations wide. The standard deviation is the sample one, dividing by n − 1, so a group of one has no spread to show and collapses to a point exactly as confidence does.
Neither transform makes the other redundant, and neither does range. On the iris flowers the confidence band is under a third as long as the deviation band: fifty measurements locate a mean precisely, and their spread stays as wide as it was. Adding rows narrows the first band, while the second stays about as wide as it was. Interval draws the two side by side and says which sentence each one supports.
range(0.25, 0.75) answers a third version of the question. It reads the sorted values, so it reports where the middle half of the values actually lie. deviation starts from the mean instead, and reports a distance out from it. On a skewed group they disagree, and the disagreement is informative rather than a defect.

“Given the score band: a ribbon from lower to upper, x is score.”
It differs from every transform above in two ways that both follow from reshaping, not computing. Its arguments are column names, not a number: it has to be told which columns hold the bounds. And it needs no y(): those two columns are the extents, so (like count, which invents its own y) the mark takes its low and high from bounds and the y axis fits them. bounds shows where gog stops computing. gog offers a small, deliberate set of statistics; everything else you compute yourself, and bounds draws a band you already have.
It is legal on the five marks that can draw a low/high pair, each a different geometry over the same pair, the No Exceptions rule that lets every mark in the bin table draw the same bins:

ribbon fills the pair (a filled band),
interval draws a whisker across it at each x,
line traces its two boundaries (the unfilled band),
step traces them as staircases (stepped control limits), and
zone shades the region between them, the band that names its own sides rather than tracking a curve.

So line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(pattern = "dashed") is the unfilled, dashed error band: the two ± curves with no fill between them. It is the same pair that ribbon * bounds fills, drawn by a different mark. gog refuses bounds on any other mark, and the message points to the band marks, or to a summary such as mean for one value per group.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.15 partition: a whole among nested parts
text:
25.15 partition: a whole among nested parts
Nearly every transform so far reads a column and writes a summary of it; bounds alone reshapes what you already had. partition reads a hierarchy: two or three columns that trace the path down to each row. It writes the region each node of that hierarchy occupies, four edges and a center, which is exactly what bin writes for a cell. That is what makes it a transform rather than a coordinate space, and it is why zone needs nothing new to draw the result.
The hierarchy’s levels can run two ways, and the difference is one parameter. Nested is the default: every level divides the same axis, and the other axis adds one band per level. On a flat plot that reading is the icicle. In polar() each band becomes a ring, which is the sunburst, and that chapter works it through in full.
Crossed is the other, and it is the one this chapter draws. The levels alternate: the first divides the width, the second divides the height within each of those columns, a third would divide the width again. The plot it makes is the mosaic.

25.15.1 The mosaic
A cross-tabulation raises two questions at once: how the two categories relate, and how many people each cell counts. A mosaic answers both in one picture.

one box per node, the plot above



The plot shows two variables, one in each direction. A column’s width is that city’s share of everyone surveyed, so Ashford’s column is three times Millbrook’s; a cell’s height is that mode’s share within its own city, so every column fills the panel whatever its width. The consequence is the one a mosaic is drawn for: a cell’s area is the number of people in it, and a reader compares those areas across the whole panel without being asked to.
That is also what makes Millbrook readable rather than misleading. Its bicycle share is the largest of the four, and its column is the narrowest. So the plot reports the finding and the number of people it is based on at once, which four equal-width stacked bars cannot do.
The two axes therefore carry different quantities, so look at both before you read a value from either. The horizontal axis runs from 0 to the total in the data’s own units, 3,790 people. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 1 and can do nothing else, because what a height means is a share of its own column and the grand total is not the thing being divided.
Compose the partition with proportion and the horizontal axis reads shares of everyone surveyed instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(commutes) + zone * partition(city, mode, cross = TRUE) * proportion +
  x(people) + color(mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("Share of people surveyed") +
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares")


(data(commutes) + zone * partition(col.city, col.mode, cross = True) * proportion +
  x(col.people) + color(col.mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("Share of people surveyed") +
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares"))


data(commutes) +
  zone * partition(:city, :mode, cross = true) * proportion + x(:people) +
  color(:mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("Share of people surveyed") +
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares")


plot(data(commutes),
  layer(zone, partition(col.city, col.mode, { cross: true }), proportion),
  x(col.people), color(col.mode),
  style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  x_label("Share of people surveyed"),
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares"))

“Given the commutes: zones derived by partition through city and mode, crossed, and proportion, x is people, color by mode.”
The columns keep their widths, and the axis under them now runs from 0 to 1. Ashford’s column ends near 0.41, its share of the 3,790 people. The heights do not change, because each was already a share of its own column.
partition writes a name column holding each node’s own label, and a text layer reads it. The sunburst uses the same kind of layer. A shallower partition of the same table puts its nodes in exactly the same places, so the second layer needs no filtering and no arithmetic of its own.

  x_label("People surveyed") +
  title("The same plot, with its columns named")

  layer(zone, partition(col.city, col.mode, { cross: true })),
  color(col.mode), style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),

The labels sit at the middle of each column because that is where the center of a column is, and style(nudge = ) is what moves them if you want them along the top. The city names would normally sit on an axis. But gog’s category axis gives every slot the same width, and the mosaic’s columns all have different widths. So the names are drawn as a layer.
The cell edges are a style() setting like any other, and they matter more here than anywhere else in the book. Without them, two neighboring cells that share a color merge into one shape and the column boundary disappears:

Both plots draw the same numbers. The second plot shows why a zone has the style(border_color = , border_size = ) settings at all. The mark has two uses. It is a highlight behind a line, where a frame would distract from the data, and it is the cells that are the data.
One level is legal and means something: the spine plot, columns of varying width and nothing dividing them, which is the marginal distribution on its own.

  color(col.city) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +

  color(:city) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("The margin alone: a spine plot")


plot(data(commutes), layer(zone, partition(col.city, { cross: true })),

partition refuses the same things whether it is crossed or nested, because the refusals are about the tree and not about the layout. A level must be a categorical column, not a continuous one. A branch may stop early, but it may not skip a level and then continue. And an interior node carrying a value of its own is the one genuine ambiguity, so it is refused rather than guessed. The Polar chapter shows each refusal where it is easiest to see.

Three marks read a flow, and a full diagram layers all three:



Mark derived by flow
Shape




ribbon * flow
the bands between the stages, the plot above


zone * flow
the slots at each stage

the name of each slot



The ribbon layer draws the bands, one per path, as thick as the path’s total at both ends. The zone layer draws each stage’s slots, stacked with no padding, so the measure axis is drawn with its usual ticks and reads true counts. A text layer names the slots. With shared = TRUE, two columns such as exporter and importer name one set of places, and every place lies on one axis, which carries no numbers. Drawn flat, it is the arc diagram; in polar(), it is the chord diagram. With layered = TRUE, each row is a link from one place to another, and gog computes a layer for each place from the links. That picture is the Sankey diagram. The Flow chapter builds the full diagram and gives the rules; this section only shows where the atom fits among the transforms.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.17 layout: a graph placed from an edge table
text:
25.17 layout: a graph placed from an edge table
partition, flow, layout and cluster each compute a whole picture rather than a column. layout is the third of them, and the first whose output draws in a space of its own. layout(from, to) reads the two endpoint columns of an edge table and computes a position for every distinct name, in the engine, the same way in every language. Three marks read the placement inside network(): edge the connections, point the nodes, text their names. Its positions mean nothing as quantities, so its space draws no axes. This section draws no layout plot. The Network chapter draws those plots and gives the rules; this section only shows where the atom fits among the transforms.

25.18 cluster: the closest leaves joined first
cluster is the fourth transform that computes a whole picture, and the question it answers is which things are most alike. It treats each category of an axis as a leaf of a tree, joins the two closest leaves, then the next two, and keeps joining until one tree holds them all. Each leaf is described by a profile: cluster(amount, over = nutrient) says that one leaf’s profile is its amount in every category of nutrient.

section: 25.19 dodge: side by side instead of on top

25.19 dodge: side by side instead of on top
Every transform above answers a question about the data. The four that remain answer none. They change where a mark sits rather than what was measured. dodge is a different kind of transform: a collision modifier. It writes no new values; it moves marks that would otherwise be drawn at one position, and sets them side by side instead.
When color splits a bar, a box or an interval into groups, the groups share their category’s slot and are drawn on top of one another. A histogram reads well that way, because the overlapping bars are translucent. A grouped bar chart does not, because there you want the groups set side by side. dodge does exactly that:

Four marks take dodge. Three share out the slot’s width among their groups, and a point moves sideways within the slot instead:

There is no width to set: dodge derives it from the number of groups (G groups, each 1/G of the slot). And because the offset resolves the overlap outright, dodged bars take the same fill a single bar does. The translucent fill exists only to see through overlapping bars, and none overlap now.
It is written after * like any transform, so it composes cleanly: bar * mean * dodge aggregates first and dodges the result; box * dodge dodges a box’s own summary; interval * range * dodge dodges grouped whiskers. Here it sets each continent’s two distributions side by side:

“Given the gapminder eras: boxes derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”
Which marks dodge serves is decided by what a mark is. On bar, box and interval it subdivides a width (a bar’s thickness, a box’s body, a whisker’s slot). A point has no width, so dodge moves it instead. Each point moves sideways within its slot, only as far as it must to touch no other point, and never along the measure axis. An area is piled rather than subdivided (that is stack, the next section). Ask for dodge on an area and gog refuses, naming the collision modifier that fits. A line takes neither dodge nor stack. It is a thin stroke, so lines that meet cross rather than cover each other. The rest of the kernel follows the same rule: an atom combines with the marks it was defined for, and the refusal names the atom that fits rather than drawing something wrong.
On a bar, box or interval, dodge also needs a split to separate: a channel that splits the rows into groups, such as color or group. Without one there is a single mark per slot and nothing to set beside anything, so bar * dodge on its own is refused, and the message asks for the split. It is never accepted as a word that quietly does nothing. A point needs no split, because points in one slot can already land on one another. With a split, each group takes its own part of the slot, as a dodged bar does, and its points are moved apart inside that part:

  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot")

  style(size = 2.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot"))


data(gm_eras) + point * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + color(:era) +
  style(size = 2.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot")


plot(data(gm_eras), layer(point, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), style({ size: 2.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot"))

“Given the gapminder eras: points derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”
The dots are drawn smaller here, with style(size = 2.5). Each era has half a slot, and at the default size Europe’s 2007 countries sit too close together to fit in it, so gog would draw some of them at the edge and say how many.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.20 stack: piled up, not side by side
text:
25.20 stack: piled up, not side by side
Side by side, two eras’ populations never show what they add up to, and when the total means something the pile is the better picture.
stack is dodge’s sibling: the other way to resolve a color split’s overlap. Where dodge sets the groups beside each other, stack piles them on top of each other along the measure axis, each group starting where the one below it ended. It is the collision modifier for the marks that accumulate: bar and area pile heights, and point piles rows.
Take the dodge example, change dodge to stack, and sum population instead of averaging life expectancy:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(continent) + y(population) + color(era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")


(data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked"))


data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")


plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.era), y_label("Population"),
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked"))






                                   Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 2000M 4000M  Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked Population Continent  Era    1957  2007 





“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and stack, x is continent, y is population, color by era.”
Three marks pile instead of overlapping:







Mark derived by stack
Shape




area * stack
each region starting at the top of the one below


point * bin * stack
one dot per row, piled into a column, which is the dot plot


bar * stack
one segment per group, piled, the plot above



The measure changed because you stack quantities that add up. Two populations can be added into one bar, while two mean life expectancies cannot: Europe’s two eras would pile into a bar reaching 144 years, so that comparison wants dodge, side by side. The grammar allows either, and the data decides which is right. Because the pile resolves the overlap, the bars take the same fill a single bar does, and the axis grows to the tallest stack: Asia passes five billion, the sum of its two eras.
Which marks stack serves is decided by what a mark is: the same rule dodge follows. What stack computes is one thing for every mark, a span from a foot to a top along the measure axis, and what differs is how a geometry draws that span. A bar fills it, and an area fills it across x. A point has no length to stretch across the span, so the span becomes how many dots there are, which is the dot plot. A box or interval is set beside its neighbors rather than piled, which is dodge. An unfilled line has nothing to fill and pile, so use area. A ribbon already spans a low to a high, so it measures no height from a baseline. Ask for stack on one of those and gog refuses, naming what fits instead. For bar and area it also needs a channel that splits the rows into groups to pile, such as color or group. bar * stack alone is refused, and the message asks for the split. It is never accepted as a word that quietly does nothing.

25.20.1 Stacked areas: the case stack was built for
A split area is where overlap matters most. Filled regions cover one another, and gog warns about it (the area chapter shows the warning and the opacity it suggests). Lowering the opacity does let you see through them, but five overlapping fills blend into colors the legend names for none of them. stack answers the same problem a different way. Each region sits on the cumulative height of the ones below, so they meet edge to edge in one band instead of covering each other, the classic “parts of a whole, over time”:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack + x(year) + y(population) + color(continent) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("World population by continent, stacked")


(data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack + x(col.year) + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("World population by continent, stacked"))


data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack + x(:year) + y(:population) +
  color(:continent) + y_label("Population") +
  title("World population by continent, stacked")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(area, sum, stack), x(col.year),
  y(col.population), color(col.continent), y_label("Population"),
  title("World population by continent, stacked"))






                                 1960 1980 2000   0 2000M 4000M 6000M  World population by continent, stacked Population Year  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given all the gapminder years: areas derived by sum and stack, x is year, y is population, color by continent.”
Asia sits at the foot; Europe, Africa, the Americas and Oceania pile on top, and the band’s upper edge is the world total. It climbs from 2.4 billion people to 6.25 billion. Read any one color’s thickness for that continent’s population.


25.20.2 stack(share = TRUE): every pile filled to one
Reading a thickness is the hard part of the plot above, because each band’s baseline moves under it. When the composition is the question and the total is not, stack(share = TRUE) divides every pile by its own slot’s total, so all of them reach 1 and only the proportions are left. That is filling the pile:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(year) + y(population) +
  color(continent) + title("Every year's composition, filled to one")


(data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = True) + x(col.year) + y(col.population) +
  color(col.continent) + title("Every year's composition, filled to one"))


data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = true) + x(:year) +
  y(:population) + color(:continent) +
  title("Every year's composition, filled to one")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(area, sum, stack({ share: true })), x(col.year),
  y(col.population), color(col.continent),
  title("Every year's composition, filled to one"))






                               1960 1980 2000   0.0 0.5 1.0  Every year's composition, filled to one Share Year  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given all the gapminder years: areas derived by sum and stack as shares, x is year, y is population, color by continent.”
Now Asia’s band holds about three fifths, and Europe’s visibly narrows across those 55 years. Both facts were also in the stacked plot before this one, where the rising total hid them. The axis says Share, because whatever the numbers were before, they are fractions of one now.
This is not a second name for proportion. The two divide by different totals. proportion divides by the whole plot’s, so its bars still say how big each slot is. This one divides by the slot’s own, which deliberately discards the slot’s size. So each year here is a set of shares of that year’s world population, a reading proportion cannot give in a single panel. Filling is a position adjustment: it changes where the marks sit and what the scale reads, never what was counted, which is why it belongs to stack and not to a statistic.
A bar fills the same way, and the result is the 100% stacked bar, worked through in the bar chapter. One parameter, both geometries, exactly as plain stack hands both marks the same span and lets each draw it: No Exceptions.


25.20.3 stack(baseline = ): where the pile sits
Two things about a pile can be changed. Its heights are one, and share is how you change them. Where the pile sits is the other, and baseline is how you change that.
The default is "zero". Every pile sits on the axis, which is both plots above. That layout has a known weakness. Only the bottom band has a shape you can read. Every band above it rests on the sum of the bands below, so its shape carries all of their movement as well as its own.
The weakness is easiest to see when each series peaks at a different time. Here are four music genres over half a year, in the listening table:

data(listening) + area * stack + x(week) + y(plays) + color(genre) +
  y_label("Plays") + title("Stacked on zero")

  y_label("Plays") + title("Stacked on zero"))


data(listening) + area * stack + x(:week) + y(:plays) + color(:genre) +
  y_label("Plays") + title("Stacked on zero")

  color(col.genre), y_label("Plays"), title("Stacked on zero"))
