Techno is the red band, the third from the bottom. It looks like it grows to about week 17 and then collapses. Part of that shape is Techno, and part of it is Folk and Jazz shrinking underneath it. You cannot tell which part is which.
"center" places each pile so that its middle is at zero:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "center") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + title("Centered: the ThemeRiver")


(data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "center") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + title("Centered: the ThemeRiver"))


data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "center") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + title("Centered: the ThemeRiver")


plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre),
  title("Centered: the ThemeRiver"))






                            5 10 15 20 25    Centered: the ThemeRiver Week  Genre    Folk  Jazz  Techno  Ambient 





“Given the listening table: areas derived by stack on the center baseline, x is week, y is plays, color by genre.”
That symmetric layout is the ThemeRiver (Havre et al., 2000), named for the plot it was built to draw: how much each theme is written about, over time.
"wiggle" instead chooses the foot that leaves the bands as flat as possible. The thickest bands move least, because a reader looks at them first. The movement is pushed into the thin bands instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + title("Flattest: the streamgraph")


(data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + title("Flattest: the streamgraph"))


data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + title("Flattest: the streamgraph")


plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack({ baseline: "wiggle" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre),
  title("Flattest: the streamgraph"))






                            5 10 15 20 25    Flattest: the streamgraph Week  Genre    Folk  Jazz  Techno  Ambient 





“Given the listening table: areas derived by stack on the wiggle baseline, x is week, y is plays, color by genre.”
Now Techno is one clean shape, widening and then narrowing, which is what the numbers actually say. Folk, the blue band, is a steady decline rather than a wedge. No band changed thickness between these three plots. Only the place each pile sits changed.
The last plot is a streamgraph (Byron & Wattenberg, 2008). The middle one is a ThemeRiver. The two are often confused and they are not the same layout: one is symmetric, the other is chosen to reduce movement. The streamgraph’s designers argue readers compare values more accurately on it, and that argument is the reason this option exists (Byron & Wattenberg, 2008).
Notice also that these two plots have no numbers on the measure axis. Once a pile has moved off zero, no value on that axis means anything. A band drawn from 12 to 20 says “this group is 8 here”, and the 12 and the 20 only record where the pile was placed. So gog draws no ticks and no axis label of its own, for the same reason it leaves an empty heatmap cell unpainted. A label you write with y_label() is still drawn, because it names the quantity and not a position. The scale is unchanged, so thicknesses stay comparable everywhere in the plot, and thickness is what a streamgraph asks you to read.
baseline is not an area-only parameter. A bar has a pile too, so it is placed the same way:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(listening) + bar * stack(baseline = "center") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + title("The same baseline, drawn as bars")


(data(listening) + bar * stack(baseline = "center") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + title("The same baseline, drawn as bars"))


data(listening) + bar * stack(baseline = "center") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + title("The same baseline, drawn as bars")


plot(data(listening), layer(bar, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre),
  title("The same baseline, drawn as bars"))






                                                                                                                         0 10 20    The same baseline, drawn as bars Week  Genre    Folk  Jazz  Techno  Ambient 





One parameter, both geometries. share follows the same rule, and so does plain stack, which hands both marks one span and lets each draw it: No Exceptions.
Once a pile is moved, zero on the measure axis no longer means anything. Only a flat plot can work without a meaningful zero, so the other spaces refuse:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + polar()


(data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + polar())


data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + polar()


plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack({ baseline: "wiggle" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre), polar())




Error:
! gog: `stack(baseline = "wiggle")` moves every pile off the origin of the measure axis, and `polar()` has no origin to spare. A displaced pile is a statement about a plane: in `polar()` the measure is an angle or a radius or a height the space has already fixed, so moving the foot asks for a place that is not on the plot. Keep the space and drop the baseline (`stack` alone, or with its `share` set to true for composition), or keep the baseline and draw it flat.

In polar() the measure is an angle or a radius. A radius of zero is the center of the circle, so moving a pile off it asks for a negative radius, which is not a place on the plot.


25.20.4 A pile has one direction
stack has a third condition. The first two, a mark that can pile and a channel that splits the rows, are about the sentence. This one is about the numbers.
In a table of sales and returns, the returns arrive as negative numbers. The question is then whether a pile can grow downward at all.
A pile puts its groups end to end. Every member must therefore point the same way.
Negative values are allowed. A pile of them grows downward from zero, exactly as a positive pile grows up:

Error:
! gog: `bar * stack` piles the groups at one position on top of one another, and at quarter = Q2 they disagree in sign — `sales` is 5 and `returns` is -3. A pile has one direction: the band going the other way is drawn *inside* the ones below it, so the plot would show a block of 3 where the number is negative and read its sign backwards. Either keep the sign and drop the pile — `bar * dodge` sets the groups side by side instead, and a dodged bar keeps its own baseline, so a negative one hangs below the axis where a reader can see that it is negative — or keep the pile and drop the sign, stacking magnitudes you took the absolute value of in the host. (A pile whose members agree stays legal both ways: all-negative grows downward from zero exactly as all-positive grows up.)

The message names the position, both groups, and both numbers. A message that said only “some values are negative” would make you search the whole table for a pile you cannot see on the page.
There are two ways to fix this, and you choose by what you want the plot to show. If the sign matters, use dodge. Each bar then keeps its own baseline, so a negative bar hangs below the axis where a reader can see that it is negative. If the total matters, take the absolute value in the host language first. You are then stacking magnitudes, so say so in the column name or the axis label.
stack(share = TRUE) fails for the same reason, and the failure is easier to see. A share is a fraction of the pile’s total. Here the total is 5 plus -3, which is 2, so the two shares are 2.5 and -1.5. No rescaling fixes that. The problem is in the pile itself, not in how the pile is drawn.
Piles at different positions may still point different ways. Each pile is read on its own. One quarter can be positive and the next negative in the same plot.


25.20.5 The dot plot
A histogram’s bars hide the rows inside them. When every country should stay visible, and countable, the mark to pile is the point.
A point has no length, so it cannot stretch across the span every other mark gets. gog fills the span with copies of the point instead: one dot per unit, piled up from the foot. The unit of a count is one row, so a pile of dots is a count you can count:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, bin, stack), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("One dot per country"))






                                                                                                                                                                            50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  One dot per country Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by bin and stack, x is life.”
That is a dot plot (Wilkinson, 1999), and it is the same sentence as the histogram at the top of this chapter with one atom changed and one added. Compare the two. bar * bin draws each tally as a length, and you read the shape from the outline. point * bin * stack draws each tally as that many dots, so every country in the table is on the page. Count the tallest pile and you get its bin’s count exactly, which no bar can offer.
Nothing here is a color split, and none is needed. bar and area pile groups, so they ask for one; a point piles rows, which every table already has. What it asks for instead is a transform that counts them, because a pile of 3.7 dots means nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean * stack + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean * stack + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))

! gog: `point * stack` piles one dot per observation along the measure axis — the dot plot — so the measure has to be a count of rows, and nothing here counts them. Add the transform that does: `point * bin * stack` for a continuous axis (dots per interval), `point * count * stack` for a categorical one (dots per category).

The refusal names the two transforms that count rows: bin for a continuous axis, and count for a categorical one. The second draws a bar chart of counts as piles of dots, one dot per row:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + x(continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + x(col.continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + x(:continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count, stack), x(col.continent),
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent"))






                                                                                                                                                                            Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  One dot per country, piled by continent Count Continent





The dots pack tightly here and loosely on a small table. No setting controls the spacing. The vertical gap between stacked dots is always one count unit on the y axis, so its size on the page depends on the tallest pile. A taller pile therefore subdivides the panel more finely, and a pile of ten dots in a tall panel leaves wide gaps. style(size = ) will enlarge the dots, but making them touch means fixing the panel’s height to the tallest pile, and no setting does that. The y axis shows real counts either way, and that choice is deliberate: the alternative is to draw the dots touching and leave the axis with no meaning.
Each pile’s height is the count, drawn on y, so a dot plot names no column there. Name one, such as y(continent), and gog refuses it. The message suggests color(continent) or a facet instead.


25.20.6 How many rows is too many?
One dot per country works at 142 rows. A table twelve times that size is where the picture stops working.
Write the same sentence for a much larger table and the dots in each pile merge into one solid shape. Every year of gapminder rather than one is 1704 rows, and the tallest pile is 314 of them:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point * bin * stack + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots")


(data(gm_all) + point * bin * stack + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots"))


data(gm_all) + point * bin * stack + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(point, bin, stack), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots"))




gog: `point * bin * stack` piled 314 dots into one column, and at that height they overlap instead of counting — a dot plot says what it says by showing every observation separately, so this is a histogram drawn dot by dot. For this many rows, `bar * bin` reads the same shape as a summary, and `line * density` as a curve. `style(size = )` shrinks the dots, which buys a little room.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    40 60 80   0 100 200 300  Every year, every country: 1704 dots Count Life expectancy (years)





gog draws it, and says what happened. The piles have become solid sticks. With 314 dots in a pile, the gap is a sixth of a dot’s width, so the dots overlap and nothing can be counted, which was this plot’s entire claim. What you are looking at is a histogram drawn dot by dot, and a costly one: it draws 1704 circles where bar * bin draws twelve rectangles.
The warning is not a row limit, and that matters. It compares the gap against one dot’s diameter, both of which gog knows once the panel is laid out. So the warning appears exactly when the picture degrades, and not when it does not. With wider bins, a smaller table gets the warning too. Shrink the dots with style(size = ) far enough and the warning stops. On this table, though, that means style(size = 0.75), a dot 1.5 pixels wide and too small to count, because size is the dot’s radius. That is why the next plot also cuts more bins. A number like “more than 500 rows” would be wrong at some panel size or dot size, and there is no need to guess one when the real condition is available.
Which also means the warning is advice, not a limit. Two atoms usually answer it without removing a single dot, and the first is the one people forget: more bins spread the same rows over more piles, so every pile gets shorter without anything getting smaller. Then the dots themselves:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point * bin(40) * stack + x(life) + style(size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller")


(data(gm_all) + point * bin(40) * stack + x(col.life) + style(size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller"))


data(gm_all) + point * bin(40) * stack + x(:life) + style(size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(point, bin(40), stack), x(col.life),
  style({ size: 1.5 }), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  40 60 80   0 50 100  The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller Count Life expectancy (years)





“Given all the gapminder years: points derived by bin into 40 and stack, x is life, with size 1.5.”
The columns are made of visible dots again, and every one of the 1704 is still on the page. Faceting is the third way, since fewer rows per panel means shorter piles in each.
What none of them changes is the arithmetic. Counting needs at least one dot-diameter of axis per row, so the tallest pile you can still count is about the panel’s height divided by a dot. That is a few hundred with dots you can see, and a few dozen if you mean to count them one by one. Past that, a summary is the better answer, and the reason is the same one that makes the dot plot useful for small tables. A bin width or a bandwidth is a guess about structure when there are thirty rows. It is a reliable description when there are ten thousand. So the dot plot stops working at the same size where a summary starts working well.


25.20.7 One bar, split into its parts
Not every question comes with a category to stand bars on. The 264 winds are one total, and the only question is how it divides by direction.
Every stacked bar so far has stood at a position, one pile per category on the x axis. Take the position away and the split still has something to divide: a single bar, showing how one total divides.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count * stack + color(direction)


data(winds) + bar * count * stack + color(col.direction)


data(winds) + bar * count * stack + color(:direction)


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count, stack), color(col.direction))






                              0 100 200  Count  Direction    N  NE  E  SE  S  SW  W  NW 





“Given the winds: bars derived by count and stack, color by direction.”
There is no x() in that sentence, and none is needed. A bar normally requires a position because it has to stand somewhere. Here the color split is what divides the bar into parts, and there is one slot for those parts to share, so the position is no longer required. Bend this same plot into a circle and it is a pie, the subject of Polar.
Without a split there is nothing to divide, so the position is required again and the refusal says so. The statistic also has to be one that means something with nothing to group by. count and sum reduce a set of rows to one number. bin and density describe how values spread along an axis, and there is no axis here.
That ends the sections on stack. Two collision modifiers remain: jitter, which spreads points within a category, and repel, which moves labels apart.

title: 25  Transforms
section: 25.21 jitter: spread sideways, along the category
text:
25.21 jitter: spread sideways, along the category
dodge and stack resolve the overlap of grouped marks. The third collision modifier resolves a mark’s own points landing on top of each other, as dodge also does on a point. jitter does it another way: it moves each point sideways by a small amount that varies from point to point. A strip plot, every country as a dot above its continent, draws its points in a single vertical line, and heavy overlap hides how many there are:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Strip plot: the points pile onto one line Life expectancy Continent





jitter nudges each point a little to the side, so the crowded points spread out and the shape of each group shows:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life.”
Africa’s long tail of low values and Europe’s tight cluster near the top were both there before; the spread is what lets you read them.
jitter moves a point along the categorical axis, never along the measured one. Look again: every dot sits at exactly the same height as before; the spread is entirely sideways. This is the rule, not a coincidence. The horizontal axis is a category, and a category has no magnitude, so nudging a point along it changes nothing you could misread. The vertical axis is a measurement, and moving a point off its measured value would misreport the data, so jitter never touches it. (Spreading in both directions is the other way to do this. It moves a point off its measured value, which is why gog spreads along one axis only.) On a horizontal strip, with the category on y, the spread is vertical instead. jitter always spreads the categorical axis and leaves the measured one exact.
The spread is deterministic: it is computed from the data itself, not from a random-number generator or the clock, so the same plot drawn twice is pixel-for-pixel the same picture. A specification always means one plot.

25.21.1 How much to spread: jitter(amount)
The default spread is one guess at what reads well, and on your figure it may be too wide or too narrow.
By default a point moves at most 0.4 of a slot from its category’s center: far enough to show how many points there are, and near enough to leave a gap between categories. For a wider or narrower spread, jitter(amount) multiplies the default by a plain number, so jitter(0.5) is half as wide (a bare jitter is jitter(1)).


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(0.5) + x(continent) + y(life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(0.5) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(0.5) + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter(0.5)), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread"))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread Life expectancy Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter at 0.5, x is continent, y is life.”
The amount can be any number from 0 to 1.25. jitter(0) moves no point. It is harmless, so gog draws the plot and prints a note that the jitter did nothing. At the other end, jitter(1.25) moves a point up to half a slot, to the edge of its slot. gog refuses a larger amount, because it would move some points into a neighboring category, where they would be read as that category’s rows:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(2) + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(2) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(2) + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter(2)), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `jitter(2)` spreads points past the edge of their own category, so some would land in the neighboring one and be read as its rows. A point moves up to 0.4 of a slot for each unit of the amount, so `jitter(1.25)` reaches the slot's edge and is the widest spread that keeps every point in its own category. Use an amount of 1.25 or less; to show where many points overlap, `style(opacity = )` or a smaller `style(size = )` does it without moving any point.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message names 1.25 as the widest amount, and style(opacity = ) as a way to show where points overlap without moving any of them.
The parameter has the same shape as density’s adjust, a dimensionless multiple of an automatic value. It is there for the same reason density and bin take a parameter while dodge does not. The jitter amount is a legibility choice with no single right value, whereas gog computes dodge’s offsets itself: from the group count on a bar, and from the other points in the slot on a point. A value you must choose takes a parameter; a value gog can compute does not.
Like dodge on a point, jitter needs no color split. It separates a mark’s own points where they land on one another, so point * jitter with only x and y is a whole sentence. It also needs a categorical position axis to spread within. Ask for jitter when both x and y are continuous and gog refuses. There is no slot to spread across, and no axis it could move a point along without misplacing its value. The answer for overplotting on two continuous axes is style(opacity = ), which shows where points are crowded without moving any of them.
Which marks jitter serves is decided by what a mark is: the rule that divides the whole trio. jitter spreads a scatter of individual points, so it is defined for point alone. A bar, box or interval has a width, and its groups are set apart by dodge; a line or area is one connected shape, not a cloud of points. Ask for jitter on any of those and gog refuses, naming the collision modifier that fits.
Three of the four collision modifiers divide the marks by geometry and by axis: dodge sets marks side by side within a slot, stack accumulates along the measure axis, jitter spreads along the categorical one. Each mark that dodge, stack or jitter serves has an answer to overlap that moves nothing off its value, and point has three. It is the one mark that can collide on either axis. Along a measure, it is piled into a countable stack of dots. Along a category, it is moved sideways within its slot, by jitter or by dodge. All three are modifiers the kernel already has, so these uses of point need no new atom.

“Given gapminder Europe: points, and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”
No two names overlap now. A label that ends up more than a line of text away from its point is joined to it by a thin line. Two rules set where each label rests. First, a label rests beside its dot, on whichever side has room. repel pulls the label toward its dot and pushes it away from every word and every dot, and the label stops where the two balance. A label with no neighbors sits just above its dot. One with neighbors moves to whichever side is free. Second, when a label is pushed by another label and by its own dot at the same time, it moves off the other label and may rest over its dot. A word over a dot is still readable. Two words over each other are not.
Like jitter, the placement is deterministic: it depends only on the labels and the rows, never on a random-number generator, so one specification always draws the same picture. Like jitter, it needs no color split, since what it separates is the layer’s own labels.
repel takes no parameter, and jitter takes one, for the same reason. A jitter’s spread has no single right value, so you choose it. A label moves exactly as far as the overlap requires and no further. That distance is computed, the way dodge computes a width, so there is nothing to set. The gap left between two labels is set by the font size. The engine sets the distance of style(nudge = ) from the font size in the same way.
Above some number of labels, no arrangement fits at all. repel draws every one of them anyway and reports how many still overlap. A plot missing the names it could not fit would read as a plot with fewer rows, and nobody looking at it would know.
repel is text-only. Each of the other three serves the marks whose geometry fits it, and a label is the only glyph made of a word. Ask for it on a point and gog refuses, naming jitter; on a bar it names dodge. Its counterpart among the settings is style(nudge = ), a fixed shift in a direction you name, described in Text. The two compose: the nudge says which side a label prefers, and repel resolves the overlaps that remain.
The four collision modifiers are one family, and two questions divide it. Three of them ask what geometry does this mark have, and answer with a width, a measure or a slot. The fourth asks what is this mark made of, and only one mark is made of words.

For bin, count, proportion and density, the new y column takes the name you bind with y(), as long as that name is not a column of your table. With no y(), the axis is labeled with the transform’s name: “Count”, “Proportion” or “Density”.
One row of that table changes when bin is composed with another statistic (see Chaining transforms). Cutting is then all it does. It writes the bin centers to x(column) as before and does not change y(column), so the statistic can reduce it. The y column then holds your column’s summary rather than a count.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.24 In short
bin, count and density write the measure axis themselves, so they need no column there and refuse a column of your table named on it. The reading transforms refuse without the column they read. A statistic runs inside each group, so binding color changes what it computes. Two transforms compose when their jobs differ and contradict when they do not. Four more transforms compute a whole picture, and four move marks that would otherwise overlap.

title: 25  Transforms
text:
25.25 What comes next
A transform changes the values of one mark and no other. Operators says how whole sentences join: how two marks share a panel, and how one plot is split or set beside another.

title: The sentences
text:
Knowing the letters is not the same as writing with them. The 1446 book, after explaining each letter class, devoted a chapter to assembly: how letters pack into syllable blocks.
This part is gog’s version of that chapter. It moves through six groups, from how words join into a sentence to what a reader does with the finished plot.
First the mechanics. The + operator layers marks in one panel, and the * operator derives a compound mark from a mark and a transform. Where you write a channel then decides whether it binds to the whole plot or to one layer. Second, one pair of operators with two uses. | and / split one plot into a grid of panels, and the same pair arranges separate plots on a page. Third, two of the transforms that compute a whole picture: flow carries a magnitude through its stages, and cluster builds the tree that puts an axis in order.
Fourth come the coordinate spaces, each a different surface to draw the plot on. space needs only one more vowel, z, to turn a flat plot into a cube. polar bends the same plane into a circle. nest divides a panel into regions, each sized by its measure, that fill it with no gaps. map flattens the earth onto the page, and globe draws it as a sphere. Each of those five takes a sentence you can already write and draws it on a new surface. network is different: its table holds relations, not positions, so a transform, layout, computes where each node goes. Fifth is time, where play cuts the plot into frames and shows them one after another. Last comes selection: with brush, the plot’s reader selects rows with the pointer, and the plot dims the rest.
Every chapter in this part depends on one law, Compositional Invariance: a composed expression means the same thing wherever it appears. What you build in one chapter keeps its meaning when you use it in the next. That is what lets you build a larger sentence from parts you learned in different chapters.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.1 +: layer
How do you put two things in one picture? You join them with an operator, and gog has exactly four. They are not atoms. They are the assembly rules: how atoms combine.
Hangeul (한글) works the same way. Its consonants and vowels are the atoms. Its operator is one rule: an initial consonant, a vowel and an optional final consonant make a syllable block. The rule never changes, and a small set of letters builds every syllable the language needs.
| and / also arrange whole plots on a page. That second use has a chapter of its own (Composition).
Every sentence you have written so far holds several atoms, and + joins most of them. Each mark, channel, label and setting enters a specification through it:
Adding a mark (point, line, bar, …) starts a new layer. A channel (x(), color(), …) written before any mark belongs to the plot, and one written after a mark belongs to that mark. A label atom (title(), x_label()) belongs to the plot wherever you write it (Encoding scope).

So if the order does not change the picture, why does this book use one order: data, mark, positions, refinements? Because a fixed order lets the code read like an English sentence, with a natural, subject-first shape:

data(...) first. It names the table the columns come from. A bare name like petal_length means nothing until a table is bound (Bind-Once), so the table is named first. The sentence must start here.
The mark and its *-chain second. This is the subject. Nothing is drawn without a mark (Minimum Syllable): bar * mean * dodge says what you are drawing and what was done to it, as one compound word. It is the initial consonant of the block; everything after is said about it.
The positions third. x and y say where the subject stands, and a mark cannot be drawn without them (the vowel to the mark’s consonant), so they follow immediately.
The refinements last. color, size, order, labels, title: everything optional. Delete every refinement and a legal plot remains; delete the mark or a position and nothing is drawn. Writing the removable parts last is also how you build a plot: the minimum sentence first, then refine (First plot).

Only two parts of the order are rules: the sentence starts with a source (data() or query()), and style() follows its mark. The rest is a reading convention: inside one layer, any arrangement draws the same plot. Where you write a channel does matter once a plot has two layers, because a channel written before a mark and one written after it bind differently. Encoding scope gives the rule. Learn one order and use it everywhere. Then your plots and the plots in this book read the same way.
Which orders matter lists what the engine enforces under + and *, and what you are free to arrange.

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”
dodge and color(era) are plainly related: on a bar, dodge has nothing to set side by side until a channel such as color names the groups. So why not write them together? Because the grammar deliberately gives them different operators. dodge belongs to *, because it modifies the mark. The same modifier works on box * dodge and interval * range * dodge, where group can make the split instead of color. color belongs to +: it binds a column to a channel. color * dodge cannot be written: * needs a mark on its left. Joining the two would make dodge depend on which channel splits the groups, and a modifier must not depend on that.
The order is not a compromise. It follows from what dodge does. dodge subdivides the x slot: each continent’s slot is cut into one bar per era. So dodge uses both atoms: x(continent) says which slot to divide, color(era) says into how many pieces. The sentence lists them in the order dodge uses them: the axis it splits along, then the groups it splits into. The positions do not separate dodge from what it needs; one of them is the slot dodge divides.
You also never have to read back through the sentence to check that the split is there. If no channel splits the mark, bar * mean * dodge is refused rather than drawn as one bar per slot. The message tells you to add a channel that splits it, such as color. So color can stand far from dodge in the sentence and still work with it.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.2 *: derive
A mark on its own draws the rows as they are. A histogram counts them first, and a trend line fits a curve to them first. That computing step needs a word of its own. * joins a transform to a mark, and the result is one compound mark.
bar * bin     # histogram
line * smooth # smoothed trend line
line * density # kernel density curve
* has one rule and one freedom. The mark goes on the left and the transforms go on the right. Among the transforms themselves, any order draws the same plot. The rest of this section explains both.

26.2.1 Why the order is fixed
Start with the rule. In Hangeul, a syllable is always initial consonant + vowel, never the reverse. gog’s * works the same way: the mark is the subject; the transform is what is done to it.
bin * bar is refused, just as ㅏ (a) + ㄱ (g) is not a valid Hangeul syllable.
bar * bin   # a bar mark, derived by binning
The refusal names the fix:

bin * bar

Error in `*.gog_atom`:
! gog: `*` not defined for transform * mark.
Use `*` to combine a mark with a transform, e.g. bar * bin.




26.2.2 One fixed place, and one free order
The mark stands on the left, always, and no transform may stand there. That is what makes bar * bin a compound mark rather than a function call. Why +, and not a pipe explains why it lets the atoms stay nouns.
Write the transforms in the order they happen. This is a reading convention: any order draws the same plot, and this one lets you follow the steps as you read. bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each one. That is the order it runs in, and there is no other order it could run in.
The reason is what mean needs. A statistic reduces a group to one number, and a continuous column has no groups: every value stands alone, so its mean is itself. Ask for the mean of life at each value of gdp, and each group holds one country:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))




gog: `point * mean` groups the rows by their value of `gdp`, and here every group holds a single row, so each `mean` is one row's own value. Drawn as asked. To summarize, cut `gdp` into ranges first, `point * bin * mean`, or group by a column whose values repeat.




                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by mean, x is gdp, y is life.”
The picture is the plain scatterplot, and the note printed with it says why: each mean is one row’s own value. bin is what makes the groups, by turning many distinct numbers into one band. So the cut comes first: without it, the mean has nothing to average.
So two transforms work together only when they do different jobs. There are four jobs: making the groups, measuring inside them, rescaling the result, and arranging the marks. A pair that does the same job twice is refused rather than run in sequence. bin and count both count the rows, so each cell would be measured twice:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(12) * count + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(12) * count + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(12) * count + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(12), count), x(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `bar * bin * count` measures each cell twice — `bin` and `count` each invent their own measurement from the rows, and neither was handed a column to give way to, so there is no reading that keeps both. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * bin` or `bar * count`. To cut an axis into cells and measure something else inside them, the second transform has to be one you hand a column: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>) + y(<column>)`. To read either as shares of the whole rather than as counts, `proportion` rescales whichever you keep: `bar * bin * proportion`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The engine decides the running order from the transforms themselves, not from where you typed them. The order you type can never be the wrong order, although the pair itself can still be refused, as the refusal above shows. Chaining transforms shows why a pair is refused, one refusal at a time, and Combinations has the whole grid of pairs.


26.2.3 Live examples
The three compound marks named when * was introduced appear in the sentences you will write most often. Here each one is drawn, so you can see what the transform did to the rows before the mark drew them.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Histogram: life expectancy across all countries in 2007
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + y(count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) + y(col.count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) + y(:count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life), y(col.count),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Count"),
  title("Distribution of life expectancy, 2007"))






                                       50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Distribution of life expectancy, 2007 Count Life expectancy (years)







RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Scatterplot, with a LOESS smooth on top
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth + title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth),
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Kernel density estimate
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) + y(density) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Density") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) + y(col.density) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Density") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) + y(:density) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Density") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  y(col.density), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Density"),
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))






                               40 60 80   0.00 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.04  Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007 Density Life expectancy (years)





“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life, y is density.”
In each plot, the compound mark draws what its transform computed rather than the rows. The bars are counts of countries in bands of life expectancy. The line through the points is a fitted curve, and the last line is an estimated density.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.3 | and /: facet, or compose
Two questions lead to the last two operators: how the same plot looks for each group, and how two different plots fit on one page. | puts things side by side and / puts one above the other. What you write on the right decides the job: a facet() splits one plot into panels, and a second plot is placed beside or below the first.
With facet(), | produces small multiples arranged in columns, one panel per category of the column it names.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
/ stacks the panels in rows. Five rows would make each panel too short, so this example uses two continents:

gm_two <- gapminder_2007[gapminder_2007$continent %in% c("Africa", "Europe"), ]
data(gm_two) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) / facet(continent)



                                                              40 50 60 70 80                                                                                         0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80    Europe  Africa  Life Gdp





“Given the gm two table: points, x is gdp, y is life, split into panel rows by continent.”
Write | and / in one sentence to combine them into a grid. Each operator applies to the facet written after it, read from left to right. See Faceting for the grid, what the panels share, and why the facet column must be categorical.
With a plot on the right, the same two operators arrange separate plots on one page, and each plot keeps its own axes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
These two measure different things on y, life expectancy and a count, so each draws its own vertical axis. When two plots side by side name the same column on y, that axis is shared and drawn once. Two plots one above the other share x the same way.
One pair of operators, two jobs. Composition covers the second.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.4 Which orders matter
Most of the order data, mark, positions, refinements is a reading convention, and the engine enforces the rest. The difference tells you where to be careful. There are three kinds of ordering, and only one of them needs your attention.









Kind
What it means
Under +
Under *




Free
Either way draws exactly the same picture.
In a plot with one mark: the mark, its positions and its other channels, in any arrangement. Labels go anywhere. Only style() must follow its mark.
Two transforms after one mark. Write them in the order they happen; the engine runs them in that order either way.


Refused
The engine stops and names what to move.
Atoms with no table named before them: point + x(gdp). A style() written before any mark.
A transform on the left: bin * bar.


Meaningful
No error, and a different picture.
A channel before the marks, or after one of them, once a plot has two. Two marks swapped: the second draws on top.
Nothing. No order under * changes the picture.



Start with the cell where * meets Meaningful. * fixes one thing only, which is that the mark stands on its left. Once the mark is there, no arrangement of what follows changes what you get.
Free covers most arrangements. The two sentences below draw the identical plot, and the book writes the first because a fixed order is easier to read:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + point + y(life))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + point + y(col.life)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + point + y(:life))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), point, y(col.life)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                                                                                                                                                                             0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K    Gdp






Both name life on y, so the two plots share that axis and it is drawn once, on the left. Each plot still draws its own gdp axis underneath it.
Refused means an atom comes before the thing it needs. A plot needs its table first, so + must have a plot on its left. A setting needs a mark, so a style() before any mark is refused:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + style(size = 3) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + style(size = 3) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + style(size = 3) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), style({ size: 3 }), point, x(col.gdp),
  y(col.life))




Error:
! gog: `style()` has no mark to style. Put it after a mark, e.g. `point + style(color = "tomato")`.


Meaningful is the only kind that needs care, because it is the only kind the engine says nothing about. With two marks in a sentence, a channel written before them belongs to the plot and reaches both, and a channel written after one belongs to that mark. Both are legal, neither warns, and they draw different pictures. That is the subject of Encoding scope. It is also why this book keeps one order: when every sentence looks the same, a different arrangement is a deliberate signal.
The marks themselves are the other case the engine does not report. Two marks swapped draw in the order you wrote them, so the second sits on top of the first.

26.4.1 What groups first
Those three kinds are about where you may put a word. Precedence answers a different question: when a sentence holds more than one operator, which one groups first. Arithmetic has the same idea. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14 and not 20, because * groups before +. It is read as 2 + (3 * 4), as if the parentheses were written. A sentence in gog is read the same way, so precedence decides which atoms each operator joins.
This order of grouping belongs to the language you write in, not to gog, and gog cannot change it. R and Python share one order. Julia differs in one place: it groups | together with +. When the two meet, the one written first groups first. The table gives the order in each of the three languages:



Groups
R
Python
Julia




First
* and /
* and /
* and /


Next
+
+
+ and \|, from left to right


Last
\|
\|




JavaScript has no column in the table, because it spells each operator as a word, such as beside(). The things the word joins are written inside its parentheses, so you see the grouping instead of remembering it (JavaScript).
For one plot, this is the order you want in all three languages. So a plot needs no parentheses of its own, even with a facet:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  across(col.continent))






                                    50 60 70 80   0 5 10 15                              50 60 70 80                                     50 60 70 80                                  50 60 70 80                              50 60 70 80      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Count Life





R reads that sentence as (data(gapminder_2007) + (bar * bin) + x(life)) | facet(continent). The transform joins its mark first, the atoms join the plot next, and the facet splits the finished plot last. Python and Julia read it the same way.
/ groups before +, so a row facet is grouped in a different order. In the row facet drawn earlier, y(life) / facet(continent) is grouped first, and + then joins that pair to the plot. A facet always splits the whole plot, whichever atom it was grouped with. So that sentence draws the same file as (data(gm_two) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) / facet(continent).
An atom can also be written after a facet, like the title in the sentence below:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) |
  facet(continent) + title("Each continent in its own panel")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) |
  facet(col.continent) + title("Each continent in its own panel"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) | facet(:continent) +
  title("Each continent in its own panel")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  across(col.continent), title("Each continent in its own panel"))






                                                               0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                        0 20K 40K                                                                                0 20K 40K                                                     0 20K 40K                              0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Each continent in its own panel Life Gdp





In R and Python, + groups before |, so title() joins the facet first, and then both join the plot. Julia groups | together with +, from left to right, so the facet joins the plot first and the title joins after it. The title appears once, above all five panels, in every language.


26.4.2 Parentheses on a page
That order works for one plot. On a page, it can group a sentence in a way you did not mean. Both sides of | or / should be whole plots, and precedence can group part of one plot with part of the other before both plots are complete. Here are the two plots from earlier in this chapter, set one above the other with no parentheses:


RPythonJulia


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) /
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) /
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) / data(gapminder_2007) +
  bar * count + x(:continent)




Error:
! gog: `/` places one plot below another, and it groups before `+`, so here it joined `y()` to the plot after it. Put each plot in parentheses: `(data(df) + point + ...) / (data(df) + bar + ...)`.


/ groups before +, so it joins only the two atoms on either side of it: y(life) and the second data(). R reads the sentence as … + x(gdp) + (y(life) / data(gapminder_2007)) + …. A facet can be grouped with one atom, because it splits the whole plot anyway. A plot cannot: / places a whole plot below another, and y(life) is not a plot. So gog refuses the sentence. Its message names y(), the atom that / joined. gog gives the same refusal in Python and Julia.
Written with | instead, the same sentence draws in R and Python. In those two languages, | groups last, so both plots are complete before | joins them. Julia groups | together with +, from left to right. So | joins the first plot to the second plot’s data() alone, and gog refuses the sentence.
So whenever this book composes plots in R, Python or Julia, it writes each plot inside its own parentheses. Then every plot is complete before | or / joins it, and the page means the same thing in all three languages. In JavaScript each plot is written as plot(…), so it is complete already.
Two more places need parentheses. The first is a page inside a page. / groups before |, so a | b / c is read as a | (b / c): one plot beside two plots, one above the other. To put a row of two above a third plot, write (a | b) / c. The second is a theme() for the whole page: put parentheses around the page before you add it. Without them, R and Python give the theme() to the second plot, because + groups before |. Julia gives it to the page (How big is the page itself?).
The table collects the rules for a page. Each (…) holds one whole plot, from its data() to its last atom, and the last column gives the same page in JavaScript’s words:








Page
R, Python and Julia
JavaScript




Two plots side by side
(…) \| (…)
beside(plot(…), plot(…))


One plot above another
(…) / (…)
below(plot(…), plot(…))


A row of two above a third
((…) \| (…)) / (…)
below(beside(plot(…), plot(…)), plot(…))


A height for the whole page
((…) \| (…)) + theme(height = 260)
beside(plot(…), plot(…), theme({ height: 260 }))



Each language’s chapter shows these rules in its own spelling: R, Python, Julia and JavaScript.


26.4.3 What parentheses may group
The table above shows what parentheses group: whole plots and whole pages. You might also try them around several marks, to give a second table to all of them. That does not work, because parentheses do not group marks. A second data() applies only to the mark written directly after it (Data):



actuals: all 5 rows


year
sales




2019

135


2021

2022
152

168






forecast: all 3 rows


year
sales




2024

210







RPythonJulia


data(actuals) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  line +
  (data(forecast) + point + area)


(data(actuals) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  line +
  (data(forecast) + point + area))


data(actuals) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line +
  (data(forecast) + point + area)




Error:
! gog: parentheses do not group marks, so everything inside these would be dropped. Write the marks in sequence instead, and repeat `data()` before each one that reads that table: `+ data(forecast) + point + data(forecast) + area`. Parentheses compose whole plots, with `|` and `/`.


gog refuses that instead of drawing it. The refusal is better than the alternative. The engine cannot give the second table to both marks inside the parentheses. Its only other choice is to discard both marks and draw a plot with two layers missing, without saying so. To put two marks on the second table, write data() before each of them.
The same refusal covers a position or a title inside the parentheses, for the same reason. In JavaScript, where the operators are words, the same mistake is a plot() handed to another plot(), and it is refused there too.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.5 Why +, and not a pipe
Readers who know R’s tidyverse packages ask why gog does not use a pipe. A pipe passes a value into a function: a |> f means f(a). Hadley Wickham, ggplot2’s author, has said publicly that the pipe would have been the better interface (Wickham, 2018). ggplot, ggplot2’s predecessor, was written as function composition, and it could have used a pipe if one had existed. ggplot2 used + instead.
He also answers the question a reader asks next: why not change ggplot2 now? It cannot change: its functions take the mapping and the data first, while a pipe needs the plot as the first argument. And he judges that a new package built only to make this change would cost more work than the change would be worth. So ggplot2’s + comes from its history, not a fresh choice, and a grammar designed today has to make that choice for itself. He gives two reasons for preferring the pipe, and neither applies to gog. A third consideration is gog’s rather than his, and it is the one that decides the question.
His first reason is about one language. A pipe is a single idea that works everywhere in R, so a grammar that spells function composition differently is one more thing to learn. Switching between the two spellings is a frequent source of errors, his own included. That is true, and it is an argument about R and its packages. gog is one syntax written in four languages, and that changes the answer. + can be given a meaning in R, Python and Julia. The pipe cannot be given a gog meaning. Julia’s |> and R’s two pipes already mean something gog must not change. Python has no pipe operator at all, and no way to add one: you can give new meanings only to the operators it already has. In R and Julia a pipe would work with the meaning it already has. Python would need another spelling, and the languages would then have two different grammars. This project exists to avoid that. JavaScript decides nothing here, because it cannot overload any operator at all, which is why it spells all four as words (JavaScript).
The second is about arithmetic, and it is the stronger of the two. You expect a + b to equal b + a, and ggplot2’s + does not always do that. That objection is answered by the six permutations drawn earlier in this chapter. Here the mark and the channels commute. Move color ahead of x, or write the positions before the mark, and the engine produces the identical file. One thing does depend on order: two marks swapped. There the order is the drawing order you asked for, and the second mark draws on top.
The other half of that objection is grouping, whether a + (b + c) means what (a + b) + c means. The question cannot arise here, because a + (b + c) cannot be written at all. + always takes a plot on its left, so two atoms with no table named before them never form a smaller expression to group. They are refused:

point + x(gdp)

Error:
! gog: these atoms have no plot to join — the sentence starts with the data: `data(df) + point + x(gdp) + ...`.


The third point is gog’s own, and it is what decides the question. It is not an argument against the pipe. It is a statement of what a pipe would remove. A pipe applies functions, so every atom would have to become a function taking a plot and returning one. Make bar a function, then ask what bar * bin could mean. There is no answer: you cannot multiply two functions and get a histogram. The derive operator exists only because marks and transforms are things rather than actions. They are values, and they combine with each other before either one is joined to a plot.
This is the decision the book opens with: a plot is a specification, not drawing code. ㄱ is a letter, not an instruction. You put it in a slot next to other letters, and the block is assembled from its pieces rather than performed in sequence. Hangeul’s atoms are nouns, which is exactly why they combine, and gog’s are nouns for the same reason. A grammar built on the pipe is a grammar of verbs: it can layer, because layering really is a sequence of additions, but it cannot derive. ggplot, ggplot2’s predecessor, was written as function composition, and it had no * either.
So + here is a choice rather than something inherited. Unlike the pipe, it can be given a meaning in R, Python and Julia. It commutes wherever order should not matter, and it leaves the atoms as nouns so that * can exist.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.6 Summary
Each operator reads as a phrase when a plot is read aloud, and | and / have two readings each:








Operator
Reads as
Example




+
“…and also…”
point + line


*
“…derived by…”
bar * bin


|
“…split into panel columns by…”
data(gm) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent)


/
“…split into panel rows by…”
data(gm) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) / facet(era)


|
“…beside…”
(one specification) | (another)


/
“…above…”
(one specification) / (another)



A finite set of rules, and more plots than you will ever need to draw.

title: 26  Operators
text:
26.7 What comes next
The operators say how atoms combine into a sentence. Where you write each atom decides what it binds to, and Encoding scope gives that rule in full.




Wickham, H. (2018). Answer on why ggplot2 uses + rather than the pipe. Posit (RStudio) Community forum, 29 January 2018.

title: 27  Encoding scope
text:
27.1 The rule
If you write one x() and then two marks, which marks use it? Both do. Each atom binds to a scope: the whole plot, or one layer. A layer is one mark and the atoms bound to it. This chapter gives the rule that decides between the two.
The rule for every atom you write with + fits in one table. Each row names an atom, the scope it binds to, and whether it matters where you write it.
In every row marked Yes, where you write the atom decides its scope. Write a channel before any mark and it binds to the plot. Write a channel or style() after a mark and it binds to that mark. data() and query() work differently. The first data() or query() opens the sentence and is the plot’s table. Each later one binds to the mark written directly after it, not to the mark before it. The atoms in the last row, marked No, belong to the plot wherever you write them. They are the title and the axis labels, palette(), theme(), order(), brush() and the spaces. The row for positions after a mark says one thing more, and the next section shows it with an example.
Where two bindings could apply, the nearest one wins. That is the same rule that lets a data() written between two marks give the next layer its own table in place of the plot’s.

title: 27  Encoding scope
text:
Atom
Scope
Depends on where you write it?

Yes


the same positions after a mark

27.2 One axis, and which column each layer reads
The rule above never gives a layer axes of its own. Every layer of a plot shares the same axes. That is what makes it one plot rather than two drawn on top of each other. gog allows no second axis: one x scale, one set of ticks, one label. So a second table’s values must be in the same units as the first table’s, such as dollars in both. Values in different units need a plot of their own. Composition covers the choice between layering, faceting, and a page of separate plots.
Sharing an axis is not the same as sharing a column name, and the two are easy to confuse. Almost always you want to bind the positions once, before the marks, so that every layer reads them:

  bar +

Here those first columns are gdp and life, written after point. The axis belongs to the plot, and only the choice of column belongs to the layer. Without this rule, you would have to rename at and value in milestones to gdp and life. Renaming is easy when you build the table yourself. When the table comes from somewhere else, renaming means changing data you did not write.
A layer that names no column of its own reads the first column written for each axis, wherever the layer is written. So point + x(gdp) + y(life) + line draws a line through the points. point + line + x(gdp) + y(life) draws the same plot: the positions are written after line, and point, which names none, reads them too. color() does not work this way. A layer names its own column, never its own scale.

27.3 Channels: plot-scoped or layer-scoped
Positions share one axis, which is why they needed a section of their own. The other channels have no shared axis between layers. They follow the same rule: where you write a channel decides its scope.
A channel is often meant for one layer alone. You may want the points colored by country, and one trend line in a single color, fitted to all of them together. Written after a mark, a channel binds to that mark alone. The table gapminder_asia holds five Asian countries, one row per country and year:

  point + color(country) +   # color applies to point only
  line * smooth              # the trend line uses a single default color

  point + color(col.country) +

  line * smooth

  color(col.country), layer(line, smooth))

“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, points colored by country, and also a line derived by smooth.”
Each point is drawn in its country’s color. The line takes no color, so it is one dark gray trend line, fitted to all five countries together. Whenever a plot has a color legend, a layer that neither maps nor sets color is drawn in this gray. No country in the legend is gray, so the line cannot be mistaken for one.
Written before any mark, a channel has no mark to bind to. It binds to the plot instead, so every layer that can accept it gets it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  point +
  line * smooth

  point +
  line * smooth)

  line * smooth

  point, layer(line, smooth))

“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, points and also lines derived by smooth.”
Now the line takes color as well. A line colored by a categorical column splits into one line per category, so the plot draws five trends, one per country.
That is the same rule that x and y follow. Written before the marks, they apply to every mark. Written after one mark, they belong to that mark. Positions add the one rule from the previous section: a layer that names no column of its own reads the first column written for that axis.

27.3.1 Why a channel binds to one mark only
Suppose you want the lines colored by country and only the points sized by population. A channel written after a mark binds to that mark alone, never to an earlier one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

# the line written above it does not change, and keeps its own color

  line  + color(country) +
  point + size(population)


(data(gapminder_asia) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line  + color(col.country) +
  point + size(col.population))


data(gapminder_asia) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line + color(:country) +
  point + size(:population)

  color(col.country), point, size(col.population))

“Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also points sized by population.”
This plot is possible only because a channel binds to one mark. If size also bound to the earlier line, gog would refuse the whole plot: a line takes one size for the whole layer, not one per row. There would then be no way to describe the plot you wanted.


27.3.2 One column per legend
Binding a channel to one mark has one limit. A plot draws one legend for color, and that legend names one column. So when two layers both map color, they must name the same column. The same is true of size, shape, pattern and opacity, the other channels that draw a legend.
Suppose the lines above stay colored by country, and the points are colored by population instead of sized by it. The one legend would name country, the first column written, and nothing would explain the colors of the points. So gog refuses the plot:

  point + color(population)

  line  + color(col.country) +
  point + color(col.population))

A plot draws one legend for `color`, and it names `country`, so `population` would be drawn with no legend to read it by. Keep one column on `color` and show `population` another way: `size(population)` on the `point`, or `opacity(population)` on the `point`.

The message names two other channels for population, each with its own legend: size or opacity on the points. The plot above uses size. Writing legend = FALSE on either color lets the plot draw, with no color legend at all.


27.3.3 A plot-scoped channel and the marks left unchanged
A channel bound to one mark must be one that mark can accept, or gog refuses the plot. A channel written for the whole plot works differently. What happens when some marks can accept it and others cannot? size written for the whole plot applies to the points, and not to the line. A line has one width for the whole layer rather than one width per row, so it has no size to map. gog applies size to every mark that has a size feature, and prints a message naming the marks it left unchanged. That message is an Assumption: gog says what it decided instead of refusing the sentence, so the plot still draws:
