beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The two plots measure entirely different things: a country’s income against its life expectancy, and how many countries each continent holds. They share nothing, not a scale, not an axis, not a legend, because there is nothing to share. Each plot sits in a cell, its own part of the page. The two cells are equal, and a narrow gap between them leaves each a little under half the width. Inside each cell, a panel holds the marks, and the axes and their labels take the rest. The page does align the two panels at the top and the bottom.
/ places the same two plots one above the other. Each one now has the full width of the page:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, above bars derived by count, x is continent.”
One above the other, the two panels align at the left and the right, even when one plot’s tick labels are wider.
Here the parentheses are required. / groups before +, so without them / would join only y(life) and the second data(), and gog would refuse that sentence. With |, gog draws the page without them in R and Python, but refuses it in Julia. So whenever this book composes plots, each plot goes inside its own parentheses, whichever operator joins them. Parentheses on a page shows how each language groups a page.
Both operators take pages as well as plots, so a page can hold another page. (a | b) / c is a row of two plots above a third. The marginal plot later in this chapter is built the other way: one plot above a row of two.
In R, Python and Julia, / groups before |, so a | b / c reads as a | (b / c). Write the parentheses whenever you mix the two operators. JavaScript spells the operators as words, so there is no order to remember. The JavaScript chapter shows those words.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.2 A shared column is a shared axis
text:
29.2 A shared column is a shared axis
The two plots in those figures share no column. One shared column changes what the page draws. When two composed plots name the same column on the same axis, both read it on one scale. The arrangement decides whether they also share one drawn axis. Plots one above the other align their x axes, and plots side by side align their y axes. When both plots name the column on the axis the arrangement aligns, gog does not draw two matching axes. It draws one axis:

The same column on the aligned axis of two composed plots is one axis: one scale, one panel extent, drawn once.

The shared column may sit on the other axis instead, such as gdp on x in two plots side by side. Each plot then draws its own copy of that axis from the one scale, so both copies mark the same values.
Here are two plots, both reading gdp on x. The theme(height = 150) on the first asks for 150 pixels of the page’s height:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp),
  theme({ height: 150 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)))






                                         0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp






“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, above points, x is gdp, y is life.”
Look at what the rule did. Both plots measure gdp over the same range, so each bar is drawn directly above the points it counts. And the gdp axis is drawn once, along the bottom, because there is only one axis to draw. Faceting makes the same decision when it draws the tick labels only under the panels with nothing below them.
A plot that does not draw an axis reserves no margin for it. That is why the histogram sits close to the scatter, with no band of tick labels between the two panels.
gog cannot know what a column measures, so on a page it compares column names. Two plots built from different tables share a scale whenever both name a column spelled the same way on the same axis. That is correct when the two columns measure the same thing, such as gdp in two tables of countries. When they measure different things, rename one of them before you compose. Otherwise the plot with the smaller values is drawn in a small part of an axis sized for the larger.
There is one case where gog does know what an axis measures, because its own transform changed it. With stack(share = TRUE) or proportion, an axis that names a column shows shares, numbers from 0 to 1, instead of that column’s values. gog never merges such an axis with another, so the plot draws its own. The Bar chapter shows such a page: two plots of people use one axis, and the plot of shares beside them draws its own.
A page reads a shared column on one scale, so both plots must write the same scale and limits for it. When you write x(gdp, scale = "log") in one plot and plain x(gdp) in the other, gog refuses the page. This is true side by side as well as one above the other. The message names both scales:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life)))




Error:
! gog: `gdp` is on the x axis of two plots on this page, one read with the default scale and one with a log scale. A page reads a column on one scale, so both plots have to read it the same way. Write the same scale and limits in both, or give the column another name in one of them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.



29.2.1 One axis, but not one legend
You have seen an axis merge, so you might expect two legends for one column to merge the same way. Compose two plots that both map color and you get two legends, one for each:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(population) + y(life) + color(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.population) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:population) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent))


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.population), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent)))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 


                                                                                                                                                                       0 500M 1000M    Population  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, beside points, x is population, y is life, color by continent.”
Look at what that figure draws once, and what it draws twice. Both plots read life on y, so that axis is shared and drawn once, on the left. Both color by continent as well, and there you get two legends, saying exactly the same thing.
Axes merge and legends do not, and that difference is deliberate. Axes merge because there is an exact test: when two plots show the same column’s values on the same axis, one scale is correct for both. A legend has no such test. These two plots do agree, because both split by continent. But nothing in the grammar makes two composed plots use color the same way. The next pair may split by different columns, or map one column onto two color scales. One legend over those two would be wrong for one of them. Nothing in the picture shows the error, because it still looks like a legend.
So gog merges no legend. Two identical legends side by side tell you that the two plots split by the same column.
When you want one legend over several panels, use faceting instead. A facet is one plot split by a column, so every panel is colored by the same scale. It draws a single legend. The choice between composing and faceting is the choice between two plots and one.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.3 The marginal plot
A scatter shows how two columns vary together, but not how the rows spread along each one alone. Go back to the histogram that shared the scatter’s gdp axis. That histogram is a marginal: one column’s distribution, drawn along the edge of the plot that uses the column. Put a second marginal on the right and the picture is the marginal plot, which most tools offer as a named chart type:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp) + theme(height = 130)) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(life) + theme(width = 130)))


((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.gdp) + theme(height = 130)) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(col.life) + theme(width = 130))))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:gdp) + theme(height = 130)) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(:life) + theme(width = 130)))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp),
  theme({ height: 130 })),
  beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), y(col.life),
  theme({ width: 130 }))))






                                         0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                                    0 10 20 30    Count






“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp; above points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by bin, y is life.”
That figure is built from three ordinary plots and two operators. The top histogram shares gdp with the scatter, so its panel is drawn exactly as wide as the scatter’s. The right-hand one shares life, so its panel is exactly as tall as the scatter’s, and the life axis is drawn once, on the left. Nothing in the sentence draws the empty top-right corner. Both marginals stop where the scatter’s panel stops, and the corner is the room left over.
The marginals need no special rule either. bar * bin + y(life) is the histogram you already know. Its bars run left to right, because y now carries the bins and the count goes on x.

29.3.1 A shared categorical column
You may want each group’s summary drawn directly above the group’s own rows. The shared column need not be continuous for that. Two plots reading the same categorical column on x share that column’s slots, so each category keeps the same place in both:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(continent) + y(life) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(gdp) + color(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.gdp) + color(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + box + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  theme(height = 150)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:gdp) +
  color(:continent))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), box, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  theme({ height: 150 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.gdp),
  color(col.continent)))






                                                                 40 50 60 70 80  Life


                                                                                                                                                                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K  Gdp Continent  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 






“Given gapminder 2007: boxes, x is continent, y is life, above points, x is continent, y is gdp, color by continent.”
The five continents take the same slots in both panels, so each continent’s box sits directly above that continent’s countries.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.4 A clustered panel decides the order
text:
29.4 A clustered panel decides the order
A categorical axis needs an order, and most plots take the one the data arrived in. A panel with cluster computes a better one. cluster builds a tree that joins the most similar categories first, and reading its leaves along the axis gives an order that puts similar categories next to each other. When a clustered panel is composed with another, the axis they share takes the order the tree computed.

A shared categorical axis takes the order a clustered panel computed for it.

The other panels need no cluster of their own, and their categories take the tree’s order. gog refuses two panels that derive different orders for one shared axis, because one axis cannot hold two orders. Give both the same columns to cluster(), or cluster in one panel alone. The Cluster chapter uses this rule: a tile plot with a tree on two of its sides, each tree deciding one axis.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.5 How thin is the marginal histogram? theme(width =, height =)
text:
29.5 How thin is the marginal histogram? theme(width =, height =)
In the marginal plot, both histograms are thin because each one asks for a small size. The top histogram asks for 130 pixels of height, and the right-hand one for 130 pixels of width. A plot asks for room in pixels with theme(width = ) and theme(height = ). The plots that ask for nothing divide what is left, so the scatter takes the rest.
On a plot drawn alone, the same two arguments set the size of the whole image:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(width = 420, height = 320)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(width = 420, height = 320)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(width = 420, height = 320)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ width: 420, height: 320 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





Alone or on a page, the two arguments mean the same thing, which is Compositional Invariance, the sixth of the nine laws. A plot that asks for 130 pixels of height is 130 pixels tall, whether it is drawn alone or above another plot. Beside another plot it is also 130 pixels tall, and the plot beside it takes the same height.
Do not confuse theme(width =, height =) with theme(ratio = ). The second one shapes the panel inside the room the plot was given, and it never resizes the image. When a plot states a ratio, the page does not align its panel with the other panels.

title: 29  Composition
section: 29.6 How big is the page itself?
text:
29.6 How big is the page itself?
A page that states no size is 800 by 600 pixels, the same as a plot that states none. Its plots can decide a different size. Plots one above the other that all ask for a height make the page as tall as their heights plus the gaps. Plots side by side that all ask for a width make it as wide as their widths plus the gaps. Each gap is 20 pixels.
Plots side by side divide the page’s width and share one height. A height written into one of them is the height of all of them, and of the page. Plots side by side that ask for different heights are refused. Plots one above the other share one width, by the same rule. The marginal plot’s page stays 800 by 600, because the scatter asks for nothing.
A plot that asks for nothing still needs room, so the other plots must leave some of the page’s height for it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + theme(height = 700)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + theme(height = 700)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(height = 700)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ height: 700 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)))




Error:
! gog: the plots below each other ask for 700px of height, and the 20px between them makes 720px; the page has 600. A `theme(height = )` on a composed plot is how much of the page that plot takes, so the ones that state it must leave room for the ones that do not.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The bottom plot asks for nothing, so the page keeps its 600 pixels. gog added the top plot’s 700 pixels and the 20-pixel gap, and compared 720 with those 600.
When the plots do not decide the page’s size, you can choose it: give the page its own theme(). Put parentheses around the whole page before you add theme() to it. In R and Python, + groups before |, so without them the theme() would go to the second plot instead of the page. Julia would give it to the page, so the parentheses also make the sentence mean the same thing in every language:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) + theme(height = 260)


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) + theme(height = 260))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) +
  theme(height = 260)


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)),
  theme({ height: 260 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent






The page is now 260 pixels tall instead of 600, and both plots take that full height. A page takes the same two size arguments as a plot.
Without the outer parentheses, this sentence would draw the same picture, because plots side by side share one height. A width would show the difference in R and Python: without the parentheses, only the second plot would change.
Sizing the page matters most when a plot cannot be stretched to fill its cell. A cube is drawn with one scale in both screen directions, so its shape is never stretched. In a tall, narrow cell the cube is therefore drawn small, with an empty band above it and another below it. The figure is then the wrong shape, and you correct it by sizing the page.
Size is the only thing a page can say. Every other property theme() sets belongs to one plot: its gridlines, its frame, its background, the angle of its tick labels. A page is not a plot, so each of those properties is refused, and the refusal says to write it into the plot it describes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) + theme(grid = "none")


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) + theme(grid = "none"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) +
  theme(grid = "none")


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)),
  theme({ grid: "none" }))




Error:
! gog: `theme(grid = )` describes a panel, and a page is plots arranged rather than a panel of its own. On a page, `theme()` states how big the figure is — `theme(width = )` and `theme(height = )` — and nothing else. Write this into the plot it describes, before composing: `(plot + theme(grid = )) | other_plot`.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.7 What a page is not
A title over two plots seems to belong to the page rather than to either plot, so you might try writing it there. A page is an arrangement of plots, so anything belonging to one plot is written into that plot before it is composed. A page accepts theme(width = ) and theme(height = ). Every other atom added to a page is refused, and the message names where it belongs:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) + title("Two views")


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) + title("Two views"))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) +
  title("Two views")


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)),
  title("Two views"))




Error:
! gog: `title()` belongs to a plot, and the left side is a page of them. Write it into the plot it describes, before composing: `(plot + title("...")) | other_plot`.


gog draws no title over a whole page. On a page of plots one above the other, the top plot’s title sits above everything else. Otherwise, write the title as the figure’s caption in your document.
And a page cannot be faceted, because a facet splits one plot by a column and a page is not one plot:


RPythonJulia


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent))) | facet(continent)


(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))) | facet(col.continent))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))) |
  facet(:continent)




Error:
! gog: `|` faceted a page of plots, and a facet splits *one* plot by a column. Facet the plots before composing them: `(plot | facet(g)) | other_plot`.


Facet first, then compose: (plot | facet(g)) | other_plot is a faceted plot beside another plot, and it is legal.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.8 Where these operators come from
You have now seen | used both ways. Neither reading is this grammar’s invention, and the two were borrowed from different places.
The facet reading is the older of the two. Trellis display wrote a conditioned plot as y ~ x | g (Becker et al., 1996), and lattice writes it that way still. There | means “given”, the same meaning it has in conditional probability. That is exactly what plot | facet(continent) says.
The composition reading comes from patchwork (Pedersen, 2019). That package writes p1 | p2 for side by side and p1 / p2 for one above the other. gog spells composition the same way on purpose. A reader who already uses that package already knows both operators. A different spelling for an idea that already has one would only be one more thing to learn.
Composing pictures with operators is older than both of them. Henderson’s Functional Geometry (Henderson, 1982) describes an algebra of pictures, and it places pictures with beside and above. The textbook Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs teaches the same picture language. Haskell’s diagrams library spells the two operations ||| and ===. The JavaScript binding has no operators to overload, so it spells the two operations as words: beside(), and below() for what Henderson called above. His above(a, b) and gog’s below(a, b) draw the same picture, with a on top and b under it.
gog follows Wilkinson in most of its decisions, and this is one place where it does not. His graph algebra also has a /, and there it means nesting (a/b, “a within b”), not one plot above another. That nesting is not gog’s nest() atom, which divides one panel into areas sized by a measure. gog’s facet operators always cross and never nest, as the Faceting chapter explains, so gog can use / to place one plot above another.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.9 Layering, faceting, or composition?
Layering, faceting and composition answer different questions, so your data decides which one you want:

Layering. The layers draw different tables that measure the same thing. One coordinate space, one pair of axes, and the second table annotates the first: a threshold, a band, a note, a forecast. Data shows how to add a second table.
Faceting. The panels show the same measurement for different subsets. One scale, one legend, and you can compare the panels directly.
Composition. The plots show different measurements that belong on one page. Each keeps its own space, and the only thing they may share is a column.

In layering, the engine cannot check that a second table measures what the axes measure, so you have to. A second table that measures something else still draws when you layer it: gog finds every column, draws every mark, and the picture is wrong. A sentence that puts sales figures on an income axis is legal, and gog draws it. So if the second table does not measure what the axes measure, compose two plots instead of layering one onto the other.
A marginal plot is composition because the histogram and the scatter measure different things: one counts countries, the other puts each country at its own position. They share gdp, and that one shared column is what the shared-axis rule turns into a single axis.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.10 In short
| and / mean faceting when a column splits one plot into panels, and composition when both sides are whole plots. Composed plots that show the same column’s values on the same axis read it on one scale. On the axis the arrangement aligns, that column is one axis, drawn once. A page draws no mark of its own, and its size is the only thing you can write on it.

title: 29  Composition
text:
29.11 What comes next
Composition arranges finished plots on a page, and none of those plots shows where each part of a total went. Flow draws that: it carries each amount through a series of stages, read from the table’s own columns.




Becker, R. A., Cleveland, W. S., & Shyu, M.-J. (1996). The visual design and control of trellis display. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics, 5(2), 123–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.1996.10474701


Henderson, P. (1982). Functional geometry. In D. P. Friedman & D. S. Wise (Eds.), Conference record of the 1982 ACM symposium on lisp and functional programming (pp. 179–187). ACM Press.


Pedersen, T. L. (2019). patchwork: The composer of plots. R package; first CRAN release 1 December 2019. https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/


Wilkinson, L. (2005). The grammar of graphics (2nd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-387-28695-0

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.1 The finished diagram
Where did each part of a total go? Some tables record movement: each row says that some amount started in one place and finished in another. A flow diagram draws that movement. The places are grouped into stages, and the stages are drawn side by side. Bands carry each amount from stage to stage. The thicker the band, the larger the amount it carries. This picture is an alluvial diagram, one kind of Sankey diagram. The section Links in layers shows a Sankey diagram drawn from a table of links, and Where the limits are says what gog does not draw. No atom spells either name, just as there is no pie() atom.
gog builds that picture out of the table’s own columns. A stage is one of the table’s categorical columns. Its distinct values are the possible places at that stage, and each row sits in one of them. The flow transform computes the whole diagram from one table of such columns. This chapter uses the passengers and crew of the Titanic, the ship that sank in 1912. titanic holds one row per group of people. Four columns describe each group: class, sex, age (child or adult) and survived. A fifth, n, counts the people in that group. The table has one row for every combination of those four columns, so some rows count zero people:
Who survived the sinking, and did class and sex change their chance of survival? The diagram below answers both:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  title("Who survived, by class and sex")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("Who survived, by class and sex"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  title("Who survived, by class and sex")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("Who survived, by class and sex"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  Who survived, by class and sex N  Survived    Yes  No
“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored by survived, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name.”
Read it from left to right. Each white rectangle marks a slot: the part of a stage that one place takes, such as a class, a sex or an outcome. Each band is a group of people who share a class, a sex and an outcome, and its color is the outcome: blue for the people who survived, orange for the people who did not. The blue bands that leave the Female slot are much thicker than the orange ones, because 344 of the 470 women and girls survived. At the Male slot the orange bands are thicker, because only 367 of the 1,731 men and boys survived. Class mattered too. 203 of the 325 people in first class survived, compared with 178 of the 706 in third class.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.2 Three layers
The sentence above has three layers. In each one, * joins the same transform, flow(...), to a different mark, and each mark draws one part of the picture:







Layer
What it draws




ribbon * flow(...)
the bands, which carry the counts from stage to stage


zone * flow(...)
the slots, one rectangle for each place at each stage


text * flow(...) + label(name)
the names, one inside each slot



The three layers compute the same positions from the same stages. So the bands end at the edges of the slots, and each name sits inside its slot. The next three sections add the layers one at a time, in the order of the table. They use two stages, class and survived, and Adding a stage then adds sex between them.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.3 The bands
To build the diagram, start with the bands alone. Class is one stage and the outcome is another. Name the stages inside flow(), from left to right, and bind the count to y:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) + y(n) +
  title("Who survived, by class")


(data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + y(col.n) +
  title("Who survived, by class"))


data(titanic) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + y(:n) +
  title("Who survived, by class")


plot(data(titanic), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  y(col.n), title("Who survived, by class"))






                                class survived   0 1K 2K  Who survived, by class N





“Given titanic: ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, y is n.”
Each band is one path: one place at each stage, here a class and then an outcome. This plot does not outline the slots or name them, so find a path by its position. Inside each stage the slots stack from the bottom, in the order the column declares: 1st to Crew, and Yes before No. So the lowest band leaves the 1st slot and arrives at the Yes slot. It carries the 203 first-class passengers who survived, and it keeps that thickness at both ends. Rows that share a path become one band: their counts are added, and the band carries the total. The four 1st rows that end in Yes differ only in sex and age, and the atom names neither, so the four become one band.
flow() also sets both axes. With the count on y, the stages are drawn along the horizontal axis, each named by its column, in the order you name them inside flow(). The vertical axis is a continuous axis for the count. The bands at each stage stack from zero with no gaps. So the top edge of any band is the total of that band and every band below it.
The count is optional. Bind nothing and every row counts as 1, and the diagram counts rows instead of summing a column. partition uses that default too, and count tallies rows the same way. This table needs y(n): it holds one row per combination, so counting its rows would count combinations rather than people.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.4 The slots
In the plot above, the bands that leave one place touch the bands that leave the next, so you cannot see where one place ends and the next begins. A zone layer draws the slots. Add zone * flow(class, survived), with the same stages as the bands. Both layers now use the count, so write y(n) before any mark, where it belongs to the plot and every layer reads it (Encoding scope):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, survived) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) +
  title("The same flow, with its slots")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  title("The same flow, with its slots"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) +
  zone * flow(:class, :survived) + title("The same flow, with its slots")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  title("The same flow, with its slots"))






                                        class survived   0 1K 2K  The same flow, with its slots N





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived.”
Each rectangle marks one slot. It covers the same part of the count axis as the bands that leave it or arrive at it, so each slot is as tall as the number of people at that place. A categorical axis also gives each category a slot, but there every slot is the same size. The top slot of the class stage is the crew, the largest group, with 885 people. At the outcome stage the larger slot is No: 1,490 of the 2,201 people did not survive.
Each slot is white with a thin black line around it, so only the bands have color and the edge of every slot is visible. Those are the defaults, and Choosing the colors shows how to change them. The slots still have no names, so you still count from the bottom to find each slot.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.5 The names
A text layer names the slots. The transform writes each slot’s name into a column called name, exactly as partition does. Add a third layer, text * flow(class, survived), with the same stages again, and bind label(name) to draw that column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, survived) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) +
  text * flow(class, survived) + label(name) +
  title("The same flow, with its slots named")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("The same flow, with its slots named"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) +
  zone * flow(:class, :survived) + text * flow(:class, :survived) +
  label(:name) + title("The same flow, with its slots named")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("The same flow, with its slots named"))






                             1st 2nd 3rd Crew Yes No              class survived   0 1K 2K  The same flow, with its slots named N





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived, and text derived by flow through class and survived, label by name.”
Each name is drawn at the center of its slot. The layers are drawn in the order they are written, so the text layer comes last. If the text layer came before the zone layer, the white slots would hide the names.
The 1st slot is now easy to find, and the thicker of its two bands arrives at Yes. It carries the 203 of the 325 people in first class who survived, the number given under the finished diagram. Every later plot in this chapter keeps the three layers.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.6 Adding a stage
The finished diagram has a third stage, sex, between class and the outcome. Add it by naming one more column inside flow(), in all three layers. Each path now passes through three stages, and each band is as thick as its count at every one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  title("Class, then sex, then survival")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("Class, then sex, then survival"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  title("Class, then sex, then survival")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("Class, then sex, then survival"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  Class, then sex, then survival N





Each band is now a group of people with one class, one sex and one outcome. sex declares no order, so its slots follow the order its values first appear in the table: Male at the bottom, then Female. The band from 1st through Female to Yes carries 141 people, the women and girls in first class who survived. Most people in the Female slot arrive at Yes, and most in the Male slot arrive at No, as in the finished diagram.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.7 Color from a stage
With three stages the bands cross one another, and when every band has the same color, one band is hard to follow through a crossing. A band runs through every stage, so any stage can color it. The finished diagram at the start of this chapter colors each band by survived, the slot it arrives at. Coloring by class gives each band the color of the slot it leaves at the first stage instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  title("The same paths, colored by class")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col["class"]) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("The same paths, colored by class"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:class) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  title("The same paths, colored by class")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), color(col.class),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("The same paths, colored by class"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  The same paths, colored by class N  Class    1st  2nd  3rd  Crew 





Now you can see which classes arrive in each later slot. Coloring by survived and coloring by class answer two questions: who lived, and where each class went.
color() is written after the ribbon layer, so it belongs to the bands alone. Written before the marks, it would reach the slots and the names as well. gog refuses that, because a slot and its name take their color from style().

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.8 Color from another column
Did the women in third class survive as often as the women in first class? A color can show it inside each band, with no third stage. Any categorical column can color the bands, not only a stage. A column that is not a stage splits each band into one part for each of its values. A categorical color splits a line the same way, into one line for each category. The parts of one band lie next to each other across its thickness and follow its path, and the slots are the same as without the color. With survived as a color instead of a stage, a flow through class and sex shows who survived in every band:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex) +
  text * flow(class, sex) + label(name) +
  title("Class, then sex, colored by survival")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex) + label(col.name) +
  title("Class, then sex, colored by survival"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex) + color(:survived) +
  zone * flow(:class, :sex) + text * flow(:class, :sex) + label(:name) +
  title("Class, then sex, colored by survival")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex)),
  color(col.survived), layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex)), label(col.name),
  title("Class, then sex, colored by survival"))






                                     1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female              class sex   0 1K 2K  Class, then sex, colored by survival N  Survived    Yes  No 





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class and sex, colored by survived, and also zones derived by flow through class and sex, and text derived by flow through class and sex, label by name.”
Each band from a class to a sex now has a blue part for the people who survived and an orange part for the people who did not. The band from 1st to Female is nearly all blue: 141 of its 145 people survived. The band from 3rd to Female is less than half blue: 90 of 196. The finished diagram shows the same split with survived as a stage, where the outcome also gets slots of its own. As a color, the outcome needs no slots of its own, and the legend names its values.
Only a categorical column can split a band, because its values are groups. A continuous column is refused, as it is on every ribbon.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.9 Choosing the colors
Every color in this chapter so far is a default. The bands take gog’s default palette and are translucent, the slots are white with a thin black line around them, and the names are near-black. You choose each one in its own layer.
The bands take their colors from a column, and palette() chooses the color for each value of that column. Write each value beside the color you want, as Colors by name explains. Name every value, since gog refuses a palette that leaves one out:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  palette(c(Yes = "steelblue", No = "darkgray")) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  title("The survivors in blue")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  palette({"Yes": "steelblue", "No": "darkgray"}) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("The survivors in blue"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + palette(["Yes" => "steelblue", "No" => "darkgray"]) +
  zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  title("The survivors in blue")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived), palette({ Yes: "steelblue", No: "darkgray" }),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("The survivors in blue"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  The survivors in blue N  Survived    Yes  No 





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored by survived, with a palette naming Yes steelblue and No darkgray, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name.”
The bands of the survivors are blue and the others are gray, so the survivors are easy to find. A band is translucent, so it looks lighter than the color you name, and two bands that cross both stay visible. To give every band the same color, leave out color() and write style(color = ) after the ribbon layer. style(opacity = ) there sets how translucent the bands are, with or without color().
A slot sits at one stage, so no single column can color every slot, and the same is true of the names. The zone and text layers take their settings from style() instead, one value for each layer. On the zone layer, color fills the slots, and border_color and border_size draw the line around each one. On the text layer, color and size set the color and the size of the names:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  palette(c(Yes = "steelblue", No = "darkgray")) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  style(color = "midnightblue", border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  style(color = "white", size = 14) +
  title("Dark slots with white names")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  palette({"Yes": "steelblue", "No": "darkgray"}) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  style(color = "midnightblue", border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  style(color = "white", size = 14) +
  title("Dark slots with white names"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + palette(["Yes" => "steelblue", "No" => "darkgray"]) +
  zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  style(color = "midnightblue", border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  style(color = "white", size = 14) + title("Dark slots with white names")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived), palette({ Yes: "steelblue", No: "darkgray" }),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  style({ color: "midnightblue", border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  style({ color: "white", size: 14 }),
  title("Dark slots with white names"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  Dark slots with white names N  Survived    Yes  No 





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored by survived, with a palette naming Yes steelblue and No darkgray, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored midnightblue, with border color white and border size 2, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name, colored white, with size 14.”
Each style() is written after the mark it changes, so it changes that layer and no other. On the dark fill, the white line shows where each slot ends, and border_size = 0 would remove it. The zone layer also takes opacity, as every mark does, and pattern, as the five filled regions do (Style).

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.10 Room for long names
In a flow that runs left to right the slots are tall and narrow. The names in titanic are short, so every one fits. A longer name, such as Member of the crew, would be wider than its slot, and gog would draw it across the slot’s edges, over the bands. There are two ways to give it more space.
The first turns the names. style(angle = 90) on the text layer turns every name upward, so it runs along its slot, as Turning a label explains:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) + style(angle = 90) +
  title("Names turned 90 degrees")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) + style(angle = 90) +
  title("Names turned 90 degrees"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  style(angle = 90) + title("Names turned 90 degrees")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  style({ angle: 90 }), title("Names turned 90 degrees"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  Names turned 90 degrees N  Survived    Yes  No 





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored by survived, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name, with angle 90.”
Each name is now written upward, so it must fit the slot’s height, not the slot’s width.
The second places the stages from top to bottom. Bind the count to x instead of y, and the first stage is at the top of the plot. Each slot is then wide and short, so a long name fits across it unless the slot’s count is small. The sentence is the finished diagram’s, with x(n) in place of y(n) and a new title. gog takes the direction from the axis that holds the count, as it does for a bar chart (Horizontal bars):


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + x(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  title("The same flow, from top to bottom")


(data(titanic) + x(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  title("The same flow, from top to bottom"))


data(titanic) + x(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  title("The same flow, from top to bottom")


plot(data(titanic), x(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("The same flow, from top to bottom"))






                                                        1st 2nd 3rd Crew Male Female Yes No               0 1K 2K   survived sex class  The same flow, from top to bottom N  Survived    Yes  No 





“Given titanic: x is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored by survived, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name.”
The stage names are now on the left: class at the top, then sex, then survived. The count is on the bottom axis, and each name fits inside its slot.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.11 Leaving out the count axis
The count axis helped while the diagram was being built: it showed that the bands at each stage add up to the same total, just over 2,000 people. A reader of the finished diagram compares the thicknesses of the bands and the slots, and needs no numbers for that. So the count axis, the gridlines and the frame (the two lines along the bottom and the left of the panel) can be left out, and the gray panel can be white. Write axis = FALSE on the count. In theme(), grid = "none" and frame = "none" leave out the gridlines and the frame, and background = "white" colors the panel (Axes, legends, gridlines and the frame). The stage names stay, because they belong to the other axis, which is still drawn:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n, axis = FALSE) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") +
  title("Who survived, by class and sex")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n, axis = False) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") +
  title("Who survived, by class and sex"))


data(titanic) + y(:n, axis = false) +
  ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + color(:survived) +
  zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white") +
  title("Who survived, by class and sex")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n, { axis: false }),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  theme({ grid: "none", frame: "none", background: "white" }),
  title("Who survived, by class and sex"))

Only the bands, the slots with their names, the legend and the stage names are left. A reader can still see that most of the women survived and most of the men did not. The exact counts are gone from the picture, so give them in the paragraph beside the plot, as The finished diagram does.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.12 Selecting one place
Color tells the bands apart, but it does not show where the people in one place went. brush keeps the color of the bands that pass through one place and dims the rest. Name a stage, and use at to name the place the selection starts with, as a brush on a categorical column does:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  text * flow(class, sex, survived) + label(name) +
  brush(sex, at = "Female") +
  title("The women and girls, and where they went")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  text * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + label(col.name) +
  brush(col.sex, at = "Female") +
  title("The women and girls, and where they went"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) + label(:name) +
  brush(:sex, at = "Female") +
  title("The women and girls, and where they went")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  brush(col.sex, { at: "Female" }),
  title("The women and girls, and where they went"))






                                    Male                                      1st 2nd 3rd Crew Female Yes No               class sex survived   0 1K 2K  The women and girls, and where they went N  Survived    Yes  No 





“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class, sex and survived, colored by survived, and also zones derived by flow through class, sex and survived, and text derived by flow through class, sex and survived, label by name, and let the reader select sex, starting with Female.”
The bands that pass through Female keep their colors, and every other band is dimmed. A brush on a stage never cuts a band in two. A band is a group of people who share a place at every stage, so either all of them are in the selection or none of them are. The Male slot is dimmed as well. The slots at the other two stages hold both women and men, so they are not dimmed.
In the web edition, a click on a sex slot selects it. Click Male and the selection moves there. Click the selected slot again, a band, or an empty part of the panel, and nothing is dimmed. With a bare brush, a click selects a slot at any stage. A drag selects nothing on a flow, and the pointer shows no values, because each band and each slot stands for many rows. In the PDF, the plot keeps the selection the sentence states.
A flow keeps or dims each band, or each part of a band, as a whole. So the brushed column must be one that each band, or each part, holds a single value of. A stage is one. So is a column given to the bands’ color, because it splits each band into parts, as Color from another column shows. Any other column can hold two values in one band, and gog refuses it. age is a column of titanic, but not a stage of this flow:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, sex, survived) + color(survived) +
  zone * flow(class, sex, survived) +
  brush(age, at = "Child")


(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) + color(col.survived) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.sex, col.survived) +
  brush(col.age, at = "Child"))


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  color(:survived) + zone * flow(:class, :sex, :survived) +
  brush(:age, at = "Child")


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  color(col.survived),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.sex, col.survived)),
  brush(col.age, { at: "Child" }))




Error:
! gog: `brush(age)` on a flow is valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it. A flow selects whole bands, and `age` is neither a stage nor a column that colors the bands, so it would cut across them. Brush a stage, such as `brush(class, at = ...)`, or map `age` to the `ribbon` layer's `color` or `pattern`, which splits each band by its values.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

section: 30.13 Two columns that name the same places
text:
30.13 Two columns that name the same places
So far each column named in flow() has been a stage of its own. Some tables record amounts between places of one kind instead. trade_partners, from the Network chapter, records trade between countries: each row says how much one country exported to another, in billions of dollars:

China appears in both columns. It exports to the United States, and it imports from Korea. A flow through exporter and importer would put each column at a stage of its own, so China would get two slots. shared = TRUE says that the two columns name one set of places. Each country then gets one slot, and every slot lies on one axis. The length of a country’s slot is the total of its exports and imports:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + x(billions) +
  ribbon * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) + color(exporter) +
  zone * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) +
  text * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) + label(name) +
  title("Trade between countries, as arcs")


(data(trade_partners) + x(col.billions) +
  ribbon * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) + color(col.exporter) +
  zone * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) +
  text * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) + label(col.name) +
  title("Trade between countries, as arcs"))


data(trade_partners) + x(:billions) +
  ribbon * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) + color(:exporter) +
  zone * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) +
  text * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) + label(:name) +
  title("Trade between countries, as arcs")


plot(data(trade_partners), x(col.billions),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  color(col.exporter),
  layer(zone, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  layer(text, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  label(col.name), title("Trade between countries, as arcs"))






                                                                          China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain        Trade between countries, as arcs  Exporter    China  Mexico  Canada  United States  Korea  Germany  Netherlands  Japan  Australia  Brazil  India  France 





“Given trade partners: x is billions, ribbons derived by flow through exporter and importer, shared, colored by exporter, and also zones derived by flow through exporter and importer, shared, and text derived by flow through exporter and importer, shared, label by name.”
This picture is an arc diagram. Each band rises from the country that exports and comes down at the country that imports. The farther apart the two countries are on the axis, the higher the band rises. Each end of a band is as wide as the amount it carries. color(exporter) gives each band the color of the country it leaves.
A country’s slot has up to two parts, with no line between them. The bands of its exports leave the white part, and the bands of its imports arrive at the gray part, to the right of the white part. Vietnam only imports, so its slot is all gray. At China, the band to the United States leaves the white part, and the band from Korea arrives at the gray part. The colors show this too: every band of China’s exports has China’s color. The two parts show it even without the legend. A style(color = ) on the zone layer colors the white part, and the gray part becomes a darker shade of that color.
The white part is for the first column in flow(), and the gray part is for the second. To put the exports in the gray part instead, name importer first:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + x(billions) +
  ribbon * flow(importer, exporter, shared = TRUE) + color(exporter) +
  zone * flow(importer, exporter, shared = TRUE) +
  text * flow(importer, exporter, shared = TRUE) + label(name) +
  title("Trade between countries, imports first")


(data(trade_partners) + x(col.billions) +
  ribbon * flow(col.importer, col.exporter, shared = True) + color(col.exporter) +
  zone * flow(col.importer, col.exporter, shared = True) +
  text * flow(col.importer, col.exporter, shared = True) + label(col.name) +
  title("Trade between countries, imports first"))


data(trade_partners) + x(:billions) +
  ribbon * flow(:importer, :exporter, shared = true) + color(:exporter) +
  zone * flow(:importer, :exporter, shared = true) +
  text * flow(:importer, :exporter, shared = true) + label(:name) +
  title("Trade between countries, imports first")


plot(data(trade_partners), x(col.billions),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.importer, col.exporter, { shared: true })),
  color(col.exporter),
  layer(zone, flow(col.importer, col.exporter, { shared: true })),
  layer(text, flow(col.importer, col.exporter, { shared: true })),
  label(col.name), title("Trade between countries, imports first"))






                                                                          United States China Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain        Trade between countries, imports first  Exporter    China  Mexico  Canada  United States  Korea  Germany  Netherlands  Japan  Australia  Brazil  India  France 





Each slot now starts with the country’s imports, in white, and its exports follow in gray. The order of the countries changes too, but only at the start: the United States now comes first and China second. gog puts the countries in the order it first reads their names. In each row it reads the first column in flow() before the second, so the first row now gives the United States before China. If the columns have a declared order, gog uses that order instead.
The axis carries no numbers. Each amount takes space on the axis twice, once at each end of its band, so an axis with numbers would end at twice the total trade. The country names are written in place of the numbers, turned to read upward when they do not fit side by side. With the amount on y, as in y(billions), the axis runs up the page, the names stand at its left, and the bands reach to the right.
The panel is white and has no frame, because the plot has no numbers to read values from. theme() changes both, as it does for any plot: background colors the panel, and frame = "axes" draws the two lines along the bottom and the left (Axes, legends, gridlines and the frame).
A shared flow, one with shared = TRUE, reads two columns: the place each amount leaves, and the place it arrives at. A third column, for a route through three places, would be valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.14 The chord diagram
Add polar() to the arc diagram’s sentence, the one with exporter first. polar() puts the amounts on the angle, as it does for a pie, so the axis bends into a ring. This picture is a chord diagram:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + x(billions) +
  ribbon * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) + color(exporter) +
  zone * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) +
  text * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) + label(name) +
  polar() + title("Trade between countries, as chords")


(data(trade_partners) + x(col.billions) +
  ribbon * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) + color(col.exporter) +
  zone * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) +
  text * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) + label(col.name) +
  polar() + title("Trade between countries, as chords"))


data(trade_partners) + x(:billions) +
  ribbon * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) + color(:exporter) +
  zone * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) +
  text * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) + label(:name) +
  polar() + title("Trade between countries, as chords")


plot(data(trade_partners), x(col.billions),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  color(col.exporter),
  layer(zone, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  layer(text, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  label(col.name), polar(), title("Trade between countries, as chords"))






                                                                        China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  Trade between countries, as chords  Exporter    China  Mexico  Canada  United States  Korea  Germany  Netherlands  Japan  Australia  Brazil  India  France 





“Given trade partners: x is billions, ribbons derived by flow through exporter and importer, shared, colored by exporter, and also zones derived by flow through exporter and importer, shared, and text derived by flow through exporter and importer, shared, label by name, in polar.”
Each country’s slot is now a piece of the ring, and its length is still the total of the country’s exports and imports. It keeps its two parts, white for exports and gray for imports. Each band curves toward the center of the circle, from the country that exports to the country that imports. Like the arc diagram’s axis, the ring carries no numbers, and the names stand outside it.
In a chord diagram, a band’s area can mislead. A band’s width at its two ends is the amount it carries, but its area is not. A band between countries far apart on the ring is long, and a band between two countries side by side on the ring is short. The countries stand around the ring in the order they first appear in the table, so the length of a band says nothing about the amounts. Canada exported 420 billion dollars to the United States, and China exported 500. Yet Canada’s band covers more of the picture, because China sits next to the United States. Read a band at its two ends. The next section shows an easier way to read the diagram: one country at a time.

title: 30  Flow
section: 30.15 Selecting a place in either column
text:
30.15 Selecting a place in either column
A brush on one column selects by that column alone. brush(exporter, at = "China") keeps the bands that leave China and dims the bands that arrive there. To keep both, brush the flow’s own name, the column that label(name) reads. That brush keeps every band that leaves or arrives at the place. Each band holds two names, one at each end. Selecting one place refuses a column with two values in one band, and name is the one exception.

data(trade_partners) + x(billions) +

  text * flow(exporter, importer, shared = TRUE) + label(name) +
  brush(name, at = "China") +
  title("What China exports and imports")


(data(trade_partners) + x(col.billions) +
  ribbon * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) + color(col.exporter) +
  zone * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) +
  text * flow(col.exporter, col.importer, shared = True) + label(col.name) +
  brush(col.name, at = "China") +
  title("What China exports and imports"))


data(trade_partners) + x(:billions) +
  ribbon * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) + color(:exporter) +
  zone * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) +
  text * flow(:exporter, :importer, shared = true) + label(:name) +
  brush(:name, at = "China") + title("What China exports and imports")


plot(data(trade_partners), x(col.billions),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  color(col.exporter),
  layer(zone, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  layer(text, flow(col.exporter, col.importer, { shared: true })),
  label(col.name), brush(col.name, { at: "China" }),
  title("What China exports and imports"))

Every band that leaves or arrives at China keeps its color. Every other band is dimmed, and so is every other country’s slot. In the web edition, a click on a country’s slot selects that country instead. A click on the selected slot, on a band, or on an empty part of the panel clears the selection. show rows lists the selected rows with both exporter and importer, so each row says whether it is an export from China or an import into China.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.16 Links in layers
Some tables record movement whose paths do not all pass through the same stages. budget holds one household’s money for a month. Two incomes are added into one, Income. From there the money goes to Taxes, Savings and four groups of spending, and each group divides again. Each row is one link, an amount that moves from one place to the next:



budget: first 5 of 22 rows


source
target
amount




Salary

1275
