Taxes and Savings are one step after Income, and no band leaves them. Rent is one step later, and no band leaves it either. Utilities, at the same step as Rent, divides again into Energy and Water. Stage columns cannot hold that, because every row would need a value at every stage. layered = TRUE says that each row is a link between two places. gog then puts the places in layers. A layer is drawn like a stage, but gog computes it from the links instead of reading a column. It is a different thing from a layer of the sentence, such as the ribbon layer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(budget) + y(amount) +
  ribbon * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) + color(source) +
  zone * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) +
  text * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) + label(name) +
  title("A month of a household's money")


(data(budget) + y(col.amount) +
  ribbon * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True) + color(col.source) +
  zone * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True) +
  text * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True) + label(col.name) +
  title("A month of a household's money"))


data(budget) + y(:amount) +
  ribbon * flow(:source, :target, layered = true) + color(:source) +
  zone * flow(:source, :target, layered = true) +
  text * flow(:source, :target, layered = true) + label(:name) +
  title("A month of a household's money")


plot(data(budget), y(col.amount),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })),
  color(col.source),
  layer(zone, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })),
  layer(text, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })),
  label(col.name), title("A month of a household's money"))






                                                       Salary Income Side work Taxes Housing Food Transport Leisure Savings Rent Utilities Repairs Energy Water Groceries Eating out Car Season ticket Fuel Insurance Holidays Hobbies Subscriptions        A month of a household's money  Source    Salary  Side work  Income  Housing  Utilities  Food  Transport  Car  Leisure 





“Given the budget: y is amount, ribbons derived by flow through source and target, layered, colored by source, and also zones derived by flow through source and target, layered, and text derived by flow through source and target, layered, label by name.”
This picture is a Sankey diagram. Each place stands in the first layer that comes after every place that sends to it. Salary and Side work send to Income, so Income stands in the second layer. Taxes stands in the third layer, and no band leaves it. Energy stands in the fifth layer, after Housing in the third and Utilities in the fourth. Each slot is as tall as the larger of what arrives at the place and what leaves it. A small gap separates the places of one layer. color(source) gives each band the color of the place it leaves.
gog also computes the order of the places in each layer. It puts each place near the places it links to, so that few bands cross. The slots are too narrow to hold a name, so each name stands beside its slot. In every layer but the last, it stands to the right, on top of any bands that leave the place. In the last layer it stands to the left. Like the shared flow, a layered flow writes no numbers on its axes. Its layers have no names to write along one axis. Along the other, the gaps between places take space too, so the edge of a slot is not a running total there.

title: 30  Flow
section: 30.17 A Sankey diagram and an alluvial diagram
text:
30.17 A Sankey diagram and an alluvial diagram
A layered flow adds up the amounts that arrive at a place. Salary and Side work both arrive at Income. The band from Income to Housing holds money from each, and the picture cannot show how much. The alluvial diagram at the start of this chapter keeps each group of people on its own band, from the first stage to the last. So when every row has a value at every stage, name those columns as stages, and each band keeps its group. Use layered = TRUE for a table of links, which stage columns cannot hold.
Adding up at each place also decides what a selection keeps. brush(name, at = "Housing") keeps the links of Housing itself: the band that arrives at Housing, and the bands that leave it for Rent, Utilities and Repairs:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(budget) + y(amount) +
  ribbon * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) + color(source) +
  zone * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) +
  text * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) + label(name) +
  brush(name, at = "Housing") +
  title("What arrives at Housing and what leaves it")


(data(budget) + y(col.amount) +
  ribbon * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True) + color(col.source) +
  zone * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True) +
  text * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True) + label(col.name) +
  brush(col.name, at = "Housing") +
  title("What arrives at Housing and what leaves it"))


data(budget) + y(:amount) +
  ribbon * flow(:source, :target, layered = true) + color(:source) +
  zone * flow(:source, :target, layered = true) +
  text * flow(:source, :target, layered = true) + label(:name) +
  brush(:name, at = "Housing") +
  title("What arrives at Housing and what leaves it")


plot(data(budget), y(col.amount),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })),
  color(col.source),
  layer(zone, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })),
  layer(text, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })),
  label(col.name), brush(col.name, { at: "Housing" }),
  title("What arrives at Housing and what leaves it"))

The bands from Utilities to Energy and Water stay dimmed, although here all of their money passed through Housing. A place can receive money from several places, as Income does. A band that leaves such a place carries some of each, and the picture cannot show how much. So a selection keeps only the bands that arrive at the place or leave it, whatever the table holds. In the web edition, a click on a slot selects that place, as on the other flows.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.18 What flow refuses
A flow needs at least two stages, because movement needs a place to start and a place to finish:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"])


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), layer(ribbon, flow(col.class)))




Error:
! gog: `flow()` needs at least two stage columns, in reading order — `flow(class, sex, survived)` runs each row from its `class` to its `survived`. One column has no between.


flow() puts the stages on the axis that does not hold the count. With y(n) that is the x axis, so x(class) asks for the same axis as the stages, and gog refuses it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + x(class) + ribbon * flow(class, survived)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + x(col["class"]) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived)


data(titanic) + y(:n) + x(:class) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), x(col.class),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)))




Error:
! gog: under `flow` one axis carries the count and the other the stages, and both `x(class)` and `y(n)` are bound. Keep `y(<amount>)` to run the stages left to right, or `x(<amount>)` to run them top to bottom.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Only ribbon, zone and text can read what flow computes. Any other mark is refused, and the message names the three:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + bar * flow(class, survived)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + bar * flow(col["class"], col.survived)


data(titanic) + y(:n) + bar * flow(:class, :survived)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), layer(bar, flow(col.class, col.survived)))




Error:
! gog: `flow` lays a path's magnitude through its stages — an interval at each stage, and a band between adjacent ones — and `bar` has no reading for that. Three marks do: `ribbon * flow(<a>, <b>)` draws the bands, `zone * flow(<a>, <b>)` draws each stage's slots, and `text * flow(<a>, <b>) + label(name)` names them. Bind `y(<amount>)` to weigh the paths, or bind nothing and each row counts 1.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And a continuous column cannot color a band, just as it cannot color any ribbon. n is a continuous column:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) + color(n)


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + color(col.n)


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + color(:n)


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), color(col.n))




Error:
! gog: `color(n)` maps a continuous (numeric) column, but `color` on `ribbon` needs a categorical (text) column.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.19 Where the limits are
The two limits below are not mistakes in your sentence. Each is valid grammar that this engine does not draw.
A flow with stages is valid grammar in polar() too. Each stage would get a ring of its own, so the picture would be a circular alluvial diagram, not the chord diagram above. This engine does not draw it, and the message points to shared = TRUE for two columns that name one set of places:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) + polar()


data(titanic) + y(col.n) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + polar()


data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + polar()


plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), polar())




Error:
! gog: `flow` in `polar()` is valid grammar, a flow bent round a rim with a ring for each stage, but this engine does not draw it. Draw the flow flat. If two columns name one set of places, `flow(class, survived)` with `shared` set to true draws them in `polar()` as the chord diagram.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A layered flow has a limit too. Its bands may skip a layer, or stop before the last layer, but its links may not form a cycle. Links that form a cycle have no layers, because no place in the cycle comes first. A household that moves money from its checking account to its savings account, and back again, makes a cycle. gog refuses it, and the message names the cycle:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


accounts <- data.frame(source = c("Checking", "Savings"),
                       target = c("Savings", "Checking"), amount = c(200, 50))
data(accounts) + y(amount) + ribbon * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE)


accounts = {
  "source": ["Checking", "Savings"],
  "target": ["Savings", "Checking"],
  "amount": [200, 50],
}
data(accounts) + y(col.amount) + ribbon * flow(col.source, col.target, layered = True)


accounts = (
  source = ["Checking", "Savings"],
  target = ["Savings", "Checking"],
  amount = [200, 50],
)
data(accounts) + y(:amount) +
  ribbon * flow(:source, :target, layered = true)


const accounts = {
  source: ["Checking", "Savings"],
  target: ["Savings", "Checking"],
  amount: [200, 50],
};
plot(data(accounts), y(col.amount),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.source, col.target, { layered: true })))




Error:
! gog: these links form a cycle, Checking → Savings → Checking, and a layered flow stands each place after every place that sends to it, so a cycle has no order. A cycle drawn as a loop is valid grammar this engine does not draw. Set `shared` to true in place of `layered`: `flow(source, target)` then puts every place on one axis and draws a cycle as arcs. Or remove one of the links.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Some tools draw a cycle as a band that runs back across the diagram. The message points to shared = TRUE instead, which puts every place on one axis and draws the same links as arcs.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.20 Choosing a flow diagram
This chapter has drawn four kinds of flow diagram: alluvial, Sankey, arc and chord. To choose one, start from what one row of your table says. The last row of the table is a fifth choice, the network diagram:



What one row says
A question it answers
The diagram




a group and its place at each of several stages, as in titanic
How did each group move from stage to stage?
an alluvial diagram (The finished diagram)


a link, an amount that moves from one place to the next, with no cycles, as in budget
Where does the total go, step by step?
a Sankey diagram (Links in layers)


an amount between two places of one kind, often in both directions, as in trade_partners
Who sends to whom, and how much each way?
an arc diagram, or the same links on a ring, a chord diagram (Two columns that name the same places)


a connection between two places, when who is connected matters more than how much
What is connected to what?
a network diagram (Network)



A flow diagram shows the pattern of the movement, but a band is hard to compare with a band in another part of the picture. A tile plot gives each pair of places its own cell, so every pair has a fixed place in a grid:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + zone + x(importer) + y(exporter) + color(billions) +
  title("Trade between countries, one cell per pair")


(data(trade_partners) + zone + x(col.importer) + y(col.exporter) + color(col.billions) +
  title("Trade between countries, one cell per pair"))


data(trade_partners) + zone + x(:importer) + y(:exporter) +
  color(:billions) + title("Trade between countries, one cell per pair")


plot(data(trade_partners), zone, x(col.importer), y(col.exporter),
  color(col.billions),
  title("Trade between countries, one cell per pair"))






                                                                                    United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea China Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Spain   France India Brazil Australia Japan Netherlands Germany Korea United States Canada Mexico China  Trade between countries, one cell per pair Exporter Importer  Billions         500 275 50 





“Given trade partners: zones, x is importer, y is exporter, color by billions.”
Each row of cells is an exporter, and each column of cells is an importer. The darkest cell is China’s exports to the United States, the largest amount in the table. The cells for Mexico and Canada are nearly as dark, so the shades alone do not say which is larger. A reader compares lengths more accurately than shades of a color, so draw the amounts as bars when the comparison must be precise.
Four more suggestions help you draw a flow diagram. First, color the bands by the column that answers your question. On a flow with stages, the first stage shows where each group goes, and the last shows the outcomes. Second, add brush to select one place: the bands that meet it keep their colors, and the others are dimmed. With brush written, a click on a slot in the web edition selects another place. Third, use few places. Before you draw, give the small places one shared name in your table, such as Other. On a layered flow, give it only to places that do not link to each other: a link from Other to Other is a cycle. Fourth, in an arc or a chord diagram, the order of the places decides how long the bands are and how often they cross. So declare an order that means something, such as by continent.

title: 30  Flow
text:
30.21 What comes next
A flow with stages stacks each stage’s slots in the order you declare, or else in the table’s order. Cluster computes an order from the data instead: it joins the categories that are most alike into a tree, and puts an axis in the tree’s order.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.1 The tree
Which categories in a table are most alike? A table of numbers holds the answer, but a reader cannot see it in the rows. The cluster transform computes it. It treats each category of an axis as a leaf of a tree. It finds the two closest leaves and joins them into one branch. Then it measures again, treating that new branch as one item, and joins the closest two again. It repeats until one tree holds every leaf. The finished tree is called a dendrogram. As with a pie chart, no atom spells that name.
This chapter builds the tree, uses it to order a tile plot, and then puts the two together as a clustered heatmap. nutrients holds one row per pair of food and nutrient. There are eight everyday foods, and each one is measured on five nutrients:
Which two of the eight foods are most alike, and which one is least like all the rest? To answer that, the engine needs to know what to compare. Each leaf is described by a profile. cluster(amount, over = nutrient) says that one leaf’s profile is its amount in every category of nutrient. So each food’s profile is five numbers. Two numbers place a point on a scatter plot, and five numbers place a point the same way, along five axes that are never drawn. The distance between two leaves is the straight-line distance between their points, the Euclidean distance. The distance between two branches is the average of the distances from every leaf on one branch to every leaf on the other. At each step the two closest branches join, and the join is drawn at that distance. This rule is called average linkage.
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of")


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of"))


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of")


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of"))






                                   chicken salmon spinach oats rice beans lentils almonds   0 20 40  Eight foods, joined by what they are made of Distance Food
“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food.”
path draws the tree. A tree is a set of points that must be joined in a fixed order, and line would sort them by x instead. path draws the rows in the order they arrive, and cluster writes them in the order the tree needs. Here you bind food to x, so x carries the leaves. This chapter calls that axis the leaf axis. You bind nothing to the other position, and cluster supplies it. The transform computes the distance at which each pair of branches joins, and it names that axis Distance.
The place where two branches meet is a join. The further a join is drawn from the leaf axis, the more different the two branches are. Beans and lentils join lowest, and rice and oats join just above them. Almonds join at the greatest distance of all, so almonds are the food least like the rest.
Bind y instead of x, and the same tree is drawn sideways, with the leaves down the left edge:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + y(food)


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + y(col.food)


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + y(:food)


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), y(col.food))






                                   0 20 40   almonds lentils beans rice oats spinach salmon chicken  Food Distance
“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, y is food.”
Whichever axis carries the leaves, the tree is the same. Two things about how cluster builds it cannot be changed. First, distance is measured on the values as they are, with no rescaling. Fat runs from 0.3 to 49.9 and iron from 0.5 to 3.7, so fat has far more effect on the distance than iron does. If you want every nutrient to count equally, rescale amount separately within each nutrient, in the host language, before you draw. Second, branches join at their average distance, so a join is never closer to the leaf axis than the joins inside its two branches. And two leaves with identical profiles are at distance zero, so their join is drawn at zero, where every leaf’s line begins.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.2 The order
Reading the finished tree along the leaf axis also gives an order, with similar foods next to each other. That order helps on a tile plot, because a pattern in the tiles is hard to see when similar foods are far apart. A tile plot of the same table draws its slots in the order the rows arrived. That order says nothing about the foods:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + zone + x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount) +
  title("In the order the rows arrived")


(data(nutrients) + zone + x(col.food) + y(col.nutrient) + color(col.amount) +
  title("In the order the rows arrived"))


data(nutrients) + zone + x(:food) + y(:nutrient) + color(:amount) +
  title("In the order the rows arrived")


plot(data(nutrients), zone, x(col.food), y(col.nutrient),
  color(col.amount), title("In the order the rows arrived"))






                                                                                salmon rice almonds lentils chicken spinach beans oats   iron fiber carbs fat protein  In the order the rows arrived Nutrient Food  Amount         49.9 24.95 0 





“Given nutrients: zones, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount.”
zone * cluster draws the same tiles. The leaf axis now runs in the tree’s order. Chicken and salmon are next to each other on the left, and oats, rice, beans and lentils are together between spinach and almonds:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over = nutrient) +
  x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount) +
  title("In the tree's order")


(data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over=col.nutrient) +
  x(col.food) + y(col.nutrient) + color(col.amount) +
  title("In the tree's order"))


data(nutrients) + zone * cluster(over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  y(:nutrient) + color(:amount) + title("In the tree's order")


plot(data(nutrients), layer(zone, cluster({ over: col.nutrient })),
  x(col.food), y(col.nutrient), color(col.amount),
  title("In the tree's order"))






                                                                                chicken salmon spinach oats rice beans lentils almonds   iron fiber carbs fat protein  In the tree's order Nutrient Food  Amount         49.9 24.95 0 





“Given nutrients: zones derived by cluster over nutrient, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount.”
On a tile plot, amount is already bound to color, so cluster does not name it again. over names the profile column, nutrient, which is on y. The other axis, food on x, holds the leaves, and that is the axis the tree reorders.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.3 The clustered heatmap
So far one tree has ordered one axis. Put a tree on two sides of the tiles, above and to the right, and each axis takes its order from the tree along that side. The result is usually called a clustered heatmap. It is three plots joined by two operators: a tree above, the tile plot below it, and a second tree to the right of the tiles. The plots align because they share axes, as the marginal plot in Composition does. A second rule from that chapter sets their order: a shared categorical axis takes the order a clustered panel computed for it. The tile plot in the middle carries no cluster of its own. It is the same plain tile plot drawn earlier in this chapter, without its title. theme(legend = "bottom") puts its legend under the tiles, so the tree on the right stands next to the tiles it orders. The tile plot takes its column order from the tree above and its row order from the tree on the right.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
   theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(food) + y(nutrient) + color(amount) +
      theme(legend = "bottom")) |
     (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = food) + y(nutrient) +
        theme(width = 150)))


((data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
   theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(col.food) + y(col.nutrient) + color(col.amount) +
      theme(legend = "bottom")) |
     (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.food) + y(col.nutrient) +
        theme(width = 150))))


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  theme(height = 150)) /
  ((data(nutrients) + zone + x(:food) + y(:nutrient) + color(:amount) +
  theme(legend = "bottom")) |
  (data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :food) +
  y(:nutrient) + theme(width = 150)))


below(plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  theme({ height: 150 })),
  beside(plot(data(nutrients), zone, x(col.food), y(col.nutrient),
  color(col.amount), theme({ legend: "bottom" })),
  plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.food })), y(col.nutrient),
  theme({ width: 150 }))))






                               0 20 40  Distance


                                                                                chicken salmon spinach oats rice beans lentils almonds   carbs fiber iron protein fat  Nutrient Food  Amount         0 24.95 49.9 


                            0 10 20 30 40    Distance






“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food; above zones, x is food, y is nutrient, color by amount, beside paths derived by cluster on amount, over food, y is nutrient.”
Each column of tiles is one food. Follow the tree upward from a column to its first join: that join shows which food, or which group of foods, the column’s food is most like. The tree on the right swaps the roles. Its leaves are the five nutrients, and each nutrient’s profile is its amount in the eight foods. Iron and fiber join first. The trees are not decoration. They decide the order of the foods across the page and of the nutrients down it.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.4 What cluster refuses
The tree decides the order of the leaf axis. You saw order() on a bar chart, where it sorted the categories along an axis, and you may want to write it here as well. An axis can hold only one order. order() sorts by a column, cluster derives an order from the tree, and writing both is a contradiction:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  order(food)


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
  order(col.food))


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  order(:food)


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  order(col.food))

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.5 Where the limits are
Each refusal above names a fix for the sentence you wrote. The limits below are different, because they are about what the engine draws and what the grammar can say.
Trees are often drawn in a circle, with the leaves around the rim, so you may want to draw one that way. polar() is what bends a plot, and a tree inside it is valid grammar that this engine does not draw. A circular tree needs curved lines, and path draws straight ones. Write polar(), and the engine says so:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) + polar()


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) + polar()

  polar()


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  polar())




Error:
! gog: a circular cluster tree is valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it: the tree's horizontal bars would bend into arcs, and a path's segments draw straight. Drop `polar()`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


You may want to color the tree by food. Every join connects two or more foods, so no single column can give its lines one color, and the engine refuses color() on the tree:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  color(food)


(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
  color(col.food))


data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  color(:food)


plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  color(col.food))




Error:
! gog: `color(...)` under `cluster` has nothing to read — the tree's strokes are computed from every row, so no column is left to split them by. `style(color = )` paints the tree; coloring its branches by a cut is not designed.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


style(color = ) paints the whole tree in one color. Coloring each group of branches below a chosen distance is not part of the grammar.
And a tree uses its second position for the distance, so it cannot share a plot with the tiles it orders. That is why the clustered heatmap composes three plots.

title: 31  Cluster
text:
31.6 What comes next
cluster reorders an axis, and the plot still uses two positions. Space adds the third position, z, and draws the marks inside a cube you can turn.

title: 32  Space
text:

  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + color(species)

  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + color(col.species))

  color(:species)

  color(col.species))

“Given the iris flowers: points, x is petal length, y is sepal length, color by species.”
Now add the third measurement as z. Nothing else about the sentence changes: the same point, the same x and y, and one more position, which the Grammar chapter calls a vowel. The flat plot becomes a cube:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + z(sepal_width) + color(species)


(data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + z(col.sepal_width) + color(col.species))


data(iris_flowers) + point + x(:petal_length) + y(:sepal_length) +
  z(:sepal_width) + color(:species)


plot(data(iris_flowers), point, x(col.petal_length), y(col.sepal_length),
  z(col.sepal_width), color(col.species))






                                                                                                                                                                               6 4 2 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 Petal Length Sepal Length Sepal Width   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica
“Given the iris flowers: points, x is petal length, y is sepal length, z is sepal width, color by species.”
That is the whole idea. A 3-D scatter is not a different chart with a different name; it is point with its third position bound, the same way a horizontal bar is just bar with its categories on y. A flat plot is a 3-D plot with z held constant. So every flat plot you have read so far was a special case of the cube, and the same rules place a mark in both.
Drawing a 3-D plot on a flat page takes two steps, and the second is the one every flat plot already uses. First the engine turns the three coordinates of every point to match the angle you are looking from. Then it draws the turned points on the page, the way it draws any flat plot. Points nearer to you are drawn last, so they cover the ones behind them. The fill is translucent, so a point behind still shows through the one in front. The drawing order is what gives a flat picture its depth.
The faint box behind the cloud of points is a guide rather than part of the data. A bare cloud of points gives you no way to tell which direction is x, which is y and which is z. The box draws the edges of the space the points stand in, and each of the three axes puts its numbers along one of those edges. Those three edges are drawn darker than the other nine.
Now look at the flowers. At this opening angle setosa sits apart from the other two, as it did on the flat page, but versicolor and virginica overlap much more than they did there. The data has not changed, so the extra overlap comes from the angle you are looking from.
In the web edition you can turn this cube yourself. Drag it in any direction and watch versicolor and virginica. Some angles separate the two colors, and others leave them mixed together. When you find an angle that separates them, read the two numbers under the plot. They are called turn and tilt, and they describe the view you are looking at. The next section shows how to write those two numbers into the sentence, so the plot opens at the angle you found.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.2 The viewing angle
A 3-D plot has to be seen from somewhere, and that angle is not part of the data. It is a property of the space the data sits in, the way a polar plot needs to know where its circle starts. Polar is the next chapter, and polar(start = ) is the same kind of parameter. So the angle is not a channel (it maps no column) and not a mark. It is space():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + z(sepal_width) + color(species) +
  space(turn = -95, tilt = 15)


(data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + z(col.sepal_width) + color(col.species) +
  space(turn = -95, tilt = 15))


data(iris_flowers) + point + x(:petal_length) + y(:sepal_length) +
  z(:sepal_width) + color(:species) + space(turn = -95, tilt = 15)


plot(data(iris_flowers), point, x(col.petal_length), y(col.sepal_length),
  z(col.sepal_width), color(col.species), space({ turn: -95, tilt: 15 }))






                                                                                                                                                                               6 4 2 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 Petal Length Sepal Length Sepal Width   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: points, x is petal length, y is sepal length, z is sepal width, color by species, turned -95, tilted 15.”
This is the first cube again, seen from another side and from a little lower down. The choice matters. From this side petal length runs across the page, and sepal length runs into the page, away from you. Virginica has the longer petals, so it sits to the right of versicolor, and the two barely overlap. At the default angle the two lengths ran in opposite directions across the page, so most of the difference between the two species was lost. The low tilt points the z axis up the page and flattens the floor. Sepal width and petal length are easy to read, but the flat floor squeezes sepal length into a short axis. A higher tilt does the reverse: the floor takes up more of the page and the heights grow shorter.
Turning the plot changes how you look at the data, never what the plot claims about it. That is why the angle is set in space(), and not by a channel or a mark. Omit space() and the plot opens at a default angle; use space() when that default hides what you want to see.
Both angles are given in degrees, and both move your eye rather than the data.
turn says which side of the cube you look at. It moves your eye around the plot, the way you walk around an object to see another side of it. At turn = 0 you look straight along the x axis, so x runs into the page. As turn grows from 0, the direction you look moves from the x axis toward the y axis. At turn = 90 you look straight along y, so y runs into the page. A negative turn moves your eye around the other way, and a full circle is 360 degrees.
tilt says how high your eye is. At tilt = 0 you are level with the floor and see the cube from the side. Raise it and you look down from higher up. At tilt = 90 you are directly above the cube, looking straight down. The floor fills the picture. The z axis now points straight at you, so it has no length left on the page and even its label disappears. A negative tilt puts your eye below the floor, looking up, as far as tilt = -90 from directly underneath. Dragging stops at tilt = 90 and at tilt = -90. A written tilt must also stay between -90 and 90, so dragging reaches every tilt you can write.
A plot with no space() opens at turn = 30, tilt = 25. That is far enough around and high enough up to show all three axes at once, which is why it is the default. Name one angle and the other keeps its default, so space(tilt = 85) looks down from high up without changing which side you stand on. Writing space() with nothing inside it takes both defaults, which is how the histogram sentences later in this chapter ask for a cube. (Astronomy calls these two angles azimuth and elevation, and the plain words say the same thing.)

title: 32  Space
text:
32.3 Turning the plot yourself
In the web edition you turn every cube in this book the same way, by dragging it. The cube follows your pointer. Drag right and the side facing you moves right; drag down and it tips down to show you the top. A row under each cube shows the two angles of the current view, and the numbers change as you drag. So you can find an angle by hand, then write it into the sentence as space(turn = , tilt = ).
A reset button sits beside those numbers. It returns the plot to the view it opened at, which is the angle the sentence asked for, or the default angle if the sentence named none. It is dimmed until you turn the plot, because until then there is nothing to undo.
The same buttons under every plot sit in a row of their own, between the plot and the angles, and each button does the same work here as on a flat plot. The camera saves the picture as you are looking at it, so the angle you turned the cube to is saved with it.
The cube differs from a flat plot in two ways, and both follow from one fact: dragging turns the cube and everything in it, rather than moving the picture across the page. So a zoomed cube cannot be dragged to one side, and the cube has a second control that undoes something: reset. The two undo different things: the frame button undoes the zoom, and reset undoes the angle. So zooming in never loses the angle you found, and going back to the opening angle keeps the zoom you set. A flat plot has no angle to restore, so it has no reset.
Turning a cube with the pointer changes nothing in its sentence. space() sets the angle the plot opens at, and dragging moves the view to any other angle from there. The data, the marks and the scales are the same at every angle.
Dragging needs the web edition. In the PDF, each plot is the still image its sentence asks for. That is the reason to name the angle even for readers who can drag: the PDF shows the view you chose, and the web edition opens at it.

title: 32  Space

32.4 path: the route through the cube
So far the cube has held one mark. A scatter is a cloud: every dot stands alone and the table’s order means nothing. When the order of the rows is what matters, the mark that says so is path, which joins rows in the order the table gives them. Give it three positions and the route runs through the cube. Here are two gliders circling one thermal (a rising column of warm air), sampled as they climb:

  color(:glider)

  color(col.glider))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude   Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider.”
Nothing in that sentence asks for a spiral. path was told to join the rows in order, and the gliders circled while they climbed. The spiral is what that looks like when it is drawn. The same three bindings would draw a straight line for an aircraft flying level, and a tangle for a tumbling one, because the route is only the order of the rows.
Look at where the two routes cross. The one in front covers the one behind, and which is which changes along the climb, so neither glider is simply “on top”. A stroke running through the cube has no single distance from the eye. Its far end and its near end are different distances. So the engine sorts the segments rather than the strokes, and sorts the segments of both routes together. Sorting whole strokes would put one glider entirely in front of the other: a picture of two coils that never meet, instead of two that pass through each other along the climb.
path is the only mark that draws a route through the cube. The reason is the one that already separates it from line on the flat page: the order of the rows. An order belongs to no axis, so it means the same thing when the plane becomes a cube. A line sorts by x and draws one y for each, read left to right along a domain. The cube has no left to right. x is one of three equal positions, and at some angles it runs straight into the page and becomes depth. A line in the cube would be sorted by an axis you cannot see, so the engine refuses it instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

plot(data(thermals), line, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude))

A `line` in space would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see, so this is refused rather than drawn. For a route through three dimensions use `path`, which is `line` with that sort removed: `path + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(altitude)`.

32.5 The 3-D histogram
Every cube so far bound a column to each of the three axes. The third axis can also carry something the data does not hold. The heatmap cuts a plane into cells and colors each one by how many rows fell in it. Those cells already cover a plane, and in the cube that plane is the floor. The color on each cell shows its count. Two shades of one color are hard to compare exactly, and two heights are easy. Here is the heatmap first, and then the same counts drawn as heights:

  style(color = "#2a9d8f")

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, in the cube.”
The mark changed from zone to bar, and space() asks for the cube. The transform is the same bin, cutting the same two axes into the same cells, and the count it invents is the same count. What differs is the mark that receives the count. The mark decides which visual attribute carries it. A zone measures nothing by length, so its count has to become a color. A bar is a length from a baseline, so its count becomes a height. The bar’s color then carries nothing, so every bar has the same color, and style() only chooses which one.
Nothing was added to the grammar to do that, and the rule that decided it was written for the flat page. How many axes a transform cuts is decided by the mark. bar * bin cuts one: a bar uses one axis for the domain and keeps the other to measure along. zone * bin cuts two, because a zone keeps none. A cube gives the bar a third axis. It can use two for the floor and still have one to measure along, so the same bar * bin that cuts one axis on the page cuts two here. Read that way, the 3-D histogram needs no feature of its own. It is what the flat rule already said, applied to three axes.
Note also what you did not have to write. There is no z() in that sentence, for the same reason a flat histogram has no y(): the count is invented rather than bound, so naming it would be naming an output.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.6 Transforms in the cube
That floor was cut from two continuous axes. A floor is made of cells, so the question is where the cells come from. The zone chapter answered it for a plane, and the same two answers hold here. A continuous axis has to be cut into cells before anything can be counted in them; a categorical axis arrives already cut, because a category is a cell. So which transform you want depends on which kind of axis you have. Two categorical axes arrive already cut:

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by count, x is continent, y is era, in the cube.”
That sentence counts the rows for every pair of categories, and each count is drawn as a bar’s height. A floor with one axis of each kind is a distribution per category, drawn as bars:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(life) + y(continent) + space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) + space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(:life) + y(:continent) + space() +
  style(color = "#2a9d8f")


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin(12)), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  space(), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }))






                                                                                                                                                          80 60 40 Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania 100 50 0 Life Continent Count 





Compare the two floors. The count floor holds a category on both axes, so its bars leave a gap in both directions. The bin floor holds one axis of each kind, so its bars touch along the binned axis and leave a gap along the categorical one. That is not a decision about how a 3-D plot should look; it is the flat rule, per axis. A histogram’s bins are adjacent intervals, so its bars fill them and meet. A category is one slot, and its neighbors are separate slots rather than adjacent intervals. A bar fills four fifths of its slot and leaves one fifth empty, and that gap is what says the categories are separate. So a floor cut on one axis and slotted on the other has no gaps one way and gaps the other. Each axis follows the rule for its own kind of column, and neither depends on the other.
Ask for a cut where there is nothing to cut and the engine names the other transform, exactly as it does on the plane:

count and bin both invent what they measure: you give count no column to reduce, because it counts rows. The other kind of statistic is the kind you give a column to reduce: a mean, a sum, a median. Those work on a floor too, and the sentence names the column on the axis that measures:

  style(color = "#2a9d8f")

  space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")

  z(col.life), space(), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is era, z is life.”
Each bar sits on the cell of one continent and one era, and its height is that group’s mean life expectancy. Read that beside the flat bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life). The rule is the same in both. A summary reduces the column on the axis the mark measures along, and groups by the other positions. On the flat page, a bar measures with y, so it groups by x and averages y. In the cube it measures with z, so it groups by the pair and averages z. Nothing about mean changed. The mark simply has one more position to group by.
That is the same rule the histogram used, applied a second time: take the positions the space offers, and set aside the one the mark measures along. Applied to bin, it says how many axes are cut. Applied to mean, it says how many columns the rows are grouped by. One rule answers both questions, and in both the answer depends on the mark.
The two kinds of statistic differ in what you give them, not in what they can draw. count and bin invent a measurement, so they need no column, and a color or a height shows the count. mean, sum, median, max, min and quantile reduce a column you name, so the sentence has to name it. Leave z() off and the engine says so rather than guessing.
One statistic does stay on the plane. It is smooth, which fits a curve instead of reducing a column:

Smooth on the plane, where there is a domain: `line * smooth + x(<a>) + y(<b>)`. To summarize a column within each pair of categories instead, the six reductions (`sum`, `mean`, `median`, `max`, `min`, `quantile`) do read a floor: `bar * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(<column>) + space()`.

The engine gives two reasons, and only the second belongs to the cube. The first would refuse the same sentence on the flat page, because both floor columns are categories. The second holds on any floor: a smoother traces a curve of one column against another, and a curve needs a domain to run along. The cube’s floor is a pair of positions with no left to right. That is why line and area cannot stand here either. It is the same reason, stated by a transform this time instead of by a mark.

title: 32  Space
section: 32.7 interval and box in the cube
text:
32.7 interval and box in the cube
A mean per cell hides how far the values in that cell spread, and the spread is often the question. A bar is not the only mark that sits in a slot and measures along the other axis. An interval does the same with a whisker, which spans a range from end to end, and a box does it with its quartiles and its median. So all three can be drawn in the cube, each on one cell of the floor, measuring along z:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + interval * range + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life) + space() +
  style(color = "#2a9d8f")


(data(gm_eras) + interval * range + x(col.continent) + y(col.era) + z(col.life) + space() +
  style(color = "#2a9d8f"))


data(gm_eras) + interval * range + x(:continent) + y(:era) + z(:life) +
  space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


plot(data(gm_eras), layer(interval, range), x(col.continent), y(col.era),
  z(col.life), space(), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }))






                                                                           Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia 1957 2007 80 60 40 Continent Era Life 





“Given the gapminder eras: intervals derived by range, x is continent, y is era, z is life.”
Every cell’s whisker spans that cell’s own low and high. The caps (the short lines across each end of a whisker) are a cross rather than a single tick, and that is not decoration. On the flat page a cap runs across the slot, in the one direction the whisker does not use. A cube has two such directions. Picking one of them would be arbitrary, and a reader would look for a meaning that is not there. So the cap runs in both.
Ask for confidence, which carries a center as well as two ends, and gog draws the pointrange: a dot at the center with a whisker on each side.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + interval * confidence + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life) +
  space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


(data(gm_eras) + interval * confidence + x(col.continent) + y(col.era) + z(col.life) +
  space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f"))


data(gm_eras) + interval * confidence + x(:continent) + y(:era) +
  z(:life) + space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


plot(data(gm_eras), layer(interval, confidence), x(col.continent),
  y(col.era), z(col.life), space(), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }))






                                                                                     Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia 1957 2007 80 70 60 50 40 Continent Era Life 





“Given the gapminder eras: intervals derived by confidence, x is continent, y is era, z is life.”
The box plot stands in the cube the same way. Its box is a solid between the two quartiles, and its whiskers reach beyond the box:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_eras) + box + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life) + space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


data(gm_eras) + box + x(col.continent) + y(col.era) + z(col.life) + space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f")


data(gm_eras) + box + x(:continent) + y(:era) + z(:life) + space() +
  style(color = "#2a9d8f")


plot(data(gm_eras), box, x(col.continent), y(col.era), z(col.life),
  space(), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }))






                                                                                                                                            Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia 1957 2007 80 60 40 Continent Era Life 





“Given the gapminder eras: boxes, x is continent, y is era, z is life.”
Look at the median on each box. It is drawn only where the box’s own sides face you. The median is a plane inside an opaque solid, so the far half of it is behind the box. That is the back-face rule (a face turned away is not drawn), the same rule the solid’s own six faces follow. One case is handled differently. When every value in a group is the same, its two quartiles are equal, so the box has no height and no sides to turn toward you. The whole median is drawn instead, as a flat rectangle. On the flat page, a box of no height becomes a single line in the same way.
The small dots beyond the whiskers are outliers, each drawn at the center of its cell. Interval and Box are the chapters for these two marks on the flat page.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.8 z_label(): naming the third axis
Those three marks all stood on the same two axes and measured along the third. Whatever stands in the cube, the third axis still needs a label. Each axis takes its label from the name of the column bound to it, and you can replace any of the three. Each position has its own label function, and z_label() is the third. Units are the usual reason to set all three at once:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) +
  x_label("Meters east") + y_label("Meters north") + z_label("Altitude (m)") +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + color(col.glider) +
  x_label("Meters east") + y_label("Meters north") + z_label("Altitude (m)") +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + x_label("Meters east") + y_label("Meters north") +
  z_label("Altitude (m)") + title("Two gliders, one thermal")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), x_label("Meters east"), y_label("Meters north"),
  z_label("Altitude (m)"), title("Two gliders, one thermal"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 Meters east Meters north Altitude (m)  Two gliders, one thermal  Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





Ask for a z_label() on a plot with no z and the label has no axis to name, so gog says so and draws the plot anyway. It is guidance rather than a refusal, because nothing else about the plot is wrong.
Path is the chapter for the mark itself; the same two gliders appear in the third-variable cookbook.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.9 What the cube refuses
Three sentences in this chapter have been refused already, each with a message that says why. What follows is what the cube itself will not do, and why. The first two are not refusals but fixed drawing orders, and the engine draws the plot without a message. The first concerns the guide box: the engine does not sort it by depth with the marks. The box is drawn behind the marks and its labels are drawn over them, whatever the angle. So an edge of the box never passes in front of a point, even where the edge is nearer to you. And no mark can cover the numbers that say what it measures, because a guide describes the scene rather than being part of it.
Turning the whole cube is cheap, and the engine does it every time you drag. Working out, piece by piece, which part of the box hides which point costs far more computing, and the renderer does not do it. That is a limit of the renderer, not a rule of the grammar, so the box stays behind the marks however far you turn the scene.
Layers keep a fixed order as well. The depth sort runs within a layer, and layers are painted in the order you wrote them, exactly as they are on the flat page. So a point cloud layered over a path sits in front of the whole route rather than passing through it. That is the ordinary layering rule applied in the cube, not a new exception, so read a layered 3-D plot as layers, not as one depth-sorted scene.
A tilt beyond 90 or -90 is refused, and a turn beyond a full circle is not. One of the two angles has an end and the other does not, and that is the whole reason:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + space(tilt = 95)


data(thermals) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + space(tilt = 95)


data(thermals) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  space(tilt = 95)


plot(data(thermals), point, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  space({ tilt: 95 }))




Error:
! gog: `space(tilt = 95)` is outside -90 to 90, which is where an elevation lives. At 90 the camera looks straight down at the floor and at -90 straight up from underneath; past either the scene turns over. Use `space(tilt = 90)` for the nearest view, or `space(turn = )` to swing around the plot instead — a bearing wraps and an elevation does not.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


tilt is how high your eye is, and there is a highest point. At 90 you are directly above the cube, and at -90 directly underneath. Going past either end would turn the scene upside down, and an upside-down cube shows nothing the sentence asked for. So dragging stops at both ends, and a written tilt must stay between them.
turn is which side you stand on, and it has no end. A full circle brings you back, so 390 is the same view as 30 and gog draws it without comment:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + space(turn = 390)


data(thermals) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + space(turn = 390)


data(thermals) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  space(turn = 390)


plot(data(thermals), point, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  space({ turn: 390 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude 





That is space(turn = 30) drawn a second time: 390 is 30 plus a full circle, so the two sentences produce exactly the same file. tilt has two ends and turn has none, so the two rules come from the angles themselves, not from a choice gog made.
When the cube does not draw a mark, there are three possible reasons, and the engine’s message says which one you have. It was decided against, or it is blocked, or it is simply not built. A blocked mark would need the renderer to work out, piece by piece, what hides what; a mark that is not built only lacks its own drawing code.
Some are decided. line, step, area and ribbon read a domain left to right. They sort by x and draw one value for each, which is what makes a line a function rather than a route. A cube has no left to right, so all four are refused there. The path section showed that refusal for line. It is a rule rather than a missing feature, and the refusal says so: the route through three dimensions is path, which is line with exactly that sort removed. On the page line and path differ by one rule: whether the rows are sorted by x. In the cube that one rule decides which of the two can be drawn at all.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.10 What the cube blocks
The second reason is blocked, and it is a different kind of refusal. A rule in a cube is a plane. It takes one position, as it does on a flat plot, and spans the other two axes. Here z(altitude) places the rule, so each row would be a horizontal plane at its own altitude, and the engine refuses the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + rule + z(altitude) + space()


data(thermals) + rule + z(col.altitude) + space()


data(thermals) + rule + z(:altitude) + space()


plot(data(thermals), rule, z(col.altitude), space())




Error:
! gog: `rule + z(altitude)` in a cube is a **plane**: it marks `altitude` on `z` and spans `x` and `y`. Marks in space are sorted by their footprint, and a plane's footprint runs across the whole floor, so it could only be drawn wholly in front of or wholly behind the data when its job is to cut through it. A plane in a cube is valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it: that would mean working out, piece by piece, what hides what. Draw the plot flat, where a rule is a line.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Marks in the cube are painted in order, from far to near. The engine places each solid, such as a bar, in that order by its footprint, the part of the floor it stands on. A horizontal plane spans the whole floor, so part of it is nearer to you than a given point and part is farther away. Drawn in one piece, it could only be entirely in front of the data or entirely behind it, but its purpose is to cut through the data. A zone in a cube is a slab, a plane with thickness, and it is refused for the same reason. Neither is drawn, because drawing one means working out, piece by piece, what hides what, and the engine does not do that.
The third reason is the simplest, and text is the example. A label at a third position is valid grammar, and no part of the grammar forbids it. The engine does not draw it, and says exactly that:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + text + x(petal_length) + y(sepal_length) + z(sepal_width) +
  label(species)


(data(iris_flowers) + text + x(col.petal_length) + y(col.sepal_length) + z(col.sepal_width) +
  label(col.species))


data(iris_flowers) + text + x(:petal_length) + y(:sepal_length) +
  z(:sepal_width) + label(:species)


plot(data(iris_flowers), text, x(col.petal_length), y(col.sepal_length),
  z(col.sepal_width), label(col.species))




Error:
! gog: `z` is valid grammar for `text`, but this engine does not draw it — `z(sepal_width)` would have no visual effect. Remove it, or use a channel that renders.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The third reason covers a scale as well. The z axis is linear, so a log z is refused, and the message says to use a log scale on x or y instead.
Every refusal above comes with a message that says why. Silence would be worse than a refusal, because a plot that quietly dropped a dimension would still look finished and would answer a question you never asked.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.11 Faceting: one cube per panel
A cube of 142 countries mixes five continents together. The question is how one continent’s cloud differs from another’s. A facet splits the rows into panels, and a panel is a rectangle. The cube is drawn inside a rectangle. So a faceted 3-D plot is one cube per panel, each projected into its own panel:

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + z(population) +
  color(continent) | facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + z(col.population) +
  color(col.continent) | facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + z(:population) +
  color(:continent) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  z(col.population), color(col.continent), across(col.continent))






                                                          50K 20K 80 70 50 1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population                                                        50K 20K 80 70 50 1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population                                                                              50K 20K 80 70 50 1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population                                                   50K 20K 80 70 50 1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population                            50K 20K 80 70 50 1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, z is population, color by continent, split into panel columns by continent.”
The scales are shared, exactly as they are on the flat page, so the five cubes share one set of axes, and a given height means the same population in every panel. Oceania holds two countries, so its cube is nearly empty, and that is the correct reading. The shared scale is what makes the difference visible.
The same split, on a route rather than a cloud:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) + color(glider) |
  facet(glider)


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) + color(col.glider) |
  facet(col.glider))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) | facet(:glider)


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), across(col.glider))






                                                                                                                                                                                                  200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude                                                                                                                                                                                                   200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude    Alpha  Bravo   Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





The guides are the one thing that needs explaining. Each cube draws its own tick numbers and its own three axis labels. A faceted flat plot writes each axis once, along an edge of the page. That is a rule rather than an oversight. A guide drawn on the panel’s boundary is drawn once, because the panels share that boundary. A guide drawn inside the panel appears in every panel, because there is no boundary to share it on. A faceted polar plot works the same way: each panel draws the category names around its own circle. A cube’s three axes are edges of the cube, and the cube sits inside the panel. A shared column of numbers beside the page would have nothing to point at. The tick reading -200 lands in a different place in every panel, because each panel projects from its own rectangle.
Each axis puts its numbers along one of the three darker edges. Which edges they are depends on the viewing angle, and the engine picks them by a rule. The cube has four edges parallel to each axis. Two of the four edges parallel to x lie on the floor, and x takes the one that is lower in the picture. y does the same with its own two floor edges. Seen from above, with a positive tilt, the lower edges are the ones nearest you. Seen from below, with a negative tilt, they are the ones farthest from you. From below, the floor edges nearest you cross the middle of the picture, so numbers on them would cover the data. In both views, the two numbered edges form a V shape at the bottom of the picture. z takes the vertical edge on the left side of the cube’s outline, the edges around the outside of the drawn cube. All three lie on that outline, so their numbers sit outside the cube, away from the marks. Surface shows the same rule: the surface fills most of the picture, and the z numbers still sit outside the surface.
Before any text is drawn, the engine checks the numbers and axis labels against each other for overlap. Where two would overlap, it moves one of them farther from the cube, or leaves it out. So numbers from two axes never overlap where their edges meet, and an axis label never covers its own numbers.
One case is left: an axis that is drawn very short. Raise the tilt and the measure axis is drawn shorter, until its numbers no longer fit. Here is the same summary at two tilts; the second is seen from almost straight above:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life) + space() +
    style(color = "#2a9d8f") +
    z_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The default view")) |
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(era) + z(life) +
      space(tilt = 85) + style(color = "#2a9d8f") +
      z_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Tilted up, with fewer numbers"))) +
  theme(height = 430)


(((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.era) + z(col.life) + space() +
    style(color = "#2a9d8f") +
    z_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The default view")) |
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.era) + z(col.life) +
      space(tilt = 85) + style(color = "#2a9d8f") +
      z_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("Tilted up, with fewer numbers"))) +
  theme(height = 430))


((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:era) + z(:life) +
  space() + style(color = "#2a9d8f") + z_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("The default view")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:era) + z(:life) +
  space(tilt = 85) + style(color = "#2a9d8f") +
  z_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Tilted up, with fewer numbers"))) + theme(height = 430)


beside(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.era),
  z(col.life), space(), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }),
  z_label("Mean life expectancy"), title("The default view")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.era),
  z(col.life), space({ tilt: 85 }), style({ color: "#2a9d8f" }),
  z_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Tilted up, with fewer numbers")), theme({ height: 430 }))






                                                         Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia 1957 2007 80 70 60 50 40 Continent Era Mean life expectancy  The default view


                                                       Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia 1957 2007 80 40 Continent Era Mean life expectancy  Tilted up, with fewer numbers






“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is era, z is life, beside the same tilted 85.”
The right-hand plot draws fewer numbers up its measure axis, and that is all it does about the crowding: it drops numbers and never changes the scale. A coarser tick step would also clear the crowding, and gog does not use it. The step decides where the axis stops, so a bigger step pushes the top of the axis above the tallest bar and leaves empty space above the bars. The numbers that remain are always a subset of the ones the left-hand plot shows. Each one sits at the same height in both, so a value read from either panel is the same value.
A second kind of split lays the panels out in time instead of across the page. play is that chapter, and it also shows the two kinds of split used together.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.12 In short
Binding z places a mark in the cube, and nothing else in the sentence changes. A transform cuts or groups by each position the mark does not measure along, so bin cuts two axes in the cube and one on the page. Only path draws a route through the cube: it follows the order of the rows, and an order belongs to no axis. Turning the plot changes how you look at it, never what it claims about the data.

title: 32  Space
text:
32.13 What comes next
A cube keeps the axes straight and adds one. Polar bends them instead: the same marks on the same data, with x running around a circle and y out from its center.

title: 33  Polar
text:
33.1 A circular variable on a straight axis
Which way does the wind blow most often? Some questions do not fit a flat page. Every plot so far has been drawn on one: an x running across, a y running up. That is one coordinate space, flat, and the kernel names six more. The flat space is also the wrong shape for a whole class of variables. Compass direction, the hour of the day, the month of the year: in each of them the last value is the neighbor of the first. A straight axis has no way to show that.
Two of the oldest statistical graphics were drawn in a circle instead, in the space gog calls polar. Playfair’s Statistical Breviary of 1801 cut a circle into sectors to show the Turkish empire’s territory, and that is the first pie chart (Playfair, 1801). Florence Nightingale’s 1858 diagram of what killed British soldiers in the Crimea (Nightingale, 1858) is a bar chart in polar coordinates. It has three names: a coxcomb, a rose, or, most precisely, a polar area diagram. That third name is the only one that says what the wedges mean. Her wedges put each month’s death rate into the wedge’s area, so their radius grows as the square root of the rate. In gog, a polar bar maps the value directly to the radius. Both are correct drawings, but they are not the same drawing, so check which one you have before you compare them. The section Nightingale’s rose, later in this chapter, draws a rose from her own numbers.
The line version has even more names: radar plot, spider plot, star plot, and Kiviat diagram in engineering. As with the rose and the pie, none of them is an atom. Each is a mark and a channel or two with polar() at the end, which is what the rest of this chapter is about.
How often the wind blew from each direction is a count per compass point, so start with the plot you know. It shows what a straight axis loses. Here are wind observations from two seasons, summer and winter, drawn as an ordinary bar chart with one bar per compass point:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction)


data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction)


data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction)


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction))






                                      N NE E SE S SW W NW   0 20 40 60  Count Direction
“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction.”
Read the two ends. North is at the far left and north-west at the far right, with the whole compass between them, although the two directions are 45 degrees apart in the world. The chart has cut the circle open and flattened it, and the cut is invisible: nothing in the picture says that the two ends belong together. A reader who did not already know the compass could not tell from this chart that north-west is next to north.
Now add one atom to the same sentence:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction) + polar()


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction), polar())






                            N NE E SE S SW W NW   20 40 60  Count Direction
“Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction, in polar.”
Same mark, same transform, same binding, same data. The only thing that changed is the space the plot is drawn in, and north-west is beside north because on the compass it is beside north. The west wind, which blew most often, is now a long wedge pointing west, rather than a tall bar you find by reading the labels.
This is what a coordinate space is for, and it is why a pie chart, a rose and a radar plot are not chart types in this grammar. They are marks you already know, read in a circle.

title: 33  Polar
section: 33.2 What polar() changes and what it keeps
text:
33.2 What polar() changes and what it keeps
One word changed the whole picture, so the next thing to settle is which of the two positions became the angle. x becomes the angle and y becomes the radius. That order is Wilkinson’s (Wilkinson, 2005). His reason is that the first position says where a mark stands, and in a circle that is an angle. The second says how much, and that becomes how far out from the center the mark reaches. (That is the rule when both positions are bound. Bind only one and there is nothing to choose, so the one you have becomes the angle: that is the pie, and it has its own section below.)
So x(direction) still says what it always said, that direction is the position each bar stands at. polar() changes one thing only: how positions are read. x now gives a direction around the circle, and y a distance from the center. A bar still runs from its baseline to its value. The baseline is the center of the circle, so the count sets how far out each wedge reaches.
The next question is whether the rest of the grammar still works in a circle: a split by season, for example, with the two seasons side by side. Nothing else in the grammar knows the space changed, so nothing else has to be rewritten for it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count * dodge + x(direction) + color(season) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count * dodge + x(col.direction) + color(col.season) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count * dodge + x(:direction) + color(:season) +
  polar()


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count, dodge), x(col.direction),
  color(col.season), polar())






                                    N NE E SE S SW W NW   10 20 30  Count Direction  Season    Summer  Winter 





“Given the winds: bars derived by count and dodge, x is direction, color by season, in polar.”
color splits the count by season, and dodge sets the two seasons’ bars side by side inside each slot instead of on top of each other. The legend decodes the colors. Every one of those works in a circle exactly as it works on a flat page, because none of them was ever written in terms of pixels.
Change dodge to stack and the seasons pile outward from the center instead, one season outside the other:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(winds) + bar * count * stack + x(direction) + color(season) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count * stack + x(col.direction) + color(col.season) + polar()


data(winds) + bar * count * stack + x(:direction) + color(:season) +
  polar()


plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count, stack), x(col.direction),
  color(col.season), polar())






                                    N NE E SE S SW W NW   20 40 60  Count Direction  Season    Summer  Winter 





“Given the winds: bars derived by count and stack, x is direction, color by season, in polar.”
Summer sits against the center and winter is stacked outside it, so each wedge now reaches the total of both seasons. West runs out to 63. In the dodged rose above, west stopped at 38, the longer of its two bars. The radial axis now reaches 63 rather than 38. That is why stack is a transform and not a drawing option: a transform runs before the scale is set, so the scale can read the totals stack adds up.
Read the pair together, because each hides what the other shows. Stacked, each wedge shows the total wind from its direction, and west is plainly the most common direction. Dodged, the seasons stand side by side, and you can see that the south-west wind comes mostly in summer (30 against 17), and the west wind mostly in winter (38 against 25). Neither is the correct rose. The rose is not a chart with its own options at all. It is bar, with its axis bent.
play also works in a circle, with no new atom. The animation chooses the rows for each frame, and polar() bends those rows into a circle, so neither step changes the other. The Play chapter’s “Frames in polar” animates a rose and two pies across half a century.

title: 33  Polar
text:
33.3 Where the circle starts
The angular axis begins at the top and runs clockwise, which is how a clock and a compass are both read. The middle of the first category’s slot sits at the top, not the edge of the slot. That is why north points straight up in the rose above: north is the first of the eight directions.
The day_cycle table holds one day of trips, hour by hour:



day_cycle: first 5 of 25 rows


hour
trips
