“Given the world borders: zones, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by country, color by continent, in the map space.”
Compare that with the earlier map that colored each continent. Apart from the title, only two things changed: path became zone, and group(piece) became group(country). A path traces one ring at a time, so it groups by ring. A zone fills a whole country, so it groups by country.

title: 35  Map
text:
35.10 Life expectancy on the map
Where in the world do people live longest? color accepts a quantity as well as a category, so the same sentence can shade each country by life expectancy. That column comes from a table you already know: gapminder_2007, the same 142 countries that the chapter A first plot draws.
Joining two tables is the host language’s job, not the grammar’s, so this chunk is shown in R only. In R the join is one call to match(), and each of the other languages has its own way to look up one table’s values in another. The plot sentence under the join is the same sentence in every language, spelled the way the tabs above spell it:

filled <- world_borders
filled$life <- gapminder_2007$life[match(filled$country,
                                         gapminder_2007$country)]
filled <- filled[!is.na(filled$life), ]

data(world_borders) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) +
  style(color = "#e6e6ec") +
  data(filled) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) + color(life) +
  map() + title("Life expectancy at birth, 2007")



                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°  Life expectancy at birth, 2007 Lat Lon  Life         82.6 62.34 42.08 





Two layers again. The first draws all 176 countries in pale gray, and the second colors the 120 whose names match() found in gapminder_2007. A name matches only when both tables spell it the same way. The outline says United States of America and gapminder_2007 says United States, so the United States stays gray, and so do 14 other countries whose names the two tables spell differently. Without the gray layer, the 56 unmatched countries would simply be absent, and a reader could not tell “no match” from “no country”.
Compare the map with the scatter plot in A first plot, which shows life expectancy against GDP per person, one point per country. The map shows that same life column. It answers a question the scatter cannot: where.

It stores the year twice: year is a number, and era is the same year as a label. A facet needs the label, because a facet column names its panels (Faceting).
The join works as in the section above, and is again shown in R only. Each year is joined to its own copy of the outline, and the table eras holds both copies. Its era column says which year each copy shows:

e57 <- gm_eras[gm_eras$era == "1957", ]
e07 <- gm_eras[gm_eras$era == "2007", ]
then <- world_borders
then$era <- "1957"
then$life <- e57$life[match(then$country, e57$country)]
now <- world_borders
now$era <- "2007"
now$life <- e07$life[match(now$country, e07$country)]
eras <- rbind(then, now)
eras <- eras[!is.na(eras$life), ]

data(world_borders) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) +
  style(color = "#e6e6ec") +
  data(eras) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) + color(life) +
  palette("viridis") + map() +
  title("Life expectancy at birth, 1957 and 2007") / facet(era)

gog: table `world_borders` has no column `era`, so its layer is drawn in every panel. If it should be split too, add `era` to that table.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   -50° 0° 50°                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     -100° 0° 100°   -50° 0° 50°    1957  2007  Life expectancy at birth, 1957 and 2007 Lat Lon  Life            82.6 56.47 30.33 





“Given the world borders: zones, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by country; then given the eras table: zones, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by country, colored by life, with the viridis palette, in the map space, split into panel rows by era.”
/ facet(era) stacks the two panels, one above the other. In the default projection a world map is about twice as wide as it is tall, so side by side each map would be about half as wide. Both panels share one color scale, and that is what makes them comparable: the same shade means the same life expectancy in 1957 and in 2007.
palette("viridis") colors the shortest life expectancy dark purple and the longest yellow. In the map above, dark meant the longest. Dark purple is clearly different from the pale gray of the unmatched countries, so a short life expectancy never looks like a missing value.
Most countries are greener or yellower in 2007 than in 1957. Counted from the table, life expectancy rose in 117 of the 120 colored countries, and the median rose from 48 years to 72. Life expectancy fell only in Lesotho, Zambia and Zimbabwe, all three in the south of Africa.
The gray layer appears in both panels. Its table, world_borders, has no era column, so gog draws that layer in every panel and says so in a message. A layer without the facet column explains the rule.

title: 35  Map
section: 35.12 Rings, and the country inside another country
text:
35.12 Rings, and the country inside another country
A zone groups by country, not by piece, so nothing in its sentence says where one ring ends. gog finds each ring by closure: a ring ends where it returns to the point it started from. Boundary data is written that way, so nothing extra has to be said.
Finding rings by closure is what lets a country contain a hole. Lesotho, one of the three countries above, lies entirely inside South Africa, and South Africa’s boundary has a second ring around Lesotho:

enclave <- world_borders[world_borders$country %in%
                           c("South Africa", "Lesotho"), ]
enclave$life <- gapminder_2007$life[match(enclave$country,
                                          gapminder_2007$country)]

data(enclave) + zone + x(lon) + y(lat) + group(country) + color(life) +
  map() + title("Lesotho is not painted on top of South Africa")



                          20° 25° 30°   -30° -25°  Lesotho is not painted on top of South Africa Lat Lon  Life         49.34 45.97 42.59 





Lesotho is a hole in South Africa, not a patch laid over it. The difference matters because the two countries have different values. A patch is right only when it is drawn after the region beneath it, and nothing in the sentence says which region is drawn first.
Real boundary data is not always written this carefully. If a ring in your data does not close, gog cannot tell where one ring ends and the next begins. It draws the region, warns you that the ring ends had to be guessed, and names what to fix.

title: 35  Map
section: 35.13 Counties: one country in finer detail
text:
35.13 Counties: one country in finer detail
Every map so far has given each country one value. One value hides how much the places inside a country differ. Each state of the United States is divided into areas called counties. A county’s poverty rate is the estimated percent of its people who live in poverty. In 2023 the median of the county rates was 13.6%. The lowest was 3.3%, and the highest was 49.6%, nearly half. A map of the counties shows where the high rates and the low rates are.
The us_counties table holds 3,109 counties: those of the 48 states between Canada and Mexico, plus the District of Columbia, which counts as one county. Alaska and Hawaii are left out. Many maps of the United States move them into small boxes beside the other states. In gog, a map draws every place at its own longitude and latitude. Alaska lies far to the northwest and Hawaii far to the southwest, so including them would make the 48 states much smaller.
The outlines and the rates both come from the US Census Bureau, for 2023. Like world_borders, the table has one row for each point of an outline, and piece names each ring. poverty holds each county’s rate, repeated on every row of its outline, so the map needs no join.
The sentence below is a choropleth, built like the map in Life expectancy on the map. group(county) says which rows make one county, and color(poverty) shades each county by its rate. Three more choices differ from that map. First, palette() names four colors, from seashell (almost white) to saddlebrown, so a county with a higher rate is drawn darker.
Second, preserve = "angle" draws the map with Mercator. The default, preserve = "area", draws only longitude 0, the line through Greenwich, as a straight vertical line. The other lines of longitude curve more the farther they lie from it. So the United States, at about 100 degrees west, would be drawn slanted. Mercator draws every line of longitude straight.
Third, theme(height = 470) sets the image’s height to 470 pixels, shorter than the default. A map keeps the proportions its projection gives it, so it never stretches to fill a tall image. Without the setting, empty space would be left above and below the map.

“Given the US counties: zones, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by county, color by poverty, with a palette of seashell, sandybrown, chocolate and saddlebrown, in the map space preserving angle.”
Mercator keeps the shape of every county, but not its size. It draws a county in South Dakota about 1.6 times as large as a county of the same area in south Texas. That is why preserve = "area" is the default, as Choosing a projection explains. So compare the counties on this map by their colors, not by how much of the map each dark region covers.
The darkest counties form three regions: along the lower Mississippi River, in the mountains of eastern Kentucky, and in South Dakota. Issaquena County, in the state of Mississippi beside the river, had the highest rate of all, 49.6%. Across the river, East Carroll Parish in Louisiana had 46.5%. Louisiana calls its counties parishes. In eastern Kentucky, Martin County had 48.1%. South Texas is lighter than these three regions. Along the border with Mexico, the six counties from Maverick County southeast to Cameron County had between 22% and 31%. That is still higher than nine counties in ten.
In South Dakota, the darkest counties lie on reservations, areas of land reserved for Native American nations. Ziebach County had 46.2%, and Oglala Lakota County had 37.1%. South Dakota also had the lowest rate of all: 3.3% in Lincoln County, which holds the southern part of the city of Sioux Falls. A map with one color for each state would give all of South Dakota one color. It would show neither Ziebach County’s rate nor Lincoln County’s.

35.14 One state over three elections
The poverty map above shows one year. To compare the same places from one election to the next, draw one map for each election, side by side: a map can be split into panels like any other plot. The ohio_turnout table holds Ohio’s 88 counties three times, once for each presidential election: 2016, 2020 and 2024. As in us_counties, each row is one point of a county’s outline, and the election column says which election the row belongs to.
A county’s turnout is the percent of its citizens aged 18 or over who voted. The number who voted is the count each county reported to the US Election Assistance Commission. The number of citizens is the Census Bureau’s estimate.

“Given the Ohio turnout: zones, x is lon without an axis, y is lat without an axis, grouped by county, color by turnout, with the viridis palette, in the map space preserving angle, split into panel columns by election.”
Counted from the table, turnout was highest in 2020 in 68 of the 88 counties. The median of the county turnouts was 62% in 2016, 66% in 2020 and 64% in 2024. The counties kept nearly the same order: a county with a high turnout in one election had a high turnout in the other two. Delaware County, the brightest county, was the highest in all three elections, with 88% in 2020. It lies in the middle of the state, just north of Columbus, the state capital. Holmes County, the darkest county, lies east of Delaware County. It was the lowest in all three, at 40% to 44%. Many of its people are Amish, members of a Christian group who mostly do not vote. They are counted among the citizens, but most of them are not among the people who voted.
The number of citizens is an average over the five years that end in the election year. In a county that grew quickly, such as Delaware County, that average is smaller than the number on election day. So the percent is a little too high.

title: 35  Map
text:
35.15 What comes next
A map flattens the sphere so a page can hold it. The next chapter, Globe, draws every mark from this chapter on the sphere itself: the same marks at the same places, seen from one side.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.1 The view
What does the data look like on the earth itself? The map chapter flattened the sphere to fit a page. This chapter keeps the sphere round, and turns it toward you.
quakes_fiji holds a thousand earthquakes recorded near Fiji, one row for each. Here is the map chapter’s first sentence, which draws them, and beside it the same sentence with globe() in place of map(), turned to face Fiji:
“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, in the map space, beside the same on the globe.”
x is longitude and y is latitude, exactly as on the map. What changed is how the two numbers become a position on the page. Each point now stands at its place on the sphere. A sphere seen from one side is a disk, and that disk is what the plot draws.
A globe shows one half of the earth, so the choice of half matters. turn and tilt name the place the view faces, and they are the same two arguments space() takes. turn is the longitude at the center of the disk, and tilt is the latitude. The chapter’s first plot faces Fiji. Leave both out and the view faces longitude zero and latitude zero, where the equator crosses the prime meridian.
turn is a longitude, so 190 and -170 name the same view: 190 degrees east is 170 degrees west. tilt is a latitude, so it runs from -90 to 90 and no further.
In the web edition the angle you write is only the view the globe opens at. Drag it and it turns, the way the cube in Space turns, and the far half of the earth comes into view. The reset button returns to the view the sentence asked for. In the PDF a plot keeps its one view, which is why this chapter also draws some data at a second angle.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.3 The graticule
Every globe so far has drawn a grid of thin gray lines over the sphere. It is the graticule, this space’s gridlines. Its meridians run from pole to pole, one every thirty degrees of longitude, and its parallels circle the earth, one every thirty degrees of latitude. A flat panel draws its gridlines straight. A globe bends its gridlines onto the sphere, the way the polar space bends them into rings and spokes.
There are no axes beside the disk, because a sphere has no straight side to write one along. The graticule is the reference instead. theme(grid = ) works on it as on any other grid: "x" keeps only the meridians, "y" keeps only the parallels, and "none" removes it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18) + theme(grid = "none") +
  title("No graticule")


(data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18) + theme(grid = "none") +
  title("No graticule"))


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18) + theme(grid = "none") +
  title("No graticule")


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  globe({ turn: 178, tilt: -18 }), theme({ grid: "none" }),
  title("No graticule"))

title: 36  Globe
section: 36.8 Thousands of storm tracks on a dark globe
text:
36.8 Thousands of storm tracks on a dark globe
The routes earlier in this chapter were a few arcs between cities. A table of real records can hold thousands of lines, and then the lines are hard to tell apart. Thin lines drawn over one another on a pale sphere merge into one gray mass, and the lines inside it can no longer be followed.
cyclones is a table of that size. It holds all 2,174 storms from 1980 to 2025 that reached hurricane strength, a wind of at least 64 knots (119 kilometers per hour). The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) keeps the record. Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are one kind of storm, with a different name in each ocean. Scientists call all three tropical cyclones, which gives the table its name.
Each row is one storm’s position at one moment, and a storm’s positions joined in order are its track. The positions are twelve hours apart. They cover only the time when the storm’s wind was at least 34 knots, or 63 kilometers per hour. At that speed a storm is given a name. category is the storm’s highest category on the Saffir-Simpson scale, which ranks a storm from 1 to 5 by its strongest wind. It holds one value for each storm, in three bands: “1 or 2”, “3 or 4” and “5”. The month column is not used in this chapter. The Play chapter uses it to show the same storms one calendar month at a time.

In the north, most tracks run west, and many then bend to the north and east. In the south, many bend to the south and east. The band along the equator stays empty: no position lies closer to it than 0.7 degrees, and only 33 of the 29,669 positions lie within 5 degrees of it.
The gold tracks lie on top because of the table’s order, not because of their color. gog draws the storms in the order the table lists them, and a track drawn later covers the tracks drawn before it. The table lists the category 5 storms last. Reverse the rows, and the gold tracks go to the bottom, under all the others.

“Given the world borders: paths, x is lon, y is lat, grouped by piece; then given the population spikes: bars, x is lon, y is lat, z is reach, colored by continent, on the globe.”
Look at the edge of the disk. The sphere itself can hide part of a spike. A spike just behind that edge has its base hidden, so only the part that rises past the edge is drawn. A spike too short to rise past that edge is not drawn at all. At the edge you see a spike from the side, along its whole length. A spike that points straight at you is seen from its tip, so it looks shorter than it is. In the web edition, turn the globe to see such a spike from the side.
Finding each country’s center and joining its population are the host language’s job, like the join for the cities above. Choosing how to scale the measure belongs there too. The square root keeps China’s spike from making every other spike too small to see. A scale keeps an axis in the column’s own units, and a globe draws no axis, so the globe refuses scale = on z().

title: 36  Globe
section: 36.10 The depth goes to the cube
text:
36.10 The depth goes to the cube
The Fiji earthquakes from the chapter’s first plot carry a third number: elevation, their depth below the surface, written as a negative number. That number is not a height to raise above the surface. It is a third coordinate of the place itself, and on the globe z belongs to bar alone. So gog refuses the sentence below rather than guessing at it. The refusal names three things you can do instead: add a bar layer, drop z(), or draw the same table in the cube.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18)


(data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  globe(turn = 178, tilt = -18))

data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  color(:slab) + space(turn = 130, tilt = 25) +
  title("The same earthquakes, read by depth")

  z(col.elevation), color(col.slab), space({ turn: 130, tilt: 25 }),
  title("The same earthquakes, read by depth"))

“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by slab.”
slab names the depth band each earthquake falls in. The globe plots looked straight down on these earthquakes, so a deep one and a shallow one were drawn at almost the same place. In the cube, depth is a third position, so they separate. Most of them lie along one sloping sheet: the ocean floor, sinking into the earth. Drag this one too. The drag that turns the earth on a globe turns the cloud of points in the cube.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.11 What a globe refuses
The map and the globe draw the same places as two pictures. The map flattens the sphere so a reader sees all of it at once. The globe keeps the sphere and hides the far half. To go from one picture to the other, you change one word.
The globe takes the map’s marks and one more: bar, which measures along the radius. It refuses the rest for the same reason the map does. Suppose you try a line through the earthquakes, as you would on a flat page. Both positions carry the place, exactly as on the map, and only bar reads the radius. So a line has no axis to measure along:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + line + x(east) + y(north) + globe()


data(quakes_fiji) + line + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + globe()


data(quakes_fiji) + line + x(:east) + y(:north) + globe()


plot(data(quakes_fiji), line, x(col.east), y(col.north), globe())




Error:
! gog: `line` measures along an axis, and a `globe()` plot has none to spare — longitude and latitude use both. Drop `globe()` to draw `line` flat, or use `point`, `bar`, `text`, `path`, `rule`, or `zone`. To carry a quantity on the globe, put it on a channel instead of an axis: `point + size(<column>)` sizes each place by it, and `color(<column>)` shades it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The refusal’s advice is to put a quantity on a channel instead, size or color. On a globe a quantity can also be a spike’s length along the radius, as in the population spikes earlier in this chapter.
A latitude past a pole names no place, so a view cannot face that latitude:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + globe(tilt = 100)


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + globe(tilt = 100)


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + globe(tilt = 100)


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  globe({ tilt: 100 }))




Error:
! gog: `globe(tilt = 100)` is outside -90 to 90, which is where a latitude lives. At 90 the view faces straight down on the north pole and at -90 on the south; there is no place past either. Use `globe(tilt = 90)` for the nearest view, or `globe(turn = )` to swing around the earth instead — a longitude wraps and a latitude does not.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And a globe draws no axes at all. So gog refuses an axis label rather than accepting it and drawing nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + globe() + x_label("Longitude")


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + globe() + x_label("Longitude")


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + globe() +
  x_label("Longitude")

  x_label("Longitude"))




Error:
! gog: an axis label names an axis, and a `globe()` plot draws none — a sphere has no straight side to write one along, and the graticule is the reference instead. Drop it; `title()` still names the plot.

title: 36  Globe
text:
36.12 What comes next
A globe can draw a row only at the place its two numbers name. Network draws tables whose rows name no place, only a connection between two nodes, and the engine computes a position for every node.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.1 One row is one edge
What is connected to what? Some tables record relations rather than measurements: each row says that one thing is related to another. A network diagram draws those relations. Each thing becomes a node, one marked place in the picture, and each relation becomes an edge, a stroke between two nodes.
Nothing in such a table says where any node should sit. Choosing those positions is the problem, and this chapter shows how gog solves it. The engine computes a position for every node. A space named network() draws the result, with no axes at all.
trade_partners holds one row per trade relation: who exports, who imports, and the value of the goods, in billions of dollars, rounded:
The first question this table raises is who trades with whom. One stroke per row answers exactly that. Write the edge mark derived by layout(), give it the from column first and the to column second, and add the space:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network())
“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network.”
Each row of the table becomes one stroke. Five pairs of countries trade in both directions, and each pair’s two strokes lie on one line. So you can see only 17 separate strokes for the 22 rows. The layout reads both columns and makes one node for each distinct name. The engine then pushes every node away from every other node, and pulls the two nodes of each row toward each other. Two countries that trade therefore sit near each other. The positions are computed by the engine that all four languages share, never by the language you write in. So this sentence draws the same picture in R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, and the four image files are identical.
The panel has no axes, no ticks and no grid, because network() draws none. A layout’s positions mean nothing as quantities. Flip the picture left to right and it means the same, so a number on an axis would state nothing about the data. gog therefore draws a layout only inside network(), and refuses it in every other space.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.2 The nodes and their names
The strokes alone do not say which node is which country, or which countries have the most trade relations. Two more layers finish the diagram. A point layer draws the nodes, and a text layer names them. Each one carries the same layout, and the engine computes it once per layer. The layout uses no random numbers, so all three layers get the same positions. That is why every dot sits exactly where its strokes end.
The layout also computes two columns for the nodes: name, and degree, the number of rows the node appears in. A pair that trades both ways counts twice, so China, which trades with 7 countries, has a degree of 9. size(degree) then draws a node larger when it appears in more rows. The text layer also composes repel, the collision modifier that moves each label off the dots and off the other labels. So a name sits just outside its dot instead of covering it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("Who trades with whom")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("Who trades with whom"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  point * layout(:exporter, :importer) + size(:degree) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel + label(:name) + network() +
  title("Who trades with whom")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("Who trades with whom"))






                                             China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  Who trades with whom  Degree    1  5  9 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
China, the United States and Germany have the largest dots, and they sit near the middle. No row of the table says that these three have the most trade relations. The layout found them by counting each country’s rows.

title: 37  Network
section: 37.3 An edge carries its own columns
text:
37.3 An edge carries its own columns
Every stroke so far is drawn alike, whether the trade is 500 billion dollars or 50 billion. Each edge is drawn from one row, so its color, its dash and its opacity can come from that row’s own columns. color and pattern need a categorical column, and opacity needs a continuous one. opacity(billions) maps each stroke’s opacity to that row’s billions, so a larger trade draws a darker stroke. A pair that trades both ways is two strokes on one line, so it looks darker than either row alone:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  size(:degree) + text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel +
  label(:name) + network() + title("More trade, darker stroke")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network(), title("More trade, darker stroke"))






                                             China United States Mexico Canada Japan Korea Germany France Poland Netherlands Vietnam Australia Brazil India Spain  More trade, darker stroke  Degree    1  5  9   Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer and repel, label by name, in the network.”
A node is different. It stands for every row it appears in, and those rows can hold different values. So the point and text layers map only name and degree, and gog refuses any other column there. Every other column belongs on the edge layer, where one row carries one value.

title: 37  Network
section: 37.4 An angle asks for the cube
text:
37.4 An angle asks for the cube
Every picture so far is flat. A plane gives the layout two directions for placing its nodes. A cube gives it three, and a cube can be turned. A crowded network has more room in three directions, and turning the cube shows which strokes pass in front of the others. Bare network() computes the layout in the plane. State a viewing angle and the same edges are laid out in a cube instead. Every node takes a new position, and the picture is drawn from the angle you asked for. This engine does not draw names in the cube, so the sentence below has no text layer:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + size(degree) +
  network(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, given depth")


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + opacity(col.billions) +
  point * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + size(col.degree) +
  network(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, given depth"))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  opacity(:billions) + point * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  size(:degree) + network(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
  title("The same network, given depth")


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), opacity(col.billions),
  layer(point, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), size(col.degree),
  network({ turn: 35, tilt: 20 }), title("The same network, given depth"))






                                                               The same network, given depth  Degree    1  5  9   Billions    50  275  500 





“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, sized by degree, in the network, turned 35, tilted 20.”
Nothing in the table gives a node a third position, so there is nothing to bind to z. The third dimension belongs to the space, exactly as the viewing angle does. The box outlines the cube, so you can see how it is turned. It has no numbers along its edges, because a layout’s positions are not measurements. The flat form has no axes for the same reason.
In the web edition the cube turns with a drag, the way the cube in Space turns. The reset button returns it to the angle the sentence asked for. In the PDF it keeps the view it was given.
A text layer in the cube is valid grammar that this engine does not draw. The refusal says so, and it suggests the flat form for the labels:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) * repel + label(name) +
  network(turn = 35, tilt = 20)


(data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) * repel + label(col.name) +
  network(turn = 35, tilt = 20))


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) * repel + label(:name) +
  network(turn = 35, tilt = 20)


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer), repel), label(col.name),
  network({ turn: 35, tilt: 20 }))




Error:
! gog: names in the network's cube are valid grammar, but this engine does not draw them. Drop the `text` layer, or drop the viewing angle and label the flat form.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.5 What the network refuses
That refusal is about something this engine does not draw. The four refusals in this section are different: each one is a mistake in the sentence. The most likely mistake is to leave network() off, because most plots need no space at all. Without it the plot would draw axes under the layout, and the numbers along them would mean nothing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer)


data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer)


plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)))




Error:
! gog: a `layout`'s positions are the graph's, not the data's — an axis under them would number something no reader can mean. Draw it in the network: `+ network()` flat, or `+ network(turn = 30, tilt = 25)` for the cube.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Only three marks read a layout. Write any other mark and the refusal names all three:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + bar * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + bar * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


data(trade_partners) + bar * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners), layer(bar, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  network())




Error:
! gog: `layout` places a graph — a position per node, computed from an edge table — and `bar` has no reading for that. Three marks do: `edge * layout(<from>, <to>)` draws the connections, `point * layout(...)` the nodes, and `text * layout(...) + label(name)` names them, all inside `network()`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The layout has already placed every node, so x() has nothing left to set:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + x(billions) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


(data(trade_partners) + x(col.billions) +
  edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network())


data(trade_partners) + x(:billions) +
  edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


plot(data(trade_partners), x(col.billions),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), network())




Error:
! gog: under `layout` the nodes place themselves, so `x(...)` has nothing left to say. Remove it — the third dimension, when you want it, is the space's: `network(turn = 30, tilt = 25)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And network() with no layout has nothing to place, so it refuses:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(trade_partners) + point + network()


data(trade_partners) + point + network()


data(trade_partners) + point + network()


plot(data(trade_partners), point, network())




Error:
! gog: `network()` draws what a `layout` places, and nothing here carries one. Compose the syllable: `edge * layout(from, to) + network()`, with `point * layout(...)` for the nodes and `text * layout(...) + label(name)` for their names.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.6 Where the limits are
A sentence can be right, and the table can still hold rows a layout cannot use. A row from a node to itself is refused, because such a stroke would have no length. The first row of this small table goes from China to China:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


self_trade <- data.frame(exporter = c("China", "Mexico"),
                         importer = c("China", "United States"),
                         billions = c(500, 455))
data(self_trade) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()


self_trade = {
  "exporter": ["China", "Mexico"],
  "importer": ["China", "United States"],
  "billions": [500, 455],
}
data(self_trade) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + network()


self_trade = (
  exporter = ["China", "Mexico"],
  importer = ["China", "United States"],
  billions = [500, 455],
)
data(self_trade) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) + network()


const self_trade = {
  exporter: ["China", "Mexico"],
  importer: ["China", "United States"],
  billions: [500, 455],
};
plot(data(self_trade), layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  network())




Error:
! gog: 1 row(s) of `self_trade` connect a node to itself, and a stroke from a point to the same point has no extent. Remove those rows in the host language: an edge joins two different nodes.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Remove the rows that connect a node to itself before you draw the plot. A row with a missing value in the from or the to column is not refused: it draws no stroke, and a message says how many rows were left out.
You may know more about each country than the edges say, such as its continent. gog does not read a second table describing the nodes, so a node shows only what the edges give it: its name and its degree. You can still show such a fact, but only on the edges. Before you draw the plot, join it onto each row in the host language, as a column such as the exporter’s continent. Then map that column on the edge layer.
You may want to drag a rectangle over part of the picture and select what it covers. A brush is refused. A brush selects a range of values on the plot’s axes, and a network has no axes. The fix is again in your table: add a column that marks the rows you want, and map it with color() on the edge layer.
If your table also has a year column, you may want to show how trade changes. For most plots, play does that: it draws one frame per year and shows the frames in order. In a network, play is valid grammar that this engine does not draw, like names in the cube.
Instead, split the plot by year with | facet(year), which draws one panel per year. All panels share one layout, so a country sits in the same place in every panel where it appears. Each panel draws only the edges from its own rows. An edge missing from a later panel is a trade relation that ended.

title: 37  Network
text:
37.7 What comes next
A network draws one table at one moment. The section above suggested panels for comparing years, because this engine does not play a network. Most other plots can be played. Play adds time to a plot: it cuts the plot into frames and runs them in order, so the reader watches the picture change.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.1 The same sentence, as panels
How did the whole picture change from year to year? play cuts the plot into frames, one picture for each value of a column, and shows them in sequence. It is faceting read in time. A facet splits the rows by a column’s distinct values and lays the pieces out across the page; play splits them exactly the same way and lays them out in time, one after another.
“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, played by year.”
Twelve frames, one per year in the data, running from 1952 to 2007. The strip above the panel names the one you are looking at.
A sequence is not the only way to show the years. Panels show them too, and the choice between the two is easiest to judge over the same rows. play and facet split the rows in the same way, so here the sentence changes only at its end: | facet(period) becomes + play(period). The years become a category first: facet names its panels and needs one, while play would take the number as a number.
gm_four <- gm_all[gm_all$year %in% c(1952, 1972, 1992, 2007), ]
gm_four$period <- factor(gm_four$year)
data(gm_four) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + color(continent) |
  facet(period)



                                                                                                                                                                        1K 10K 100K   40 60 80                                                                                                                                                                      1K 10K 100K                                                                                                                                                                        1K 10K 100K                                                                                                                                                                        1K 10K 100K      1952  1972  1992  2007  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given four of the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, split into panel columns by period.”
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_four) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + color(continent) +
  play(period)


(data(gm_four) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  play(col.period))


data(gm_four) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + play(:period)


plot(data(gm_four), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), play(col.period))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    1K 10K 100K   40 60 80     1952    1972    1992    2007    Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
Four panels, then four frames, over identical rows. The grid is better for comparing two moments carefully, because both are in front of you and your eye can move between them freely. The sequence is better for seeing movement, because you watch a point move right and up instead of finding the same point twice in two panels. The two are not different plots. They are one plot read two ways, which is why one grammar draws both, with one column bound differently.
In the PDF, only the first frame is drawn: 1952, with its strip. There, the faceted version above is what a reader sees instead of the motion.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.2 The column’s order
play and facet split the rows the same way, so you might expect the same columns to suit both. The same columns do not suit both. The test for playing a column is not its type. It is whether the column has an order.
A facet lays its panels out across the page, and you can read a page in any order you like. Your eye goes to any panel you choose, then comes back. A sequence lays its pieces out in time, and time arrives in one order only. So a sequence claims something a grid never claims: this frame comes after that one.
Bind a column with no order, and the plot shows movement the data does not have:

gog: `play(continent)` has no stated order, so each frame is a snapshot of one `continent` and the frames run in the order the rows arrive: Asia, Europe, Africa, Americas, Oceania. A sequence claims that one frame comes after another. Declare the column's levels in the table (a factor in R, `ordered()` in Python, Julia and JavaScript), or use `facet(continent)`, which claims no order.




                                                                                                                                                                                                 1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80     Asia    Europe    Africa    Americas    Oceania    Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





Watch the strip: Asia, Europe, Africa, Americas, Oceania. That order is not alphabetical, and it is not geographic. It is the order the continents first appear in the table, because the rows are sorted by country and Afghanistan comes before Albania. The sequence is showing you how a file was sorted. The points jump between frames, and none of the jumps mean anything.
gog draws the plot anyway, because nothing about the sentence is malformed and you may have meant that order. The message above the plot names the order it had to choose, and two answers: declare the column’s levels, or facet instead. Give the column its levels and the frames follow them. Bind facet(continent) instead and the panels claim no order at all.
Channels describes the opposite mistake. There the data had an order the hues could not carry; here the frames carry an order the data does not have, so a reader looks for a pattern that was never there.
A column does not have to hold numbers to be ordered. A year is ordered, and so is a date. So is a categorical column whose levels you declared: months in calendar order, or a rating from low to high. gog runs the frames in the order the levels declare, the same order it uses on an axis (Data). A categorical column with no declared levels takes the order its values first appear in, which is the mistake the plot above showed.
Having an order is not on its own a reason to play a column. A sequence should move only when its frames hold the same things in different states. Then a reader can follow one of those things across the frames. The four frames above are that case: the same countries at four dates, and the cloud climbs. The five continent frames above are not that case: each holds different countries, so nothing moves between them. The reader waits, and then has to remember what a facet would have shown at once. This needs saying plainly, because animation is the choice most people want to make.
How many values there are is a separate question, and the next section answers it. The gapminder years give twelve frames, and the glider flight in the next section gives 170. Both are worth animating, because in both the same things change from frame to frame. A long sequence takes more of the reader’s time without being harder to understand, and speed is there for that.

title: 38  Play
section: 38.3 Too many panels for one page
text:
38.3 Too many panels for one page
Whether a column has an order decides whether it should be played. How many values it has decides something else: whether a facet of it is still readable. A facet has to fit every piece on one page. A sequence shows them one at a time, so nothing limits how many it holds.
A facet’s limit is the point where its panels stop being readable. They share one page, so every panel added makes every panel smaller. wrap folds a long line into a rectangle, which makes each panel wider and shorter (Faceting). The rectangle is still one page.
Here are the two gliders from the cube, with one panel for each sample of the flight, taken every two seconds:

thermal_moments$moment <- factor(thermal_moments$second)
data(thermal_moments) + point + x(east) + y(north) + color(glider) |
  facet(moment, wrap = 13)

gog drew both of those sentences. It refuses neither, and it never will. A plot is refused for not being well formed, never for being a poor idea (Design laws). Which of the two says more about gliders is your judgment, not the engine’s. What the engine does instead is name the one cost it can measure. The message above counts the frames and reports how long one loop takes. It offers two answers: speed, or a column with fewer values.
Choose between the facet and the sequence before anyone else sees the plot. A reader needs one glance to see that a facet was the wrong choice. A sequence has to be watched for as long as the loop runs. If it then shows nothing new, the reader has waited for nothing.
The choice is easiest to see when the number of pieces is large. Imagine a year of hourly temperatures for New York, drawn as one curve for each day. As a facet that is 365 panels, and no fold leaves a curve large enough to read. As a sequence it is 365 frames, and a reader watches a year of weather pass. Below about ten pieces the panels usually read better, and Faceting shows ten of them wrapped and readable. Well above that the panels stop being readable, as the 170 glider panels did, and a sequence is the picture that still works.
A sequence can hold more pieces, and that alone does not make it the better picture. It loses the thing a facet does best: two pieces side by side, where a reader compares them instead of remembering them.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.4 What every frame shares
When a plot is cut into frames, can one frame still be compared with the next? Every scale, the color palette and every legend are fitted across the whole sequence at once, never per frame. That shared fitting is what makes a sequence worth trusting, and the fastest way to see why is to imagine a plot without it. If each frame fitted its own axis, 1952’s poorest countries and 2007’s would both sit at the left edge. A world whose incomes tripled would draw as a world standing still. The only thing actually moving would be the axis, silently, with nothing on the page to say so. So free, which fits a scale to each panel, is refused on a played plot, as Faceting shows.
Because the frames share their scales, movement on the page is movement in the data. In the gapminder sequence this chapter opened with, the cloud genuinely moves right and up, and a country whose point stays in place had no change in income or life expectancy.
The color palette is shared for a second reason. A reader follows a point by its color, so a palette that changed partway through would take away the one thing they are following. Every continent keeps its color in every frame, including frames where it happens to have no rows.
The statistics are not shared. A transform sees each frame’s rows as if they were the whole table, exactly as it sees a facet panel’s rows. That is the No Exceptions law, applied to frames:

gm_past60 <- gm_all[gm_all$life > 60, ]
data(gm_past60) + bar * count + x(continent) + play(year)



                                                                                                                                               Americas Oceania Europe Asia Africa   0 10 20 30     1952    1957    1962    1967    1972    1977    1982    1987    1992    1997    2002    2007    Count Continent





“Given the gapminder past 60 table: bars derived by count, x is continent, played by year.”
Each bar is that year’s tally of the countries that had passed sixty years of life expectancy. Asia climbs from four to thirty, Africa opens with none and ends with twelve, and Europe starts at twenty-three and then runs out of countries to add.
A tally can also be the same in every frame. Then bars that stay still are a correct result, not a mistake:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * count + x(continent) + play(year)


data(gm_all) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + play(col.year)


data(gm_all) + bar * count + x(:continent) + play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent), play(col.year))






                                                                                                                                               Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40     1952    1957    1962    1967    1972    1977    1982    1987    1992    1997    2002    2007    Count Continent





Twelve frames run and not a bar moves. The statistic is recomputed in every frame, and every frame gets the same number. The gapminder table holds the same 142 countries in every year, so each frame counts the same countries. Only the strip changes, and bars that stay still under a changing strip report that the count did not change. The plot above this one filters the rows first, and that is what turns a count of countries into a count of countries whose life expectancy passed sixty.
What the frames do share is the cut, when there is one. A bin’s edges are positions on the axis, and the axis is shared. One set of bins is cut from every frame’s rows at once, and each frame then counts only its own rows into those bins. Faceting explains why, and the rule is the same with “panel” read as “frame”.

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin, x is life, played by year.”
The distribution moves right across half a century. Every frame uses the same bins, and that is what makes the movement readable.
A density shares one thing across the frames too: its bandwidth, which sets how smooth the curve is. It is the average of the bandwidths each frame’s rows would get alone. A change in the curve’s shape from frame to frame therefore comes from the data and not from the smoothing.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.5 A layer with no frames
So far every layer in a plot has been cut into the same frames. A layer does not have to be. play is a channel, so it obeys the ordinary scope rule: written before any mark it reaches every layer, and written after one it binds that layer alone. A layer that never names it is drawn whole in every frame, which is how a fixed reference sits behind something that moves.

One detail of the second table changes the number of frames, but not what the plot shows. thermal_marks calls its time column instant where thermals calls the same measurement second. text:
38.6 How fast
Two sequences in this chapter have already carried speed = 3. A slow loop makes a reader wait for a pattern they have already seen. speed is a multiple of the normal pace, which shows a frame for 0.8 seconds. It is written inside the binding, the way scale and limits are written inside theirs, because it belongs to play and to nothing else:

  play(col.year, speed = 3))

  color(:continent) + play(:year, speed = 3)

These are the same twelve frames the chapter opened with, running three times as fast. speed = 0.5 would run them at half pace. speed exists for long sequences. The length of a loop is a default you did not choose, and the sentence does not show it. So when a sequence runs past thirty frames at the normal pace, gog reports how many seconds one loop takes.
When the played column holds numbers or dates, gog shows each frame for a time in proportion to the gap between its value and the next. Each sequence is timed against its own gaps: a frame whose gap is the middle one, when the gaps are put in order, shows for the normal 0.8 seconds. The gapminder years are all five years apart, so their frames all show for the same time. Here are the four years drawn as panels earlier, played by the number year instead of the category period:

Twenty years separate 1952 from 1972 and 1972 from 1992, so 1952 and 1972 show for 0.8 seconds. Only fifteen separate 1992 from 2007, so 1992 shows for 0.6. The last frame has no next value and shows for 0.8. Categories have an order but no distance between them, so the earlier play(period) shows every frame for the same time. A frame shows for at most four times the normal 0.8 seconds, so one long gap cannot make the sequence seem to stop. It shows for at least a quarter of 0.8 seconds, however short its gap.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.9 Frames in the cube
The gapminder cloud has a third measurement, population, and the whole cloud moves through the years. play does not depend on a flat plot. A frame is a subset of the rows, and the third position is a way of looking at whatever rows you have, so the two compose, and neither needed anything added for the other:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + z(population) +
  color(continent) + play(year)


(data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + z(col.population) +
  color(col.continent) + play(col.year))


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  z(:population) + color(:continent) + play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  z(col.population), color(col.continent), play(col.year))

1000M 500M 0 Gdp Life Population     1952    1957    1962    1967    1972    1977    1982    1987    1992    1997    2002    2007     Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, z is population, color by continent, played by year.”
Three of the kernel’s ideas meet in that sentence: the third position, the frames, and the selection. None of them was designed around the others, so they combine with no new rule. The sentence above uses two of them, and Selection adds the third to the same sentence.
The cube is fitted once across the whole sequence, exactly as a flat plot’s axes are. A box that resized itself per frame would move its own corners while the cloud stayed where it was, and every apparent motion would belong to the guide rather than to the countries. Fitted once, the height axis has room for 2007’s China from the first frame onward. That is why 1952 opens with the cloud pressed low and only China and India far above the floor.
A transform inside the cube is the same transform. The floor is cut once from every frame’s rows and each frame then counts only its own into the cells, which is this chapter’s shared-cut rule read with a second axis present:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(life) + y(continent) + color(continent) +
  palette("okabe") + space() + play(year)


(data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) + color(col.continent) +
  palette("okabe") + space() + play(col.year))


data(gm_all) + bar * bin(12) + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  color(:continent) + palette("okabe") + space() + play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin(12)), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  color(col.continent), palette("okabe"), space(), play(col.year))

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 12, x is life, y is continent, color by continent, with the okabe palette, in the cube, played by year.”
Follow one continent’s row of bars rather than the whole floor. Each pile slides toward longer lives as the sequence runs, and it slides against cells that never move, so what you are watching is the countries changing which cell they fall in. color(continent) names the same column the y axis does, and it is there so that following one row is possible at all. A floor axis in a cube runs diagonally into the picture. Finding a row along that axis means tracing a receding edge while five rows of bars block the view. The legend names the row at once; the axis makes you trace it.
The sentence sets the palette by hand, and the cube is the reason for choosing the okabe set. A solid in space is shaded per face, so one category is already three tones before any two categories are compared. Shading has therefore narrowed the gap between hues before the reader looks, and a palette whose hues sit close together narrows it again. Okabe and Ito’s eight are spaced for readers who cannot separate some hues at all, which is the same requirement as separating them once shading has removed a third of the light.
What the frames do not touch is the viewing angle. space(turn = , tilt = ) is a property of the space rather than of the data, so one angle serves the whole sequence and every frame is seen from the same place. That is a design choice, not something missing. A viewing angle that swung while the sequence played would add motion that no column asked for, and a reader would then have to separate it from the motion a column does explain. play moves the data, and the viewing angle stays fixed.
You can still turn the plot yourself while it runs, and that is not the same as a viewing angle that moves on its own. A reader who drags knows which motion is theirs, and can stop it. Turning matters more in this chapter than anywhere else in the book, because something is moving inside a solid shape. The only way to see what the near edge hides is to turn the cube and look from another side.
Panels and frames still compose in the cube. facet and play each split the rows by their own column, so crossing the two needs no new rule. Each panel draws its cube at whatever size its own rectangle allows.

data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + z(population) +
  color(continent) + play(year) | facet(continent, wrap = 3)


(data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + z(col.population) +
  color(col.continent) + play(col.year) | facet(col.continent, wrap = 3))


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  z(:population) + color(:continent) + play(:year) |
  facet(:continent, wrap = 3)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  z(col.population), color(col.continent), play(col.year),
  across(col.continent, { wrap: 3 }))

“Given the ripples: a surface, x is across, y is along, z is height, color by height, with the plasma palette, played by instant at speed 4, split into panel columns by tank.”
Watch one arc leave the corner and cross the floor. In the PDF you see the first instant, with the arcs already spread across both tanks and closer together in the shallow one. It is the same tapping in both panels, and the panels share every scale, so the closer spacing in the shallow tank is a shorter wavelength, not a different scale. speed = 4 matters here: at the normal pace twelve frames take nearly ten seconds, which is a slideshow of a wave rather than a wave.
The height is said twice, once as the third position and once as the color, and that is deliberate rather than a redundancy. A sheet seen from one angle hides part of itself. The far corner is foreshortened, and the near crests stand in front of the troughs behind them, so a shape that is clear at the front has to be guessed at the back. Bright crest bands stay readable after the projection where the height alone does not, and the wavelength this plot exists to compare is the spacing of those bands. palette("plasma") runs dark blue through magenta and orange to yellow. Channels has the rest, including two diverging ramps whose neutral color would sit at the still-water line if the sign of the height were the point.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.10 Frames in polar
Every picture in the polar chapter held one moment, and a rose can grow across the years too. Polar is the second space this chapter plays a sequence in, and it composes with frames for the same reason the cube does. polar() bends the panel, the frames choose the rows, and neither has to know about the other:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + polar() + play(year)


data(gm_all) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + polar() + play(col.year)


data(gm_all) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) + polar() +
  play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  polar(), play(col.year))






                                                                                                                                        Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   20 40 60 80     1952    1957    1962    1967    1972    1977    1982    1987    1992    1997    2002    2007    Life Continent





“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, in polar, played by year.”
A rose of mean life expectancy, one petal per continent, opening across half a century. The radial axis is fitted over the whole sequence exactly as a flat one is. That is why the ring at 80 is already drawn in 1952 with nothing reaching it: the petals grow inside a circle that does not resize under them. Asia’s petal changes most, from 46 years to 71. Africa’s climbs steadily until the late 1980s and then stops for fifteen years. The pause is in the data, and the mean shows it rather than hiding it.
A pie is where that shared axis does something surprising. No new rule applies here, only the flat rule bent into a circle:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * sum * stack + y(population) + color(continent) + polar() +
  play(year)


(data(gm_all) + bar * sum * stack + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) + polar() +
  play(col.year))


data(gm_all) + bar * sum * stack + y(:population) + color(:continent) +
  polar() + play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, sum, stack), y(col.population),
  color(col.continent), polar(), play(col.year))






                                                                                                                               1952    1957    1962    1967    1972    1977    1982    1987    1992    1997    2002    2007    Population  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by sum and stack, y is population, color by continent, in polar, played by year.”
The circle does not close until the last frame. A pie’s turn is its measure axis, and that axis is fitted across the whole sequence like every other. 1952’s world population is a little under two fifths of 2007’s, so 1952 sweeps a little under two fifths of the turn. The identical sentence without polar() draws a stacked bar that stops far below the top of its axis, and nobody finds that surprising. A pie that does not close is that stacked bar bent.
If the question is each year’s shares rather than each year’s total, the sentence can say so, and then every frame closes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + y(population) + color(continent) +
  polar() + play(year)


(data(gm_all) + bar * sum * stack(share = True) + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) +
  polar() + play(col.year))


data(gm_all) + bar * sum * stack(share = true) + y(:population) +
  color(:continent) + polar() + play(:year)


plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, sum, stack({ share: true })),
  y(col.population), color(col.continent), polar(), play(col.year))






                                                                                                                               1952    1957    1962    1967    1972    1977    1982    1987    1992    1997    2002    2007    Share  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by sum and stack as shares, y is population, color by continent, in polar, played by year.”
The turn is one whole in every frame now, and what moves is how it divides. Asia widens a little from 58% to 61%, Europe falls from 17% to 9%, and Africa grows by half, from 10% to 15%. The two sentences differ by one argument, share = TRUE, and they answer two different questions about the same column. Choosing between them belongs to the reader; the grammar only has to let you write both.
