Twelve frames, one for each calendar month, and each frame holds 46 years of that month. From June to November most storms are in the Northern Hemisphere, and almost half of those are in the western North Pacific. September has the most storms of any month: 477 in the north over the 46 years. From December to April most storms are south of the equator, in the southern Indian Ocean, near northern Australia and in the South Pacific. February is the busiest southern month. No storm appears south of the equator in July or August. May is the quietest month of the year.
Two rules from earlier in this chapter make the sequence work. The frames follow the calendar because month has a declared order, as The column’s order explained. The land has no play of its own, so it is drawn whole in every frame, like the reference lines in A layer with no frames. Only the storms change from one frame to the next.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.12 Taking the sequence with you
You may want to send one of these sequences to someone. Every sequence on this page moves because the SVG carries its own timing, and a browser reads that timing. Most other places do not. A chat with a friend, a slide in a talk, a post on a social site: each of them shows the first frame and stops.
save_gif() writes the same sequence as a file that those places will play:

wave <- file.path(tempdir(), "wave.gif")
save_gif(data(ripples) + surface + x(across) + y(along) + z(height) +
           color(height) + palette("plasma") + play(instant, speed = 4) |
           facet(tank),
         wave, scale = 2)
cat(basename(wave), round(file.size(wave) / 1024), "KB\n")

wave.gif 739 KB


Nothing has to be installed first. The engine converts and encodes the file itself, so the same line works on every machine that can draw the plot at all.
scale multiplies the canvas. A plot is 800 by 600 pixels unless its theme says otherwise, which is small for a post, so scale = 2 doubles both numbers. You do not restate the pace. This sequence was written with speed = 4, so each frame holds for a fifth of a second in the file, exactly as it does on the page.
The file cannot disagree with the plot beside it, and the reason is the one Design laws gives for having one renderer. The frames are not drawn again one at a time. The plot is drawn once, with every scale, the color palette and each legend fitted across the whole sequence. What you see at any time is that single drawing with only one frame visible, so there is no second set of decisions that could differ.
save_gif() refuses some calls. A plot with no play() has no frames to write, and saying so is more useful than writing a file of one frame:

still <- data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
save_gif(still, file.path(tempdir(), "still.gif"))

Error:
! gog: a GIF of a still plot is valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it: this plot does not play, so it has no frames to write. Bind a column with an order to `play` — `play(year)` — or save the still picture it already is.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


And the path has to end in .gif, because the name of a file is a claim about what is inside it:

moving <- data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + play(year)
save_gif(moving, "wave.png")

Error:
! gog: `save_gif()` writes a GIF, so the path ends in `.gif` — `save_gif(p, "wave.gif")`.


A page of two plots is refused as well, because each plot keeps its own clock and nothing says which one the file should follow. Save the played plot on its own.
One thing changes when the file is written, and you should know it before you send the file rather than after. A GIF is pixels. The text stops being text, so it no longer sharpens when a reader zooms in, and every color in the plot is matched to one of 256. The SVG remains the plot itself. The GIF is a copy of it made for somewhere that cannot read the original.

38.12.1 Why a GIF and not a video
A video file would be smaller and sharper than a GIF, and a few places accept video and nothing else. gog writes no video, and the reason is about what a package can carry rather than about what a plot is.
Making a video needs a video encoder. The one nearly everybody uses is more than ten times the size of this whole engine, and a package would need one copy for every platform it supports. Its license also does not allow it to be included in a package licensed the way this one is. The other choice is to require the reader to install the encoder separately. That sounds harmless, until you count the readers who cannot install a separate program. A prebuilt package cannot supply the encoder for them either, because the encoder cannot be included in it. The feature would work for some readers and refuse for others, which is a worse answer than not having it.
A GIF needs nothing else installed. The engine writes it on every machine that can draw the plot, in every one of the four languages. When the file looks blurry, raise scale. When you genuinely need a video, converting a GIF into one is easy, and free converters online do it in one step.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.13 What it refuses
Two more sentences are refused, and neither has appeared yet. Earlier in this chapter, frames and panels were used together, so you may try one column for both. A column names the panels or the frames, not both. If it were drawn, every panel but one would be empty in every frame:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_four) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + play(period) | facet(period)


data(gm_four) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + play(col.period) | facet(col.period)


data(gm_four) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + play(:period) |
  facet(:period)


plot(data(gm_four), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), play(col.period),
  across(col.period))




Error:
! gog: `period` cannot both name the frames and name the panels — every panel but one would be empty in every frame. Split the page by one column and the time by another, or drop `| facet(period)` and let `play(period)` carry it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A speed of zero or less is refused as soon as play() is written:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + play(year, speed = 0)


data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + play(col.year, speed = 0)


data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + play(:year, speed = 0)


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  play(col.year, { speed: 0 }))




Error:
! gog: `speed = 0` — a speed is a multiple of the normal pace, so it has to be above zero. `speed = 2` is twice as fast, `speed = 0.5` half.


speed belongs to play and to nothing else, because nothing else in the grammar takes time to draw: a color is drawn all at once, so there is no duration for a multiplier to scale. This page cannot show a refusal for speed on another channel. None of the four packages gives any other channel a speed argument at all, so color(continent, speed = 2) fails in R, Python, Julia or JavaScript before a specification is ever built. The engine still checks it, because a specification can also be written by hand. You will never see that message from a sentence, though: the language you are writing in refuses first, which is the earlier and better place for it.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.14 What the page adds
A played plot on a web page carries three more buttons. They sit on the same line as the four every plot has, a little to the right of them, and they control the clock:







Control
What it does




the left arrow
Goes back one frame, and stops the clock


the pause
Stops the clock. It becomes a play arrow, which starts it again


the right arrow
Goes forward one frame, and stops the clock



Stepping stops the clock, and it has to. A running clock would move past the frame you just asked for, often in less than a second. So the arrows stop it, and the middle button is how you start it again.
The two ends are connected. Go back from the first frame and you arrive at the last. The sequence already runs that way: it loops, so the last frame is followed by the first, every time. Buttons that stopped at the ends would disagree with the sequence they control.
No button shows which frame you are on, because the strip above the panel already names it. That strip is the sequence’s guide, drawn on every played plot, the way an axis is drawn for x.
None of the three buttons is in the sentence, and that is the rule rather than an omission. Every frame is already in the file: the whole sequence is drawn once, and a clock decides which frame you see at each moment. Stepping moves that clock. It chooses no rows, hides no rows, and changes nothing the sentence said. So it is like turning a cube (Space), which changes how you look at the plot and never what is drawn. Neither one needs a word in the grammar.
Stop the clock and the camera photographs the frame you stopped on. That follows from the camera’s own rule, not from a rule about animation: it saves what you are looking at, the same way it saves how far you have zoomed in.
The PDF shows no buttons, because they belong to the web page rather than to the plot.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.15 Why points jump between frames
The arrows move from one frame to the next, which raises a question about what happens in between. Nothing happens in between. Frames do not blend into one another: the frame for 1957 and the frame for 1962 are two complete pictures shown in turn. Moving a point smoothly between them needs a key, something that says Afghanistan in one frame is the same country as Afghanistan in the next. The grammar has no such word. group looks like that word, and it is not: a point does not take group. The mark everyone imagines moving smoothly is exactly the mark that cannot carry a key. So what is missing is a word in the vocabulary, not an ability in the engine.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.16 In short
play splits the rows exactly as a facet does and lays the pieces out in time. One set of scales and one palette serve every frame. A sequence claims that one frame follows another, so playing an unordered column prints a message naming the two answers. A line draws a curve along the column bound to x, so playing that same column leaves one position in every frame, and gog refuses the pair.

title: 38  Play
text:
38.17 What comes next
Play runs the frames and you watch them. In Selection you use the pointer instead: drag across a group of rows, and the plot dims the ones you did not choose.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.1 Saying where the selection starts
Which countries in a scatter are the rich ones, and where do they sit? Finding them among 142 dots takes a long time. Add one word, brush, to the sentence and the reader can draw a box around any group. The countries inside the box keep their color, and the rest are dimmed:
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, and let the reader select.”
In the web edition, drag across that plot. In the PDF it is the plain scatter, because a bare brush selects nothing until a reader drags.
Bare brush means the positions this plot binds, so here it is a region over gdp and life together. The sentence offers the reader a selection without choosing in advance which part of the plot to select.
Every country is still drawn while you drag, so the group is read against what it was taken from. Remove the other rows and the plot no longer shows that the rich countries sit at the top right of the whole world.
In the PDF nothing can be dragged, so a reader of the first plot must still find the rich countries without help. Name a column and the brush states a bound on it: the low and high values the selection starts at. That is how you point at something rather than let a reader look for it:
RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), theme({ width: 620 }),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }))






                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 20000 to 60000.”
The thirty or so countries above 20,000 dollars keep their color, and almost all of them sit above 75 years. A bound written into the sentence points the reader at a group, as a note on the plot would. The sentence has done the selecting, and a reader can still drag across the panel to replace the bound.
The two forms differ in who chooses the group. brush leaves the choice to the reader. brush(gdp, at = ...) makes the choice in the sentence, so the selection also appears in the PDF.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.2 Highlighting, never removing rows
A brush highlights rows and never removes them. That rule separates brush from an atom you already know. limits also takes a range in a column’s own units, and it puts that range to a different use.
limits on a column of the table runs before the statistics. It removes rows, and the transform then reads the rows that are left as if they were the whole table. brush runs after the axes and statistics are computed. It removes nothing and recomputes nothing.
One range, one mark, two outcomes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, limits = c(20000, 60000)) + y(life) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 300) + title("limits: 109 countries gone")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, limits = [20000, 60000]) + y(col.life) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 300) + title("limits: 109 countries gone"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, limits = [20000, 60000]) +
  y(:life) + theme(width = 620, height = 300) +
  title("limits: 109 countries gone")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { limits: [20000, 60000] }),
  y(col.life), theme({ width: 620, height: 300 }),
  title("limits: 109 countries gone"))




gog: `x(gdp, limits = …)` excludes 109 of 142 rows, which fall outside [20000, 60000]. Stating a domain is what removes them — widen the limits if they should be drawn.




                                                                   20K 30K 40K 50K 60K   74 76 78 80 82  limits: 109 countries gone Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp from 20000 to 60000, y is life.”


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 300) + brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000)) +
  title("brush: all 142 still here")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 300) + brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) +
  title("brush: all 142 still here"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 300) + brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) +
  title("brush: all 142 still here")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  theme({ width: 620, height: 300 }),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }),
  title("brush: all 142 still here"))






                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  brush: all 142 still here Life Gdp





The limits plot is drawn from fewer rows. Its axis runs from 20,000 to 60,000, only the countries inside that range are drawn, and both axes were fitted to the rows that were left. Look at its y axis: the lowest number on it is 74, because the poorer countries were removed, and they included every country with a low life expectancy. gog prints how many it removed rather than removing them in silence.
The brush plot is the whole world, with one group keeping its color. Its axes are the axes of all 142 countries, so the selected points are exactly where an unbrushed plot would have put them.
The two plots do not share an axis, even though one is drawn above the other. A country at 30,000 dollars sits a quarter of the way along the top plot’s axis and more than halfway along the bottom one’s. Read each plot against its own axes.
Which of the two you want depends on your question, and the grammar lets you write either one. Ask how does this subgroup look on its own and you want limits. Ask where does this subgroup sit inside the whole and you want brush.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.3 Two bounds make a rectangle
Which of the rich countries also live longest? That is two conditions on one row. One brush tests one column. Write two, and a row has to satisfy both:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000)) + brush(life, at = c(78, 85))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) + brush(col.life, at = [78, 85]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) +
  brush(:life, at = [78, 85])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), theme({ width: 620 }),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }),
  brush(col.life, { at: [78, 85] }))






                                                                                                                                                                                       0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 20000 to 60000, and life, starting from 78 to 85.”
These are the rich countries that also live longest. Six countries inside the gdp bound fall outside the life bound, and you can see which six, because they are still drawn, dimmed.
Two bounds needed brush written twice, and that follows the rest of the grammar. A position is one column at a time, and so is a bound.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.4 A categorical column selects slots
Both bounds so far have been ranges of numbers. What happens when the column holds names instead? at is still where the selection starts, and the column decides which reading you get, in the same way it decides whether color uses a ramp or a palette. Numbers are a range. Names are a set of slots:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(continent, at = c("Europe", "Oceania"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  theme(width = 620) + brush(col.continent, at = ["Europe", "Oceania"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + theme(width = 620) +
  brush(:continent, at = ["Europe", "Oceania"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), theme({ width: 620 }),
  brush(col.continent, { at: ["Europe", "Oceania"] }))






                                                                                                                                                                                     Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Life Continent  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life, color by continent, and let the reader select continent, starting with Europe and Oceania.”
Drag across the slots and the selection follows them, whole slots at a time, because a slot cannot be split.
The column is on the x axis here, and that matters. A drag can only change a bound on a column that one of the panel’s axes shows. Add the same brush(continent, at = ...) to the first scatter in this chapter, where continent is only a color. The sentence is still legal and still dims the right countries. But no axis shows continents, so a drag cannot change the selection the sentence chose.
It does not matter which axis places the column. Here is the same sentence with x and y exchanged, in a shorter panel:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(life) + y(continent) + color(continent) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 320) + brush(continent, at = c("Europe", "Oceania"))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) + color(col.continent) +
  theme(width = 620, height = 320) + brush(col.continent, at = ["Europe", "Oceania"]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  color(:continent) + theme(width = 620, height = 320) +
  brush(:continent, at = ["Europe", "Oceania"])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  color(col.continent), theme({ width: 620, height: 320 }),
  brush(col.continent, { at: ["Europe", "Oceania"] }))






                                                                                                                                                                                     40 50 60 70 80   Oceania Americas Africa Europe Asia  Continent Life  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





The slots now run up the left side, and the same two continents keep their color. Drag on the panel and the selected band is horizontal instead of vertical, still one whole slot at a time. The bound never mentions an axis. It names a column, so moving the column to the other axis turns the drag from vertical to horizontal, and the brush stays exactly as it was written.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.5 Two views, one selection
A brush is most useful across two plots. A selection inside one plot marks a group you can already see there. The useful question is where does this group sit in a different picture, and that needs a second picture:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000)) + theme(height = 230)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(population, scale = "log") +
     brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000)) + theme(height = 200))


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
   brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) + theme(height = 230)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.population, scale = "log") +
     brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) + theme(height = 200)))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) + theme(height = 230)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) +
  y(:population, scale = "log") + brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) +
  theme(height = 200))


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }), theme({ height: 230 })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp),
  y(col.population, { scale: "log" }),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }), theme({ height: 200 })))






                                                                                                                                                                                     40 50 60 70 80  Life


                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   1M 10M 100M 1B  Population Gdp






“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 20000 to 60000, above points, x is gdp, y is population on a log scale, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 20000 to 60000.”
Two plots sit on one page. In both plots, the same countries keep their color. Drag in either and the other follows. The top plot says the rich countries live long. The bottom plot says their populations run from under a million to over three hundred million. Neither plot could have told you both.
Nothing was added to the grammar to link them. Look at what the two sentences share: each one says brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000)). A bound is a fact about a column’s values rather than about a panel, so two plots that brush the same column answer the same question. There is no name to declare, no identifier to match, and no third atom joining them.
Composition has a matching rule for axes. Two composed plots naming the same column on the same axis share that axis, which is why these two are the same width and the gdp numbers are written once. The selection is shared for a related reason: both sentences brush the same column.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.6 One bound reaches every panel
Faceting is the other way to get more than one panel, and a brush treats it the same way. The bound is a fact about a column, and every panel reads that column, so every panel answers:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000)) | facet(continent)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) | facet(col.continent))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000]) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }), across(col.continent))






                                                                    0 20K 40K   40 50 60 70 80                                                             0 20K 40K                                                                                   0 20K 40K                                                          0 20K 40K                                 0 20K 40K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 20000 to 60000, split into panel columns by continent.”
Five panels, one bound, and the rich countries keeping their color. Europe has many and Africa has none, which is the comparison the split was made for. facet divides the rows into panels, brush dims the rows outside the bound, and neither atom refers to the other.
In the web edition, resting the pointer on a mark shows that row’s values. A bound is shared across panels, because it names a column. The pointer is not: its values come from the panel you are pointing at, never from a row another panel drew.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.7 Which one is that?
A selection shows you where a group sits. It does not say which country each dot is, and that is usually the next question. Layer text over the points, and the bound decides which labels stay legible:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  text + label(country) + style(size = 7) +
  brush(gdp, at = c(30000, 60000)) + theme(width = 620)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  text + label(col.country) + style(size = 7) +
  brush(col.gdp, at = [30000, 60000]) + theme(width = 620))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + text +
  label(:country) + style(size = 7) + brush(:gdp, at = [30000, 60000]) +
  theme(width = 620)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), text,
  label(col.country), style({ size: 7 }),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [30000, 60000] }), theme({ width: 620 }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also text, label by country, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 30000 to 60000.”
A hundred and forty-two labels on one scatter cannot be read, and a selection solves that here. The labels you did not select are dimmed with their points, and twenty names keep their color. Drag across the panel for a new bound, and a different group of names becomes readable.
This works because text, like point, draws one shape for each row, so a brush can dim each label on its own. No special rule joins brush to text: each atom follows its own rule, and this plot uses both.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.8 What can be brushed
A selection marks rows, so a shape can be brushed only when all of its rows are selected, or none are. The simplest case is one row is one shape. Four marks meet that test and draw a selection: point, text, rule and zone. An interval with the bounds transform meets the test too, because each whisker’s two ends come from one row.
A plain bar meets the test as well and still refuses. One row is one bar, but a bar’s thickness comes from the smallest gap between neighboring bars. The engine draws the selected rows and the other rows as two groups, and each group would measure its own gap, so the two groups would get different thicknesses. A jittered point and a repelled text refuse for a similar reason. A jittered point’s offset is derived from its place in the table. A repelled label is placed by what the other labels around it are doing. In both cases every mark would move when the selection changed. An edge meets the test too, and it still refuses. The Network chapter gives the reason: a network has no axes, so there is nothing for a range of values to be measured on.
A line does not meet the test at all. It draws one shape through many rows, so a row is a corner of the line rather than a thing of its own. Selecting half of a line would mean cutting it in two. group() cuts a line into pieces, but each piece still runs through many rows, so the engine refuses even this sentence:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  brush(life, at = c(60, 80))


(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) +
  brush(col.life, at = [60, 80]))


data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) +

plot(data(gapminder_asia), line, x(col.year), y(col.life),

Error:
! gog: a `line` draws one shape through many rows, so there is no single row to select. Brush a layer that draws a selection: `point`, `text`, `rule`, `zone` and `interval * bounds`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The refusal lists the layers that draw a selection. A brushed plot needs at least one of them.
A summarized layer refuses for a different reason. A bar of bar * count stands for as many as fifty-two countries at once. There is no way to draw “twelve of these are selected”: dimming the whole bar would be wrong, and dimming part of it would invent a mark nobody asked for. gog says so instead of guessing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000))


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]))


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }))




Error:
! gog: a brush on `bar * count` is valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it: `count` summarizes many rows into one, and the engine cannot say which of them you selected. Brush the layer that draws the rows themselves, or drop the brush.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A flow is the only summary that answers a brush. Each band stands for the rows that share a place at every stage, so a brush on a stage keeps or dims a whole band, and never part of one.
Apart from the edge’s, none of the refusals above applies when the plot also carries a layer that can answer. The plot draws, and gog reports which layer it left whole:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  line * smooth +
  brush(gdp, at = c(20000, 60000))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  line * smooth +
  brush(col.gdp, at = [20000, 60000]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + line * smooth +
  brush(:gdp, at = [20000, 60000])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  layer(line, smooth), brush(col.gdp, { at: [20000, 60000] }))




gog: the `line` layer is drawn whole, because it draws one shape through many rows and there is no single row to select. The selection still reads on the rest of the plot.




                                                                                                                                                                                          0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also a line derived by smooth, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 20000 to 60000.”
The points answer the selection and the trend line does not, so the line is drawn once, undimmed, through all 142 countries. That is the right answer: a trend fitted to the selection alone would be a different statistic, and the sentence did not ask for one.
A range written from high to low selects nothing, so it is a mistake rather than an empty selection:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  brush(gdp, at = c(60000, 20000))


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  brush(col.gdp, at = [60000, 20000]))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  brush(:gdp, at = [60000, 20000])


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  brush(col.gdp, { at: [60000, 20000] }))




Error:
! gog: `brush(gdp)` at 60000 to 20000 selects nothing, because the range does not run upward. Write the smaller number first.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A map cannot be brushed at all. It projects longitude and latitude to new positions before it draws anything, and a brush on it would count one set of places while it dims another. “Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, played by year, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 3000 to 20000.”
In the web edition, watch countries cross into the selection, frame by frame. In the PDF, the plot shows the first frame, 1952. The bound stays at 3,000 to 20,000 dollars while the countries move. In 1952 the selected group is that year’s middle-income countries. By 2007 many have grown past 20,000 and poorer ones have grown into the range. A brush does not pause the sequence or skip a frame.

39.9.1 What the count includes
Stop the clock, draw a small box, and the count under the plot (the line reading 17 of 1704 selected) looks far too large. The number is right. A bound is a test on a column’s values, so it is true or false for every row in the table. It does not stop at the frame you can see. The count and show rows, a button under the plot, report the whole selection across every frame. The picture shows you one frame of it.
The played plot in this section makes that concrete. gm_all is 1,704 rows, which is 142 countries in each of twelve years, and one frame draws 142 of them. Stop on 1982 and drag across the four countries furthest to the left, and the count reads far more than four. This brush tests only gdp, so the box covers the whole height of the panel, and it tests every year’s rows, not only 1982’s. In other years, other countries had a gdp in that range too. The four you can see are the 1982 rows of a selection that spans all twelve years.
The table that show rows opens is where you check it. It lists the year of every selected row, beside the other columns the sentence maps. You can see which frame each row belongs to, and pick out the four that belong to the frame on screen.
A faceted plot never raises this question. There every selected row is drawn at once, so a count of the whole selection is a count of what you see. A sequence shows one frame of twelve at a time, so most of the selected rows are not on the screen. They are in other frames. The rule is the same one; only the picture differs.


39.9.2 Choosing a bound the data crosses
A bound chosen for the late frames can mislead a reader in the early ones. Count what a bound selects in each frame before you write it down. From 3,000 to 20,000 dollars selects between 52 and 74 countries in every frame here. From 20,000 to 60,000 dollars selects none at all in 1952 and 1957, one in 1962, and four by 1972. The second bound draws a true picture, and it still reads as a broken plot, because a reader cannot tell nothing is selected here from this is not working. To see it, drag across the panel from 20,000 to 60,000 dollars and step back to 1952: every country in that frame is dimmed.
One column cannot both cut the frames and carry a bound. Brushing the column the frames are cut on would select frames rather than rows inside one, and that is a control for moving through time rather than a selection:

data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + play(year) + brush(year, at = c(1980, 2007))

  brush(:year, at = [1980, 2007])


plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), play(col.year),
  brush(col.year, { at: [1980, 2007] }))

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.10 All three at once
A bound and a sequence combined without a new rule, and a third position joins them the same way. Play drew the cube of countries through the years, and nothing in it marks the middle-income countries. The third position, the frames and the selection are three separate ideas, and none of them was designed around the others. So all three can be written in one sentence, and none of them changes what the others do:

“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, z is population, color by continent, played by year, and let the reader select gdp, starting from 3000 to 20000.”
A cube of 142 countries, twelve frames, and one bound tested inside every one of them. Drag the plot to turn it and the selection turns with the cloud. The bound picks rows and the drag picks the viewing angle, and neither one depends on the other.
One thing is different in the cube. There the drag turns the plot, so it cannot also draw a selection, and you name the bound in the sentence. brush on its own would declare a region that no drag could draw. The rule is the one behind every plot in this chapter: a drag does one thing at a time, and in the cube that one thing is turning.
So in the cube you cannot change the selection, but you can still read it. The count and show rows sit on their own line under the plot, and you can read the selected rows while you turn it.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.11 Changing the bound yourself
After the first one, every brushed plot in this chapter states where its selection starts. In the web edition, drag across a flat panel and your range replaces the sentence’s bound. The plot redraws as you drag. On a flow, a click on a slot moves the bound instead, as Selecting one place shows.
This changes nothing about the sentence, and it is the same arrangement the cube uses. space(turn =, tilt =) chooses the angle a plot starts at, and the pointer moves it from there. brush(gdp, at = ) chooses the bound a plot starts with, and the pointer replaces it from there. Drag to find a selection, read its two ends off the axis, and write them into the sentence.
In the PDF, each plot shows the bound its sentence asked for. That is why naming it matters even though a reader of the web edition can replace it: that reader starts from it too.
A brush that names a column but no at also selects nothing until a reader drags. On a polar plot, a drag never changes the selection, and the section Where the page cannot find a row explains why.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.12 What the page adds
A flat brushed plot on a web page carries two lines of controls under it. None of them are in the sentence, and that is the rule rather than an omission. They report a selection, or they change how you look at one. Not one of them changes what the plot claims about the data, so none of them needs a word in the grammar. A plot in the cube follows the same rule: space() names the angle the plot starts at, and turning it needs no word. It carries two lines of controls, or three when it is brushed.
The first line is the one every plot carries:







Control
What it does




the magnifiers, − and +
Makes the picture smaller or larger


the frame button (four corners around a small square)
Returns to the whole picture


the camera
Saves what you are looking at as a picture file



It sits first, directly under the picture, on a plain plot and a brushed one alike. This matters. A reader who has found the magnifiers once finds them in the same place under every plot in this book, rather than in a place that moves with whatever else the plot needed.
A plot that also plays carries three more buttons at the end of that same line, which pause the sequence and step through its frames. Play sets them out.
The second line is what a brush adds:



Control
What it does




drag: and its icons
Says what dragging the plot will do, and switches it: a rectangle, a free shape, or moving the picture. Absent on a flow, where a click on a slot selects


40 of 142 selected
How many rows the current bound selects. On a played plot this counts every frame, not the one on screen. Plots composed with | or / share this count. When they read the same table, each row is counted once, and only if all their bounds select it


show rows
Opens a table of those rows; while the table is open the button reads hide rows. A long selection arrives ten at a time, with ‹ and › under the table


clear
Puts the selection back to what the sentence asked for


unstamp
Removes every stamp at once (Stamping a point explains stamps). With two or more, the button shows how many. Absent until you have made one



In the cube and on a polar plot, the line a brush adds holds only the count and show rows. In the cube it comes third, under the line that shows the angle.
A control drawn as an icon names itself when the pointer rests on it. So do clear and unstamp, which say what they undo.

39.12.1 Dragging a box
A bound written in the sentence is a starting point, and a drag replaces it. Drag across the panel. A dotted box follows the pointer, and it shows exactly what is bound. On a plot with one brush the box spans the whole panel in the other direction, because that direction was not selected. On a plot with two, it is a rectangle. A box that narrowed an axis you never bound would claim a range you did not choose. The box disappears when you release the pointer, and from then on the dimming shows the bound.
Dragging in either direction gives the same bound, so you can start from any corner. A click on empty space empties the selection, so nothing is dimmed. A click that lands on a mark does something else, and Stamping a point is about that.


39.12.2 Drawing around a group
A rectangle is what a sentence can say. Some groups are not rectangles. A cloud of points often has a shape: a narrow tail to one side, a curve, a group sitting apart from the rest. A box drawn around such a group includes points you did not mean.
The second icon beside drag: is the free shape. Choose it, then draw around the group with the pointer held down. The outline closes itself when you release the pointer, and everything inside it is selected. The count and the row table read exactly as they do for a box, because a shape and a bound ask the same question: which rows do you mean.
Nothing about the sentence changes. You do not type a shape, and the PDF still shows the bound the sentence named. Drawing one is a way of looking, like turning a cube, rather than a claim about the data.
That is also why the grammar has no word for it. Other tools call the gesture a lasso, and gog has no such word. Written down, a drawn shape is a long list of corner points, too long to type or read as part of a sentence. So you can draw the shape, but you cannot write it.
Two restrictions apply. A free shape needs two continuous axes, so where one axis is categorical the drag stays a rectangle. And clear removes a free shape and returns to the bound the sentence named. It cannot restore the shape, because no sentence can state a drawn shape.


39.12.3 Reading what you selected
The dimming shows where a group sits, but not which rows are in it. The count says how many rows are selected, and show rows opens the row table. It lists the columns the sentence maps, not every column of your data, because the columns you did not plot are not what you are looking at. On a flow it also lists the columns named in flow(), so each row shows its place in each of them.
A long selection arrives ten rows at a time. The line under the table says which rows you are reading, as 11–20 of 40, and the two arrows beside it move you through the rest. Every row you selected is reachable, and none of them pushes the plot off the screen. A selection short enough to fit shows no arrows at all.
The row table lists every row you selected, with those columns, in one place, away from the picture. It shows country names only when the sentence maps country, as the labeled plot in Which one is that? does. Draw a bound tight around one point and the table lists that point alone.


39.12.4 Stamping a point
The pointer shows one row’s values at a time, and they disappear as soon as you move away from the mark. That is right for a quick look and wrong for a comparison. Suppose three points on a scatter interest you. Reading them one after another means remembering the first two while you look at the third.
Click a mark and its values stay. That is a stamp: a dot on the mark, a short line, and a small card saying what the pointer said. Click as many as you want to compare. The card sits on the picture beside the mark it belongs to, which is the difference between a stamp and the row table. The row table names rows. A stamp labels the plot.
A card needs space on the picture. On a crowded scatter a card can cover the points you want to read. So drag a card and it goes where you put it. The line stretches to follow, and a long line ends in an arrowhead at the stamped point. Move four cards out to the edges and the picture underneath stays whole.
A card keeps the distance you gave it from its point. Zoom in, pan across, or drag a new bound, and the card moves with its point. Zoom far enough that the point leaves the picture on screen, and the whole stamp goes out of sight with it. It has nothing left to point at, and a card left over an unrelated corner would claim a point that is not there. Bring the point back and the card is where you left it.
A played plot works the same way, for the same reason. A row there is one country in one year, so a stamp made in 1972 names something the 1987 frame does not draw. The stamp is hidden while the other frames run, and it returns to its point when the sequence comes back to 1972. The card names the year it holds. Stamp the same country in three frames and each card appears in its own frame.
There are three ways to take a stamp off. The × in the corner of a card removes that card. Clicking the card itself does the same, as long as you did not move it: if the pointer moved between press and release, the click counted as a drag instead. unstamp removes every card at once.
clear does not remove the cards, because a stamp is not a selection. A click on empty space does not remove them either. It empties the selection, so every point returns to full strength, and every card is still there. clear, unstamp and the frame button each undo one thing, which Three controls, three things sets out.
The camera saves the cards too. Arrange the cards, press the camera, and the picture file carries the plot with your annotations on it, each card where you put it and each line pointing at its row. The camera saves what you are looking at, the same way it saves how far you have zoomed in and the angle a cube is turned to.
You do not type a stamp, and the PDF carries none.
A stamp is for deciding which points are worth naming. A plot with a name on every point is unreadable, and a plot with a name on the few that matter is the one you wanted. Stamping lets you try a few before you choose. Then put those rows in a small table of their own, give it to a text layer, and the picture carries the names itself, in the web edition and the PDF alike. A note is a layer shows how.
Arranging the cards by hand has a written form too. text * repel does the same job inside the sentence. Every label is placed outside its own dot, and one that moved far keeps a thin line back to the point it names. That is the stamp’s line again, written down rather than dragged. Stamp to decide what is worth naming, then write the labels down and let repel place them.
A stamp is for looking at the data. text is for telling a reader what it says.
Both can go into a presentation, and they are not the same there. A saved picture is fixed: it keeps one moment of one session and cannot be drawn again. A sentence with text in it draws again for anyone who has the data, in the PDF and on the page and in all four languages. Stamp and save to keep this one picture. Write the labels down to keep the plot itself.


39.12.5 Where the page cannot find a row
On a brushed polar plot, the pointer shows no values. The reason is how the page finds the row under the pointer. From each row’s own values and the values at the ends of each axis, it computes where that row was drawn. That is exact when both axes are straight lines. A polar plot has no straight axes: it draws x as an angle and y as a distance from the center.
So the pointer shows nothing, rather than the values of the wrong row. Nothing can be stamped either. The page never reads positions from the picture itself. It only computes them.
The same reason applies to a drag. The page would read the box you drag as a range of values on a straight axis. On a polar plot, the rows in that range are drawn somewhere else, not under the box. So on a brushed polar plot, a drag never changes the selection.
The bound the sentence names still works: gog tests it against each row’s values, so the count and the dimmed marks agree. That is why a polar plot keeps its brush and a map does not. As in the cube, the only way to choose the selection is to name the bound in the sentence. On a polar plot, a brush with no at never selects a row. The brush adds only the count and show rows under the plot.
In the cube, as on a polar plot, the pointer shows no values, and nothing can be stamped. There the viewing angle moves every mark, so the page cannot compute where each row was drawn.
The pointer still shows values on a plot with a layer whose marks do not stand at their rows’ values. jitter sets each point beside its value, repel moves each label away from the others, and a summary such as bin or mean draws one shape for many rows. As What can be brushed showed, a layer like that either refuses the brush or is drawn whole beside a layer that answers it. The pointer then reads that other layer, whose marks stand at their values. A flow is the exception. Its layers answer the brush, but none of its marks stands at a row’s value, so the pointer shows no values there.


39.12.6 Looking closer
A crowded corner is easier to read when it is larger. + and − magnify the picture, and the frame button returns to the whole of it. Zooming in switches the drag to panning, because a reader who has just looked closer usually wants to move around inside the picture. The frame button sets the drag back to selecting. You can switch by hand at any time with the icons beside drag:. The pointer also tells you which mode you are in: a crosshair to draw a box, an open hand to move the picture. A brushed polar plot has no drag: icons, because a drag there never selects. There, once you zoom in, a drag moves the picture.
This is a view, so it recomputes nothing. The bars are the same bars and the ticks are the same ticks, drawn larger. Zoom far enough into a histogram and you will see the same bins, not finer ones. If you want the statistics re-run over a narrower range, that is limits, the atom this chapter compared with brush.


39.12.7 Three controls, three things
Three of these controls undo something, and pressing the wrong one removes work you meant to keep. clear acts on the selection, unstamp acts on the stamps, and the frame button acts on the view. Each one undoes only its own thing, so pressing one never costs you the other two. The frame button sits a line above the other two, beside the magnifiers. It puts back the view they changed.
The × on a card is a fourth undo, and it is not under the plot at all. It belongs to the card rather than to the plot. A control under the picture acts on the whole plot: all the cards, the whole selection or the whole view. A control on a card acts on that card alone.
The PDF has none of these controls, and it shows the bound the sentence named.


39.12.8 Your data on the page
Before you publish a brushed plot, know what data it carries. The browser redraws the plot as the reader drags, so the table has to be in the page. The page carries every row of the table, but only the columns the sentence names.
The rows are all there, though, each with its exact values in the columns the page carries. So check those values before you publish, the way you would check any file before sharing it. Plots that carry the table lists every kind of plot that carries its table, and what a saved SVG file carries instead.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.13 In short
A selection runs after the axes and statistics are computed: it dims rows, removes none, and leaves the axes where they were. The column decides the reading, a range for numbers and a set for categories. A bound tests a column’s values rather than a panel, so plots that brush the same column share the selection. Everything a brush needs is already inside the web page: every row of the table, but only the columns the sentence names.

title: 39  Selection
text:
39.14 What comes next
Selection is the last atom this book teaches. The chapters so far started from the grammar; the cookbook starts from your data instead: one variable first, then two, then more.

title: The cookbook
text:
The 1446 book ends its explanations with a list: ninety-four everyday words, written out in the new letters. Persimmon, ice, tiger, star. It shows usage, not rules: the new letters could spell the words of daily life.
You have now met every word of gog, and every way of joining them into a sentence. What is left is practice on real questions. This part is gog’s version of the 1446 list. It is organized by your columns and your question, because you know those before you know a chart’s name. You will not find a chapter called “Histograms”. You will find a recipe called How is a measurement distributed?, and the sentence that answers it. (If you already know the chart’s name, the chart names appendix translates it into a sentence.)
The recipes use the book’s shared tables, which you can download from The book’s data. Each recipe chapter shows the first rows of every shared table before drawing from it. The recipes use only atoms taught in Parts I to III, and most link back to the chapters that own their atoms.
Almost every recipe has the same shape: the question, the sentence that answers it, the plot, and a line or two on why it works. Many then show what is one atom away: the same sentence with one small change, such as an atom swapped or one of its arguments changed. That is the real lesson. A cookbook of finished charts teaches you charts. This one teaches you that the recipes are connected: swap one atom in a recipe and you have another.

title: 40  One variable
text:
40.1 How many of each?
You have one column. What can it tell you? Which question you can ask depends on the column’s type. With a categorical column you ask how many rows fall in each category. The invented count axis has moved to x, so each bar’s length is read from left to right. Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

title: 40  One variable
section: 40.2 What share of the whole is each?
text:
40.2 What share of the whole is each?
In both count plots above, Africa has the longest bar: 52 countries. A count alone cannot say whether 52 is many or few. The table holds 142 countries in all, so Africa holds 52 of the 142, a share of about 0.37. When the question is each continent’s share of the whole, swap count for proportion. The counts become fractions that sum to one:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent))






                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0.0 0.1 0.2 0.3  Proportion Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent.”
One atom away. Swap proportion back to count for the counts themselves. The bars above follow the order the continents first appear in the table. To draw them in another order, use order(), which sorts them by the values in a column of the table: order(continent) sorts them alphabetically, by their own names. The transform invents the share, so the table has no column of shares, and gog refuses order(proportion). Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

The first question is where the values cluster and how far they spread. bin cuts the axis into equal-width bins and counts the rows in each. bar draws those counts as touching rectangles, so a gap is a bin with no rows. “Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length.” The gap near 2.5 cm is an empty bin. No flower in the table has a petal length between 1.9 and 3.0 cm. One species has much shorter petals than the other two, and the empty bin is part of the space between them.
One atom away. When the automatic choice makes the shape hard to read, give bin a number of bins or a bin width. bin(30) asks for thirty bins; bin(width = 0.5) asks for bins 0.5 cm wide:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  x(col.petal_length))

The width 0.5 suits these lengths: they are recorded to one decimal place, so every bin holds exactly five possible values. Choosing a width explains how to pick a width for your own column.
A line * bin is the frequency polygon: a line through the same counts, placed at the center of each bin. Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

title: 40  One variable
text:
40.4 What is its smooth shape?
A histogram’s shape depends on the choice of bin edges. A reader can mistake that choice for a feature of the data. When the shape of the distribution itself is the answer, density draws a curve with no bin edges at all. Here is the histogram’s own column again, the petal lengths:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(col.petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + line * density + x(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(line, density), x(col.petal_length))






                               0 2 4 6 8   0.0 0.1 0.2  Density Petal Length





“Given the iris flowers: a line derived by density, x is petal length.” This answers the question the histogram answered, for the same column, with density in place of bin and a line to draw it. The two groups of petals are now two peaks, and the valley between them lies over the empty bin. Draw both when the number of peaks matters, because a histogram and a density curve can show a different number of peaks.
The curve starts below zero, although no petal is shorter than 1 cm. A density spreads each row into a small smooth bump, and the bumps of the shortest petals reach past zero.
The width of each bump is the bandwidth, and it sets how smooth the curve is. A number written alone multiplies the default bandwidth: density(0.5) is half as smooth as the default and density(2) is twice as smooth. density(bandwidth = 0.5) sets the bandwidth itself instead, in the column’s own unit, so here it is half a centimeter. Write one of the two forms, never both. Owning chapters: Line, Transforms.

title: 40  One variable
section: 40.5 How does the distribution look as a staircase?
text:
40.5 How does the distribution look as a staircase?
The histogram drew bin with bar. step can draw it too, tracing the bin tops as a staircase outline with no fill. It is most useful when several distributions share one axis, as in Many groups, because unfilled outlines do not cover each other. This plot draws the histogram’s distribution again, so you can compare the two marks directly:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(col.petal_length)


data(iris_flowers) + step * bin + x(:petal_length)


plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(step, bin), x(col.petal_length))






                               2 4 6   0 10 20 30 40  Count Petal Length





“Given the iris flowers: a step outline derived by bin, x is petal length.”
This is the histogram’s sentence with one atom changed, step in place of bar. The bins are the same, the empty one included, and only the mark that draws them changed. With the line * bin named earlier, that is three marks on one transform. That is the No Exceptions law: a transform behaves the same on every mark. Owning chapters: Step, Transforms.

40.7 What this section refuses
Every recipe above that used density or bin gave it a continuous column. Suppose you give density the continent column instead. density estimates a continuous distribution, so gog refuses the sentence. For a categorical column, use the share recipe in What share of the whole is each?. The message says which kind of column density needs, and it names the same fix, bar * proportion:

41.1 Are two measurements related?
You have two columns. What can they tell you together? The two kinds of column, continuous and categorical, decide which question you can ask. Two measurements ask about relationship: when one is high, is the other high too? When one measurement is a time, the question can be quantity: how large was the value in each year? A category and a measurement ask about comparison: is the measurement larger in some groups than in others?

title: 41  Two variables
section: 41.2 What is the trend through the points?
text:
41.2 What is the trend through the points?
The first scatter in this chapter draws one dot for each of 142 countries. The dots show that life expectancy rises with GDP per person. Below $5,000, though, they spread from 40 to 74 years, so the typical value is hard to see. You want the trend, and you still want every country on the page. Layering a derived line over the points gives you both. + puts both marks in one panel, and * smooth fits one trend curve through all the points:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth


(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth)


data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth


plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth))






                                                                                                                                                                                     0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania 





“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”
The curve climbs steeply on the left and much more slowly on the right. Most of its rise happens below $10,000 of GDP per person. At the far right the curve runs above the dots of the five richest countries. A smooth curve is least reliable at the edge of the data, where there are few points.
The positions are written before any mark, so both layers share them. color is written after point, so only the points are split into one group per continent. The curve is fitted to all 142 countries, not to any one continent. Owning chapters: Transforms for smooth, Encoding scope for that rule.

section: 41.3 How much was there at each time?
text:
41.3 How much was there at each time?
The second question in the opening was quantity, which pairs a time with an amount. The actuals table holds one sales figure per year. Sometimes the question is not whether sales rose but how large they were in each year. A line says where the value was; an area says how much there was. The fill is the quantity, so it starts from zero:

“Given the actuals: an area, x is year, y is sales.”
Sales stay between 120 and 168 in every year. Measured from zero, the fall in 2021, from 135 to 128, is small.
One atom away. Some quantities have no true zero, where zero means none at all, such as a temperature in degrees Celsius. For those, write line instead of area. Owning chapters: Line, Area.

title: 41  Two variables
section: 41.4 What is the typical value per group?
text:
41.4 What is the typical value per group?
The last question in the opening was comparison, which pairs a category with a measurement. Each continent holds many countries, and each country has its own life expectancy. To compare the continents you need one number for each, so you summarize the measurement within each category. The transforms that summarize this way are the aggregation family: sum, mean, median, max, min and quantile. Each one groups the rows by the category and reduces the measurement to one value per group. Only quantile needs a number of its own, the probability: quantile(0.9) gives the 90th percentile of each group. Here is mean, the average life expectancy in each continent:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
Oceania’s countries average 81 years and Europe’s 78, while Africa’s average 55.
One atom away. A few very high or very low values can change a mean noticeably. They change a median much less. When that matters, swap mean for median:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, median), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))






                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by median, x is continent, y is life.”
Africa’s bar falls by about two years and Asia’s rises by about the same. The other three change by less than a year. Where the two bars differ, a few very high or very low values have moved the mean. In Africa, seven countries live 71 to 76 years, well above the other 45. Owning chapters: Bar, Transforms.

title: 41  Two variables
section: 41.5 What does every value per group look like?
text:
41.5 What does every value per group look like?
A bar * mean gives each continent one number. That number hides how much life expectancy differs among the continent’s countries. Sometimes you want to see every country, not the mean. The plot that shows every row is the strip plot. Its sentence differs from the bar * mean sentence in two places: * mean is gone, and point is written where bar was. Each row is one dot, at its own height in its category’s slot:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life.”
On each vertical line, dots with nearly the same value cover each other, and * jitter spreads them sideways. It moves them along the category axis only, so every dot keeps its exact height. style() sets a value instead of mapping a column. Here it sets opacity to 0.6, below the default, so you can see where the dots overlap:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.6)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.6)


data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.6)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.6 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   40 50 60 70 80  Life Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life.”
One atom away. Swap the positions and the strips run horizontally, which helps when the category names are long. Owning chapters: Point, Transforms, Setting vs mapping.

title: 41  Two variables
text:
41.7 What this section refuses
Every recipe in this chapter used at least one continuous column. Suppose both of your columns are categorical, a country and its continent. You write bar, with one column on each axis. A bar needs at least one continuous axis, because the value on that axis is what sets the length of the bar. Two categories give the bar nothing to measure. The one number you can still make from them is a count of rows, so the refusal names count:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(country) + y(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(:country) + y(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), bar, x(col.country), y(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: `bar` has categorical columns on both axes — `x(country)` and `y(continent)` — so there is nothing for it to measure. One axis must be a number: that is the length of the bar. To count the rows instead, count one column, `bar * count + x(country)` or `bar * count + x(continent)`, and `color()` splits each bar by the other. To keep both, `bar * count + x(country) + y(continent) + space()` stands one bar on each pair in the cube.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Adding * count to this sentence still refuses. bar * count draws its count along the axis that has no column, so one axis must stay empty. To count the countries in each continent, remove country and write bar * count + x(continent), the sentence of How many of each?.

title: 42  A third variable, and more
text:
42.1 Which group does each row belong to?
You have more columns than the flat page has positions. Where do the rest go? x and y are already taken. A further variable can go in one of four places. The first is a refining channel: color, size, shape, pattern or opacity. The second is the third position, z. The third is play, which gives the variable one frame per value, and the fourth is facet, which gives it one panel per value. This chapter uses all four. Each channel answers one kind of question, and a refining channel gets the legend that decodes it.

42.3 How big is each observation?
The last two recipes put a category on a channel. This one puts a measurement there, and it returns to the countries. Population is a third measurement of each country, and both positions are already taken by GDP per person and life expectancy. A magnitude is carried by size. That channel answers the question how much, so it accepts a continuous column and nothing else:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript

  size(population)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  size(col.population))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  size(:population)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), size(col.population))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, size by population.”
The two largest circles are China and India. A legend decodes the radius. Owning chapter: Channels.

title: 42  A third variable, and more
text:
42.4 What if four variables matter?
The recipes so far bound color to the continent and size to the population, one column at a time. You may need both at once, to see which continent a country is in and how many people live there. Channels compose: any channel a mark accepts works beside any other channel it accepts. That rule is Orthogonality. GDP per person, life expectancy, population and continent in one sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point +
  x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + size(col.population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + size(:population) +
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.continent), size(col.population),
  title("The health and wealth of nations, 2007"))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  The health and wealth of nations, 2007 Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
Every channel keeps its own rule and its own legend; none of them changed meaning by being combined. Four variables are usually the most a single plot can carry. Beyond four, use panels instead of more channels.

section: 42.5 What if the third variable is continuous?
text:
42.5 What if the third variable is continuous?
Now return to three columns. A continuous third column does not have to go on size. Here population goes on color instead, so every dot keeps the same size and the color carries the number. color accepts either kind of column. A continuous column gets a sequential ramp, from light to dark, instead of a categorical palette. A skewed column reads better on a log ramp. On a linear ramp, China and India would sit alone at the dark end, and almost every other country would get the same light shade:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.population, scale = "log"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:population, scale = "log")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.population, { scale: "log" }))






                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Population         1.3B 16.2M 199.6K 





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by population on a log scale.”
The legend becomes a labeled ramp. The channel and its rule did not change; only the kind of column did. Scales owns the log scale.

section: 42.6 What if three measurements matter equally?
text:
42.6 What if three measurements matter equally?
The iris flowers from the grayscale recipe above carry three measurements each, and none of them is less important than the others. color or size would make the third measurement a refinement, and the plot would still be about the other two. When three measurements matter equally, the third one is a position, not a refinement. Put one measurement on each of x, y and z, and the plot becomes a cube:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species)


(data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.sepal_width) + z(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species))


data(iris_flowers) + point + x(:sepal_length) + y(:sepal_width) +
  z(:petal_length) + color(:species)


plot(data(iris_flowers), point, x(col.sepal_length), y(col.sepal_width),
  z(col.petal_length), color(col.species))






                                                                                                                                                                               8 7 6 5 4 3 2 6 4 2 Sepal Length Sepal Width Petal Length   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal length, color by species.”
Setosa sits apart, near the bottom of the cube, because its petals are short. Versicolor and virginica sit higher, and from this side they overlap.
One atom away. The viewing angle is a property of the space, not of the data. turn says which side of the cube you look at, and tilt says how high your eye is:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(sepal_length) + y(sepal_width) + z(petal_length) +
  color(species) +
  space(turn = -50, tilt = 15)


(data(iris_flowers) + point +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.sepal_width) + z(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) +
  space(turn = -50, tilt = 15))


data(iris_flowers) + point + x(:sepal_length) + y(:sepal_width) +
  z(:petal_length) + color(:species) + space(turn = -50, tilt = 15)


plot(data(iris_flowers), point, x(col.sepal_length), y(col.sepal_width),
  z(col.petal_length), color(col.species), space({ turn: -50, tilt: 15 }))






                                                                                                                                                                               8 7 6 5 4 3 2 6 4 2 Sepal Length Sepal Width Petal Length   Species    setosa  versicolor  virginica 





“Given the iris flowers: points, x is sepal length, y is sepal width, z is petal length, color by species, turned -50, tilted 15.”
From this side versicolor and virginica overlap less. Space owns the third dimension.
