42.7 What if the rows form a route?
Each flower in the iris cube is its own dot, and the order of the rows means nothing. Sometimes the order is what matters. Here are the two gliders from Path again. Each row records where one glider was at one moment, and that glider’s next row is two seconds later. So the rows have to be joined in the order they were recorded. The mark that joins rows in table order is path:

  color(glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) +
  color(col.glider) +
  title("Two gliders, one thermal"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + title("Two gliders, one thermal")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), title("Two gliders, one thermal"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude  Two gliders, one thermal  Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider.”
Each route rises because each glider gains altitude. Both gliders start at 900 meters and were recorded for the same 338 seconds. Bravo’s first point is drawn higher than Alpha’s, but only because it sits at the back of the cube. In this view, the back is drawn higher on the page. By the end, Bravo has reached about 2,500 meters and Alpha about 2,100, so Bravo climbs faster.
Nothing in the sentence draws a spiral. The sentence asks path to connect the rows in order. Each glider moves in a circle while it rises, so the connected rows form a spiral. Look at the crossings as well. At each one the route nearer to the eye is drawn over the route behind it, and which route is nearer changes as the two gliders climb. Neither route is drawn entirely in front of the other: the pieces of both routes are sorted by depth together, as Path explains.
Turn the view, and the same two routes answer a different question. No binding changes:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(thermals) + path + x(east) + y(north) + z(altitude) +
  color(glider) +
  space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead")


(data(thermals) + path + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.altitude) +
  color(col.glider) +
  space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead"))


data(thermals) + path + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider) + space(turn = 20, tilt = 80) +
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead")


plot(data(thermals), path, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider), space({ turn: 20, tilt: 80 }),
  title("The same two routes, seen from overhead"))






                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           200 0 -200 200 0 -200 2500 2000 1500 1000 East North Altitude  The same two routes, seen from overhead  Glider    Alpha  Bravo 





“Given the thermals: paths, x is east, y is north, z is altitude, color by glider, turned 20, tilted 80.”
Seen from nearly overhead the climb is no longer visible, and you are looking down at two circles, one inside the other. Bravo’s circle is half as wide as Alpha’s. Together, the two views show that Bravo climbs faster and turns in a tighter circle.
These two plots raise one more question. line, step, area and ribbon also join their rows, so why is path the only one of the five that takes z? The answer is the difference that separates path from line on the flat page: the order in which each one joins its rows. A path joins rows in the table’s order. That order does not depend on any axis, so a third axis does not change it. A line sorts its rows by x. In the cube, x is one of three equal positions. At some angles it points straight into the page, and then you cannot see the order the line was sorted in. That is why a rising route is drawn with path, and why line refuses z rather than draw a stroke you cannot read:

data(thermals) + line + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:altitude) +
  color(:glider)


plot(data(thermals), line, x(col.east), y(col.north), z(col.altitude),
  color(col.glider))

A `line` in space would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see, so this is refused rather than drawn. For a route through three dimensions use `path`, which is `line` with that sort removed: `path + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(altitude)`.

  title("A thousand earthquakes, and the sheet they lie on")

  z(col.elevation), color(col.magnitude), palette("viridis"),
  space({ turn: 120, tilt: 20 }),
  title("A thousand earthquakes, and the sheet they lie on"))

“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, color by magnitude.”
Color carries a fourth column here, the magnitude of each quake. The vertical axis is elevation, the height above sea level, so a quake 680 km down has the value −680. That is the deepest quake in the table.
The quakes are not scattered through the cube. They trace a sheet of ocean floor sinking into the earth. At this angle, east is on the left. The sheet begins near the surface at the eastern edge and dips west. About a third of the way from that edge, it is more than 600 km down. The shallower quakes farther west do not lie on this sheet. They form a separate group. That sheet lies in three dimensions, so drawing it takes three positions. Any two of them show it flattened onto the page.
Now cut the quakes into slices of depth and show the slices one after another. play(slab) steps through slab, a column that holds the depth in 90 km bands:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(east) + y(north) + z(elevation) +
  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) + play(slab)


(data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(col.east) + y(col.north) + z(col.elevation) +
  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) + play(col.slab))


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) + play(:slab)


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), space({ turn: 120, tilt: 20 }), play(col.slab))

In the web edition the frames play one after another. As they run, the points move down, and their eastern end moves west. That movement is the slope of the sheet, read one slice at a time. The frames are not time here. play advances through the levels of an ordered column, and whether that column measures years or kilometers is a fact about the column, not about play. The same atom that steps through years steps through depths here.
In the PDF, only the first frame is drawn, the slice from 0 to 90 km, and the panels below replace the motion. They lay the same slices out across the page instead of showing them one after another in time:

  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) | facet(col.slab, wrap = 4))


data(quakes_fiji) + point + x(:east) + y(:north) + z(:elevation) +
  space(turn = 120, tilt = 20) | facet(:slab, wrap = 4)


plot(data(quakes_fiji), point, x(col.east), y(col.north),
  z(col.elevation), space({ turn: 120, tilt: 20 }),
  across(col.slab, { wrap: 4 }))

“Given quakes Fiji: points, x is east, y is north, z is elevation, split into panel columns by slab, wrapped at 4.”
The eight panels share one set of scales. You compare two depths by looking from one panel to the next, not by remembering the frame that just played. Whether you choose panels or frames depends on your readers. Panels let them compare any two slices, and frames let them see the movement. Play owns that choice.

42.9 Which categories are alike?
The nutrients table gives the amount of five nutrients in each of eight foods. The question is which foods resemble each other, and which nutrients are found in the same foods. Two categorical axes and one value make a tile plot, with the amount on color. The slot order on each axis is the order the rows arrived in, and that order carries no meaning. So here the amount also sets the order of both axes. Build a cluster tree on each axis, then compose the three plots: the tree above, the tiles below it, and the second tree on the right. theme(legend = "bottom") puts the tile plot’s legend under the tiles, so the tree on the right stands next to them. title: 43  Over time
text:
43.1 How did it change?
How did a measurement change over time? Time is not a chart type in this grammar. It is a column like any other, and you decide where it goes. Most recipes here put it on x, which gives the familiar time series. One gives it to play instead, to show where earthquakes happened, one week at a time. The last section asks for one panel per year, which gog refuses.
The actuals table holds one sales figure per year. The question is whether sales rose or fell. A line with year on x answers it:
actuals: all 5 rows

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(actuals) + line + x(year) + y(sales)


data(actuals) + line + x(col.year) + y(col.sales)


data(actuals) + line + x(:year) + y(:sales)


plot(data(actuals), line, x(col.year), y(col.sales))






                                     2019 2020 2021 2022 2023   120 130 140 150 160 170  Sales Year
“Given the actuals: a line, x is year, y is sales.”
Sales rose over the five years, from 120 to 168, and fell only once, in 2021. A line sorts the rows by x and joins each row’s point to the next. With years on x, the stroke runs from the earliest year to the latest. Owning chapter: Line.
One atom away. If the question is how large sales were in each year, not whether they rose, swap line for area. An area fills from zero up to each value, so the height of the fill is the amount itself. Two variables draws that plot on this table.

title: 43  Over time
text:
43.2 How did several things change?
The recipe above needed only one line, because actuals holds one row per year. The gapminder_asia table holds five countries, each with one row for the same twelve years, 1952 to 2007. A zone needs sides, and a year is a number, which has no width. bin(width = 5) gives the years their sides. It cuts the axis into cells five years wide, from 1950 to 2010, and each cell holds one of the table’s twelve years. mean then colors each cell by life. Read across a row for one country’s change, and down a column to compare the countries in one year. Sorted this way, the colors run from dark at the bottom left (Afghanistan in 1952) to light at the top right (Japan in 2007). Life expectancy was higher in 2007 than in 1952 in every country, and Oman gained the most, from 38 years to 76. In Iraq, it fell from 65.0 years in 1987 to 59.5 in 1992, and it was still below 65 in 2007. Owning chapters: Zone, Channels.

The recipes so far put time on x or gave it to play. Suppose instead you want one scatter of GDP per person and life expectancy for each year, with the years side by side. One panel per year is what faceting does. A facet column names its panels, so it must be categorical, but year holds numbers. gog refuses the sentence, and the message names two fixes:

  across(col.year))




Error:
! gog: `facet(year)` splits on a number column, but a facet variable names the panels, so it must be a category column. Store `year` as text or categories before plotting, or cut it into named groups first.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The first fix turns year into text. The gm_eras table already holds each year as text, in the column era. Many groups draws a plot split by era, with one row of panels for each of the two years.

Each panel column holds one continent, and its two panels show 1957 and 2007, fifty years apart. Read a panel column downward to see what changed. The plot is split by era, not by year. A facet column must be categorical, because it names its panels, and year holds numbers. Over time shows the refusal you get for facet(year).

text:
44.6 Which group is biggest?
The medals table lists five countries, and the question is which of them won the most gold. A comparison is easiest to read when it is sorted. gog draws the categories of a column of text in the order their rows appear in the table, and order() lets you choose another order:

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + order(gold)


data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + order(col.gold)


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + order(:gold)


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), order(col.gold))






                                  Germany Russia Great Britain China USA   0 10 20 30 40  Gold Country





“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, smallest first.”
The bars rise from left to right, from Germany’s 17 gold medals to the USA’s 46, so the country with the most gold comes last. order() names gold here, not the categorical column country. You name the column that holds the values, and the categories are sorted by those values.
One atom away. desc = TRUE puts the largest first. The table already lists the countries from most gold to least, so with desc = TRUE the bars keep the table’s own order. A sentence with no order() draws the same plot. Writing the order anyway keeps the plot sorted if a later version of the table lists the countries in a different order.
order() overrides a declared order as well. The next recipe uses it another way: it sorts by a column’s declared order, not by size.

title: 44  Many groups
section: 44.7 Where does a population pyramid come from?
text:
44.7 Where does a population pyramid come from?
Two cities each have a population count in every age band, and the question is how the two age structures compare. The chart drawn for that question is the population pyramid. It is a named chart type, and no atom in the kernel carries that name. You never ask for a pyramid; you describe one.
The census table has three columns: an age band, a city (Busan or Seoul), and a population. age holds the band names as text, from 0 to 85, in a declared order from youngest to oldest. Each city has 18 bands, so the table holds 36 rows. The numbers are invented; the columns are the ones a census would hold.

The mirrored shape comes from one minus sign. Busan’s populations are negated, so Busan’s bars run to the left of zero. That is arithmetic, so it happens in the table, before the sentence:

mirrored <- census
mirrored$population <- ifelse(mirrored$city == "Busan",
                              -mirrored$population, mirrored$population)

The negation above is shown in R only; Python, Julia and JavaScript each negate a column in their own way. What follows is the sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(mirrored) + bar + y(age) + x(population) + color(city) +
  order(age, desc = TRUE)


(data(mirrored) + bar + y(col.age) + x(col.population) + color(col.city) +
  order(col.age, desc = True))


data(mirrored) + bar + y(:age) + x(:population) + color(:city) +
  order(:age, desc = true)


plot(data(mirrored), bar, y(col.age), x(col.population), color(col.city),
  order(col.age, { desc: true }))






                                                                              -40K -20K 0 20K 40K   0 5 10 15 20 25 30 35 40 45 50 55 60 65 70 75 80 85  Age Population  City    Busan  Seoul 





“Given the mirrored table: bars, y is age, x is population, color by city, ordered by age, largest first.”
No new atom, and none was needed. The pyramid comes from three rules the grammar already states. First, the engine takes the orientation from the bindings, so a category on y makes the bars horizontal. Second, a bar runs from the zero baseline to its value, on whichever side of zero that value is, so a negative bar is not a special case. It is the same rectangle, extending the other way. Third, stack is something you ask for, never something the engine does on its own. This sentence does not ask for it, so the two bars in one slot sit on opposite sides of zero. If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip() or matplotlib’s barh(), gog has no such word, because it would be a second way to say one thing.
order(age, desc = TRUE) is the atom from the medals recipe, used in a second way. There it named gold, a different column from the one on the axis. Here it names the categorical column itself, so it asks for that column’s own order: the declared order, youngest first. desc = TRUE reverses it. gog puts the first category at the top when the category is on y, so without desc = TRUE age 0 would sit at the top. A pyramid needs its youngest band at the bottom.
Now look at the left half of the population axis. It reads -40K, not 40K.
Many versions of this chart replace each tick’s text with its absolute value. The minus sign that placed one city’s bars then disappears. gog keeps every tick showing the number at its own position, and this plot shows why. If the ticks were relabeled, the axis would carry two ticks reading 40K. Only a reader who knows the convention would know that the left 40K marks the position -40K. That reader could read -40K just as well, so the relabeling does not help. Any other reader gets bars whose positions no longer match the numbers on the axis. gog gives you no way to write your own tick text, and Coverage lists that among the capabilities with no decision recorded. These reasons argue against adding one.

title: 44  Many groups
text:
44.8 What this section refuses
Most recipes here separated groups with color, group or a panel. shape separates categories too, with one glyph per category on a point, and you might expect the same on a bar. A bar is a rectangle; it has no glyph to vary, so shape on a bar is refused outright:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + shape(country)


data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + shape(col.country)


data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + shape(:country)


plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), shape(col.country))




Error:
! gog: `shape` cannot be bound to `bar` — a bar has no shape feature. Remove the `country` mapping from `shape`, or use a mark that maps it: `point`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The message says a bar has no shape feature, and tells you to remove shape or to use a mark that has one. point is the only mark that does. One rule table decides every pairing of a mark and a channel, and it makes no exception for any mark. The companion grid prints all of it.

title: The reasons
text:
The most remarkable chapter of the 1446 book is the one that explains why: why ㄱ (g) is shaped like the back of the tongue blocking the throat, why the vowels are built from three shapes. That chapter was lost for nearly five hundred years, so the world had the letters but not the reasons. A surviving copy was found in 1940. The letters worked the whole time. But a system whose reasons are lost cannot be extended, only used.
This part is gog’s reasons, published with the package on purpose. It states the nine laws the package never breaks. It says why the engine refuses what it refuses, and why every refusal comes with a direction. None of it is required to use gog. The earlier parts cite these laws by name, and never ask you to have read them. It is here for the moment you want to know why the grammar is shaped the way it is. The laws also let you predict what the engine will do in a case no chapter covers.
The laws all refuse the same thing, and it has a name: the expert’s shortcut. It saves an expert a few keystrokes and gives every beginner one more exception to learn.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.1 Law 1: Orthogonality
gog is governed by nine laws. They are not preferences or style guides; they are rules the package never breaks.
Every new feature, every argument, every naming decision is checked against these rules. If a proposed addition breaks one, it is rejected.
Laws 1 to 5 govern the grammar you write every day. Laws 6 to 8 govern the grammar’s structure: what composes, what renders, and what the engine may refuse. Those three follow Hangeul (한글), the Korean alphabet, most closely, and each opens with an example from it. Law 9 says what a specification is, and what it must never contain.
color works with point, line, bar, area, and every other mark. Whenever a mark’s geometry can show a channel, gog accepts that channel on that mark. A mark can still limit the kind of column: a bar takes a categorical color only.
One rule follows from this. A mark-specific version of a channel, such as point_color beside bar_color, breaks the law. The channel must be generalized, not specialized. This section shows no refusal, because gog has no mark-specific channel to refuse.

title: 45  Design laws
text: Every compatible atom combines with every other atom. No atom is redundant.

A transform behaves identically on every mark. No per-mark special cases. No silent letters.

Without this law you would have to learn each transform again for every mark that can read it. bin makes the same bins and counts the same rows, whichever mark reads it. Change only the mark, and what changes is the geometry:

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, beside a line derived by bin, x is life; above an area derived by bin, x is life, beside a step outline derived by bin, x is life.”
The same bins and the same counts are drawn four ways. You get rectangles, a line through the bin centers, that same line filled, and the counts as a staircase. Read any bar’s height, then read the same bin in the panel beside it: the number is the same. The transform never asks which mark will draw its result. A transform that one mark ignored would be a silent letter: a letter that is written but never pronounced, like the k in knife.
This is the hardest law to keep as the package grows. Every user request that begins “but for maps I need…” or “histograms are special because…” is asking for this law to be broken. The engine keeps the law in two places. The code that computes a transform never looks at the mark, and one table records a decision for every pair of a mark and a transform, even when the decision is a refusal.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.3 Law 3: Plain Names

Every taught name is a common English word. No acronyms. No abbreviations. Two words maximum, joined by _. The only exceptions are x, y and z.

If a new user has to look up what a name means, it fails this law. svg and gif are acronyms, but a new user does not have to look them up: they are the usual names of two file formats. So render_svg(), save_svg() and save_gif() keep them. The table pairs a name you may know from another library with the plain name gog uses:







The name you may know
The plain name here




alpha
opacity


loess, stat_smooth
smooth


coord_polar
polar


geom_point, aes
point, and channels called by their plain names: x( ), color( )


color_by, size_by
color, size



In the last row a word was removed rather than replaced: the by of color_by. A plotting library could reasonably write color_by(species) and size_by(population). The suffix marks the argument as a column, which adds nothing in gog, because every channel takes a column. Now read color(continent) aloud. It is “color by continent”. The word by is already in how you read the sentence, so writing it into the name says it twice. In Law 2’s terms, that is a silent letter, and every channel would have had to carry one.

45.3.1 One spelling of English
The same reasoning decides how words are spelled. gog writes American English everywhere: color, center, the gray palette, and every word of the kernel. There is no British alternative. ggplot2 takes both spellings, so scale_colour_manual() and scale_color_manual() are one function in that package. gog has one spelling and no second one to learn.
Two spellings for one word is a silent letter, and Law 2 refuses silent letters in the vocabulary as well as in the grammar. The person who already knows both spellings notices nothing. Everyone else has more to learn and more to check. If gog took both spellings, a reader of your code would have to know both, a search for color( would miss every colour(, and every list of the vocabulary would list some words twice.
Many readers meet the spelling rule for the first time by typing colour, so the refusal names the word to write instead:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(colour = "tomato")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(colour = "tomato")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(colour = "tomato")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ colour: "tomato" }))




Error:
! gog: `style(colour = )` is not a setting. gog spells it `color`: American English is the grammar's only spelling, and unlike ggplot2 there is no British alternative.


That refusal was for a setting, a fixed value written in style(). Writing colour as a channel is refused the same way. colour() is not a channel: it exists only so that gog can name the channel you meant.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + colour(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + colour(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + colour(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  colour(col.continent))




Error:
! gog: there is no `colour()` channel. gog spells it `color(<column>)`: American English is the grammar's only spelling, and unlike ggplot2 there is no British alternative.


border_colour, centre and palette("grey") are refused too, each with the American word in its message. A color value is different: it is one of the color names web pages use, not a word of the grammar, and that list holds both gray and grey.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.4 Law 4: Bind Once

A table is named once. Columns are then bare names. The nearest data() wins.

Other plotting libraries often repeat the table in every call, or quote each column as a string. Naming the table once is what lets the rest of the sentence read as plain words.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Correct: table named once, columns bare
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life.”
Quoting a column name is not a typo. It is a habit brought from other plotting libraries, so gog names the fix instead of only reporting the error:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y("life")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x("gdp"), y("life"))




Error:
! gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*: `x(gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.


This law makes a plot specification readable as an English sentence. It also lets gog refuse a quoted column as soon as the sentence runs, before the engine draws anything.
The law’s third line is about a second table. A data() written directly before a mark is the nearest one, and that mark reads it. Every other mark reads the plot’s table, the one named first. Data draws both cases.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.5 Law 5: Explicit Over Implicit

Short is better than long, unless short is ambiguous. Then write the longer form.

Implicit behavior saves typing now and costs clarity later. gog chooses clarity: when a short spelling would make a reader guess what the engine decided, gog asks you for the longer form.
This law also decides what an error message must say. A refusal tells you what gog cannot do and what to write instead, never only that something went wrong.

45.5.1 Setting is not mapping
The clearest case of a short spelling that would make a reader guess is one fixed color for every row. The spelling a reader might try first is color("red"): the same channel, with quotes to say that red is a value and not a column. The quotes cannot always decide. color("continent") is genuinely ambiguous: a column, or a color named “continent”. gog could decide by asking “is this a column in the table?”. Then the same expression would mean one thing with one table and something else with the next.
So gog does not reuse the channel. A fixed value gets a word of its own instead: mapping is a channel, and setting is style():


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.5)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.5))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 0.5)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ color: "seagreen", opacity: 0.5 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored seagreen, with opacity 0.5.”
Separating them also lets each operation follow its own rules. A mapping gets a legend and a setting does not. And line cannot map opacity, because one stroke has one opacity, but it can still set it.
ggplot2 puts the boundary between mapping and setting in a different place. There the boundary is a pair of parentheses: color = "red" inside aes() is a mapping, and the same words outside aes() are a setting. gog moves that boundary from a punctuation mark to a word, so the atom you write says which one you meant. The parentheses can fail in one way a word cannot. aes(color = "red") is legal, and it maps every row to one category whose only level is “red”. You get a legend with one entry labeled “red”, and points drawn in the palette’s first color rather than in red.


45.5.2 An unknown name must not become a default
A palette name that matches nothing could be answered two ways: refuse it, or quietly draw in the default colors. gog refuses, and the message lists every name it would have accepted:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + palette("red")


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + palette("red"))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent) +
  palette("red")


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), palette("red"))




Error:
! gog: `palette("red")` is not a known palette. Named palettes are gog, okabe, soft for categories; blue, viridis, magma, inferno, plasma, cividis, gray for numbers; blue_red, brown_teal for numbers that diverge from a center. `"red"` is a color, not a palette. To paint every mark one color use `style(color = "red")`; to give each category its own color, give `palette()` several colors, "red" among them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


A default breaks this law without announcing it: the plot still appears, so nothing looks wrong, and the person reading the plot is the one misled.


45.5.3 Illegal is not the same as unsupported
Refusing is not enough by itself. gog separates two kinds of refusal, because each one needs you to do something different:








Refusal
Meaning
What to do




Illegal
The grammar forbids it.
Rewrite the sentence.


Unsupported
The grammar allows it; this engine does not draw it.
Remove the atom the message names, or use one this engine draws.



Calling a valid combination “illegal” would teach you a rule that does not exist. So an Unsupported refusal says that the grammar allows the sentence and the engine does not draw it. An Illegal refusal gives the reason the grammar forbids it. Here are three Illegal refusals, each for a different reason:

# but a `line` is read along its x axis, and a cube has no left to right

data(medals) + line + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + z(col.silver)

Error:
! gog: `line` reads a *domain* left to right — it sorts by `x` and draws one value for each — and a cube has no left to right: `x` is one of three equal positions, and at some viewing angles it runs into the page and becomes depth. A `line` in space would be sorted by an axis the reader cannot see, so this is refused rather than drawn. For a route through three dimensions use `path`, which is `line` with that sort removed: `path + x(<a>) + y(<b>) + z(silver)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The third refusal is easy to mistake for an Unsupported one. It is not: the grammar forbids a 3-D line, and the refusal above gives the reason. In a cube you can look straight along x, and a line sorted along x would then have no order you can see. The refusal suggests path instead, which is line without that sort, and path draws in space.
An Unsupported refusal is worded differently. It says that what you wrote is valid grammar, but this engine does not draw it:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Unsupported: `z` is valid grammar for `text`; this engine does not draw it
data(medals) + text + x(country) + y(gold) + z(silver) + label(country)


data(medals) + text + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + z(col.silver) + label(col.country)


data(medals) + text + x(:country) + y(:gold) + z(:silver) +
  label(:country)


plot(data(medals), text, x(col.country), y(col.gold), z(col.silver),
  label(col.country))




Error:
! gog: `z` is valid grammar for `text`, but this engine does not draw it — `z(silver)` would have no visual effect. Remove it, or use a channel that renders.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


In every case gog refuses to render. It does not quietly drop the channel and return a plot that looks finished. A silently ignored mapping is a silent letter in software. You wrote it, and it changes nothing in the picture.
An Illegal refusal instead says why the grammar forbids what you wrote. That is the whole distinction. All four refusals are live: the engine prints them when this page is built. A check re-runs every refused sentence in the book, and fails if one draws a plot.


45.5.4 Drawing it anyway
Every refusal the engine makes ends with the same offer: fix it, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway. That switch turns refusals into warnings. You get the same message, in the same words, and the plot is drawn as well.
Set GOG_STRICT on a line of its own, before the sentence you want drawn. The table gives that line in each language, and the line that clears the variable again:








Language
Set it with
Clear it with




R
Sys.setenv(GOG_STRICT = 0)
Sys.unsetenv("GOG_STRICT")


Python
os.environ["GOG_STRICT"] = "0"
del os.environ["GOG_STRICT"]


Julia
ENV["GOG_STRICT"] = "0"
delete!(ENV, "GOG_STRICT")


JavaScript
process.env.GOG_STRICT = "0"
delete process.env.GOG_STRICT


Shell
export GOG_STRICT=0
unset GOG_STRICT



Only 0 works. GOG_STRICT=false and GOG_STRICT=no still refuse, because a switch this simple is better with one spelling than with a list of words to guess at.
What you get is the plot the engine can still draw. The refused mapping is not always dropped: bar + size(gold) draws the bars at one width, and beside them a size legend running from 17 to 46 that matches no bar. That mismatch is what the refusal was protecting you from.
GOG_STRICT then stays set for the rest of your session. That is the part to remember: every later refusal is a warning too, and after many warnings, people stop reading them. Clear it once you have seen the plot you wanted.
Your binding makes some refusals before the engine is ever asked. The switch cannot change those, because only the engine reads it, and the engine is never reached. Your binding catches a quoted column name, a British spelling such as colour, a sentence that does not begin with data(), and a malformed atom such as box(whiskers = "middle").

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.6 Law 6: Compositional Invariance

A composed sub-expression means the same thing in every context. No enclosing expression may silently reinterpret an inner one.

The Korean syllable 하 (ha) is pronounced identically in 하늘 (haneul, sky), 하루 (haru, a day), and 하지만 (hajiman, but). 하 can be reused because its sound never changes, not because it carries a meaning of its own. English letters do not keep their sound: “ough” is a different sound in though, through, thought, tough, cough, and bough. A gog expression must be 하, never “ough”: layering, faceting, or animating a plot may add to it, but may not change what the existing part meant.
You can see the law by using one sub-expression in two sentences. bar * bin is one sub-expression: a mark and its transform, composed once.


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life))






                                       50 60 70 80   0 10 20 30  Count Life





Now put that same sub-expression inside a faceted sentence:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) | facet(continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) | facet(col.continent)


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) | facet(:continent)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  across(col.continent))






                                    50 60 70 80   0 5 10 15                              50 60 70 80                                     50 60 70 80                                  50 60 70 80                              50 60 70 80      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Count Life





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
The enclosing expression added panels. It did not reinterpret the sub-expression: each panel bins and counts exactly as the single plot did. That is the whole law, and it is what lets you read a long sentence one piece at a time. A sub-expression can also be kept in a variable, and the variable then stands for bar * bin wherever you write it.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.7 Law 7: Minimum Syllable

A visible plot is a mark plus its required positions. A mark alone is silent; a position alone has no carrier.

In Hangeul the smallest pronounceable unit is a consonant plus a vowel: ㄱ (g) alone is silent, and 가 (ga) is the minimum syllable. A bare vowel cannot stand alone either: ㅏ (a) is written 아 (a), with the silent consonant ㅇ in front of it as its carrier.
A mark is the silent consonant: point with no positions draws nothing, because there is nowhere to draw it. gog refuses that sentence, and the refusal names each position that is missing:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(gapminder_2007) + point


data(gapminder_2007) + point


data(gapminder_2007) + point


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point)




Error:
! gog: `point` needs `x()` but none is set. Add `x(<column>)` — a point cannot be drawn without it.
gog: `point` needs `y()` but none is set. Add `y(<column>)` — a point cannot be drawn without it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Add x(gdp) and y(life) and the same sentence draws. A position with no mark is the vowel with no carrier: x(gdp) alone answers no question, because nothing says what sits at that x.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.8 Law 8: Pronounceable ≠ Usable

The grammar guarantees well-formedness, never good taste. Grammar is law; taste is advice.

꿲 (kkwek) obeys every Hangeul syllable rule and you can pronounce it, yet no Korean word uses it. Plots work the same way. This renders, because it is grammatically sound; whether it says anything is your judgment, not the engine’s:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


# Legal, and nearly invisible: the engine obeys the grammar and does not judge
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(opacity = 0.05)


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  style(opacity = 0.05))


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + style(opacity = 0.05)


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.05 }))






                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





It draws, and almost nothing is visible. No legal combination is ever refused for being ugly. A combination that looks pointless to one person can be exactly the plot another person needs.
The law has a second half, that well-formedness is enforced, and two space() arguments show it. space(turn = 390) is a full circle plus 30 degrees, so it is the same view as space(turn = 30), and gog draws it without comment. space(tilt = 95) is refused. The difference is not that one is uglier. A turn repeats every 360 degrees, so 390 is the same direction as 30, and you can stand there. A tilt stops at 90, where you are looking straight down, and going past 90 would turn the scene upside down. Taste never makes gog refuse a plot, and gog enforces well-formedness with no exceptions. Space shows both sentences, and shows why one of them is refused.
The engine will not judge, so here is the advice instead. gog exists so that you can describe a plot in clean, minimal syntax. It will let you combine anything the grammar allows, and that includes combinations that hide what you wanted to show. Leave out anything that does not help the reader see the main idea.
That advice is about the picture. A sentence needs the same care, because other people read it too. Two sentences can draw the identical plot while one is much harder to follow. As Law 4 says, a second data() applies only to the mark written directly after it, and the mark after that one reads the plot’s table again. A reader who does not know this reads such a sentence wrong. The grammar accepts the marks in either order, so the fix is a writing habit: write each mark next to the table it draws from. Data shows both orders.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.9 Law 9: Universal Transcription

A specification describes the visual, never one renderer’s drawing commands.

A specification is declarative: you say what you want to see, never how to draw it. The form is far older than software. “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light” (King James Bible, 1769, Genesis 1:3) states an outcome and nothing else. There is no procedure in it, no order of steps, and no mention of how the light is made. Every declarative sentence leaves that part out, and something else has to supply it. In gog the engine does, and every stroke on these pages was drawn from a sentence that never mentioned strokes.
What you write becomes a small, renderer-neutral specification: which marks, which columns on which channels, which transforms. One renderer reads that specification, and that renderer draws every SVG on these pages. The same specification, unchanged, is what all four bindings build. Being renderer-neutral also means that a specification holds no drawing command, such as “draw a line from here to there”: it says what to see, and the renderer decides how to draw it.

45.9.1 Why that renderer writes SVG
The law says the specification is neutral. It does not say which format the renderer writes, and SVG is a choice with reasons.
The first reason is visible in the picture itself. An SVG stores shapes and coordinates, not a grid of colored dots. A plot therefore redraws at any size it is given, and stays sharp at every one. Print one at poster size and its curves are still curves.
The second is that text stays text. Every axis label, tick number and title is written as characters in the file, not drawn as a picture of characters. You can select them, a search can find them, and a screen reader can read them aloud. It is also what lets a plot in this book carry Hangeul, or any other writing system, without the engine drawing a single letter: it writes the characters, and the font draws them.
The third reason is the one this project depends on most, and it is the least obvious. An SVG is a text file, so two of them can be compared character by character. That is what makes the promise of four bindings checkable: every sentence in this book is drawn from R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, and the four files must match exactly. Comparing pictures instead would mean comparing colored dots, and those dots change with the version of whatever drew them. An exact test would become an approximate one, and a small disagreement between two languages could be mistaken for a rounding difference.
The fourth is motion. A play animation is written into the same file as the plot, using SVG’s own timing elements. A time-lapse is one picture that moves, with no video file and no JavaScript beside it.


45.9.2 Why there is one renderer
Those four reasons decide the format. One question is left: why only one renderer writes it. gog has exactly one renderer, and the reason is the set of decisions a second renderer would have to copy.
A renderer decides five things the specification does not name: layout, tick selection, palettes, axis ranges, and label formatting. Write a second renderer beside the first and those five decisions exist twice. Two copies of a decision do not stay equal. One renderer would put ticks at 0, 20 and 40, the other at 0, 25 and 50, and one specification would then draw two different pictures.
That would break Law 9 from the renderer’s side: one specification would no longer describe one picture, and nothing in the design would show it. So there is exactly one renderer. A second one is possible only once those five decisions live in a single shared layer that both would read.
Raster output, a picture stored as a grid of colored dots such as a PNG file, comes from converting the SVG rather than from a second renderer. render_svg(), described in Functions around the grammar, returns the plot as ordinary text. It has the same name in all four languages, and the block below is R:

svg <- render_svg(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life))
cat(substr(svg, 1, 51))

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="800"


Those are the first 51 characters; svg holds the whole plot, about 15,000 of them. Write it to a file and you have the plot on disk. A tool that reads SVG can convert that file to another format. rsvg-convert, a command-line SVG converter, gives you a raster image with rsvg-convert -w 1600 plot.svg -o plot.png, and its -f pdf option is what places each plot in this book’s PDF. Converting is the deliberate answer rather than a missing feature. It keeps every decision about what a plot looks like in the one place that is allowed to make them, which is exactly what Law 9 requires.
The engine does that conversion itself in one case, and that case shows where drawing stops and converting begins. A plot that binds play() moves in a browser and nowhere else, so save_gif() writes the same sequence as a picture that a slide or a message will play. That is still conversion in the sense this section means. The frames are drawn by the one renderer, and the GIF writer only turns them into pixels. It chooses no tick and no layout. Its one decision is how to fit each frame into the 256 colors a GIF file can hold.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.10 The settable rule
The nine laws are stated. One case needs a full explanation: a setting. It is where readers most often expect to find an exception.
A setting (style(…)) is an atom like any other, so Orthogonality and No Exceptions govern it as well. A setting is available on every mark whose geometry can carry it, and it behaves the same way on all of them. That uniformity is No Exceptions: there is no mark-specific gap you have to memorize. A setting is absent only where composing two marks already says the same thing better, and that absence follows Law 1’s second line: no atom is redundant.
style(border_color =, border_size =) draws an outline distinct from the fill. It is available on all five closed-shape fills: bar, box, point, zone and surface. No second layer can draw their perimeter, so a setting is the only way to draw it. An area or a ribbon is filled too, but a layered line traces its edge, so neither takes a border. The letters of a label are filled shapes too, so text takes both settings, and there they draw a halo, a band of color under the letters. One setting takes one form in each class, as pattern does below.
style(pattern = ) gives a mark’s paint a texture, and each class of geometry shows that texture its own way. On the six path strokes (line, step, interval, path, rule, edge) it is a dash. On the five filled regions (bar, box, area, ribbon, zone) it is a hatch. One setting takes one form in each class. That is what color already does: a stroke on a line, a fill on a bar.
A curve fill (area, ribbon) takes the hatch, because a region can be textured. It takes no border, because its edge is a data curve, which already is a line (area + line, line * bounds) and can do more than any border. The class decides which settings a mark takes, not the individual mark, and Setting vs mapping defines each class.
This prevents one particular surprise: you learn a setting on one mark, then find it missing on a sibling mark for no reason you can see. A setting written outside its class is refused, and the refusal is Illegal: the grammar forbids it.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.11 Why these laws matter
Each law refuses the same thing, the expert’s shortcut: a special case that saves an expert a few keystrokes and gives every beginner one more exception to learn. Nobody asks for it by that name. It arrives as a request like these:

“Can bar have a different color scale than point?”
“Can smooth have a span parameter?”
“Can I just write alpha? Everyone knows what it means.”

Each one is reasonable on its own, and each one costs more than the one before it: the tenth exception makes the first nine harder to remember.
The laws are the answer: not “no, because we don’t want to,” but “no, because that would break Law 2 / Law 3 / …” The rule, not the maintainer, says no.

title: 45  Design laws
text:
45.12 What comes next
The laws say what the grammar will and will not do, in any language. R opens the four chapters that say what belongs to your language instead, such as how you install gog and how it reads from a database.




King James Bible. (1769). Oxford University Press.

title: The host language
text:
The 1446 book had no host language to explain: its letters were the whole system. gog’s letters are typed in four programming languages, and this part says what each language adds.
Everything so far has been the same in every language, because the grammar does not change with the language you type it in. One engine reads one specification, so the same sentence draws the same plot in every language.
Some things belong to the language you type in rather than to the grammar, and they cannot be stated once for everybody. How does a table reach data()? How does a plot display where you work? How does gog’s + work beside the operators the language already has? Those are real questions. One answer in the grammar chapters would be wrong for readers of the other three languages.
Each of the four languages has a chapter here (Bezanson et al., 2017; Ecma International, 2025; R Core Team, 2026; Van Rossum & Drake, 2009). A language’s gog package is called a binding. The same word also names a channel with its column, such as x(gdp); in this part, binding means the package. The grammar chapters mention a language only where something belongs to that language alone, such as R’s factor(), and this part holds the rest.
The four chapters are ordered R, Python, Julia, JavaScript, and the order has a reason. You write the same sentence in the first three. The operators are identical, and the main change is the column name: a bare gdp, then col.gdp, then :gdp. Values such as TRUE and c("a", "b") also take each language’s own spelling. If you have read the R in this book you can read the Python and the Julia already. JavaScript is the one that genuinely reads differently. It is the only one of the four that cannot give +, *, | and / new meanings, so it spells them as words. It is last for that reason, so the pattern the other three share is read first.
The claim that one sentence draws one plot in every language is tested. Every sentence in this book that describes a plot was translated into each language and drawn by its binding, and the four plots match byte for byte. The four bindings refuse the same sentences: in the engine’s own words where the engine refuses, and in each language’s own spelling where the binding refuses. The test skips only the sentences about a host language itself, and two that write a file rather than draw a plot.




Bezanson, J., Edelman, A., Karpinski, S., & Shah, V. B. (2017). Julia: A fresh approach to numerical computing. SIAM Review, 59(1), 65–98. https://doi.org/10.1137/141000671


Ecma International. (2025). ECMAScript 2025 language specification (16th ed.). Ecma International. https://www.ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-262/


R Core Team. (2026). R: A language and environment for statistical computing. R Foundation for Statistical Computing. https://www.R-project.org/


Van Rossum, G., & Drake, F. L. (2009). Python 3 reference manual. CreateSpace. https://www.python.org/

title: 46  R
text:
46.1 Pipes
Every sentence in this book so far was written first in R, and each tab for another language shows a translation of it. So this chapter adds nothing to the grammar. It answers the six questions R raises. The first two are how the two pipes reach data() and how R groups the operators. Then come where a plot appears, which of gog’s words R’s own packages already use, how a database table reaches a plot, and how the package installs. Data covers what a table is and how you pass one. A table is an ordinary R data frame, and needs no package of its own.
Every R block on this page ran when the page was built, except the database and install commands, which are shown but not run. Every plot came from the same engine every other chapter uses.
Much R code prepares a table in a chain of steps joined by a pipe, and you will often want the last step to be a plot. R has two pipes in common use, and which one you write decides whether gog learns the table’s name (Data explains why the name matters). Write the native pipe, |>: it keeps the name, and draws exactly the plot that data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) draws.

quote(gapminder_2007 |> data() + point + x(gdp) + y(life))

Two facts about R make that work, and both are needed.
The first is precedence, the order in which a language groups its operators (Operators). |> groups before +, so gapminder_2007 |> data() is complete before + joins anything to it. * groups after |> and before +, so a transform still joins its mark first:

That timing matters because data() reads the table’s name from the expression you wrote, and the native pipe leaves that expression a bare name. data() keeps the name as well as the rows (Data), and a later layer looks up its columns in the table with that name.
The piped table fills the first argument, so any argument you write yourself follows it:

title: 46  R
text:
46.2 If your code uses %>%
The magrittr pipe, %>%, is the one most R code still uses, and it does not keep the table’s name. It is an ordinary function rather than a rule of the parser, so it evaluates the left side and gives data() the placeholder . instead of the table’s name:

library(magrittr)
gapminder_2007 %>% data() + point + x(gdp) + y(life)

Warning: gog: magrittr's `%>%` replaced this table with its placeholder `.`
before `data()` could read the name, so gog calls the table `data`, or `data2`
and on when that name is taken. Either name it — `data(name = "...")` — or use
R's native pipe, which keeps the name: `df |> data()` reads as `data(df)`.




                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





The plot is correct. With one table, the missing name changes nothing in the plot, but gog warns you anyway and says how to supply it. Either use the native pipe, or name the table yourself:

gapminder_2007 %>% data(name = "gapminder_2007") + point + x(gdp) + y(life)



                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





Only the placeholder . raises that warning. The native pipe raises none, even when what you pipe in is an expression rather than a bare name. Its most useful case is filtering the table before data(). Unlike ., that expression is different for every table, so gog uses the whole expression as the table’s name.

gm_all |> subset(year == 2007 & continent == "Europe") |> data() +
  point + x(gdp) + y(life)



                                                                  10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   72 74 76 78 80 82  Life Gdp





gog drops the quotation marks, so the table there is called subset(gm_all, year == 2007 & continent == Europe). That name is long, and it still works. name = gives the table a shorter name:

gm_all |> subset(year == 2007 & continent == "Europe") |> data(name = "europe") +
  point + x(gdp) + y(life)



                                                                  10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   72 74 76 78 80 82  Life Gdp

46.3 Two tables with one name
The name matters once a plot has two tables. A second data() gives a layer its own table, and the “nearest table wins” rule finds each table by name. So gog refuses two different tables that you gave the same name:

  data(forecast, name = "series") + point

  data(forecast, name = "series") + point)

  data(forecast, name = "series") + point

  data(forecast, { name: "series" }), point)




Error:
! gog: two different tables are both called `series` — a layer resolves its bare columns against the nearest table by name, so one of these can never be reached. Give them distinct names: `data(name = "...")`.


Without that refusal the plot would draw the first table twice and report the second table’s columns as misspellings. You would have spelled the columns correctly, and gog would have checked them against the wrong table. Two %>% tables do not cause this refusal. gog calls them data and data2, warns once for each, and draws the plot. Naming the tables yourself removes both warnings.

title: 46  R
section: 46.4 What the pipe does not change
text:
46.4 What the pipe does not change
The pipe supplies the table that data() names. It does not replace +, and there is no piped form of the rest of the sentence. Marks, channels, and transforms compose with + and * as they do everywhere else in this book. gog has no pipe of its own, because R already has two.
The pipe question is R’s alone. Julia has a |>, but Julia’s data() never reads a table’s name from your code, so its pipe changes nothing. Neither Python nor JavaScript has a pipe operator. The other three chapters do not raise it.

title: 46  R
text:
46.5 The operators, and their precedence
That was the first question. The second is how R groups the four operators of a sentence. The pipe section used one case of precedence: |> groups before * and +. Among gog’s operators, R groups * and / first, then +, then |. That order is R’s, not gog’s, so it applies to every sentence you write (What groups first).
In that order, one plot needs no parentheses, even with a facet. A page is different, because R groups / before + and | after it. gog draws a page written with | and no parentheses, because | groups last, after both plots are complete. It refuses the same page written with /, because / joins the first plot’s last atom to the second plot’s data(). Inside a page, / also groups before |, so a | b / c is read as a | (b / c). And a theme() added after a page with no parentheses around it goes to the second plot, not to the page, because + groups before |.
So write each plot on a page inside its own parentheses, whichever operator joins them. Put a page inside a page in parentheses too, and the whole page before a theme() for it. The page then means the same thing in all three languages, including Julia, which groups | together with + (Parentheses on a page).

title: 46  R
text:
46.6 Showing the plot
The third question is where a plot appears once you have written its sentence. You do not call anything to show it: R shows a plot as soon as you run its sentence, and where it appears depends on where you work:

At the console, it opens in the viewer pane of RStudio or Positron. Without a viewer pane, it opens in your web browser.
In a Quarto or R Markdown document, it is drawn under the chunk, as every plot in this book is.
In a Jupyter notebook with the R kernel, it appears under the cell. print() shows it too, so a loop can show several plots one after another.

To keep the drawing itself, render_svg() returns it as text.

title: 46  R
text:
46.7 Twenty names R already uses
The fourth question is which of gog’s words are already R’s. Twenty of the names gog provides are also names in the packages R loads when it starts, and library(gog) lists eleven of them. Here are all twenty:



from
names




stats
density line median quantile smooth step


graphics
box layout text title


grDevices
palette


utils
data stack


base
jitter max mean min order range sum



Nine of the twenty cannot affect an ordinary call, and library(gog) leaves those nine out of its message. A rule in R itself is the reason. A mark that takes no argument is an object rather than a function, and so is a transform that takes no argument. When R evaluates a call, it looks for a function of that name and skips any object of that name that is not a function. So a call still reaches base R’s mean, even though library(gog) attached its own:

is.function(mean)   # gog's `mean` is an object, so a call cannot reach it

[1] FALSE

mean(1:10)          # and base R's function answers anyway

[1] 5.5


The same is usually true when you pass mean to another function, because most functions look the name up the same way; the exceptions come later in this chapter:

sapply(gapminder_2007["life"], mean)

    life 
67.00742 


The other eleven are functions, and a call does reach gog’s: box, data, density, jitter, layout, order, palette, quantile, range, stack and title. To choose one, give it a prefix: the package’s name and ::, as in base::order. Both remain available:








you write
you get
for R’s own, write




order(population)
the plot’s sort order
base::order(df$population)


data(gapminder_2007)
the plot’s table
utils::data(mtcars)


density(2)
the density transform
stats::density(x)


jitter(0.5)
the offset transform
base::jitter(x)


layout(exporter, importer)
the layout transform
graphics::layout(mat)


quantile(0.9)
the 90th percentile transform
stats::quantile(df$gdp)


range(0.25, 0.75)
the band transform
base::range(df$gdp)


stack(share = TRUE)
the piling transform
utils::stack(df)


palette("soft")
the plot’s colors
grDevices::palette()


title("Life expectancy")
the plot’s title
graphics::title(main = "…")


box()
the box-and-whisker mark
graphics::box()



gog’s range takes two numbers, so it is a function rather than an object, and R does not skip past it. Writing range(0.25, 0.75) therefore reaches gog’s range and never base R’s. gog then reads the argument you passed. If you pass a vector where gog expects two numbers between 0 and 1, you meant base R’s range, and gog’s refusal says so:

range(c(3, 1, 4, 1, 5))

Error:
! gog: `range()` takes the band's two ends, each one number between 0 and 1, e.g. `range(0.25, 0.75)`. It was given 5 numbers. For the smallest and largest of a vector, gog masks that name: use `base::range()`.


Of the eleven, order causes the most errors, because you often sort a table while you are making plots. gog’s order returns an atom, not the row positions that [ expects. Without a refusal, R would stop with invalid subscript type 'list', which names neither order nor gog. So whenever the argument is not a bare name, the refusal says which function you reached and how to reach the other one:

gapminder_2007[order(gapminder_2007$population), ]

Error:
! gog: `order(gapminder_2007$population)` is not a column name. gog's `order()` takes a bare column, as in `order(population, desc = TRUE)`. To sort a vector, the base function is still there as `base::order(gapminder_2007$population)`.


With the prefix, it sorts:

ranked <- gapminder_2007[base::order(-gapminder_2007$population), ]
head(ranked[c("country", "population")], 3)

          country population
25          China 1318683096
59          India 1110396331
135 United States  301139947


Several other chapters write base::order for exactly this reason.
Three of the eleven refuse nothing, because gog cannot tell from the argument which function you meant. data(mtcars) is well formed for both. It starts a plot and raises no complaint, so write utils::data() when you mean to load a dataset. title("...") is the same case: a string is what both want. So is box(), which both accept with no argument at all. Six of the others report the mistake, because what R’s function usually takes, a vector, a matrix or a table, is an argument gog refuses. The last two catch only part of it. order reports order(df$population) but not order(pop), where pop is a bare name holding a vector. palette reports palette() but not palette("R4"), because a palette name is what both want.
The names stay as they are, because renaming order to sort_by would replace a word every reader knows with one that only gog uses. The grammar chapter gives the full reason and compares how each language handles a name it already uses. R’s own packages are not the only source of a collision. Another package may define a name gog also defines. Load gog with library(gog) after that package, so R finds gog’s name first, or write the name with the prefix gog::.

title: 46  R
section: 46.8 Five calls that still need a prefix
text:
46.8 Five calls that still need a prefix
The nine words that are objects in gog, such as mean, are safe in ordinary code, and sapply() was only one example: lapply(), tapply(), mapply(), Map(), Reduce() and apply() are all safe for the same reason.
Five ways of writing a call still fail, for two different reasons. The first is a name that one function passes to a second function before R looks it up:

aggregate(life ~ continent, gapminder_2007, mean)

Error in `get()`:
! object 'FUN' of mode 'function' was not found


When R finally looks the name up, it is looking for FUN, the name aggregate() gave the function you passed, and not for mean. So the message names neither mean nor gog. by() and ave(..., FUN = mean) fail the same way. Writing base::mean fixes all three. The data frame form of aggregate() looks the name up one step earlier, so aggregate(gapminder_2007["life"], gapminder_2007["continent"], mean) works unchanged.
The second reason is a name used as a value rather than called. do.call(sum, list(x)) wants a function and receives an object, so write do.call("sum", list(x)) or do.call(base::sum, list(x)). And f <- mean copies the object, so f(x) reports that it could not find a function called f.
That is the whole cost, and one habit avoids all five failures: when you pass one of those nine words to another function, or store it in a variable, write it with its prefix, as in base::mean. The functions listed above work without the prefix, but the prefixed name works everywhere. Only four of the nine are base R’s own: max, mean, min and sum. line, median, smooth and step belong to stats, and text belongs to graphics, so write stats::median; base::median is itself an error.

title: 46  R
text:
46.9 Reading from a database
The fifth question is how a table in a database reaches a plot. query() runs a query on a database, and it takes a DBI connection. DBI is R’s database standard, so the same call reaches SQLite, Postgres, MariaDB, BigQuery, and anything with an ODBC driver.
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "sales.db")

query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(status) + y(revenue)
DBI and the drivers are optional: gog’s DESCRIPTION file lists DBI and RSQLite under Suggests, R’s field for optional packages, so installing gog does not install them. If you never write SQL, you need neither. If you do, install DBI and the one driver your database needs:
install.packages(c("DBI", "RSQLite"))    # or RPostgres, RMariaDB, odbc, bigrquery
You open the connection with DBI yourself, as the example above does, and pass it to query(). gog never opens one and never stores a password. Data covers what query() sends and how much data comes back.

title: 46  R
text:
46.10 Installing gog
The last question is how you install gog. Every plot is drawn by the engine, a separate program written in Rust, so the R package has to be able to find it. An installed copy of the package carries its own engine. The package’s configure script, which runs during the install, puts the engine inside the package, and it stops the install rather than leave you a package that cannot draw.
install.packages("gog", repos = c("https://psychometrician.r-universe.dev",
                                  "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
gog is published on r-universe. For the current version of R and the one before it, r-universe builds a ready-to-install copy of the package for macOS and Windows, with the engine already inside it, so installing needs no Rust toolchain. With an older version of R, the command installs from source, as it does on Linux.
On Linux the same command installs from source, and the source build compiles the engine. That needs Rust 1.75 or newer and a network connection. If the machine has no Rust, or only an older version, install the latest version first:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
Then install gog with the install.packages() call at the start of this section. The build runs once, while the package installs.
The repos argument names two addresses because gog is not on CRAN. The first address is the r-universe repository that holds gog. The second is an ordinary CRAN mirror. It is there for jsonlite, the one package gog needs that r-universe does not hold.
There is another way to install gog: straight from its source code on GitHub, for when you want a particular version rather than the build r-universe published. It needs the remotes package first, so install that if you do not have it:
install.packages("remotes")
Then install gog:
remotes::install_github("psychometrician/gog", subdir = "r-pkg/gog",
                        build = FALSE)
A download from GitHub holds the whole repository, including the engine’s Rust source code, and configure compiles the engine during the install. So installing this way needs Rust 1.75 or newer on every system, including macOS and Windows, where the r-universe install needs no Rust. The build = FALSE argument keeps the Rust source in the download. Without it, remotes first copies the package folder alone into a new archive, the Rust source is left out, and the install stops with a message that names the argument. To install one particular branch, tag or commit instead of the newest, add ref = "name" to the call.
You can also work from a checkout, a copy of gog’s source repository on your own computer; that is how you change gog itself. Besides the packages that come with R, gog needs one package, jsonlite, which turns the sentence you write into the JSON that the engine reads. install.packages() and remotes::install_github() both install it along with gog. Loading from a checkout needs pkgload as well, which loads a package from a folder instead of from a library. Working from a checkout installs neither, so install both if you do not have them:
install.packages(c("jsonlite", "pkgload"))
If one is missing, the step that needs it stops immediately, and the message names the missing package.
Then, from the checkout’s top folder, build the engine once (this needs Rust) and load the package from its folder:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
pkgload::load_all("r-pkg/gog")
If you change gog’s source, installing from the checkout checks more than loading it does, because the install runs configure, which puts the engine inside the installed package:
R CMD INSTALL r-pkg/gog
The R package looks for the engine in five places. In order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, a target/ build in a surrounding checkout, the copy inside the installed package, gog-cli on your PATH, and last a search upward from the working directory. A checkout is searched before the bundled copy on purpose. Inside a checkout the bundled engine is a copy an earlier install left behind. Using it would draw with an old engine while you are changing the engine’s source.

title: 46  R
text:
46.11 What comes next
R’s sentence is the one every chapter before this has written. Python writes the same sentence with col.gdp where R writes a bare name, and draws the same picture, byte for byte.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.1 A column is written col.gdp
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in Python as it is in R. What differs is short enough to state in one chapter. The sections below cover how a column is named, how a sentence is written over several lines, how values are written, and what counts as a table. Then come computed columns, showing a plot, and the six names Python already uses. After them comes the operators section. Python groups the operators in the same order as R, and a page needs two kinds of parentheses. The vocabulary and the refusals follow, and they do not change. Reading from a database and installing the package come last.
Every Python block on this page was run when the page was built, through the same engine every other chapter uses. Each block runs after from gog import *, and after gapminder_2007 is read as the section The table shows. The blocks leave those lines out. The database and install commands at the end are shown, not run.
In Python, gog marks each column with four characters, col., so that a column is never mistaken for a value. R writes a column as a bare name and Julia as a symbol. Python writes it through col, a small object called an accessor: col.gdp names the column gdp:
gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows
