data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale='log') + y(col.life) + color(col.continent)


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
This is the sentence from A first plot, without its title and with col. in front of each column. The four characters are needed because R and Python pass an argument differently. In R, the call x(gdp) receives the word gdp itself, not a value. Python always passes values, so a bare gdp would have to be a variable you defined earlier. In this grammar, a plain string is how you spell a value: style(color="tomato"), title("…"), palette("okabe"). Without the accessor, a column and a value would both be plain strings, and gog could not tell which one you meant.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x('gdp') + y(col.life)
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. Python has no bare names, so a column is written with the accessor: `x(col.gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.
The message names the column spelling, x(col.gdp). Where one name is both a channel and a setting, such as color, the message gives both spellings, because the two do different things. A channel maps a column and the plot gets a legend for it; a setting sets one value and gets none (Setting vs mapping). The opposite mistake, a column where a value belongs, is refused the same way:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + style(color=col.continent)
gog: `style(color=)` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `col.continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(col.continent)`.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.1.1 Names that need brackets
After col., Python accepts only an identifier: a name made of letters, digits and underscores that does not start with a digit. Any other name is written in square brackets instead: col["life exp"], col["gdp.2007"], col["2007"]. Inside the brackets the name is a string, but col still marks it as a column. Be careful with a hyphen: Python reads col.life-exp as col.life minus a variable named exp, so write col["life-exp"].
Python also keeps some words for its own syntax, such as class, from and global. These reserved words need brackets too: col["class"]. If you write col.class, Python stops with SyntaxError: invalid syntax before any gog code runs. Unlike gog’s messages above, this message comes from Python, so it cannot tell you to write col["class"]. help("keywords") prints the full list.
A name in another writing system needs no brackets: col.국가 (country) works with the dot. Python accepts letters from any writing system in a name. The bracket form works for any name.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.2 A sentence over several lines
The second thing you type differently is about lines rather than names. R continues a line that ends in +. Python ends the statement there, so a sentence spanning several lines is wrapped in parentheses:


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale='log') + y(col.life)
 + color(col.continent) + size(col.population)
 + title('Wealth and life expectancy, 2007'))


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Wealth and life expectancy, 2007 Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
That is Python’s rule about lines, not a rule of gog’s. Those parentheses and the accessor are nearly the only things you will type differently. The rest is as in R, except that values take Python’s spelling.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.3 How values are written
In the other chapters, a code block that is a sentence has a tab for each language. Code written inside the text has none, so it is written in R, as in x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)). Most of it reads the same in Python once col. is written before each column. The values are what change. R writes several values inside c(), and Python writes them in a list, inside square brackets. The table gives the Python spelling of each kind of value the book uses:








Kind of value
R
Python




true or false
TRUE, FALSE
True, False


several numbers
c(37.5, 87.5)
[37.5, 87.5]


several strings, such as colors
c("tomato", "steelblue")
["tomato", "steelblue"]


a color for each category
c(Asia = "tomato", Europe = "steelblue")
{"Asia": "tomato", "Europe": "steelblue"}


a missing value
NA
None


the number e
exp(1)
math.e, after import math


a declared order
factor(values, levels = c("Low", "High"))
ordered(values, ["Low", "High"])



So x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) in the text is x(col.life, limits=[37.5, 87.5]) in Python. A tuple works too: limits=(37.5, 87.5). A named argument is written as in R, because Python has named arguments of its own: legend = FALSE is legend=False. ordered() declares the order of a column’s categories, as R’s factor() does. The next section says more about it, and about a pandas column that already carries an order.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.4 The table
The simplest table is a dict of columns, so a first plot needs no package besides gog:


data({'level': ['Low', 'Medium', 'High'], 'count': [30.0, 20.0, 10.0]},
     name='small') + bar + x(col.level) + y(col.count)


                            Low Medium High   0 10 20 30  Count Level




“Given the small table: bars, x is level, y is count.”
Any object with a .columns attribute that you can index by column name is also a table, which covers pandas and polars. The binding imports neither one, so neither is a dependency. You read a file the way you already do. GAPMINDER_CSV here is the path to the book’s gapminder_2007.csv, and The book’s data says where to get that file:


import pandas as pd

gapminder_2007 = pd.read_csv(GAPMINDER_CSV)
print(gapminder_2007.shape, list(gapminder_2007.columns))
(142, 6) ['country', 'continent', 'year', 'life', 'population', 'gdp']


Apart from the small bar plot above, every plot on this page draws from this table or from a table computed from it.
The column kinds follow the Python types. A column of numbers is read as continuous, and a column of text as categorical. A column of datetime64, date or datetime values is drawn on a calendar axis. NaN and None are missing values. A row with one in a column the plot maps is left out, and the engine says how many rows it left out. A pandas Categorical keeps its declared order when the engine reads it. It is the pandas counterpart of R’s factor(x, levels = …). A plain dict of lists declares the same order with ordered(values, levels), which the Data chapter describes. A column with a declared order is categorical even when its values are numbers, such as years.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.5 Computing a column first
A channel takes a column name and never an expression. That rule is the same in all four languages. There is no x(log(col.gdp)), and gog has no language of its own for deriving values, because Python already has one. So compute the column first, then bind it by name.
Dividing a column inside the channel is a natural thing to try. gog refuses it, and says where the computation belongs:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp / 1000) + y(col.life)
gog: a channel takes a column name, not an expression — gog has no computed channels. Compute the column in Python first and bind the result: `df['ratio'] = df['a'] / df['b']`, then `col.ratio` where the expression was.




europe = gapminder_2007[gapminder_2007.continent == 'Europe'].copy()
europe['gdp_thousands'] = europe.gdp / 1000
europe = europe.sort_values('life', ascending=False)
print(europe[['country', 'gdp_thousands', 'life']].head(3).to_string(index=False))
country  gdp_thousands   life
    Iceland      36.180789 81.757
Switzerland      37.506419 81.701
      Spain      28.821064 80.941


That result is a table like any other, and the sentence that draws from it is one you already know:


(data(europe) + point + x(col.gdp_thousands) + y(col.life)
 + size(col.population) + style(color='steelblue')
 + x_label('GDP per person (thousands)')
 + title('Europe, 2007'))


                                                                  10 20 30 40 50   72 74 76 78 80 82  Europe, 2007 Life GDP per person (thousands)  Population    301.9K  41.4M  82.4M 




You did the division in pandas, in a line of your own code that you can check. The plot then names a column that exists. Keeping the computing and the plotting apart is deliberate rather than a missing feature. A plot is a mapping from a table (Data), so a channel names one of its columns. Anything you want to compute is computed before you write the sentence.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.6 Showing the plot
The plots above appear on this page because the book drew each one when it was built. In your own session, where a plot appears depends on how you are running Python. In a Jupyter notebook, a plot on the last line of a cell is drawn below that cell, as the R console draws a plot you type. A script displays nothing on its own, so you ask for the picture yourself:


plot = data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
print(plot)
print(save_svg(plot, '/tmp/life.svg'))
<gog plot: point on gapminder_2007>
/tmp/life.svg


Printing a plot gives one line, naming its mark and its table. It does not give the picture. save_svg() writes the SVG to a file and returns its path, which is the second line printed above. plot.show() opens the SVG in a browser, and render_svg(plot) returns it as a string. R’s print() draws the picture, and Python’s does not. Each language is following the convention it already has.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.7 Six names Python already uses
Six of gog’s names are also Python builtins, the functions Python provides without any import: bin, map, max, min, range and sum. After from gog import *, those six names mean gog’s atoms, not Python’s builtins, for the rest of the file or notebook. gog’s R package shares names with R as well, and max, min, range and sum are four of them. gog does not rename an atom to avoid a name the language already uses. If you call sum, min, max or map as you would call Python’s builtin, gog refuses the call. So does range with whole numbers outside 0 to 1. The message says the name is gog’s, and how to reach Python’s builtin:


try:
    range(10)
except GogError as error:
    print(error)
gog: `range()` takes the band's two ends, each one number between 0 and 1, e.g. `range(0.25, 0.75)`. For a sequence of integers, gog shadows that name: use `builtins.range` for Python's.


That is range’s message. Its word for this is shadows: after the import, the name reaches gog’s atom instead of Python’s builtin. sum, min, max and map share a different message, which lists all six names and says how to reach Python’s builtin.
One name, bin, gives no message at all. bin(5) is also how you ask gog for five bins, so it returns a transform instead of Python’s string '0b101'.
If a file needs Python’s builtins as well as gog, write import gog and then gog.point, or restore one builtin with from builtins import sum.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.8 The operators, and their precedence
The four operators do not change from R to Python, and neither does their precedence, the order in which they group. * and / group first, then +, then |. That order is Python’s own, and R’s is the same. So bar * mean below becomes one compound mark before any + joins it, exactly as in Operators:


(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
 + order(col.life, desc=True)
 + title('Mean life expectancy, highest first'))


                                  Oceania Europe Americas Asia Africa   0 20 40 60 80  Mean life expectancy, highest first Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, ordered by life, largest first.”
The same order decides where a page needs parentheses. On a page, Python has two kinds of parentheses, and they do different jobs. The outer pair, around the whole sentence, lets it continue on the next line (A sentence over several lines). It groups nothing inside the sentence. So a page inside that pair alone is still refused when / joins its plots. / groups before +, so it joins the first plot’s last atom to the second plot’s data():


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) /
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent))
gog: `/` places one plot below another, and it groups before `+`, so here it joined `y()` to the plot after it. Put each plot in parentheses: `(data(df) + point + ...) / (data(df) + bar + ...)`.


The inner pairs, one around each plot, are the ones that group. Each plot is then complete before / joins it. This book writes both kinds whenever it composes plots:


((data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent)))


                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, above bars derived by count, x is continent.”
With | between the plots, gog draws the page without the inner pairs, because | groups after +. Write them anyway. The page then means the same thing with either operator, and the same as in Julia, which groups | together with +. A page inside a page needs a pair of its own too, and so does a whole page before a theme() for it. Inside a page, / groups before |, so a | b / c is read as a | (b / c). Without the pair around a whole page, + groups before |, and the theme() goes to the second plot (Parentheses on a page).

title: 47  Python
section: 47.9 The same vocabulary and the same refusals
text:
47.9 The same vocabulary and the same refusals
Like the operators, the vocabulary does not change: every mark, transform, channel, setting and plot-level atom in the kernel card keeps its name in Python. An engine refusal does not change either. The engine does not know which binding asked, so it sends you the same words it sends an R user:


data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.continent)
gog: `bar` needs `y()` but none is set. Add `y(<column>)` — a bar cannot be drawn without it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


The refusals that differ are the binding’s own, like the two about the accessor. Each of those has to teach the spelling of the language you are writing in.
This chapter’s examples are only a small sample. On every change to the project, its automated tests translate the book’s sentences into Python and draw them again. How far the two spellings differ was measured that way, sentence by sentence. Of the book’s 926 sentences, eleven have no Python spelling at all. Nine are in the R chapter and use R’s own syntax, such as the pipe. Two are the GIF exports in the Play chapter. Every one of the rest was translated by rule and run through the Python binding. Of those, 708 drew the same plot, byte for byte, and 187 gave the same refusal, word for word. The other 20 were refused in both languages, in a message worded for each one. Two rewrites do nearly all of the translating. The accessor is needed in 909 sentences, and the parentheses in 635.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.10 Reading from a database
Your table may be stored in a database rather than held in your session. Python’s database standard is DB-API, also called PEP 249, and query() reads any connection that follows it. It also reads a Spark session, because many Python users reach their data through Spark.
Any connection with a .cursor() method works: sqlite3 from Python’s standard library, DuckDB, psycopg, pyodbc, Snowflake’s connector, and the Databricks SQL connector.
import sqlite3
from gog import query, bar, x, y, col, save_svg

con = sqlite3.connect("sales.db")
plot = query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(col.status) + y(col.revenue)
save_svg(plot, "orders.svg")
Pass the Spark session itself to query(). In the SQL, write the table’s full name as Spark lists it, such as main.sales.orders. This is how you read a Databricks table:
plot = query(spark, "SELECT status, revenue FROM main.sales.orders") + bar + x(col.status) + y(col.revenue)
In a Databricks notebook the session is already there, under the name spark, and %pip install gog is the only setup step.
Neither way adds a dependency to gog. You open the connection, and gog only reads rows from it.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.11 Installing gog
A plot is drawn by the engine, which is a compiled Rust binary, so the Python package has to be able to find one. The released package carries it. A Python package is released as wheels, ready-built files for one platform each, and each wheel holds the engine built for its platform. So installing needs no Rust toolchain.
pip install gog
That command works. gog is on PyPI as five wheels. They cover macOS on Intel and ARM processors, Linux on Intel, AMD and ARM processors, and Windows on Intel and AMD processors. On any other platform, pip install gog stops with an error, because there is no wheel for it. The other three bindings install from their own registries, and the preface lists all four commands.
To work from a checkout instead, a copy of gog’s source repository, build the engine once. Then start Python in the repository’s top folder and import the package from there:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "py-pkg/gog")

from gog import *
The engine is looked for in four places, in this order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, the copy inside the installed package, gog-cli on your PATH, and a local target/release build. Only a checkout has the fourth, which also accepts a target/debug build. This page used the first: the book sets GOG_CLI_PATH to a local build before any Python runs.

title: 47  Python
text:
47.12 What comes next
Python’s differences are spelling rather than grammar. Julia has four differences of its own. A column is a symbol, | has a different precedence, nine names need one extra import line, and the package has a different name.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.1 A column is a symbol
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in Julia as it is in R.
Of the three languages that are not R, Julia asks for the fewest changes to the sentence you already know. Like R and Python, it lets a package give +, *, | and / new meanings. Like R, it also keeps a column apart from a value in the syntax itself. So the sentence below differs from the R version only by a colon in front of each column:
The first sections cover how a column is written, how to break a sentence across lines, and how values are written. The next one shows where Julia groups the operators differently from R. Then come the tables Julia accepts, showing a plot, the nine names gog shares with Base, reading from a database, and installing the package.
Every Julia block on this page that shows a plot, a refusal or printed output ran when the page was built, through the same engine every other chapter uses. The other blocks are shown but not run. Each block ran after gapminder_2007 was fetched as The table shows, and after these two lines, which Nine names Julia already uses explains:
The colon is the main change to the sentence, so this section shows it in a plot. R writes a column as a bare name, Python as col.gdp, and Julia as a symbol, a name written after a colon, such as :gdp:
gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows

data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + color(:continent)


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
That is the sentence from A first plot, without its title and with a colon in front of each column. In this grammar a plain string spells a value, as in style(color = "tomato") or palette("okabe"). A symbol is visibly not a string, so the colon does the same work as R’s bare name and Python’s col. accessor. A channel takes a column and never a value. Because a symbol and a string look different, both you and the package can see when a value is written where a column belongs.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x("gdp") + y(:life)
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. In Julia a column is a symbol, which is what keeps the two apart: `x(:gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.
The opposite mistake, a column where a value belongs, is refused the same way and for the same reason (Setting vs mapping):
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + style(color = :continent)
gog: `style(color = )` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `:continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(:continent)`.
A column name with a space or a dot in it is written Symbol("life exp"). A name in another writing system needs no Symbol(): :지역 (region) is an ordinary symbol. Julia accepts letters from any writing system in a name.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.2 A sentence over several lines
A long sentence can be broken across lines, and Julia asks for nothing extra. Like R, it continues a line that ends in +:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
    color(:continent) +
    size(:population)


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania   Population    199.6K  659.4M  1.3B 




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, size by population.”
What does not work is the opposite arrangement, where a line starts with the operator. Julia ends the statement at the line break and reads the next line on its own, so it reports an error about + instead of drawing. To write a sentence that way, put the whole sentence inside parentheses. The Python chapter writes every multi-line sentence this way (Python), and inside parentheses a line may begin with + in Julia too. Values also take Julia’s spelling, as the next section shows.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.3 How values are written
In the other chapters, a code block that is a sentence has a tab for each language. Code written inside the text has none, so it is written in R, as in x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)). Most of it reads the same in Julia once each column is a symbol. The values are what change. R writes several values inside c(), and Julia writes them in a vector, inside square brackets. The table gives the Julia spelling of each kind of value the book uses:








Kind of value
R
Julia




true or false
TRUE, FALSE
true, false


several numbers
c(37.5, 87.5)
[37.5, 87.5]


several strings, such as colors
c("tomato", "steelblue")
["tomato", "steelblue"]


a color for each category
c(Asia = "tomato", Europe = "steelblue")
["Asia" => "tomato", "Europe" => "steelblue"]


a missing value
NA
missing


the number e
exp(1)
exp(1), or ℯ


a declared order
factor(values, levels = c("Low", "High"))
ordered(values, ["Low", "High"])



So x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) in the text is x(:life, limits = [37.5, 87.5]) in Julia. Write several values in square brackets. A tuple in parentheses also works for limits, but palette() and ordered() do not accept one. A named argument is written as in R, because Julia has named arguments of its own: legend = FALSE is legend = false. ordered() declares the order of a column’s categories, as R’s factor() does, and the Data chapter describes it.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.4 The operators, and their precedence
A sentence can use up to four operators, so it matters which one Julia groups first. That order is called precedence, and Julia’s is not R’s. R and Python group | after +, and Julia groups | together with +, from left to right. That difference could change how a sentence is grouped, so the table compares four expressions in the three languages:



Written
Julia reads it as
R and Python read it as




a + b + c \| d
(a + b + c) \| d
the same


a \| b / c
a \| (b / c)
the same


a * b + c
(a * b) + c
the same


a \| b + c
(a \| b) + c
a \| (b + c)



The first three rows are read the same way in all three languages. In the first, Julia groups | together with +, from left to right, so everything left of the | is joined first. In the second and third, * and / group first in every language. Only the last row differs, because it is the only one with a + after the |. When b is a facet and c an atom such as title(), the difference does not change the plot. R joins the atom to the facet first, and Julia joins it to the plot directly. Both draw the same plot as a sentence with the atom written before the facet.
Faceting therefore reads exactly as it does in R:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) | facet(:continent)


                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                      1K 10K                                                                              1K 10K                                                   1K 10K                            1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
A transform joins its mark first, as in R, because * groups before + in both languages:


data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)


                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
A page is where the last row matters. The plot on the right of | starts with its own data(), and its other atoms follow with +. So a page written out in full has a + after the |. Without parentheses, Julia groups the first plot with that data() alone, and gog refuses a page that it draws in R and Python:


data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) |
  data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent)
gog: `|` places one plot beside another, and the plot beside it holds nothing but its table. Julia groups `|` with `+`, from left to right, so `|` joined that table before `+` could add the rest of its plot. Put each plot in parentheses: `(data(df) + point + ...) | (data(df) + bar + ...)`.


So put each plot on a page inside its own parentheses, with | as well as with /, which groups before + in all three languages. Each plot is then complete before | joins it, and the page draws as it does in R:


(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life)) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent))


                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The same row decides where a theme() for the whole page goes. Written after a page with no parentheses around it, the theme() goes to the page in Julia, and to the second plot in R and Python. Put parentheses around the page before the theme(), as in ((…) | (…)) + theme(height = 260). Then the theme() goes to the page in all three languages (Parentheses on a page).

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.5 The table
Every sentence starts from a table. The simplest table in Julia is a named tuple of columns, which the language provides, so a first plot needs nothing installed:


data((person = ["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"], cm = [160.0, 172.0, 181.0]),
     name = "heights") + bar + x(:person) + y(:cm)


                            Ada Alan Grace   0 50 100 150  Cm Person




The table holds three people and their heights, written directly inside the call. A Dict of columns works too. So does any object that supports names(table) and table[!, col], as a DataFrame does. The package never imports DataFrames, so if you do not use one, you install nothing extra.
The other plots use gapminder_2007, one of the book’s shared tables, and gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007") fetches it. gog_table() fetches any of the shared tables by name, as it does in the other three languages (The book’s data).
Julia has both a Date and a DateTime. R and Python each have the same pair of types under their own names. A Date column never gets clock ticks, and a DateTime column can, because it stores a time of day (Scales). The package tells the two apart by type, so nothing is guessed.
In R, data() reads a table’s name from the expression you wrote. In Julia, data() receives only the table itself, so an unnamed table gets a generated name instead: data, then data2. Some messages name the table they are about, such as the warning about missing values, so write data(df, name = "notes") when you want that message to say notes (Data).

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.6 Showing the plot
The plots on this page appear under their code. In your own session, where a plot appears depends on where you run it. In a notebook, such as Jupyter or Pluto, the notebook asks the package for a picture, and the plot is drawn under the cell. At the REPL, Julia’s prompt in a terminal, a plot prints as one line of text, such as <gog plot: bar on heights> for the heights plot in The table. To see the picture, assign the plot to a variable such as p, write it to a file with save_svg(p, "plot.svg"), and open that file in a web browser. render_svg(p) returns the same drawing as text.
Julia also exports three functions that R and Python do not. You need them only to build a tool with gog, such as a web server, and never to write a sentence. svg_block(svg) puts the text from render_svg() in centered HTML for a web page. Given the plot too, svg_block(svg, p) adds its controls. find_gog_cli() returns the path of the engine the package found (Installing gog). to_wire(table, name) returns the table as gog sends it to the engine, before it becomes JSON; name labels its messages. JavaScript exports the same three.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.7 Nine names Julia already uses
Every plot above ran after two lines that its block leaves out, and this section explains them. Nine of the kernel’s words are also names in Base: count, sum, min, max, range, size, step, stack and map. Julia will not choose between two modules that export the same name, and the rule is the language’s own. Writing one of these nine without an import stops with an UndefVarError and a hint, rather than quietly calling the wrong function. The fix is one more import line:
using GrammarOfGraphics
using GrammarOfGraphics: count, sum, min, max, range, size, step, stack, map
With them, a bare sum is gog’s transform, and Base.sum still adds numbers:


println(sum)
println(Base.sum([1, 2, 3]))
<gog sum>
6


bin is not in the import line, because Base.bin is not exported, so there is no second bin to choose between.
The import line treats the nine names alike, but your existing code does not use them equally. map and size appear in ordinary Julia code constantly. After the import, a call such as map(f, xs) or size(A) in that code reaches gog’s word instead, and the error appears on a line you did not change. Write Base.map or Base.size there, and the same prefix works for any of the nine.
R, Python and Julia all have this problem, and each one solves it in its own way. R’s range, sum and min belong to base R, Python’s bin, sum and max are builtins, and Julia’s belong to Base. A grammar keeps its own vocabulary; what changes is how each language asks you to say which one you meant.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.8 Reading from a database
Your table may be stored in a database rather than in your session. query() runs a SQL query on that database, and it takes a DBInterface.jl connection. DBInterface.jl is Julia’s database standard, and SQLite.jl, LibPQ.jl, MySQL.jl and DuckDB.jl all implement it.
using DBInterface, SQLite, GrammarOfGraphics

con = SQLite.DB("sales.db")
query(con, "SELECT status, revenue FROM orders") + bar + x(:status) + y(:revenue)
GrammarOfGraphics does not depend on DBInterface. Every dependency the package declares is a Julia standard library, and many readers never write SQL, so none of them should have to install a database package. Instead, the package uses the DBInterface that your driver loads. If no driver is loaded, drawing the plot stops with a message that names DBInterface and the line that loads it.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.9 Installing gog
The Julia package is named GrammarOfGraphics. The name is longer than the one R and Python use, and the registry is the reason. Julia’s registry checks a new name automatically. The name must be at least five letters long and must start with a capital. A lowercase gog is too short and has no capital.
Every plot is drawn by the engine, a separate program written in Rust, so the Julia package has to be able to find it. Python and JavaScript each publish the engine built for every common platform, and the install picks the one for your computer. R builds it during the install, or installs one already built. Julia fetches it as an artifact, which is how a Julia package distributes a program it needs. Pkg downloads the copy of the engine built for your computer along with the package, so one call to Pkg.add installs everything:
using Pkg
Pkg.add("GrammarOfGraphics")
To work from a checkout, a copy of gog’s source repository on your own computer, first build the engine once from the checkout’s top folder (this needs Rust):
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
Then run Pkg.develop from the same folder:
using Pkg
Pkg.develop(path = "jl-pkg/GrammarOfGraphics")

using GrammarOfGraphics
The Julia package looks for the engine in six places. In order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, a build in the checkout the package sits in, the artifact the install fetched, a copy you placed inside the package yourself, gog-cli on your PATH, and last a build found by searching upward from the working directory. The search stops at the first place that holds the engine. An installed copy is not inside a checkout, so it uses the artifact. Inside a checkout, your own build is searched before the artifact on purpose. The artifact is the engine of the last release, and using it would draw with an old engine while you are changing the engine’s source.

title: 48  Julia
text:
48.10 What comes next
R, Python and Julia write one sentence three ways, and the main difference is how a column is named. JavaScript reads differently, because it cannot give + * | / new meanings, so it spells them as words.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.1 The comma is +
The grammar does not change when the language does. One engine reads one specification, so a sentence means the same thing no matter who wrote it. Everything in this book up to here is as true in JavaScript as it is in R.
The sentence is spelled differently here, and the operators are the reason. Every other binding joins the same words with the same four operators. JavaScript cannot join words that way, because +, *, | and / cannot be given a meaning on objects. For two objects a and b, a + b joins them into one piece of text, a * b is NaN, and a | b is the number 0. There is no version of the language in which data(gm) + point builds a plot.
So JavaScript spells the four operators as six words: plot(), layer(), across(), down(), beside() and below(). That is the change this chapter starts from. Read the two lines together, the R first and the JavaScript under it:
Every JavaScript block with a plot, a message or a printed line under it was run when the page was built, through the same engine every other chapter uses. The database and install commands are shown, not run. In your own code, import the words you use, such as import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "grammar-of-graphics". The blocks on this page leave that line out, and also the line that reads the table: const gapminder_2007 = await gog_table("gapminder_2007");.
JavaScript brings in only the names you list, and none of gog’s names is already a name in the language. So, unlike the R, Python and Julia chapters, this one has no section on names the language already uses. If a gog word matches a name your own script uses, such as path beside Node.js’s node:path, import it under another name with as. The sections below take the four operators first. Then come how a column, a named argument and a table are written, a plot for a web page, reading from a database, and installing the package.
A gog sentence is a list of words, and in JavaScript it is a list of arguments. A comma means nothing on its own. Inside plot(), the commas join the words, exactly as + joins them in R. A named argument is written differently: it goes into an object at the end of the call. The section on named arguments, below, sets that out in full.

plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log' }), y(col.life), color(col.continent))


                                                                                                                                                                          1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp  Continent    Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania
“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent.”
Those are the words of A first plot without its title, in the same order, reading the same way. Where you write a word still decides its scope (Encoding scope). A channel written after a mark belongs to that mark, and one written before any mark belongs to the plot. The commas change nothing about that; they are the + signs.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.2 layer() is *
The commas replaced +. * cannot become a comma, because R groups * before +. That order is called precedence, and it is how bar * bin + x(life) reads as a binned bar rather than a bar plus a bin. JavaScript writes function calls rather than operators here, so there is no precedence to use. Nesting does the same work:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.life))


                                  Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40 60 80  Life Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life.”
Nesting is clearer than precedence. A reader who does not know that * groups before + has to be told. A reader looking at layer(bar, mean) can see it.
Just over half the sentences in this book need no layer() at all, because they are a flat list of words. Where one is needed, it usually holds two words:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent), style({ color: 'steelblue' }))


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent




“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”
The two words are a mark and the transform that derives it. The color here is a setting, written as an object inside style().

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.3 across() and down() are | and /
Two operators are left, | and /. With facet() on their right, both split one plot into panels. Faceting in R is plot | facet(era), panels side by side, or plot / facet(era), panels stacked. In R, facet() means nothing on its own: it always follows a | or a /. JavaScript writes that whole phrase as one word:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log' }), y(col.life), across(col.continent))


                                                             1K 10K   40 50 60 70 80                                                      1K 10K                                                                              1K 10K                                                   1K 10K                            1K 10K      Asia  Europe  Africa  Americas  Oceania  Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, split into panel columns by continent.”
down() stacks the panels instead. Writing both gives a grid: one panel column per value of the column in across(), and one panel row per value of the column in down(). That is what plot | facet(a) / facet(b) does in R.
Because the operator and facet() are one word here, there is no separate facet() to write. Writing facet(), as the other three languages do, is refused, and the message names the two words to use instead:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), facet(col.continent))
gog: JavaScript has no `facet()`, because it has no `|` or `/` to join it with — the pair is one word here. Panels side by side: `across(col.continent)`. Panels stacked: `down(col.continent)`.

title: 49  JavaScript
section: 49.4 Composing two plots: beside() and below()
text:
49.4 Composing two plots: beside() and below()
The | you have just replaced had a second job in R. What is on its right decides which job it does: plot | facet(g) splits one plot into panels, and plot_a | plot_b arranges two plots on a page. JavaScript cannot overload |, so the two meanings never share a symbol. The second one gets its own word, beside(), and below() for /:


below(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.gdp), theme({ height: 130 })), plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)))


                                         0 20 40 60  Count


                                                                                                                                                                                  0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp





“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, above points, x is gdp, y is life.”
The two words come from an algebra of pictures published in 1982. Henderson’s Functional Geometry (Henderson, 1982) combines pictures with beside and above. His above(a, b) and gog’s below(a, b) draw the same picture, with a on top and b under it. Composition gives the history. Both words also take a page, the result of an earlier beside() or below(), so one page can hold another. below(top, beside(main, right)) is the marginal plot, exactly as top / (main | right) is in R: a histogram above a scatter, and another to its right. The spelling does not decide what two composed plots share; the engine does. Plots one above the other align their x axes, and plots side by side align their y axes. When both plots put the same column on that aligned axis, it becomes one axis: one scale, both panels the same length along it, drawn once.
That marginal plot, below(top, beside(main, right)), needs no parentheses beyond the calls themselves. In R, Python and Julia, this book puts each plot on a page inside its own parentheses. Without them, precedence can group parts of two plots together (Parentheses on a page). JavaScript needs none of those parentheses. Each plot is already one plot() call, and beside() and below() take whole plots and pages as their arguments, so the nesting shows the grouping. This book writes a theme() for the whole page as the last argument of beside() or below():


beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life)), plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent)), theme({ height: 260 }))


                                                                                                                                                                                    0 10K 20K 30K 40K 50K   40 50 60 70 80  Life Gdp


                              Asia Europe Africa Americas Oceania   0 20 40  Count Continent





“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by count, x is continent.”
In R, Python and Julia, a theme() for the whole page follows parentheses around the page, as in ((…) | (…)) + theme(height = 260). In JavaScript, the theme() goes inside the call that makes the page, so no extra parentheses are needed.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.5 A column is written col.gdp
The operators are the largest change JavaScript makes to a sentence. Three smaller ones are left, and the first is how a column is named. R writes a column as a bare name and Julia as a symbol. Python and JavaScript write it through col, a small object called an accessor: col.gdp names the column gdp. Both languages make that choice for the same reason. In this grammar a plain string is how you spell a value, as in style({ color: "tomato" }), title("…"), palette("okabe"). Without the accessor, a column and a value would both be plain strings, and gog could not tell which one you meant.
So a string where a column belongs is refused, and the message says what to write:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x('gdp'), y(col.life))
gog: `x("gdp")` binds a *value*, and a channel takes a *column*. JavaScript has no bare names, so a column is written with the accessor: `x(col.gdp)` maps the column called `gdp`.


The message names the column spelling, x(col.gdp). A channel takes a column, and a string is a value (Setting vs mapping). The opposite mistake, a column where a value belongs, is refused the same way:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), style({ color: col.continent }))
gog: `style({ color: … })` fixes one value for the whole layer, and `col.continent` is a column. To *map* it — one value per category, with a legend to decode it — that is a channel: `color(col.continent)`.


A column name with a space or a dot in it is not a JavaScript identifier, the kind of name that can follow a dot. Write it in the bracket form instead: col["life exp"]. A name in another writing system needs no brackets. JavaScript accepts letters from any writing system in an identifier, so col.지역 (region) works.

title: 49  JavaScript
section: 49.6 A named argument is one trailing object
text:
49.6 A named argument is one trailing object
That was the first of the smaller differences. The second is how a named argument is written. R writes x(gdp, scale = "log"). JavaScript has no syntax for a named argument. You put the named ones into a single object at the end, and the positional ones stay where they are:


plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: 'log', base: 2 }), y(col.life), title('Doublings of income'))


                                                                                                                                                                                      256 512 1024 2048 4096 8192 16384 32768   40 50 60 70 80  Doublings of income Life Gdp




“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale in base 2, y is life.”
style() is the case where every argument is named, so it is written as one object throughout the book: style({ color: "tomato", size: 3 }).

49.6.1 How values are written
In the other chapters, a code block that is a sentence has a tab for each language. Code written inside the text has none, so it is written in R, as in x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)). In JavaScript, limits goes into the trailing object, and its value takes JavaScript’s spelling. R writes several values inside c(), and JavaScript writes them in an array, inside square brackets. The table gives the JavaScript spelling of each kind of value the book uses:








Kind of value
R
JavaScript




true or false
TRUE, FALSE
true, false


several numbers
c(37.5, 87.5)
[37.5, 87.5]


several strings, such as colors
c("tomato", "steelblue")
["tomato", "steelblue"]


a color for each category
c(Asia = "tomato", Europe = "steelblue")
{ Asia: "tomato", Europe: "steelblue" }


a missing value
NA
null


the number e
exp(1)
Math.E


a declared order
factor(values, levels = c("Low", "High"))
ordered(values, ["Low", "High"])



So x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) in the text is x(col.life, { limits: [37.5, 87.5] }) in JavaScript, and legend = FALSE is { legend: false }. ordered() declares the order of a column’s categories, as R’s factor() does, and the Data chapter describes it.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.7 The table, and its name
The third difference is how a table gets its name. A table is an object of columns, or an array of rows, one object per row. Neither needs a package besides gog, and this one is written in place:
const heights = { person: ["Ada", "Alan", "Grace"], cm: [160, 172, 181] };


plot(data(heights), bar, x(col.person), y(col.cm))


                            Ada Alan Grace   0 50 100 150  Cm Person




R reads the table’s name from the expression you wrote, and Python from the variable you passed. JavaScript can do neither. The name matters, because a layer looks up its columns in the nearest table, and it finds that table by name (Data). So an unnamed table gets a generated name instead, such as data or data2, which is enough to tell two tables in one sentence apart. Some messages name the table they are about, such as the warning about missing values. Write data(df, { name: "notes" }) when you want such a message to say notes.
A column of Date values is drawn on a calendar axis. gog reads each Date in local time, the time shown by the clock of the computer that runs your code. So new Date(2024, 0, 1, 12), noon on January 1, is drawn at 12:00. JavaScript’s Date type holds both a date and a date-time, so gog distinguishes the two by their values. If every value in a column is midnight in local time, as new Date(2024, 0, 1) is, gog reads the column as dates and never gives it clock ticks. JavaScript reads the text in new Date("2024-01-01") as midnight in UTC, the time every time zone is counted from. On a computer in New York, gog draws that value at 19:00 on December 31, 2023. On a computer in Seoul it is 09:00 on January 1: the right day, but not midnight, so the column is read as date-times. To get midnight in every time zone, write a time after the date: new Date("2024-01-01T00:00") is midnight in local time.
Three more things have a JavaScript spelling. A missing value is null, undefined or NaN: a row with one in a column the plot maps is left out, and gog says how many rows it left out. ordered(values, levels) declares the order of a column’s categories, which the Data chapter describes. And the book’s own tables come from gog_table(), which fetches them over the network. It returns a Promise, JavaScript’s object for a value that arrives later, so you write await before it, as The book’s data shows.

title: 49  JavaScript
49  JavaScript
section: 49.9 A plot for a web page: html_block()

title: 49  JavaScript
49  JavaScript
text:
49.11 Installing gog
Every plot is drawn by the engine, a separate program written in Rust, so the npm package has to be able to find it.
npm install grammar-of-graphics
That command works. The package is on npm, and the name is written in full because npm already had a package called gog. The registry also forbids capital letters in a new name, so this is Julia’s GrammarOfGraphics written the way npm writes names.
The engine is installed with it. There are five more packages on npm, one per platform, each holding the engine compiled for that platform. The main package lists all five as optional dependencies. The install takes the one that matches your computer and skips the other four. So there is nothing to put on your PATH, nothing to build, and no Rust toolchain to install. The five cover macOS on Intel and ARM processors, Linux on Intel, AMD and ARM processors, and Windows on Intel and AMD processors. On any other computer the install still succeeds, and the first plot stops with an error that says no engine is published for that computer.
The binding itself only builds the specification and hands it to that engine, and it depends on nothing else:
import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "grammar-of-graphics";

const gm = { gdp: [1000, 2000, 3000], life: [60, 70, 80] };
console.log(render_svg(plot(data(gm), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life))));
The package runs in Node.js and not in a browser, because it starts the engine as a separate program. On a server, you send the SVG string as the response, and the page puts it straight into its DOM. Nothing has to open a viewer window, and nothing has to be turned into pixels first. What the engine returns is already the finished picture.
To work from a checkout instead, a copy of gog’s source repository, build the engine once. Then import the package by its path, from the repository’s top folder:
cargo build --release -p gog-cli
import { plot, data, point, x, y, col, render_svg } from "./js-pkg/gog/src/index.js";
The engine is looked for in four places, in this order: the GOG_CLI_PATH environment variable, the platform package installed beside the main one, gog-cli on your PATH, and a target/release build in a surrounding checkout. The search stops at the first place that holds the engine, so an installed copy normally stops at the platform package. GOG_CLI_PATH is how this page was rendered.

title: 49  JavaScript
text:
49.12 What comes next
These four chapters are about spelling, and none of them changes what a sentence means. The afterword closes the book with the ten-day challenge, and the one goal that remains.




Henderson, P. (1982). Functional geometry. In D. P. Friedman & D. S. Wise (Eds.), Conference record of the 1982 ACM symposium on lisp and functional programming (pp. 179–187). ACM Press.

title: Afterword
text:
The ten-day challenge
The 1446 book closed with a postface, and it made two claims for its little alphabet. The first was that a wise man could learn it before the morning was over, and a slow one within ten days. The second was that it could write down any sound at all: the wind, the cry of a crane, the crowing of a cock, the barking of a dog. This book closes by restating both, because they are its own measures of success.
The first claim was about speed, and the preface restated it for this book: read the whole grammar in a morning, and write it fluently within ten days. You have done the reading. Here is the rest of the promise. For the next ten days, ask one question a day of your own data, not of the book’s cast of tables, and answer it in one sentence. Start where the cookbook starts: with your columns and your question. By day three the recipes will read as ordinary sentences, because you will have written sentences like them yourself. By day ten you should be writing sentences this book never showed you. That is the one outcome that proves you learned the grammar and not the examples.
During those ten days, report two kinds of result: a sentence that renders when you expected a refusal, and a refusal whose direction you disagree with. Reports like these are how the grammar’s mistakes are found.

title: Afterword
text:
Growth without new words
The second claim was about what the letters could write: any sound at all. gog has the same goal for plots, but it does not promise that every plot is possible. The kernel you learned is its whole vocabulary. The engine draws every word in it, though not every pairing of words. Combinations shows which pairs it draws and which it refuses.
A new kind of plot does not need a new word. The choropleth is an example of that. It is a map that shades each country by a value, and no atom was added for it. What it needed was a different kind of table: one row for every point along a country’s border, so that many rows make up one country. A zone is a filled region, and several things can decide its sides. One of them is a boundary, the outline those rows trace, and group already says which rows belong to one country. Map shows the choropleth drawn with the words the kernel already had.
The vocabulary is also the same in all four languages. Whatever sentence you write, all four bindings build the same specification from its words. The main difference is how each binding names a column. JavaScript also cannot give the operators new meanings, so it spells them as words. Each language has a chapter of its own, listing what differs: R, Python, Julia, JavaScript. Here is one sentence from A first plot in all four:
# R
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
# Python
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
  + color(col.continent))
# Julia
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)
// JavaScript
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent))
All four draw the same plot, byte for byte.

title: Afterword
text:
One goal left
Those four spellings are finished work. One thing this project planned to do is not finished, and it is written down here so you can check later whether the project did it. Half of it already works: the engine itself runs inside the page, which is how a 3-D plot turns when you drag it in the web edition. The other half is making every example in this book editable on the page. You could then change color(continent) to shape(continent) and watch the plot redraw. This book is ready for editable examples, because no plot in it is a screenshot: the engine draws every one from its specification.

title: Afterword
section: Writing quickly is not writing well
text:
Writing quickly is not writing well
Both claims of 1446 are about the letters: how fast they can be learned, and what they can write. Neither says how well anyone will write with them.
I think Hangeul (한글) is the best writing system in the world. I should admit that I may be biased, because it is the alphabet I write with. Most people agree that it is quick to learn, to read and to write.
Writing quickly is not the same as writing well. Good writing cannot be learned quickly: you read good writing, and you practice. Visualization is no different. This tool is new and still has problems, but I hope it is already a good tool to practice with.
The 1446 story makes the same distinction, between making a writing system and writing with it. King Sejong made the alphabet. Other people wrote most of the books that used it. I designed gog, but I am not a great author of plots. What I do have is twenty years as a user of visualization tools, watching and listening and reading. The design comes from that experience, and the result is a tool that is easy to learn and easy to use.
I hope you do good work with it.

title: Afterword
text:
The gap
A specification is a sentence written before the picture exists. Between writing it and the moment the engine shows you what you said, there is a gap, and everyone who writes a specification waits in it. The package is gog. The state you are in while you wait is agog: eager to see what comes next. I hope the book kept you agog.

Be agog. Use gog.

title: Appendix A — The kernel card
text:
The whole grammar, on one page. The table below is the kernel, the list of every word in the grammar. Each word is an atom, and the operators join atoms into a sentence that describes a plot. The table is copied from The kernel each time the book is built, so it always matches that chapter. Functions you never write into a sentence, such as render_svg(), are in Functions around the grammar.







Kind
The words




Sources
data query


Marks
point line area bar step interval box ribbon text path rule zone surface edge


Channels
x y z color size shape pattern opacity group label play


Transforms
bin smooth count density proportion sum mean median max min quantile range confidence deviation smooth_band bounds partition flow layout cluster, and the four collision modifiers, dodge stack jitter repel


Operators
+ layers, * derives, | and / arrange


Scales
linear log time category order


Spaces
flat space polar nest map globe network


Settings
style theme palette


Labels
title x_label y_label z_label


Facets
facet


Selections
brush



The minimum sentence is a source, a mark, and the position channels that mark needs:
data(table) + mark + x(column) + y(column)
The order of + matters in a few places only. Each mark starts a layer: the mark, and the channels and settings that apply to it. In a plot with one mark, the mark and its channels may be written in any order. This book usually writes a sentence as data, mark, positions, refinements, where the refinements are the optional parts, such as color and title. Only two parts of the order are rules. A sentence must start with a source (data() or query()), and a style() needs a mark before it. The engine refuses a sentence that breaks either rule.
What the order does change is which marks each channel or table applies to, and which mark is drawn on top. A channel written before any mark applies to every layer that can accept it, and this book writes a channel there when every layer should use it. A channel such as color, written after a mark, belongs to that mark alone. Positions are the exception: a mark with no x or y of its own reads the first ones written. Each later data() applies to the mark written directly after it, and a style() styles the nearest mark before it. Two marks draw in the order you wrote them, so the second sits on top of the first. Which orders matter and Encoding scope have the rules in full.
Deriving is what * does: it joins a transform to a mark, and the mark is always on the left. More than one transform can follow one mark: bar * bin * mean cuts the x axis into bands, then averages y inside each band. Transforms on one mark must each do a different job, and each job is done at its own step. So the order you write them in does not change the picture, and writing them in the order they happen is the convention. Chaining transforms names the four jobs.
Precedence is the order in which a language groups its operators. In R and Python, * and / group first, then +, then |. Julia groups | together with +, from left to right. JavaScript spells the operators as words, so it has no precedence to remember. In every language, one plot needs no parentheses, even with a facet: data(table) + bar * bin + x(a) | facet(g).
Two whole plots joined by | or / make a page. On a page, put each plot inside its own parentheses: (…) / (…). Without them, / groups before + and joins the first plot’s last atom to the second plot’s data(), and gog refuses that sentence. Put parentheses around a page inside a page too: ((…) | (…)) / (…). Put them around a whole page before you add a theme() to it. What groups first gives the order in each language, and Parentheses on a page shows how each one groups a page.
When gog refuses, the message names the rule, and says what to write instead. Illegal means the grammar forbids the sentence you wrote: rewrite it. Unsupported means the grammar allows it and this engine does not draw it: remove the atom the message names, or use one this engine draws. Illegal is not the same as unsupported has the rule, and a refusal of each kind, printed by the engine when the book is built.
When gog assumes instead of refusing, the plot still draws. The message is an Assumption: it says what gog decided for you. Read it, and check that the decision was what you meant.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.1 render_svg()
Every word in the kernel belongs to a sentence. point is a mark, x is a channel, bin is a transform, and none of them means anything on its own. They are words, and a word needs a sentence.
The functions in this appendix are not words. Three of them take a finished plot and act on it. The fourth gives you a table that your sentence can name. None of them can be written into a sentence with + or *, and none of them is part of the grammar.
The name alone will not tell you whether a function is a word of the grammar. x_label is a word of the grammar, and its name joins two parts with an underscore, exactly as render_svg does. What separates them is where each one is written. A word of the grammar is written inside a sentence. The four functions below are always written outside one, which is why none of them appears in The kernel card.
Each function has a section below, in the same order as the rows above. The first turns a finished plot into text. The last section lists the buttons under each plot in the web edition. They are neither words nor functions.
A plot is a specification until the engine draws it. Sometimes you want the drawing itself: to save it as a file, or to put it in a web page of your own. render_svg() draws the plot and gives you the drawing as ordinary text. It takes the plot as its only argument, and it has the same name in all four languages:

The first line of output shows where that text begins. The second line gives its whole length. So every plot in this book is also a piece of text. It starts with <svg and gives the width of the picture. After that it gives the position of every point, every tick and every label.
That text is the whole picture. A notebook displays it, and so does this book. Write it to a file whose name ends in .svg, and any web browser can open that file as a picture. A vector drawing program, such as Inkscape, can edit it too, because the file describes shapes rather than a grid of colored dots.
save_svg() writes that file for you, in all four languages.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.1.1 What the file carries
An SVG file is text, so anyone who opens it in a text editor can read everything in it. The file carries the drawing and nothing else, but the drawing itself can show private values. If your table holds something private, open the file and read it yourself before you publish.
A plot uses only the columns its sentence names. Columns the sentence never names are absent from the file, and so are their names:

patients <- data.frame(
  patient = c("A. Kim", "B. Lee", "C. Park", "D. Choi"),
  email   = c("ak@ex.com", "bl@ex.com", "cp@ex.com", "dc@ex.com"),
  weight  = c(61.2, 74.8, 55.4, 68.0)
)

picture <- render_svg(data(patients) + bar * bin + x(weight))
sapply(c("A. Kim", "email", "ex.com", "61.2"), grepl, x = picture, fixed = TRUE)

A. Kim  email ex.com   61.2 
 FALSE  FALSE  FALSE  FALSE 


None of the four searches finds anything. The sentence names one column, so the drawing uses one column. Even the weights are gone: bin cuts the weights into intervals and counts the rows in each, so the bars show only the counts.
The weights are absent because of the transform, not because a plot never carries values. A point with no transform draws one glyph per row, and each glyph is placed from one value:

picture <- render_svg(data(patients) + point + x(weight) + y(patient))
lengths(gregexpr("<circle", picture))

[1] 4


The four rows are drawn as four circles, and the four patient names are printed along the axis. This is not special to gog: a scatterplot in any plotting tool draws a point for every row you give it.
The weights are not written in the file as numbers. But each circle is placed by its weight, so a reader who measures the drawing can recover every weight.
So the rule is not that the file is safe. It is narrower: what your sentence names is what you publish. That includes a column named only in facet(), whose values are printed as panel labels. A column the sentence never names cannot be recovered from the file, so it stays private.


B.1.2 Plots that carry the table
A saved SVG file carries only the drawing. A web page can carry more, and that includes a page that a notebook or Quarto makes for you. You should know what it carries before you publish it.
Some plots are drawn twice. The engine makes the first drawing. The reader’s browser makes the second, because the reader can move a selection or turn the view. Four kinds of plot do this: one that binds brush(), one in the cube, one on the globe, and a network given an angle. The second drawing needs the numbers, so the web page also holds a copy of the table. That copy is in the page’s code: the screen does not show it, but anyone who opens the page’s code can read it.
The copy holds every row of the table, but only the columns the sentence names. As in a saved SVG file, a column the sentence never names is not in the page. The difference is in the values: the page holds each row’s exact numbers, and the file holds only a drawing of them. Here is patients again, with a brush:


RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(patients) + point + x(weight) + y(patient) + brush(weight)


data(patients) + point + x(col.weight) + y(col.patient) + brush(col.weight)


data(patients) + point + x(:weight) + y(:patient) + brush(:weight)


plot(data(patients), point, x(col.weight), y(col.patient),
  brush(col.weight))






                                     55 60 65 70 75   D. Choi C. Park B. Lee A. Kim  Patient Weight





“Given the patients: points, x is weight, y is patient, and let the reader select weight.”
That sentence names a brush, so the web version of this page carries a copy of the table. The copy has two columns, weight and patient, because the sentence names those two. The email column is not in that copy at all. In the web version, the plot has a show rows button under it, which Selection explains. The table that button opens lists the same two columns.
An SVG file never carries the table, even when its sentence names a brush. render_svg() returns only the picture.


B.1.3 What “byte for byte” means
This book says in several places that the four languages draw the same picture byte for byte. That claim is about the text that render_svg() returns.
A plot looks like a picture on your screen, and that picture is drawn from this text. A byte is the unit a computer stores text in: one English letter, digit or space takes one byte. Two plots are the same when their text is the same, byte for byte. Text that is only similar does not count, even when the two pictures look the same.
That is how gog checks that the four languages draw the same picture. Nearly every sentence in this book is written in R, in Python, in Julia and in JavaScript. Each one that draws is turned into its text, and the text from Python, Julia and JavaScript is compared with R’s, byte for byte. One wrong byte counts as a disagreement, and one disagreement makes the whole check fail.
A test that allowed small differences would accept pictures that are not the same. The pictures are not compared by eye, because a person cannot see a bar that is half a pixel too wide, or a color that is slightly wrong. Comparing the text finds both differences, and it works the same way every time.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.2 save_svg()
save_svg() draws the plot and writes the drawing to a file. It takes the plot and a path that ends in .svg, and it has the same name in all four languages:

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "life.svg")
save_svg(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life), path)
cat(basename(path), file.size(path), "bytes\n")

life.svg 14710 bytes


The output names the file that was written and its size. The file holds the text that render_svg() returns, byte for byte, so the same plot gives the same file in every language. For a plot p, the call is the same in all four:



R
save_svg(p, "life.svg")


Python
save_svg(p, "life.svg")


Julia
save_svg(p, "life.svg")


JavaScript
save_svg(p, "life.svg")



A path that does not end in .svg is refused, and the message repeats the path with the right ending. gog draws the plot before it writes anything. So when gog refuses the plot, a file already at that path stays unchanged.

           play(year),
         ring, scale = 2)
cat(basename(ring), round(file.size(ring) / 1024), "KB\n")

ring.gif 708 KB


The output names the file that was written and its size. The engine writes the GIF itself, so no other program has to be installed.
scale multiplies the width and the height of the picture. A plot is 800 by 600 pixels unless its theme says otherwise, so scale = 2 writes a GIF of 1600 by 1200 pixels.
Three of the four languages take scale as a named argument. JavaScript has no named arguments, so it takes scale in an object at the end of the call:



R
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", scale = 2)


Python
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", scale=2)


Julia

JavaScript
save_gif(p, "ring.gif", { scale: 2 })



A plot with no play() is refused rather than written as a file of one frame. The Play chapter shows that refusal. It also explains why gog writes no video.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
text:
B.4 gog_table()
Every example in this book starts from a table. The examples draw from a set of shared tables, such as gapminder_2007, and each one is published with the book as a CSV file. gog_table() reads one by its name, so you can run any example without finding and saving the file yourself. Unlike the other three, this function comes before the plot rather than after it:
gapminder_2007 <- gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
No plot appears under that block, because the book does not run it. The call reads the table over the network, and running it here would mean the book could be built only with a network connection.
gog_table() is there so that you can run this book’s examples, not for your own work. When the data is yours, bind it with data() and skip gog_table() entirely.
gog_table() takes a second argument, text. A CSV file records each value but never what kind of value it is. A column of 01, 02, 03 looks like numbers, so it is read as 1, 2, 3, and the leading zeros are lost. To keep such a column as text, list it in text. Labels that look like numbers names the three columns in the book’s tables that need it.
The book’s data explains this function in full. It lists every shared table in the book and shows the call in each of the four languages.

title: Appendix B — Functions around the grammar
section: B.5 The buttons under a plot
text:
B.5 The buttons under a plot
In the web edition, a line of buttons sits under every plot. Each one changes how you look at the plot, or saves what you see, and none changes its sentence. So none of them is a word of the grammar:







Button
What it does




the magnifiers, − and +
Make the picture smaller or larger


the frame button (four corners around a small square)
Returns to the whole picture


the camera
Saves what you are looking at as a PNG file, large enough for a slide or a journal figure



A plot that plays adds three buttons to the same line: they pause the sequence and step through its frames (Play). A brushed plot adds a line of controls for its selection (Selection), and a plot in the cube adds a line for its viewing angle (Space). The buttons under every plot introduces this line.

title: Appendix C — Combinations
text:
C.1 Marks and channels
This page holds the whole of what the grammar lets you combine, in four crossings. The first is what a mark lets you map, which is the channels. The second is what a mark lets you derive, which is the transforms. The third is which two transforms can be chained on one mark. The fourth is where a mark can be drawn, which is the coordinate spaces. Three of them show what a mark takes, what it does not, and the surprising pairings that are legal anyway. The third asks the same question of two transforms.
These grids are the orthogonality law made visible. Law 1 says every compatible atom combines with every other; a table is that promise enumerated, one cell at a time. It is the direct analog of the letter chart a Hangeul (한글) learner reads, with the consonants down one side and the vowels across the top. A syllable block is what those letters assemble into. This book has used that pairing from the start: a mark is a consonant and a position is a vowel, and neither draws alone. Every syllable the grammar can form appears somewhere in these grids.
Legal is not the same as useful. Law 8, Pronounceable ≠ Usable, guarantees only that the engine draws what a ✓︎ cell allows. Whether it should be drawn is your judgment. A cell the engine refuses teaches as much as one it draws. It records a real limit of the geometry, a ruling, or a part of the engine that is not built, and never an oversight.
Every crossing here is generated live from the engine’s own rule table, each time the book is built. That is the same table the engine consults to accept or refuse your plot. A grid written by hand can stop matching the code; a grid generated from it cannot. Add a mark, a channel, a transform or a space, and this page gains the row or the column by itself.
Start with the channels. The marks run down the side and the channels across the top, and each cell says whether you may map a column to that channel on that mark.
Reading the five glyphs:
With the glyphs read, the grid itself shows five patterns:
