● must: a required channel. The mark does not render without it. A point needs an x and a y; a text needs its label.
✓︎ maps: bind a column here and the engine draws it. This is the ordinary case: the channel shows the column.
○ set: the mark has this feature, but not row by row. A line is one stroke, so its size and opacity are a single value for the whole layer, fixed with style() rather than mapped. Those constants have their own settings grid. Eight of them never appear on the channel grid at all: border_color, border_size, caps, center, nudge, angle, arrow and reach are settings and nothing else. Two questions, not one shows in one table where each of five properties can be mapped and where it can only be set.
◌ not drawn: the engine refuses this pairing and gives you a direction instead of a wrong picture. The glyph covers two verdicts, and each has its own refusal message. Not built: a mapped size or opacity on text, and z on text. Blocked: z on rule and on zone. Their 3-D forms are a plane and a slab with no single depth to sort by (Space). Drawing one means working out what hides what, and the engine does not do that.
— none: the mark has no such feature, or the grammar does not allow the pairing. A bar has no glyph for shape to change, and a point has no line for group to divide. Either binding means nothing, and the engine says so. Decided: z on line, step, area and ribbon. These marks sort by x, and in a cube x can point into the page, so the order cannot be seen. The refusal points to path instead, which for an area or a ribbon draws only the edge.



group splits a line, not a bar. Read down the group column: — on the five marks that draw one shape per row (point, bar, text, rule, edge), ✓︎ on every mark that builds one shape out of many rows. A bar is split into groups by color, then piled or set side by side with stack / dodge. A bare group has no line to divide.
label belongs to text alone. Its column is ● on text and — everywhere else. A labeled scatter is two layers, point + text, never a label given to the point.
Categories on x and on y. A category on x reaches every mark that has positions except surface, and on y it reaches fewer of them. Read the x and y columns against each other. Which types each accepts is in Channels, and the split divides the other marks with positions in two. The marks that sit at one place (point, text) and the marks that sit in a slot and measure along the other axis (bar, interval, box) take either type on both positions. A point’s or a label’s two axes are the same kind, which is why it takes either type on both. That one rule is where a strip plot, a horizontal bar and a categorical box all come from. Three more marks do the same. A path sorts nothing, so it has no domain. A rule measures nothing on either axis. A zone measures nothing by length, and that is what makes a heatmap cell a zone rather than a second kind of bar. The stroke and region marks (line, step, area, ribbon) take either type on x alone. Their x is the domain the mark is read along, and their y is the quantity it traces. Those are two different kinds of axis. surface stands outside the split, because both of its positions measure. A sheet is a height, and the two positions say where that height is read.
Three rows have no ● at all. rule and zone show ✓︎ on both positions and ● on neither, because no single cell can state what they need. A rule needs exactly one of the two, and the panel supplies the other (Rule). A zone has no fixed need: a categorical position, bounds, bin, density or a boundary on a map can each give it its sides (Zone). edge is the third, and it takes no position at all. Those obligations are stated once in the engine instead.
zone and surface take either type on color. Of the five filled regions, zone is the only one that takes a number: bar, box, area and ribbon take a category only. surface, a sheet rather than a region, takes a number as well, and both read the ramp.

text:
C.2 Marks and transforms
The second crossing: not what a mark maps, but what it derives. A transform enters through * (bar * bin, interval * range, point * jitter), and which transform a mark takes is decided by the mark’s geometry against the transform’s kind. There are three kinds, and each has its own grid below.
Each cell holds one of three glyphs:

✓︎ combines: the transform applies to this mark and renders.
● required: on interval, ribbon and edge, the mark does not draw until one of its ● transforms is present, so that transform is part of its minimum syllable. The ● cells in a row are a choice, not a list: pick one. A zone is the exception. Each ● is one way to give it its sides, and a categorical position is another, so a zone can draw with no transform at all.
— none: the mark has no use for this kind of transform, and the engine refuses it with a direction toward the transform its geometry does want.


C.2.1 Statistics: a value per group
The first of the three kinds is also the largest. Most summarizing transforms reduce the data to one value at each x: a bin’s count, a group’s mean, a smoothed height. Any mark that draws a value at each x can draw that summary, so those marks are ✓︎ under every summary. That is why a distribution has several spellings rather than one histogram with a shape option: bar * bin is the histogram, line * bin is the frequency polygon, and step * bin is the staircase.

A bare interval is refused, and interval * range with an x and a y is the whole minimum syllable. A ribbon needs a pair too, or one of the two statistics that draw it as a band, density and flow. On a zone, the ● under bounds is one of the ways it gets its sides. A line or a step already draws on its own, so the same transform is optional there, a second way to use the mark. Everywhere else there is nothing for the pair to draw. On a point or a bar, gog refuses it and names the two span marks instead, interval and ribbon. On an area it names ribbon, which is the area with two boundaries instead of a baseline.


C.2.3 Collision modifiers: an offset, not a statistic
When marks collide at one position, four offsets separate them, and which one a mark takes is decided by its geometry and by the axis the collision is on. On the marks that have a width (bar, box, interval), dodge subdivides it. A point has no width, so dodge moves each point sideways within its category’s slot, only as far as it must to touch no other point: the beeswarm. stack piles marks along the measure axis. A bar or an area piles as lengths. A point has no length of its own, so it piles as dots, which is the dot plot. jitter also moves a point along a categorical axis, by a small amount that varies from point to point, and it serves point alone. Which marks take repel is decided by a different question: not what geometry a mark has, but what it is made of. A label is as wide as the word it draws, so two labels overlap where their points do not, and text is the only mark made of words.

Six marks take an offset. bar takes two, point takes three, and the other four take one. bar has both a width and a measure axis, so it takes dodge and stack. For a point, stack answers an overlap along the measure axis, which is a pile of dots you can count. jitter and dodge answer the same overlap by moving points along a categorical axis, which carries no magnitude, so no value changes. jitter moves each point a small amount that varies from point to point; dodge moves each only as far as it must to touch no other point. Each of the six takes a known offset, so when you ask one of them for an offset it does not take, the engine can name one it does: area * dodge names stack. A box shows most clearly that an offset is not a statistic. It takes no statistic, because its own is built in, yet it still takes dodge. Setting grouped boxes side by side is a question about position, and that is orthogonal to the summary each box already carries.

title: Appendix C — Combinations
text:
C.3 Transforms and transforms
The third crossing is the only one where a mark does not appear. Two transforms can follow one mark: bar * bin * mean cuts the axis into bands, then averages inside each. Which pairs can do that is decided by the transforms alone, and by one rule.
A transform has a job. There are four of them, and every transform in gog fills at least one, except repel:








job
the question it answers
the transforms that answer it




extent
where are the cells?
bin, density, smooth, smooth_band, partition, and bounds on a zone


measure
what is in them?
count, sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, range, confidence, deviation, bounds


scale
what scale is the answer read on?
proportion, and stack(share = TRUE)


position
where do the marks sit?
dodge, stack, jitter


all four at once
what is the whole picture?
flow, layout, cluster



repel fills no job at all. It moves a label after every job has run, so it contradicts nothing. Its row in the grid below is the only one that is ✓︎ in every column, and that includes the other three offsets. flow, layout and cluster fill all four jobs at once. Each computes the whole picture, so repel is the only transform that can follow one.
Two transforms compose when they do different jobs, and contradict when they do the same one. Each cell a transform computes (a bin, a group, a point on a curve) holds one extent, one measure, one scale and one position. So a second transform doing a job the first already did leaves the engine no reading that keeps both, and it refuses rather than drawing one and discarding the other.
One transform is the exception, and it is the exception that makes chaining useful. bin does two jobs: it cuts the axis, and it counts what lands in each band. The count is a by-product of the cut, so bin does not have to keep it. It hands the measure job to a transform that reduces a column you named, such as mean. The other extent transforms do two jobs as well, and none of them can hand one over. A density or a smooth cell is a point on an estimated curve, which sits between the rows rather than holding any of them, so there is nothing inside it to reduce. That is why bar * bin * mean composes: bin supplies the cells and mean supplies their value. And it is why bar * bin * count does not, since count was never handed a column to reduce.

The grid is symmetric, and the rule is the reason. Whether two transforms contradict is a fact about their jobs, and it has nothing to do with which one you typed first. So the order is yours to choose. Each job has its own step in the engine, extent first and position last. Write the transforms in that order, and the sentence reads the way it runs. The · on the diagonal pairs a transform with itself. Written twice, a transform repeats its own job, and the engine refuses it like any other repeat. repel has no job to repeat, so it is the one transform the engine lets you write twice.
Eleven transforms measure, so no two of them combine: read their rows against each other, and every cell between two of them is —. That is why chains such as bar * count * mean, bar * mean * sum and interval * range * confidence are refused. Now compare bin’s row with smooth’s and density’s. Those two chain with no measure transform at all. bin chains with ten of the eleven, every one but count. That is the exception above, written out in the grid.
Two contradictions do not fit the grid, because each depends on something outside the pair. stack(share = TRUE) divides each pile by its own total, which is a scale. proportion divides again, and a number divided twice is not a share of anything. And bounds says where a zone’s sides are. On that one mark it does the extent job, so it contradicts bin. On every other mark it names the low and the high on the measure axis. The engine refuses both, and the grid shows the common case: stack without share, and bounds on any mark but zone.
Chaining stops at four, and the number was not chosen. There are four jobs and each takes at most one transform, so a fifth transform has to repeat a job on the same mark. Repeating one is the contradiction this whole section is about.

C.3.1 The shapes a long chain can take
The rule above allows chains of three and four, so the next question is how many there are. The answer is a short list. Once each job is filled at most once, and the marks are asked which transforms they take, every chain of three or four takes one of the shapes below. Two slots stand for a family rather than a transform: <aggregation> is any of sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, and <collision modifier> is dodge, stack or jitter, whichever the mark takes.

Read the four-transform row first, because it is the longest chain there is. It fills each job exactly once, and two of its four slots are decided before you choose anything. bin is the only extent transform that gives its measurement to another, and proportion is the only transform whose whole job is to rescale. That leaves two choices: the aggregation, which is free among six, and the offset, which the mark narrows to one or two. So chains of four exist, but with two slots fixed there are few of them.
The shapes say what the transforms allow. A mark can still refuse a chain whose every pair is ✓︎, for a reason about its own geometry, and no grid shows it. point * proportion * stack is the clearest case. A dot plot piles one whole dot per observation, and a share is less than one dot. So the chain is refused on point and drawn on bar.

C.4 Marks and spaces
The fourth crossing is not about the mark itself. It is the coordinate space the whole plot sits in, and it asks a different question of every mark. Once the plane is bent, or extended into a cube, can this geometry still be drawn? A polar() bar is a wedge, a polar() line runs around the center, and a z scatter is a projected cloud, all from the same sentences that draw them flat.
Two glyphs here, not five. Either the engine draws this mark in this space, or it does not and says so:

✓︎ drawn: the mark renders in this space.
— not drawn: refused with direction, never half-drawn. In the space column, — has three verdicts: not built, blocked and decided. On the channel grid, the verdicts not built and blocked show as ◌, and decided shows as —. Every other blank is simpler: the mark needs what the space lacks, as a surface needs the cube. The paragraphs under the table say why each column’s blanks are blank.

flat holds every mark except surface and edge. Read surface first: it does not draw in the plane at all. Five of the marks that draw there also draw in the cube. A surface is a sheet through three positions, and there is no such thing without the third, so its minimum syllable includes the cube. It is the only mark that draws in the cube and not in the plane (Surface). An edge is the other kind of blank, and it is blank in every column but the last. It takes no position at all, so it draws only in network(), the space that draws the places layout computes. In the columns that follow, ignore the edge row: every blank in it has this one reason.
space holds six marks, and one rule explains all six: each means the same thing in the cube as on the page. A point is a place, a path is its rows in order, a surface is a sheet. bar, interval and box sit in a slot and measure along the other axis. A bar gives a length, an interval a span, a box a summary, and the grammar treats the three as one family.
The blanks in that column carry three different verdicts, and each has its own refusal message. line, step, area and ribbon read a domain left to right, and a cube has no left to right. So they are decided: the grammar forbids them in a cube, and the refusal points to path instead. rule and zone are blocked, the same verdict their z cells carry. A plane and a slab have no single depth to sort by. Placing one among the data means working out what hides what, and the engine does not do that (Space). text is not built: the engine does not draw a label in the cube, so it refuses instead of drawing one flat (Space).
polar matches flat: the same twelve marks draw, and the same two do not. Every mark that draws on the page also draws in the circle. Bending the plane changes only how a mark’s outline is drawn: a held value becomes an arc, and a line between two points becomes a straight chord. A ribbon’s boundaries are the same chords a line draws. The two blanks are surface and edge, and neither is a polar refusal: a sheet needs the cube, and an edge needs network() (Polar).
nest is a column of the opposite shape: two cells filled and the rest blank. Those blanks are not unfinished work. This space asks a different question from flat, space, polar, globe and map. In those five, a mark draws if its geometry survives what the space does to the plane. A nesting is not a transformation of the plane at all, so it can draw any mark that accepts a rectangle. A bar accepts one, because a bar is a measure. A measure has been a length on the page and a radius or an angle in the circle, and here it becomes the size of a rectangle. text can take one too, and it is the only mark here that names a region rather than filling one. The rectangle is already computed, so the label goes to its center. That is what a published treemap shows. A legend cannot name a hundred regions, so the label has to sit in the rectangle (Nest).
Apart from edge, the blanks share one reason: they are the marks placed by a position. point needs somewhere to sit. line, step, area, ribbon and path join places in order, and two touching regions here are not near each other in the data. rule and zone span an axis that is not there, and box, interval and surface measure along one. text is missing from that list because no position places it here. The region places it, and the region is what places the bar too.
map, the sixth column, fills five cells, and the shape of its column comes from one fact: longitude and latitude use both positions for the place. The marks that draw are the ones that place something. A point is a place, a path is a route, and a text is a name at a place. A rule at one position spans the other, which makes it a meridian or a parallel. A zone takes its sides from a boundary, which is the choropleth (Map). The blanks share one reason: each of them needs an axis of its own, either to measure along or to read a domain along, and a map has neither to give. The quantity moves to size or color instead, which is what cartography does with a measure once both positions are gone.
globe, the column before it, fills six cells. Five of them are map’s five, and the sixth is one a flat map cannot have. A globe and a map answer one question: where a place is. So the marks that place something draw on both, and only the reader’s view changes. The far half of the earth is hidden behind the sphere. A route bends along a great circle, and a rule draws the whole meridian or parallel it sits on. The sixth cell is bar, because only the sphere leaves one direction free: the radius, which runs straight out from the surface at every place. A bar drawn along it is a spike, with z naming its measure (Globe). The blanks are map’s, minus that bar, and they are blank for the same reason. A sphere has no axis of its own to give them either.
network holds three cells, and one of its marks draws in no other space. edge draws nowhere else, because an edge is placed by neither position: layout computes where every node sits, network() draws those places, and the edge joins two of them (Network). point and text join it there, as the nodes and their names. The blanks are the marks a layout does not place.
That is the last column. Three of the four crossings have a mark on every row, so one mark can also be read across all three at once. A path takes nearly every channel on Mark × Channel and almost nothing on Mark × Transform, because a path is its rows in order and every statistic replaces them. rule reads the same way on the transform grid, and for the reason the statistics grid already gave: it takes its length from the panel, so it has no measure to compute. And surface’s row on the statistics grid holds the transforms that cover a plane. density estimates a value at every point of a grid and bin cuts adjacent cells, while sum, mean, median, max and min reduce the rows in each cell to one height. path derives two things. With density it draws the contour of a field, the same field a surface lifts into a sheet. With cluster it draws the dendrogram, the tree that joins similar categories.
With these four crossings and the settings grid, the orthogonality law is stated in full: what each mark maps, what it sets, what it derives, which transforms can chain on it, and where it can be drawn.

title: Appendix D — Chart names, translated
text:
D.1 Names with a one-line answer
gog has no chart-type atoms: a histogram is a sentence, not a word. But people look for plots by name, so this appendix is the index of names. It is the one place organized by chart name. The cookbook covers the same plots organized by question, which is usually the better place to start.
The column names in these sentences are placeholders, such as a, b, category and measure. Replace them with columns from your own table. Three names are not placeholders, because gog computes those columns for you: depth, degree, and name after partition, flow or layout.
Each of these names is answered by one gog sentence. The left column is the name you know, and the right column is the sentence that draws it. Where a name needs a note as well, the note follows the sentence in the same cell.

title: Appendix D — Chart names, translated
text:
The name you know
The sentence




Scatterplot
point + x(a) + y(b)


Bubble chart
point + x(a) + y(b) + size(c)


Labeled scatter, names not overlapping
point + text * repel + x(a) + y(b) + label(name), where the repel collision modifier moves each label off the other labels and off the dots. When a label has moved far, repel draws a thin line back to its point


Strip plot
point + x(category) + y(measure), or swap the axes to draw it sideways


Jittered strip plot
point * jitter + x(category) + y(measure), the strip plot with each point moved a little along the category axis, so that points with the same value stop covering each other. The measured value does not move


Beeswarm
point * dodge + x(category) + y(measure), the strip plot with each point moved sideways only as far as it must to touch no other point, so the outline of each group shows its distribution. The measured value does not move (Point)


Dot plot
point * bin * stack + x(measure), one dot per row, piled above the bin it falls in (Transforms)


Bar chart / column chart
bar + x(category) + y(measure)


Horizontal bar chart
bar + x(measure) + y(category)


Hatched (print-safe) bars
bar + x(category) + y(measure) + style(pattern = "hatch"), also "crosshatch"/"stripes"/"grid"/"dots"


Count (frequency) chart
bar * count + x(category)


Proportion chart
bar * proportion + x(category)


Histogram
bar * bin + x(measure); bin(30) sets the number of bins and bin(width = 5) sets their width


Relative-frequency histogram
bar * bin * proportion + x(measure), the histogram with each bar’s count divided by the number of rows, so the bars add up to 1. The bins stay where bar * bin puts them


Frequency polygon
line * bin + x(measure)


Outline (step) histogram
step * bin + x(measure)


Overlaid histograms
bar * bin + x(measure) + color(group)


Density plot
line * density + x(measure)


Box plot / box-and-whisker plot / schematic plot
box + x(category) + y(measure), Tukey’s box plot per category: quartiles, median, whiskers, and each outlier drawn as a dot (Box)


Range bar
box(whiskers = "range") + x(category) + y(measure), the whole five-number summary per category: whiskers to the smallest and largest values, with no value drawn as a separate dot. Mary Eleanor Spear drew the box this way in 1952 (Box)


Violin plot
ribbon * density + x(category) + y(measure), the whole distribution that a box plot reduces to a few numbers. By default each violin’s area follows its category’s row count; density(compare = "shape") gives every violin the same area


Half violin
area * density + x(category) + y(measure): the same estimate, closed on the slot’s center line instead of on its own mirror image, so it draws one half of the violin


Line chart / time series
line + x(time) + y(measure)


Multi-series lines by dash (no color)
line + x(time) + y(measure) + pattern(series), add color(series) for redundant encoding


Step chart
step + x(a) + y(b)


Empirical CDF
step + x(measure) + y(share), over a table sorted by measure, where share is each row’s position divided by the number of rows, computed in your host language (Step)


Survival curve (Kaplan–Meier) / failure plot
step + x(time) + y(survival), over survival probabilities you computed in your host language: the curve holds its value between events and drops at each one. Start the table with a row at time 0 and survival 1, or the first drop is not drawn (Step)


Area chart
area + x(a) + y(b)


Spread / range band
ribbon * range + x(a) + y(b), split by group with color(group)


Fan chart
x(a) + y(b) + ribbon * range(0.1, 0.9) + ribbon * range(0.25, 0.75) + line * median, two bands of quantiles nested around the median. Give each layer its own style(color = , opacity = ), as the worked example does (Ribbon)


Confidence band (computed)
ribbon * confidence(0.95) + x(a) + y(b), often under a line * mean trend


Confidence band (pre-computed)
ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(a), two ends you already hold as columns, such as an estimate plus and minus 1.96 standard errors


Unfilled (dashed) error band
line * bounds(lower, upper) + x(a) + style(pattern = "dashed"), the upper and lower edges drawn as two lines, with nothing filled between them


Min–max envelope, as two lines
line * range + x(a) + y(b), the unfilled counterpart to ribbon * range


Error bar
interval * confidence(0.95) + x(category) + y(measure), one whisker per category, with a dot at each category’s mean. The transform says what the whisker measures. confidence gives a confidence interval, deviation one standard deviation each side of the mean, range the extremes, and bounds(lower, upper) two ends you computed yourself (Interval)


Pointrange
the error bar above as it stands: confidence and deviation compute a mean, and interval draws a dot there. range and bounds compute no center, so they draw no dot (Interval)


Linerange
any interval sentence + style(caps = FALSE), the whisker without the short lines across its ends. With confidence or deviation, write style(caps = FALSE, center = FALSE) to remove the dot too


Coefficient plot
interval * bounds(lo, hi) + y(term), one whisker for each model term, with its two ends read from two columns you already have (Interval)


Dashed / dotted line
any line/step + style(pattern = "dashed") (or "dotted")


Trend line / smoother / LOESS
line * smooth + x(a) + y(b)


Trend line with a confidence band
x(a) + y(b) + ribbon * smooth_band + line * smooth


Reference line / threshold line
+ data(thresholds) + rule, layered over the plot. thresholds has one column with the same name as the plot’s x or y column, and each row draws one line across the panel (Rule)


Rug
+ rule + x(measure) + style(reach = "edge"), layered over the plot: one short tick per row, at its value, along the bottom edge of the panel. y(measure) puts the ticks up the left edge instead (Rule)


Summary bars (mean per group)
bar * mean + x(category) + y(measure), also sum, median, max, min


Grouped bars (side by side)
bar * mean * dodge + x(category) + y(measure) + color(group), where * dodge gives each group its own bar side by side inside the category’s slot


Colorblind-safe grouped bars
add + pattern(group) to the grouped bars: one column sets both the color and the hatch, so the two share one merged legend


Stacked bars / areas
bar * sum * stack + x(category) + y(measure) + color(group), the groups piled on top of each other inside each category’s slot. area in place of bar stacks areas, and grouped bars write dodge in place of stack


Ranked bars
add + order(measure, desc = TRUE)


Small multiples / trellis / conditioning plot / facets
plot | facet(category) puts the panels side by side, plot / facet(category) puts them one above another, and both together make a grid


Animated (time-lapse) chart
any sentence + play(year): one frame for each value of year, shown one after another, where a facet would show them side by side


Small multiples of 3-D plots
any 3-D sentence | facet(category): each panel holds its own cube, all drawn from the same angle


3-D scatter
point + x(a) + y(b) + z(c), view angle via space(turn = , tilt = )


3-D trajectory / space curve
path + x(a) + y(b) + z(c), the rows joined in table order, in the cube


Surface plot / wireframe
surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(c) over a table with one row per (x, y) crossing, so every a value is paired with every b value. style(border_color = "white") draws the mesh lines, and color(c) shades the sheet by height


Terrain / elevation / bathymetry
the same sentence: a height over a plane is a surface, whatever the height means


Response surface
surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(response) over the design grid, with a and b stored as numbers, because a surface refuses a categorical column. From a fitted model, predict onto a grid first and name that table in the sentence


3-D density surface
surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space(), the estimate raised as height. zone * density paints the same estimate as colored cells, and path * density traces it as contour lines


Profile plot (categories joined)
line * mean + x(category) + y(measure), one mean per category, joined by a line; step stays flat between categories instead of sloping


Filled profile
area * mean + x(category) + y(measure), the same boundary filled to the baseline


Connected scatterplot
path + x(a) + y(b), the rows joined in the table’s order rather than sorted by x; style(arrow = "end") says which end is last


Trajectory / route / hysteresis loop
the same sentence: when the row order in the table is the reading order, the mark is path, not line


Annotation arrow / callout
data(two_rows) + path + style(arrow = "end"), layered over the plot; the note itself is data(one_row) + text + label(note)


Rose / coxcomb / polar area diagram / wind rose
bar * count + x(direction) + polar(), the bar chart read in a circle. The count sets each wedge’s radius, so a count twice as large gets four times the area; Nightingale’s polar area diagram put her value, a death rate, in the area instead (Polar)


Radar / spider / star plot / Kiviat diagram
line * mean + x(category) + y(measure) + polar(), the profile bent into a circle; area fills it


Radar band
ribbon * range + x(category) + y(measure) + polar(), a band around the circle from each category’s lowest value to its highest (Polar)


Pie chart
bar * count * stack + color(category) + polar(), a stacked bar in polar coordinates; the category is a split, not a position


Pie of a measure
bar * sum * stack + y(amount) + color(category) + polar(); write sum * proportion in place of sum for shares on the axis


Share-of-total column
the same sentence without polar(), one segmented bar


Treemap
bar * sum + y(value) + color(category) + nest(), the pie of a measure’s shares, carried by area rather than by angle (Nest)


Nested treemap
the same, plus x(group): one region per group, its rows packed inside


Polar histogram
bar * bin + x(bearing) + polar(), bins as wedges of a measured angle


Circular (cyclical) line
line + x(hour) + y(measure) + polar(). The line closes into a loop only when the table holds both ends of the cycle, such as hour 0 and hour 24


Polar scatter
point + x(bearing) + y(measure) + polar()


Contour plot / density contours
path * density + x(a) + y(b), the contours of a density estimated over the plane; density(levels = ) says how many contour lines, and group(category) estimates one field per group


2-D density heatmap
zone * density + x(a) + y(b), the same field painted as cells instead of traced as lines


Filled contour / filled density
zone * density(levels = 8) + x(a) + y(b), eight bands on the levels a path traces. Each band is filled with its holes cut out, so a ring of points leaves its middle unpainted


Binned heatmap
zone * bin + x(a) + y(b), cells colored by how many rows fell in each


Hexbin
zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(a) + y(b), the binned heatmap with hexagons for cells. Hexagons form no straight rows or columns, so the grid itself cannot be mistaken for a pattern in the data


Heat strip / binned distribution per group
zone * bin + x(measure) + y(category), the mixed mesh: the continuous axis cut into cells, one row of cells per category. Every row is cut on the same edges, so the cells line up down the plot


Tile plot / calendar heatmap
zone + x(a) + y(b) + color(value), one cell per pair of categories, each cell as wide and as tall as its two categories’ slots


Mosaic plot
zone * partition(a, b, cross = TRUE) + x(measure) + color(b) + style(border_color = "white"): a divides the width, and b divides the height inside each of those columns. The white border shows where one cell ends and the next begins, even when the two have the same color (Transforms)


Spine plot
zone * partition(a, cross = TRUE) + x(measure) + style(border_color = "white"), the mosaic with one level: one column per category, as wide as its share, with nothing dividing it (Transforms)


Choropleth
zone with group(country) and map(): group says which rows belong to one region, and the region’s own boundary becomes the zone’s sides (Map)


Proportional-symbol map
point + x(lon) + y(lat) + size(measure) + map(), the bubble chart’s sentence in the map space, usually drawn over a boundary table with path (Map)

title: Appendix D — Chart names, translated
text:
D.2 Names that need more
These names need a paragraph rather than a line. gog draws each of them, and the entry gives the sentence and what to know about it.



The name you know
The sentence, and what to know




Ridgeline plot / joyplot
area * density(reach = 2.5) + x(measure) + y(category), the half violin with its axes exchanged: one density per category, each rising from its own category’s place on the y axis, all sharing one measure axis. reach is measured in slots, from a category’s line to the top of the tallest ridge. Above 0.5 that ridge reaches into the next category’s slot, and at 2.5, as here, the ridges overlap, which is what makes a joyplot. To outline it, add a layer: line * density(reach = 2.5) + style(color = "black") reads the same estimate, with the same reach, and traces the top of the fill


100% stacked bar / filled area
bar * count * stack(share = TRUE) + x(a) + color(b), every pile is divided by its own slot’s total. Each pile then reaches 1, so the plot shows composition and no longer shows size. Other summaries work the same way: bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) with a y column, and area * sum * stack(share = TRUE) for the filled area


Streamgraph
area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(t) + y(v) + color(g), worked example in Transforms. The foot of each pile is placed so that the bands move as little as possible, the thickest bands least of all. A thick band’s shape then shows its own values rather than the movement of the bands under it. share and baseline are the pile’s two independent choices, and you can use them together


ThemeRiver
area * stack(baseline = "center"), the same sentence with the symmetric layout instead (Havre et al., 2000). Readers often confuse it with the streamgraph, and it is a different plot. This one centers every pile, while the streamgraph keeps its bands as flat as possible. The streamgraph’s designers argue that readers compare values more accurately on it (Byron & Wattenberg, 2008)


Alluvial diagram
ribbon * flow(a, b, c) + y(amount), with zone * flow(...) for the stage slots and text * flow(...) + label(name) for their names, worked example in Flow. Each row follows one path through the stages, and rows on the same path are merged into one band, as thick as their total. Bind the amount to x instead, x(amount), and the stages run from top to bottom. A stage in color() colors each band by its place at that stage, and any other categorical column in color() splits each band into one part for each value


Sankey diagram
ribbon * flow(source, target, layered = TRUE) + y(amount), with zone * flow(...) for each place’s slot and text * flow(...) + label(name) for its name, worked example in Flow. Each row is a link from one place to another, and layered = TRUE puts each place in the first layer after every place that sends to it, so a band can skip a layer, and a flow can stop before the last layer. The amounts that arrive at a place are added up there, so a band cannot be followed past it. When every row passes through the same stages in order, the alluvial sentence above keeps each path. Links that form a cycle are refused


Arc diagram
ribbon * flow(a, b, shared = TRUE) + x(amount), with zone * flow(...) for each place’s slot and text * flow(...) + label(name) for its name, worked example in Flow. shared = TRUE says the two columns name one set of places, so each place is one slot on one axis. A slot’s length is the total the place sends and receives. It has two parts, with no line between them: what the place sends, then what it receives, in a darker shade. Each band is an arc from one place to another. The axis carries no numbers, and the names are written where the numbers would be. With the amount on y the axis runs up the page


Chord diagram
The arc diagram’s sentence with polar() added: ribbon * flow(a, b, shared = TRUE) + x(amount) + polar(), worked example in Flow. Each place is a piece of the ring, and each band curves toward the center. A band’s area depends on how far apart its places sit on the ring, so read a band at its two ends, or one place at a time with brush(name, at = ...). A flow with stages in polar() is a different picture, and gog refuses it with a message


Network diagram / node-link graph
edge * layout(from, to) + network() draws the edges, worked example in Network. point * layout(...) adds the nodes, size(degree) draws a node larger when it appears in more rows, and text * layout(...) + label(name) writes their names. State an angle, network(turn = 35, tilt = 20), and gog lays the nodes out again in a cube, which the reader can turn with a drag in the web edition. gog refuses names in the cube, so leave out the text layer there (Network)


Heatmap
A heatmap is drawn on two continuous axes, on two categorical axes, or on one of each. The transform you need depends on which kinds you have. A continuous axis needs cutting, so zone * bin counts the rows per cell: both axes for the classic heatmap, one for the mixed mesh. A categorical axis is already divided into slots. On two categorical axes, zone * count tallies the rows into those slots, and zone + color(value) draws a table you already have. zone * density is one more route, for two continuous axes: it estimates a value at each cell of the plane rather than counting rows


Summary heatmap / matrix of means
zone * mean + x(a) + y(b) + color(column) reduces the named column inside every cell where two categories cross, and sum/median/max/min read the same mesh. The column is named on color because a zone shows its measurement as color, and the mean is drawn on that same channel. On two continuous axes, cut them into cells first: zone * bin * mean


Confusion matrix
zone * count + x(actual) + y(predicted) tallies the raw rows; zone * proportion reads them as shares of the whole. Normalizing per true class means a share within each column of this grid, one column per actual class, and neither transform does that. Compute those shares in your host language and draw them as a tile plot: zone + x(actual) + y(predicted) + color(share)


Correlation matrix / corrplot
Drawn as a tile plot, once the correlations are a table. Compute them in your host language, then reshape the result so that each row holds one pair of variables and their correlation. zone + x(var1) + y(var2) + color(r) draws that table


Sunburst
zone * partition(a, b, c) + x(measure) + color(a) + style(border_color = "white") + polar(), worked example in Polar. One ring per level of a tree, each arc as wide as its share. The hierarchy is columns, named from the top of the tree down, so the first column is the innermost ring. A missing value in a level ends that branch early, so the branch does not reach the outer ring. The outer edge of the plot is then uneven. y(depth, limits = c(0, k + 1)), for a tree k levels deep, puts the hole in the middle, and text * partition(a, b) + label(name) names the nodes, reading the same centers the zone computed


Icicle / partition chart
the sunburst’s sentence with polar() taken off, which is the only difference: depth up the y axis, share across the x. One polar() separates the two names, exactly as it separates a rose from a bar chart, or a pie from a stacked bar


Donut chart
zone * partition(category) + x(measure) + y(depth, limits = c(0, 2)) + color(category) + polar(), worked example in Polar. A donut is a sunburst of a tree one level deep. Its one ring sits between 1 and 2 on depth, so limits = c(0, 2) leaves the inner half of the radius empty, and that empty part is the hole. The plain pie (bar * count * stack) cannot have a hole, because it binds nothing to the radius


Labeled treemap
bar + y(value) + color(category) + text + label(name) + nest(), over a table with one row per region. Each name is written at the center of its own region, which helps when there are too many regions for a legend. The text layer does not follow a sum in the bar layer, so with bar * sum the names land in the wrong regions. To name summed regions, sum the table in your host language first. A name that does not fit inside its region is left out, and a message says how many names were drawn (Nest)


Population pyramid
bar + y(age) + x(population) + color(group) + order(age, desc = TRUE), over a table where one group’s populations were made negative in your host language, so its bars run left of zero. age needs its declared order, youngest first, and desc = TRUE puts the youngest band at the bottom (Many groups)


Candlestick / OHLC chart
two layers over one table, worked example in Zone: interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) is the whisker and zone * bounds(body_lo, body_hi, start = left, end = right) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1) the body, over x(session). Compute body_lo, body_hi, dir, left and right in your host language, as the worked example does. One session gives four numbers, and gog needs no new channel to carry them. bounds reads a low value and a high value, and a rectangle’s bottom and top are the same two numbers. A zone whose sides you name is translucent, because a rectangle you chose is usually a highlight. Here the rectangle is the data, so style(opacity = 1) draws it solid, and left and right make each body narrower than its slot


Waterfall / bridge chart
zone * bounds(base, top, start = left, end = right) + x(step) + color(dir) + style(opacity = 1), worked example in Zone. stack accumulates within one position, and a waterfall accumulates across positions. So compute the running total in your host language, as new columns of the table. The subtotal blocks start at 0. left and right sit just inside each slot’s edges, which is what leaves a gap between the blocks


Funnel chart
zone * bounds(lo, hi) + y(stage) + style(opacity = 1), with text + label(n) + x(mid) for the numbers inside, worked example in Zone. A funnel is a bar chart whose blocks are centered on zero. Compute lo and hi as -n/2 and n/2 in your host language, and mid as a column of zeros. The blocks lie across the page because y(stage) is a category, so the measure goes on x. gog draws no sloped connectors between the stages, because the space between two categories holds no data


Significance brackets / p-value stars
box + x(category) + y(measure), with two more layers over tables the host language builds from a statistical test: path + group(pair) joins the four corners of each bracket, and text + label(stars) + style(nudge = "up") writes the stars above the group compared, worked example in Coverage


Survival curve with a risk table
the Kaplan–Meier step above a second plot, text + x(time) + y(group) + label(at_risk), joined by / so that the two share the time axis. Name each group’s color in palette() in both plots, so the colors agree, and write legend = FALSE in the second (Coverage)


Direct labels / names at the line ends
line + x(time) + y(measure) + color(series, legend = FALSE), then a second table with one row per line, at its last time: text + label(series) + color(series) + style(nudge = "right"). Widen the time axis with limits so the names fit (Coverage)


UpSet plot
the count for each combination of sets as bar, above a grid of dots, point + x(combination) + y(set) + color(member), with path + group(combination) joining the sets in each combination. The host language counts the combinations and writes the tables (Coverage)


Horizon chart
area + x(time) + y(part) + color(band) + style(opacity = 1), one panel per series with / facet(series), over bands the host language cuts: each difference from a chosen value, split into slices of fixed height. List each lighter band before the darker one drawn over it, because a band is drawn in the order it first appears (Coverage)


Marginal / joint plot (scatter with histograms in its margins)
top / (main | right): three ordinary plots and the two composition operators (Composition). Each marginal lines up with the main plot because it names the same column on the same axis. The top plot names the main plot’s x column, and the right plot names its y column. Along the top, a marginal can be a histogram, a density curve or a dot plot. Down the side, a histogram works (bar * bin + y(b)), and a density curve or a dot plot is refused. A box or a violin needs a category on its other axis, and then draws one per category


Dendrogram / cluster tree
path * cluster(value, over = profile) + x(item) joins the closest leaves one pair at a time. Each join is drawn at its distance on the other axis, which cluster fills and titles Distance. item is the column that names the leaves, and binding it to y instead lays the tree on its side (Cluster). Dendrogram comes from the Greek words for tree and drawing


Clustered heatmap
zone * cluster(over = profile) reorders a tile plot’s slots into the tree’s leaf order. The full figure is built like the marginal plot, with one tree over the tiles and one beside them, and each shared axis takes its tree’s order (Cluster)


3-D surface
The same sentence as Surface plot / wireframe in the first table, surface + x(a) + y(b) + z(c) over a grid table, or surface * density + x(a) + y(b) + space() to raise an estimated field. A scatter cannot be one. gog refuses it and names point instead of drawing an empty sheet, because a surface’s faces span the gaps between its samples. A surface needs its samples on a grid


Terraced / stepped surface (one value per cell)
surface * bin(3) * mean + x(a) + y(b) + z(v) cuts the floor into a 3 × 3 grid of cells and lays a flat plateau on each, with a vertical face at every step. This is the sentence for a design that measures one number per condition, here three levels on each axis. Give bin that number of levels: with more cells than conditions, the plateaus stand apart with empty cells between them. An interpolated sheet would show a slope nobody observed (Surface)



If the name you are looking for is in neither table, it is usually one of the listed plots with a different mark, transform or setting. Ask what question the chart answers, and start from the cookbook. If the name is one of ggplot2’s function names, the phrasebook gives the gog sentence for each call, and Coverage says which of those plots gog draws at all. Each plot that gog does not draw is in one of four groups there: refused, the host language’s job, missing with the direction settled, and not decided either way.




Byron, L., & Wattenberg, M. (2008). Stacked graphs – geometry & aesthetics. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 14(6), 1245–1252. https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2008.166


Havre, S., Hetzler, B., & Nowell, L. (2000). ThemeRiver: Visualizing theme changes over time. Proceedings of the IEEE Symposium on Information Visualization 2000, 115–123. https://doi.org/10.1109/INFVIS.2000.885098

title: Appendix E — The ggplot2 phrasebook
text:
E.1 Side by side
ggplot2 proved that a grammar of graphics could be a working tool and not only a theory. Most readers of this book already know it. gog follows the same grammar and decides the details differently. This appendix answers two questions: what to write in gog, and what behaves differently. The ggplot2 calls on this page are those of ggplot2 4.0.3 (Wickham et al., 2026).
The translations assume gog can draw the plot you want. To find out whether it can, read Coverage. That appendix compares ggplot2’s whole reference index with gog’s kernel, in both directions: what gog draws that ggplot2 does not, and what ggplot2 draws that gog does not.
This first table compares the two systems as a whole, rather than term by term.

title: Appendix E — The ggplot2 phrasebook
text:
ggplot2
gog




Languages
R
R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, all four calling one engine


Naming
geom_point, aes, alpha
point, channels by plain name, opacity


Where x/y are written
aes() at the plot or the layer, and a layer may override the plot’s aes()
before any mark, for every layer; after a mark, for that mark. A layer with no column of its own reads the first column written for that axis.


The histogram
geom_histogram() or stat_bin(geom = "bar")
bar * bin


Log axis
scale_x_log10()
x(gdp, scale = "log"), written on the binding


3-D
external packages
one more position: z


Animation
gganimate, a separate package
play is a channel of the kernel: + play(year)

title: Appendix E — The ggplot2 phrasebook
text:
E.2 Translations
This table is term by term. Find the ggplot2 call on the left; the gog spelling that does the same job is beside it on the right.



You write in ggplot2
You write in gog




ggplot(df, aes(x = a, y = b))
data(df) + x(a) + y(b) + …


geom_point()
point


geom_line()
line


geom_step()
step


geom_area()
area


geom_col()
bar, one bar per row; with several rows per category, bar * sum gives their total


geom_bar(), which counts the rows for you
bar * count, because bar alone counts nothing


geom_histogram(bins = 30)
bar * bin(30). The thirty bins sit differently: gog’s run exactly from the smallest value to the largest, while geom_histogram() makes each bin a little wider and centers the first and last on the smallest and largest values (Where the bin edges fall)


geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
bar * bin(width = 5). The width is the same, but the edges differ: gog puts an edge at zero, so the bins run 35 to 40, while geom_histogram() centers a bin on zero, so they run 37.5 to 42.5 (Choosing a width)


position = "stack", "dodge" or "fill" inside a geom_*()
a collision modifier after the statistic: bar * count * stack, bar * count * dodge or bar * count * stack(share = TRUE), and the same after bin for a histogram. With share = TRUE, each segment is divided by its bar’s total, so every bar reaches 1. With no position written, ggplot2 stacks the groups and gog overlays them, so write stack to get ggplot2’s default (The 100% stacked bar)


geom_freqpoly()
line * bin. The line starts at the first bin’s count and ends at the last one’s. geom_freqpoly() adds an empty bin at each end, so its line starts and ends at zero. It also uses 30 bins by default, and line * bin(30) gives the same number


geom_density()
line * density


geom_smooth()
ribbon * smooth_band + line * smooth: the band and the curve are two layers. smooth fits a straight line locally and geom_smooth() fits a parabola, so the two curves can differ where the relationship is curved (LOESS trend line)


geom_smooth(se = FALSE)
line * smooth: the curve of the row above, without its band


stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar")
bar * mean


geom_boxplot()
box, which computes its own summary, as geom_boxplot() does


geom_violin()
ribbon * density, with the categories on x. The default shapes differ. gog’s violins run past the data and narrow to a point, weight each area by row count, and share one bandwidth. geom_violin() cuts each end flat, draws equal areas, and gives each violin its own bandwidth. density(compare = "shape") gives equal areas (Compared with ggplot2’s violin)


geom_jitter()
point * jitter, on a categorical axis. On two continuous axes gog refuses it and suggests style(opacity = ) instead.


geom_errorbar(), geom_linerange()
interval * bounds(lower, upper) for ends you already have, or interval * confidence to compute them; style(caps = FALSE) removes the caps, which gives a linerange


geom_ribbon()
ribbon * bounds(lower, upper)


geom_tile()
zone + x(a) + y(b) + color(v), with a and b categorical: each category gets its own slot


geom_bin_2d(), geom_bin2d()
zone * bin + x(a) + y(b): bin cuts both axes into cells, and the count in each cell becomes its color, with no color() written (Cells cut from the data: the heatmap)


geom_hex()
zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(a) + y(b): the same count, in hexagonal cells (Hexagons: the other mesh)


stat_summary_2d(aes(z = v), fun = mean)
zone * bin * mean + x(a) + y(b) + color(v): the column to summarize goes on color, because a zone shows its value as color. sum, median, max and min work the same way (Cells cut, then summarized: the summary heatmap)


geom_hline(), geom_vline()
data(t) + rule + y(v) for horizontal lines, and x(v) for vertical ones, where the table t holds the positions


geom_text()
text + label(g)


geom_text(angle = 90)
text + label(g) + style(angle = 90): one angle for every label in the layer, in degrees counterclockwise (Turning a label)


geom_path()
path, which joins the rows in the table’s order


aes(color = g)
color(g)


aes(fill = g)
color(g): one channel colors a bar’s fill and a line’s stroke, and there is no fill


aes(size = v)
size(v)


aes(shape = g)
shape(g)


aes(alpha = v)
opacity(v)


aes(linetype = g)
pattern(g): a dash on a line, a hatch on a filled region


aes(group = g)
group(g)


scale_x_log10()
x(v, scale = "log")


xlim(58, 68), scale_x_continuous(limits = c(58, 68))
x(v, limits = c(58, 68)). As in ggplot2, the rows outside the limits are removed, and both report how many. When no row is left, gog refuses, where ggplot2 draws an empty panel (limits: stating the range yourself)


scale_color_viridis_c()
color(v) + palette("viridis")


scale_color_manual(values = c(a = "red", b = "blue"))
color(g) + palette(c(a = "red", b = "blue")): each color is written beside its category’s name, so sorting the rows cannot change it. gog refuses a name the column does not hold and a category left without a name (Colors by name)


guides(color = "none"), show.legend = FALSE
color(g, legend = FALSE), written on the channel whose legend you leave out


guides(x = "none") with labs(x = NULL), or theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_blank())
x(v, axis = FALSE), written on the position whose axis you leave out. The numbers, the tick marks and the name are left out together, and the scale is unchanged (axis: leaving an axis out)


theme(legend.position = "bottom")
theme(legend = "bottom"). The other sides are "top" and "left", and "right" is the default. Above or below the panel, a legend’s entries are placed side by side (Legend placement). ggplot2’s legend.position = "none" removes every legend, and in gog you write legend = FALSE on each channel, as in color(g, legend = FALSE)


facet_grid(r ~ c)
\| facet(c) / facet(r)


facet_wrap(~ g, ncol = 4)
\| facet(g, wrap = 4) puts four panels in each row, and / facet(g, wrap = 4) puts four in each column. The operator says the direction, so one number replaces both nrow and ncol.


facet_*(scales = "free_y")
y(v, free = TRUE), written on the axis you are freeing. You do not choose the axis a second time, because the binding already says which one.


patchwork’s p1 | p2, p1 / p2
plot_a | plot_b, plot_a / plot_b: the same two operators. What is written on the right decides what happens: a plot is placed beside or below, and a facet() splits the plot into panels.


ggrepel’s geom_text_repel()
text * repel, one of the four collision modifiers, with dodge, stack and jitter


ggExtra’s ggMarginal()
top / (main | right), three ordinary plots (Composition)


patchwork’s plot_spacer(), plot_layout(widths = )
theme(width = ) on a plot placed beside others, or theme(height = ) on one stacked above or below, in pixels; the plots that ask for nothing share what is left. In the marginal layout above, the empty corner needs no spacer.


coord_flip()
swap the x and y bindings: orientation is taken from whichever axis carries the categories, so there is nothing to switch


coord_polar()
polar()


labs(title = , x = , y = )
title(), x_label(), y_label(), z_label()


color = "red", alpha = 0.5 inside a geom_*()
style(color = "red", opacity = 0.5)


theme(…)
theme(), for what belongs to the whole plot rather than one layer, such as its size, gridlines and background; style() belongs to one layer


ggsave("plot.svg")
save_svg(p, "plot.svg"). gog draws every plot as SVG, so the file name must end in .svg. Functions around the grammar shows the call, which is the same in every language.

title: Appendix E — The ggplot2 phrasebook
text:
E.3 Six differences to expect
The words translate, but six things work differently in gog.

+ is still +, and on purpose. ggplot2’s author has said the pipe would have been the better interface (Wickham, 2018). gog chose + for two reasons. A pipe cannot be given a gog meaning: Python has no pipe operator, and the pipes of R and Julia already mean something else. A pipe also makes every atom a function, and bar * bin has no meaning once both sides are functions. Operators covers this in full, including which atoms give the same plot in any order.
A count is a word you write. bar draws your numbers unchanged. geom_bar() counts rows on its own, and gog counts only when you write a counting transform, such as count or bin. The one mark that computes by itself is box, because a box plot is a summary.
There is one spelling. There are no geom/stat pairs, so you never choose between two functions. If two different atoms in gog do the same job, that is a bug: report it on the project’s repository.
The scale belongs to the binding. Options such as scale, limits, free, legend and axis are arguments of the binding, as in x(gdp, scale = "log") or color(g, legend = FALSE), and there is no scale_*() function. The colors of a color scale come from palette(), which belongs to the whole plot.
Setting is not mapping. A constant maps no column, so it gets no legend. Write it in style(). In ggplot2 aes(color = "red") is legal and draws a legend with one entry called “red”. Here a channel takes a column, not a value, so gog refuses color("red") and names style(color = "red") as the fix.
Refusals name the fix. A sentence gog cannot draw is refused, and the message says what to change. Where ggplot2 warns about an unknown argument and draws anyway, gog stops and draws nothing. This book shows refusals on purpose: it runs the refused sentence and prints the message you would see.

If a call you use is in neither table, Coverage says whether gog draws that plot at all.




Wickham, H. (2018). Answer on why ggplot2 uses + rather than the pipe. Posit (RStudio) Community forum, 29 January 2018.


Wickham, H., Chang, W., Henry, L., Pedersen, T. L., Takahashi, K., Wilke, C., Woo, K., Yutani, H., Dunnington, D., & Brand, T. van den. (2026). ggplot2: Create elegant data visualisations using the grammar of graphics. R package version 4.0.3, published 22 April 2026. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ggplot2

title: Appendix F — Coverage, both directions
text:
F.1 What gog does that ggplot2 does not
The phrasebook answers “how do I spell this in gog”. This appendix answers the question underneath it: can it be spelled. Every entry in ggplot2’s reference index was read against the kernel. The result is two lists of very different lengths, and a table of differences between them.
Each table below has a ggplot2 column, and it is dated on purpose, because nothing here can check it: reference index of ggplot2 4.0.3, read 2026-07-26 (Wickham et al., 2026). ggplot2 is deliberately not a dependency of this book, so building the book never runs it. The plots on this page, and the one refusal shown further down, are different: the engine draws them each time the book is built.
The first list is short: what gog does that ggplot2 does not. The second is long: what ggplot2 draws that gog does not. Each gap on it is one of four kinds, and three of the four were decided on purpose. A later section turns to ggplot2’s extension packages, which the reading of the index did not include, and draws five of their plots from tables the host language computes.
The first section below shows a picture ggplot2 cannot draw. The other two show differences in vocabulary, not in what can be drawn.

title: Appendix F — Coverage, both directions
section: F.2 What is different rather than missing
text:
F.2 What is different rather than missing
The rest is not about pictures at all. These rows are differences in how the two packages work: each one follows from what its own package was built for.




ggplot2
gog




Where it runs
R
R, Python, Julia and JavaScript, one engine, the same SVG out of each


What a plot is
R closures, alive in the session
an engine-neutral JSON specification you can store, compare, send or generate


A sentence the package cannot draw
a warning, and a plot with those rows removed (Removed 12 rows containing missing values)
no plot, and a message naming the sentence it would accept


What combines with what
documented per geom
one rule table, every pair decided, dumped from the engine into Combinations


Picking out a subset with the pointer
outside the package: the plot is a still image, and the answer is plotly or shiny
brush is a word in the sentence, so the selection appears in the PDF as well as on screen. It dims what you did not pick and removes no rows. Selection is the chapter


Moving overlapping labels apart
ggrepel, a separate package, with a geom of its own to use instead
text * repel, a collision modifier beside dodge, stack and jitter, so it composes with the text mark that was already there. It draws a thin line back to the point when a label has moved far, and where no arrangement fits, it still draws every label and reports how many overlap


Spellings per plot
often two (geom_bar/geom_col, geom_histogram/stat_bin)
one


Saying “log”
scale_x_log10(), a scale function per transformation
x(gdp, scale = "log"), written on the binding


Non-positive values on a log axis
dropped, with a warning
refused, with the fix named


A mean under a log axis
the geometric mean
computed in the data’s own units


Centering a diverging ramp
scale_color_gradient2(midpoint = 0), which fixes the midpoint and stretches each side to the data’s own ends
limits = c(-k, k), the atom that already states a domain. The middle of a domain is a midpoint, so no parameter is added, and the ramp is linear on each side of the middle.

title: Appendix F — Coverage, both directions
section: F.3 What ggplot2 draws that gog does not
text:
F.3 What ggplot2 draws that gog does not
The gaps below are sorted into four tables by reason, because the reason tells you whether a gap is final. A gap with a written ruling behind it is a different thing from a gap nobody has ruled on.

F.3.1 Refused, with the ruling on record
gog will not draw these. Each has a written ruling, and the ruling names the direction to go instead. Design laws is where the laws behind them live.



In ggplot2
The ruling




sec_axis(), dup_axis()
A second y-axis is two coordinate spaces drawn in one panel. Facet on the measure, or layer if the units really are shared.


annotate() at page coordinates, annotation_custom(), annotation_raster()
A shape at pixel (120, 340) is a drawing command, and the specification has to mean the same thing at another size, in a facet, or on a sphere. Annotation in data space needs no new word: layer a mark over a small table.


ggproto(), user-written geoms and stats
Every promise on the Combinations grid depends on the vocabulary being fixed. An atom missing from the rule table has no row on that grid, breaks No Exceptions, and cannot be written into the JSON. Compose instead.


coord_flip()
Nothing to write: orientation is read from which axis carries the categories, so swapping the two bindings turns the plot sideways. ggplot2 has since superseded it.


geom_bar() beside geom_col(); geom_histogram() beside stat_bin(geom = "bar")
gog spells each of these one way. bar draws your numbers, bar * count counts them, bar * bin bins them.


geom_smooth(method = "lm")
A family of fits behind one argument is exactly the enumeration this grammar refuses. A least-squares line is a different statistic from a local smoother, so it needs its own plain name.


scale_x_log10(), scale_x_sqrt() as names
One parameter derives the family: base = 2, base = 10, base = exp(1).


coord_polar(theta = "y")
Which axis is the angle is read from the bindings, not chosen by an argument.


qplot(), and plotting bare vectors
A plot is a mapping from a table. Put the vectors in one.


geom_vline(), geom_hline() as separate marks
Three marks for one idea. They are one rule, which takes a column, so a table of thresholds draws all of them at once, and which is also the rug via style(reach = "edge").


plotmath, label_parsed(), label_bquote()
A TeX engine belongs to one output format, not to the grammar. Unicode covers what readers need: superscript powers on log ticks, Greek, sub- and superscripts in a label.


coord_cartesian(xlim = )
This ggplot2 name covers two different operations. Narrowing the domain and running the statistics again is limits, which already reports how many rows it removed. Magnifying the finished picture changes how you look at it and not what the plot claims. So magnifying needs no word. Under every plot in the web edition, − and + magnify the picture, and the frame button returns to the whole of it.


plotly-style interaction: click a point, and read what it is
This needs no word in the kernel, and the survey of what other tools do is what decided it. Plotly hands your application an event; Vega-Lite puts a predicate over named fields in the specification; D3 asks the author for a row identity, and uses it for animation rather than for selection. gog answers each of the three elsewhere. Reading a row belongs to the page a plot is shown on, not to the sentence. On a flat plot that carries brush, resting the pointer on a mark shows that row’s values. A click keeps them on the plot as a stamp. A predicate over a column is brush. A row identity is what an animation needs, and the grammar has no word for it (Animation).


a free-shape selection, drawn around some points with the pointer
There is no lasso word in the kernel. Every other selection can be written down: brush(gdp, at = c(1200, 45000)) names a range, and the PDF then shows the plot that range asks for. A free shape can only be written as a long list of corners, which nobody writes in a sentence. The act was not refused, only the word: in the web edition you draw the shape with the pointer and the sentence still says brush.



The refusal a ggplot2 reader is most likely to meet is the first one, so here it is, live. Two series in different units, the second asking for its own scale:

year
sales

RPythonJuliaJavaScript


data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) + line +
  point + y(sales, scale = "log")


(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + line +
  point + y(col.sales, scale = "log"))


data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line + point +
  y(:sales, scale = "log")


plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line, point,
  y(col.sales, { scale: "log" }))




Error:
! gog: this layer's `y(sales, …)` gives it its own scale, and the layers of one plot share one y axis — two scales on it would be two coordinate spaces in one panel, where every mark reads against an axis the expression never named. Set the scale once for the plot, before the marks: `y(<column>, scale = "log")`. A layer may name its own *column* for the shared axis — `y(sales)` on its own is fine — but not its own scale. If the two series are genuinely in different units, facet on the measure instead.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.


Every refusal in gog has that shape: it says what the rule is, and what to write instead.


F.3.2 The host language’s job
These are computations, not pictures. gog draws the table you give it. Compute the fitted value, the theoretical quantile or a model turned into a table before the plot, in R, Python, Julia or JavaScript. Those languages already have better tools for them.







In ggplot2
Where it goes




stat_ecdf()
compute the cumulative shares, then step


stat_qq(), stat_qq_line()
compute the theoretical quantiles, then point and line


stat_ellipse()
compute the ellipse, then path


stat_quantile()
fit the quantile regression, then line


stat_function(), geom_function()
evaluate the function onto a grid, then line


stat_unique()
de-duplicate the table


cut_interval(), cut_number(), cut_width()
cut the column, or use bin


mean_cl_boot()
bootstrap a lower and an upper bound, then ribbon * bounds(lower, upper). Two helpers documented beside it are gog atoms instead: mean_sdl() is deviation, and median_hilow() is range(0.025, 0.975) with point * median


fortify(), autoplot(), map_data()
get the model or the map boundaries in the host, then give gog a table


a correlation matrix
cor() where the data lives, reshape it long, then zone + x(var1) + y(var2) + color(r)



The table makes the split between gog and the host language look simpler than it is. gog does compute: bin cuts, density estimates, smooth fits a local regression, confidence builds an interval, deviation measures spread, and quantile cuts a distribution. The test is whether the picture can exist without the computation. A histogram has no bars until something bins. A quantile regression is a separate answer that is then drawn as a line. How the test applies to a new case is not settled.


F.3.3 Missing, with the direction already settled
gog does not draw these. Each one belongs to a family the grammar already has, and nothing about them is disputed.



In ggplot2
Here




labs(subtitle =, caption =)
more of the label family; title() is the one that exists


geom_sf(), geom_map(), coord_sf(), borders()
the map space draws, so a mark at a place on a projected earth is an ordinary sentence, and zone with group(country) fills each region from a boundary the data carries, holes included (Map). gog reads no spatial file. A boundary arrives as an ordinary table of points, which is the shape map_data() returns


geom_dotplot()
gog would need a mesh that follows the data’s clusters, and a second rule for choosing bin edges


scale_x_binned(), equal-count bins
the other cutpoint rule, the same parameter





F.3.4 Not decided either way
None of these has a ruling in either direction. Many groups gives reasons against custom tick text, but that is an argument, not a ruling.



In ggplot2
What is missing here




scale_*_continuous(breaks =, labels =)
tick positions and tick text. tick_count asks for a number of ticks and the engine chooses them, so “tick at 0, 50 and 100” and relabeling a category cannot be written.


scale_y_reverse()
a reversed continuous axis. x(continent) + order(continent, desc = TRUE) sorts a categorical axis from Z to A, or a declared order from last to first.


scale_x_sqrt(), coord_trans()
a power scale. The log10-style naming is refused; the capability never was.


linewidth as an aesthetic
a column mapped to stroke width. size can be set on a stroke for the whole layer, not mapped per row.


labs(alt = ), get_alt_text()
alt text on the rendered plot


geom_label()
text in a box, rather than bare text


geom_curve()
a curved connector between two points; path joins them straight


after_stat(), after_scale(), stage(), and geom_count() with them
sending a transform’s output to a channel rather than to a position. point * count + size(count) is refused, because the count a transform invented is not a column the sentence can name, so sizing a point by how many rows landed on it has no spelling. In ggplot2, all four functions in this row do this one job, and it is the largest gap on this list.


geom_contour() over a supplied z
iso-lines of a field you computed. path * density traces a field gog estimated.


aes(angle = ) on geom_text(), and ggplot2’s polar text generally
a separate angle for each label. style(angle = ) turns every label in a layer by the same angle, so a sunburst cannot turn each label along its own arc, and the labels of small wedges overlap. Every plot in polar has this gap, not only the sunburst.

title: Appendix F — Coverage, both directions
text:
F.4 What the extensions add
Every table above compares gog with ggplot2 itself. Many plots drawn with ggplot2 come instead from its extension packages: separate packages that add new plots to ggplot2. gog already draws several of these plots: the node-link diagram in Network, the alluvial diagram in Flow, the beeswarm, ridgelines, a halo behind a label, and animation with play. Other extension plots need a computation first, then an ordinary drawing. The host language computes the tables, and gog draws them with words it already has. Five of these plots follow.

F.4.1 Stars from a significance test
Packages such as ggsignif and ggpubr mark a plot with the result of a statistical test. The test is a computation, so it belongs to the host language, which builds two small tables from its result. One holds the corners of each bracket: a line that joins the two groups compared, with a short leg down at each end. The other holds the stars that stand for each p-value. “Given the iris flowers: boxes, x is species, y is petal length, and also paths from the petal brackets, grouped by pair, and also text from the petal stars, label by stars.”
Each bracket is four rows, which path joins in order: up from setosa, across, and down to the species compared. group(pair) keeps the two brackets apart. The stars sit above the species compared, and three stars mean a p-value below 0.001.

Each plot chooses its own colors, so the palette is written in both plots. It ties each sex to one color, whatever the order of the rows, and legend = FALSE leaves the second legend out. The counts fall faster than the curves, because 63 patients left the study alive, and a patient counts as at risk only while the study still follows them.

F.4.4 How sets overlap
When a person can give several answers, the question is how many gave each combination. An UpSet plot shows this. Packages such as UpSetR and ComplexUpset draw one bar for each combination of sets. F.4.5 A horizon chart
A horizon chart draws a long time series in a panel of small height. Each value is measured from one chosen value, here the mean. Differences above it rise from the baseline in shades of one color. Differences below it are turned upward too, in shades of a second color. Each band holds a slice of fixed height, and the part of a difference that does not fit is drawn again from the baseline, in a darker shade, over the lighter band. Packages such as ggHoriPlot draw it. Cutting each difference into slices is simple arithmetic, so the host language does it. This table holds New York’s daily high temperature from May to September 1973, in degrees Fahrenheit, from R’s airquality data. Each row holds one day and one band: the part of that day’s distance from the mean that falls in the band, with three bands above the mean and three below:

Each month is one panel. Red shows the days warmer than the mean, blue the cooler days, and a darker band a larger difference. style(opacity = 1) draws each band solid, so a darker band hides the lighter one beneath it. F.5 If your plot is not here
This chapter compares gog with ggplot2’s reference index, not with its extensions. So a plot from an extension may be absent from this chapter, unless What the extensions add draws it.
For a plot you can name, Chart names is the dictionary and says which ones are drawn. For a question rather than a name, start at the cookbook.
